senses.d: the nineteenth letter of the English alphabet, is a consonant, and is often called a sibilant, in allusion to its hissing sound. It has two principal sounds; one a mere hissing, as in sack, this; the other a vocal hissing (the same as that of z), as in is, wise. Besides these it sometimes has the sounds of sh and zh, as in sure, measure. It generally has its hissing sound at the beginning of words, but in the middle and at the end of words its sound is determined by usage. In a few words it is silent, as in isle, débris. With the letter h it forms the digraph sh. See Guide to pronunciation, §§ 255-261.
Armies; hosts.
Incorrectly, the Sabbath.

Sabaoth.etym: [Heb. tsebā'ōth, pl. of tsābā', an army or host, fr. tsābā', to go forth to war.]

senses.d: A season or day of rest; one day in seven appointed for rest or worship, the observance of which was enjoined upon the Jews in the Decalogue, and has been continued by the Christian church with a transference of the day observed from the last to the first day of the week, which is called also Lord's Day.
q: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

senses.d: The seventh year, observed among the Israelites as one of rest and festival.
Fig.: A time of rest or repose; intermission of pain, effort, sorrow, or the like.
q: Peaceful sleep out the sabbath of the tomb.

Sabbath.etym: [OE. sabat, sabbat, F. sabbat, L. sabbatum, Gr. σάββατον, fr. Heb. shabbāth, fr. shābath to rest from labor. Cf. Sabbat.]

senses.d: Same as Sabian.
A name formerly given to various dry Spanish wines.

Sack.etym: [OE. seck, F. sec dry (cf. Sp. seco, It. secco), from L. siccus dry, harsh; perhaps akin to Gr. ισχνὄσ, Skr. sikata sand, Ir. sesc dry, W. hysp. Cf. Desiccate.]

senses.d: A bag for holding and carrying goods of any kind; a receptacle made of some kind of pliable material, as cloth, leather, and the like; a large pouch.
A measure of varying capacity, according to local usage and the substance. The American sack of salt is 215 pounds; the sack of wheat, two bushels.

Originally, a loosely hanging garment for women, worn like a cloak about the shoulders, and serving as a decorative appendage to the gown; now, an outer garment with sleeves, worn by women; as, a dressing sack.
A sack coat; a kind of coat worn by men, and extending from top to bottom without a cross seam.

Sack.etym: [OE. sak, sek, AS. sacc, sæcc, L. saccus, Gr. σάκκοσ from Heb. sak; cf. F. sac, from the Latin. Cf. Sac, Satchel, Sack to plunder.]

senses.d: To put in a sack; to bag; as, to sack corn.
q: Bolsters sacked in cloth, blue and crimson.

senses.d: To bear or carry in a sack upon the back or the shoulders.
The pillage or plunder, as of a town or city; the storm and plunder of a town; devastation; ravage.
q: The town was stormed, and delivered up to sack, — by which phrase is to be understood the perpetration of all those outrages which the ruthless code of war allowed, in that age, on the persons and property of the defenseless inhabitants, without regard to sex or age.

Sack.etym: [F. sac plunder, pillage, originally, a pack, packet, booty packed up, fr. L. saccus. See Sack a bag.]

senses.d: To plunder or pillage, as a town or city; to devastate; to ravage.
q: The Romans lay under the apprehensions of seeing their city sacked by a barbarous enemy.

senses.d: A brass wind instrument, like a bass trumpet, so contrived that it can be lengthened or shortened according to the tone required; — said to be the same as the trombone.

Sackbut.etym: [F. saquebute, OF. saqueboute a sackbut, earlier, a sort of hook attached to the end of a lance used by foot soldiers to unhorse cavalrymen; prop. meaning, pull and push; fr. saquier, sachier, to pull, draw (perhaps originally, to put into a bag or take out from a bag; see Sack a bag) + bouter to pu

senses.d: Linen or cotton cloth such as sacks are made of; coarse cloth; anciently, a cloth or garment worn in mourning, distress, mortification, or penitence.
q: Gird you with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.
Thus with sackcloth I invest my woe.

senses.d: Employed in sacrifice.
The offering of anything to God, or to a god; consecratory rite.
q: Great pomp, and sacrifice, and praises loud, To Dagon.

senses.d: Anything consecrated and offered to God, or to a divinity; an immolated victim, or an offering of any kind, laid upon an altar, or otherwise presented in the way of religious thanksgiving, atonement, or conciliation.
q: Moloch, horrid king, besmeared with blood Of human sacrifice.
My life, if thou preserv'st my life, Thy sacrifice shall be.

senses.d: Destruction or surrender of anything for the sake of something else; devotion of some desirable object in behalf of a higher object, or to a claim deemed more pressing; hence, also, the thing so devoted or given up; as, the sacrifice of interest to pleasure, or of pleasure to interest.
A sale at a price less than the cost or the actual value.

Sacrifice.etym: [OE. sacrifise, sacrifice, F. sacrifice, fr. L. sacrificium; sacer sacred + facere to make. See Sacred, and Fact.]

senses.d: To make an offering of; to consecrate or present to a divinity by way of expiation or propitiation, or as a token acknowledgment or thanksgiving; to immolate on the altar of God, in order to atone for sin, to procure favor, or to express thankfulness; as, to sacrifice an ox or a sheep.
q: Oft sacrificing bullock, lamb, or kid.

senses.d: Hence, to destroy, surrender, or suffer to be lost, for the sake of obtaining something; to give up in favor of a higher or more imperative object or duty; to devote, with loss or suffering.
q: Condemned to sacrifice his childish years To babbling ignorance, and to empty fears.
The Baronet had sacrificed a large sum . . . for the sake of . . . making this boy his heir.

senses.d: To destroy; to kill.
To sell at a price less than the cost or the actual value.

Sacrifice.etym: [From Sacrifice, n.: cf. F. sacrifier, L. sacrificare; sacer sacred, holy + -ficare (only in comp.) to make. See -fy.]

senses.d: To make offerings to God, or to a deity, of things consumed on the altar; to offer sacrifice.
q: O teacher, some great mischief hath befallen To that meek man, who well had sacrificed.

senses.d: The sin or crime of violating or profaning sacred things; the alienating to laymen, or to common purposes, what has been appropriated or consecrated to religious persons or uses.
q: And the hid treasures in her sacred tomb With sacrilege to dig.
Families raised upon the ruins of churches, and enriched with the spoils of sacrilege.

Sacrilege.etym: [F. sacrilège, L. sacrilegium, from sacrilegus that steals, properly, gathers or picks up, sacred things; sacer sacred + legere to gather, pick up. See Sacred, and Legend.]

senses.d: Sated; satisfied; weary; tired.
q: Yet of that art they can not waxen sad, For unto them it is a bitter sweet.

senses.d: Heavy; weighty; ponderous; close; hard.
q: His hand, more sad than lump of lead.
Chalky lands are naturally cold and sad.

senses.d: Dull; grave; dark; somber; — said of colors.
q: Woad, or wade, is used by the dyers to lay the foundation of all sad colors.

senses.d: Serious; grave; sober; steadfast; not light or frivolous.
q: Lady Catharine, a sad and religious woman.
Which treaty was wisely handled by sad and discrete counsel of both parties.

senses.d: Affected with grief or unhappiness; cast down with affliction; downcast; gloomy; mournful.
q: First were we sad, fearing you would not come; Now sadder, that you come so unprovided.
The angelic guards ascended, mute and sad.

senses.d: Afflictive; calamitous; causing sorrow; as, a sad accident; a sad misfortune.
Hence, bad; naughty; troublesome; wicked.

Sad.syn: Sorrowful; mournful; gloomy; dejected; depressed; cheerless; downcast; sedate; serious; grave; grievous; afflictive; calamitous.
Sad.etym: [OE. sad sated, tired, satisfied, firm, steadfast, AS. sæd satisfied, sated; akin to D. zat, OS. sad, G. satt, OHG. sat, Icel. saðr, saddr, Goth. saþs, Lith. sotus, L. sat, satis, enough, satur sated, Gr. ἄμεναι to satiate, ἄδνη enough. Cf. Assets, Sate, Satiate, Satisfy, Satire.]

senses.d: To make sorrowful; to sadden.
q: How it sadded the minister's spirits!

senses.d: A seat for a rider, — usually made of leather, padded to span comfortably a horse's back, furnished with stirrups for the rider's feet to rest in, and fastened in place with a girth; also, a seat for the rider on a bicycle or tricycle.
A padded part of a harness which is worn on a horse's back, being fastened in place with a girth. It serves various purposes, as to keep the breeching in place, carry guides for the reins, etc.
A piece of meat containing a part of the backbone of an animal with the ribs on each side; as, a saddle of mutton, of venison, etc.
A block of wood, usually fastened to some spar, and shaped to receive the end of another spar.
A part, as a flange, which is hollowed out to fit upon a convex surface and serve as a means of attachment or support.
The clitellus of an earthworm.
The threshold of a door, when a separate piece from the floor or landing; — so called because it spans and covers the joint between two floors.

Saddle.etym: [OE. sadel, AS. sadol; akin to D. zadel, G. sattel, OHG. satal, satul, Icel. söðull, Dan. & Sw. sadel; cf. Russ. siedlo; all perh. ultimately from the root of E. sit.]

senses.d: To put a saddle upon; to equip (a beast) for riding.
q: Abraham rose up early, . . . and saddled his ass.

senses.d: Hence: To fix as a charge or burden upon; to load; to encumber; as, to saddle a town with the expense of bridges and highways.
A ridge connected two higher elevations; a low point in the crest line of a ridge; a col.
A formation of gold-bearing quartz occurring along the crest of an anticlinal fold, esp. in Australia.
Having a broad patch of color across the back, like a saddle; saddle-backed.
One of a sect among the ancient Jews, who denied the resurrection, a future state, and the existence of angels.

Sadducee.etym: [L. Sadducaei, p., Gr. �, Heb. Tsaddūkīm; — so called from Tsādōk, the founder of the sect.]

senses.d: Wearily; heavily; firmly.
q: In go the spears full sadly in arest.

senses.d: Seriously; soberly; gravely.
q: To tell thee sadly, shepherd, without blame Or our neglect, we lost her as we came.

senses.d: Grievously; deeply; sorrowfully; miserably.
Heaviness; firmness.
Seriousness; gravity; discretion.
q: Her sadness and her benignity.

senses.d: Quality of being sad, or unhappy; gloominess; sorrowfulness; dejection.
q: Dim sadness did not spare That time celestial visages.

senses.d: Free from harm, injury, or risk; untouched or unthreatened by danger or injury; unharmed; unhurt; secure; whole; as, safe from disease; safe from storms; safe from foes.
q: They escaped all safe to land.
Established in a safe, unenvied throne.

senses.d: Conferring safety; securing from harm; not exposing to danger; confining securely; to be relied upon; not dangerous; as, a safe harbor; a safe bridge, etc.
q: The King of heaven hath doomed This place our dungeon, not our safe retreat.

senses.d: Incapable of doing harm; no longer dangerous; in secure care or custody; as, the prisoner is safe.
q: But Banquo's safe? Ay, my good lord, safe in a ditch he bides.

Safe.etym: [OE. sauf, F. sauf, fr. L. salvus, akin to salus health, welfare, safety. Cf. Salute, Salvation, Sage a plant, Save, Salvo an exception.]

senses.d: A place for keeping things in safety.
A strong and fireproof receptacle (as a movable chest of steel, etc., or a closet or vault of brickwork) for containing money, valuable papers, or the like.
A ventilated or refrigerated chest or closet for securing provisions from noxious animals or insects.
To render safe; to make right.
One who, or that which, defends or protects; defense; protection.
q: Thy sword, the safeguard of thy brother's throne.

senses.d: A convoy or guard to protect a traveler or property.
A pass; a passport; a safe-conduct.
To guard; to protect.
In a safe manner; danger, injury, loss, or evil consequences.
The condition or state of being safe; freedom from danger or hazard; exemption from hurt, injury, or loss.
q: Up led by thee, Into the heaven I have presumed, An earthly guest . . . With like safety guided down, Return me to my native element.

senses.d: Freedom from whatever exposes one to danger or from liability to cause danger or harm; safeness; hence, the quality of making safe or secure, or of giving confidence, justifying trust, insuring against harm or loss, etc.
q: Would there were any safety in thy sex, That I might put a thousand sorrows off, And credit thy repentance!

senses.d: Preservation from escape; close custody.
q: Imprison him, . . . Deliver him to safety; and return.

senses.d: Same as Safety touchdown, below.
A safety touchdown.
Short for Safety bicycle.
A bulbous iridaceous plant (Crocus sativus) having blue flowers with large yellow stigmas. See Crocus.

The aromatic, pungent, dried stigmas, usually with part of the stile, of the Crocus sativus. Saffron is used in cookery, and in coloring confectionery, liquors, varnishes, etc., and was formerly much used in medicine.
An orange or deep yellow color, like that of the stigmas of the Crocus sativus.

Saffron.etym: [OE. saffran, F. safran; cf. It. zafferano, Sp. azafran, Pg. açafrão; all fr. Ar. & Per. za' farān.]

senses.d: Having the color of the stigmas of saffron flowers; deep orange-yellow; as, a saffron face; a saffron streamer.
To give color and flavor to, as by means of saffron; to spice.
q: And in Latyn I speak a wordes few, To saffron with my predication.

senses.d: Before-mentioned; already spoken of or specified; aforesaid; — used chiefly in legal style.
An extent of canvas or other fabric by means of which the wind is made serviceable as a power for propelling vessels through the water.
q: Behoves him now both sail and oar.

senses.d: Anything resembling a sail, or regarded as a sail.
A wing; a van.
q: Like an eagle soaring To weather his broad sails.

senses.d: The extended surface of the arm of a windmill.
A sailing vessel; a vessel of any kind; a craft.
A passage by a sailing vessel; a journey or excursion upon the water.

Sail.etym: [OE. seil, AS. segel, segl; akin to D. zeil, OHG. segal, G. & Sw. segel, Icel. segl, Dan. seil. √ 153.]

senses.d: To be impelled or driven forward by the action of wind upon sails, as a ship on water; to be impelled on a body of water by the action of steam or other power.
To move through or on the water; to swim, as a fish or a water fowl.
To be conveyed in a vessel on water; to pass by water; as, they sailed from London to Canton.
To set sail; to begin a voyage.
To move smoothly through the air; to glide through the air without apparent exertion, as a bird.
q: As is a winged messenger of heaven, . . . When he bestrides the lazy pacing clouds, And sails upon the bosom of the air.

senses.d: To pass or move upon, as in a ship, by means of sails; hence, to move or journey upon (the water) by means of steam or other force.
q: A thousand ships were manned to sail the sea.

senses.d: To fly through; to glide or move smoothly through.
q: Sublime she sails The aërial space, and mounts the wingèd gales.

senses.d: To direct or manage the motion of, as a vessel; as, to sail one's own ship.
The act of one who, or that which, sails; the motion of a vessel on water, impelled by wind or steam; the act of starting on a voyage.
The art of managing a vessel; seamanship; navigation; as, globular sailing; oblique sailing.
One who follows the business of navigating ships or other vessels; one who understands the practical management of ships; one of the crew of a vessel; a mariner; a common seaman.
A person sanctified; a holy or godly person; one eminent for piety and virtue; any true Christian, as being redeemed and consecrated to God.
q: Them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints.

senses.d: One of the blessed in heaven.
q: Then shall thy saints, unmixed, and from the impure Far separate, circling thy holy mount, Unfeigned hallelujahs to thee sing.

senses.d: One canonized by the church.

Saint.etym: [F., fr. L. sanctus sacred, properly p. p. of sancire to render sacred by a religious act, to appoint as sacred; akin to sacer sacred. Cf. Sacred, Sanctity, Sanctum, Sanctus.]

senses.d: To make a saint of; to enroll among the saints by an offical act, as of the pope; to canonize; to give the title or reputation of a saint to (some one).
q: A large hospital, erected by a shoemaker who has been beatified, though never sainted.

senses.d: To act or live as a saint.

Final cause; end; purpose of obtaining; cause; motive; reason; interest; concern; account; regard or respect; — used chiefly in such phrases as, for the sake of, for his sake, for man's sake, for mercy's sake, and the like; as, to commit crime for the sake of gain; to go abroad for the sake of one's health.
q: Moved with wrath and shame and ladies' sake.
I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake.
Will he draw out, For anger's sake, finite to infinite?
Knowledge is for the sake of man, and not man for the sake of knowledge.

Sake.etym: [OE. sake cause, also, lawsuit, fault, AS. sacu strife, a cause or suit at law; akin to D. zaak cause, thing, affair, G. sache thing, cause in law, OHG. sahha, Icel. sök, Sw. sak, Dan. sag, Goth. sakjō strife, AS. sacan to contend, strive, Goth. sakam, Icel. saka to contend, strive, blame, OHG. sahh

senses.d: The act of selling; the transfer of property, or a contract to transfer the ownership of property, from one person to another for a valuable consideration, or for a price in money.
Opportunity of selling; demand; market.
q: They shall have ready sale for them.

senses.d: Public disposal to the highest bidder, or exposure of goods in market; auction.

Sale.etym: [Icel. sala, sal, akin to E. sell. See Sell, v. t.]

senses.d: Any one of several species of fishes of the genus Salmo and allied genera. The common salmon (Salmo salar) of Northern Europe and Eastern North America, and the California salmon, or quinnat, are the most important species. They are extensively preserved for food. See Quinnat.
A reddish yellow or orange color, like the flesh of the salmon.

Salmon.etym: [OE. saumoun, salmon, F. saumon, fr. L. salmo, salmonis, perhaps from salire to leap. Cf. Sally, v.]

senses.d: Of a reddish yellow or orange color, like that of the flesh of the salmon.

The chloride of sodium, a substance used for seasoning food, for the preservation of meat, etc. It is found native in the earth, and is also produced, by evaporation and crystallization, from sea water and other water impregnated with saline particles.
Hence, flavor; taste; savor; smack; seasoning.
q: Though we are justices and doctors and churchmen . . . we have some salt of our youth in us.

senses.d: Hence, also, piquancy; wit; sense; as, Attic salt.
A dish for salt at table; a saltcellar.
q: I out and bought some things; among others, a dozen of silver salts.

senses.d: A sailor; — usually qualified by old.
q: Around the door are generally to be seen, laughing and gossiping, clusters of old salts.

senses.d: The neutral compound formed by the union of an acid and a base; thus, sulphuric acid and iron form the salt sulphate of iron or green vitriol.
Fig.: That which preserves from corruption or error; that which purifies; a corrective; an antiseptic; also, an allowance or deduction; as, his statements must be taken with a grain of salt.
q: Ye are the salt of the earth.

senses.d: Any mineral salt used as an aperient or cathartic, especially Epsom salts, Rochelle salt, or Glauber's salt.
Marshes flooded by the tide.

Salt.etym: [AS. sealt; akin to OS. & OFries. salt, D. zout, G. salz, Icel., Sw., & Dan. salt, L. sal, Gr. �, Russ. sole, Ir. & Gael. salann, W. halen, of unknown origin. Cf. Sal, Salad, Salary, Saline, Sauce, Sausage.]

senses.d: Of or relating to salt; abounding in, or containing, salt; prepared or preserved with, or tasting of, salt; salted; as, salt beef; salt water.
Overflowed with, or growing in, salt water; as, a salt marsh; salt grass.
Fig.: Bitter; sharp; pungent.
q: I have a salt and sorry rheum offends me.

senses.d: Fig.: Salacious; lecherous; lustful.
To sprinkle, impregnate, or season with salt; to preserve with salt or in brine; to supply with salt; as, to salt fish, beef, or pork; to salt cattle.
To fill with salt between the timbers and planks, as a ship, for the preservation of the timber.
To deposit salt as a saline solution; as, the brine begins to salt.
The act of leaping or jumping; a leap.
The quality or state of being salt, or state of being salt, or impregnated with salt; salt taste; as, the saltness of sea water.

The act of saluting, or paying respect or reverence, by the customary words or actions; the act of greeting, or expressing good will or courtesy; also, that which is uttered or done in saluting or greeting.
q: In all public meetings or private addresses, use those forms of salutation, reverence, and decency usual amongst the most sober persons.
Woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye love the uppermost seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the markets.
When Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb.
I shall not trouble my reader with the first salutes of our three friends.

Salutation.etym: [L. salutatio: cf. F. salutation. See Salute.]

senses.d: To address, as with expressions of kind wishes and courtesy; to greet; to hail.
q: I salute you with this kingly title.

senses.d: Hence, to give a sign of good will; to compliment by an act or ceremony, as a kiss, a bow, etc.
q: You have the prettiest tip of a finger . . . I must take the freedom to salute it.

senses.d: To honor, as some day, person, or nation, by a discharge of cannon or small arms, by dipping colors, by cheers, etc.
To promote the welfare and safety of; to benefit; to gratify.

Salute.etym: [L. salutare, salutatum, from salus, -utis, health, safety. See Salubrious.]

senses.d: The act of saluting, or expressing kind wishes or respect; salutation; greeting.
A sign, token, or ceremony, expressing good will, compliment, or respect, as a kiss, a bow, etc.

A token of respect or honor for some distinguished or official personage, for a foreign vessel or flag, or for some festival or event, as by presenting arms, by a discharge of cannon, volleys of small arms, dipping the colors or the topsails, etc.
The act of saving; preservation or deliverance from destruction, danger, or great calamity.
The redemption of man from the bondage of sin and liability to eternal death, and the conferring on him of everlasting happiness.
q: To earn salvation for the sons of men.
Godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation.

senses.d: Saving power; that which saves.
q: Fear ye not; stand still, and see the salvation of the Lord, which he will show to you to-day.

Salvation.etym: [OE. salvacioun, sauvacion, F. salvation, fr. L. salvatio, fr. salvare to save. See Save.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Samaria, in Palestine.
A native or inhabitant of Samaria; also, the language of Samaria.
Not different or other; not another or others; identical; unchanged.
q: Thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end.

senses.d: Of like kind, species, sort, dimensions, or the like; not differing in character or in the quality or qualities compared; corresponding; not discordant; similar; like.
q: The ethereal vigor is in all the same.

senses.d: Just mentioned, or just about to be mentioned.
q: What ye know, the same do I know.
Do but think how well the same he spends, Who spends his blood his country to relieve.
Bees like the same odors as we do.
held the same political opinions with his illustrious friend.

Same.etym: [AS. same, adv.; akin to OS. sama, samo, adv., OHG. sam, a., sama, adv., Icel. samr, a., Sw. samme, samma, Dan. samme, Goth. sama, Russ. samuii, Gr. �, Skr. sama, Gr. � like, L. simul at the same time, similis like, and E. some, a., -some. √191. Cf. Anomalous, Assemble, Homeopathy, Homily, Seem, v.

senses.d: An Israelite of Bible record (see Judges xiii.), distinguished for his great strength; hence, a man of extraordinary physical strength.
The act of sanctifying or making holy; the state of being sanctified or made holy;
q: God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth.

senses.d: The act of consecrating, or of setting apart for a sacred purpose; consecration.
Made holy; also, made to have the air of sanctity; sanctimonious.
To make sacred or holy; to set apart to a holy or religious use; to consecrate by appropriate rites; to hallow.
q: God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.
Moses . . . sanctified Aaron and his garments.

senses.d: To make free from sin; to cleanse from moral corruption and pollution; to purify.
q: Sanctify them through thy truth.

senses.d: To make efficient as the means of holiness; to render productive of holiness or piety.
q: A means which his mercy hath sanctified so to me as to make me repent of that unjust act.

senses.d: To impart or impute sacredness, venerableness, inviolability, title to reverence and respect, or the like, to; to secure from violation; to give sanction to.
q: The holy man, amazed at what he saw, Made haste to sanctify the bliss by law.
Truth guards the poet, sanctifies the line.

Sanctify.etym: [F. sanctifier, L. sanctificare; sanctus holy + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Saint, and -fy.]

senses.d: A sacred place; a consecrated spot; a holy and inviolable site.

The most retired part of the temple at Jerusalem, called the Holy of Holies, in which was kept the ark of the covenant, and into which no person was permitted to enter except the high priest, and he only once a year, to intercede for the people; also, the most sacred part of the tabernacle; also, the temple at Jerusalem.
The most sacred part of any religious building, esp. that part of a Christian church in which the altar is placed.
A house consecrated to the worship of God; a place where divine service is performed; a church, temple, or other place of worship.
A sacred and inviolable asylum; a place of refuge and protection; shelter; refuge; protection.
q: These laws, whoever made them, bestowed on temples the privilege of sanctuary.
The admirable works of painting were made fuel for the fire; but some relics of it took sanctuary under ground, and escaped the common destiny.

Sanctuary.etym: [OE. seintuarie, OF. saintuaire, F. sanctuaire, fr. L. sanctuarium, from sanctus sacred, holy. See Saint.]

senses.d: Fine particles of stone, esp. of siliceous stone, but not reduced to dust; comminuted stone in the form of loose grains, which are not coherent when wet.
q: That finer matter, called sand, is no other than very small pebbles.

senses.d: A single particle of such stone.
The sand in the hourglass; hence, a moment or interval of time; the term or extent of one's life.
q: The sands are numbered that make up my life.

senses.d: Tracts of land consisting of sand, like the deserts of Arabia and Africa; also, extensive tracts of sand exposed by the ebb of the tide.
Courage; pluck; grit.

Sand.etym: [AS. sand; akin to D. zand, G. sand, OHG. sant, Icel. sandr, Dan. & Sw. sand, Gr. �.]

senses.d: To sprinkle or cover with sand.
To drive upon the sand.
To bury (oysters) beneath drifting sand or mud.
To mix with sand for purposes of fraud; as, to sand sugar.
Same as Sendal.
q: Sails of silk and ropes of sandal.

senses.d: Sandalwood.
A kind of shoe consisting of a sole strapped to the foot; a protection for the foot, covering its lower surface, but not its upper.
A kind of slipper.
An overshoe with parallel openings across the instep.

Sandal.etym: [F. sandale, L. sandalium, Gr. �, dim. of �, probably from Per. sandal.]

senses.d: The juice of plants of any kind, especially the ascending and descending juices or circulating fluid essential to nutrition.
The sapwood, or alburnum, of a tree.
A simpleton; a saphead; a milksop.

Sap.etym: [AS. sæp; akin to OHG. saf, G. saft, Icel. safi; of uncertain origin; possibly akin to L. sapere to taste, to be wise, sapa must or new wine boiled thick. Cf. Sapid, Sapient.]

senses.d: To subvert by digging or wearing away; to mine; to undermine; to destroy the foundation of.
q: Nor safe their dwellings were, for sapped by floods, Their houses fell upon their household gods.

senses.d: To pierce with saps.
To make unstable or infirm; to unsettle; to weaken.
q: Ring out the grief that saps the mind.

Sap.etym: [F. saper (cf. Sp. zapar, It. zapare), fr. sape a sort of scythe, LL. sappa a sort of mattock.]

senses.d: To proceed by mining, or by secretly undermining; to execute saps.
q: Both assaults are carried on by sapping.

senses.d: A narrow ditch or trench made from the foremost parallel toward the glacis or covert way of a besieged place by digging under cover of gabions, etc.
Native alumina or aluminium sesquioxide, Al2O3; corundum; esp., the blue transparent variety of corundum, highly prized as a gem.
q: Of rubies, sapphires, and of pearlés white.

senses.d: The color of the gem; bright blue.
Any humming bird of the genus Hylocharis, native of South America. The throat and breast are usually bright blue.

Sapphire.etym: [OE. saphir, F. saphir, L. sapphirus, Gr. �, of Oriental origin; cf. Heb. sappīr.]

senses.d: Of or resembling sapphire; sapphirine; blue.

Any one of several small species of herring which are commonly preserved in olive oil for food, especially the pilchard, or European sardine (Clupea pilchardus). The California sardine (Clupea sagax) is similar. The American sardines of the Atlantic coast are mostly the young of the common herring and of the menhaden.

Sardine.etym: [F. sardine (cf. Sp. sardina, sarda, It. sardina, sardella), L. sardina, sarda; cf. Gr. �, �; so called from the island of Sardinia, Gr. �.]

senses.d: A precious stone, probably a carnelian, one of which was set in Aaron's breastplate.

Sardius.etym: [L. sardius, lapis sardinus, Gr. �, �, �. See Sard.]

senses.d: A variety of onyx consisting of sard and white chalcedony in alternate layers.

Sardonyx.etym: [L., fr. Gr. �. See Sard, and Onyx.]

senses.d: Same as Saree.
The grand adversary of man; the Devil, or Prince of darkness; the chief of the fallen angels; the archfiend.
q: I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven.

Satan.etym: [Heb. sātān an adversary, fr. sātan to be adverse, to persecute: cf. Gr. �, �, L. Satan, Satanas.]

senses.d: To satisfy the desire or appetite of; to satiate; to glut; to surfeit.
q: Crowds of wanderers sated with the business and pleasure of great cities.

Sate.etym: [Probably shortened fr. satiate: cf. L. satur full. See Satiate.]

senses.d: Filled to satiety; glutted; sated; — followed by with or of.

Satiate.etym: [L. satiatus, p. p. of satiare to satisfy, from sat, satis, enough. See Sad, a., and cf. Sate.]

senses.d: To satisfy the appetite or desire of; to feed to the full; to furnish enjoyment to, to the extent of desire; to sate; as, to satiate appetite or sense.
q: These rather woo the sense than satiate it.
I may yet survive the malice of my enemies, although they should be satiated with my blood.

senses.d: To full beyond natural desire; to gratify to repletion or loathing; to surfeit; to glut.
To saturate.
q: Content with science in the vale of peace.
His whole felicity is endless strife; No peace, no satisfaction, crowns his life.
He may be satiated, but not satisfied.

Satiate.syn: To satisfy; sate; suffice; cloy; gorge; overfill; surfeit; glut.

senses.d: The act of satisfying, or the state of being satisfied; gratification of desire; contentment in possession and enjoyment; repose of mind resulting from compliance with its desires or demands.
q: The mind having a power to suspend the execution and satisfaction of any of its desires.

senses.d: Settlement of a claim, due, or demand; payment; indemnification; adequate compensation.
q: We shall make full satisfaction.

senses.d: That which satisfies or gratifies; atonement.
q: Die he, or justice must; unless for him Some other, able, and as willing, pay The rigid satisfaction, death for death.

Satisfaction.syn: Contentment; content; gratification; pleasure; recompense; compensation; amends; remuneration; indemnification; atonement.
Satisfaction.etym: [OE. satisfaccioun, F. satisfaction, fr. L. satisfactio, fr. satisfacere to satisfy. See Satisfy.]

senses.d: In general, to fill up the measure of a want of (a person or a thing); hence, to grafity fully the desire of; to make content; to supply to the full, or so far as to give contentment with what is wished for.
q: Death shall . . . with us two Be forced to satisfy his ravenous maw.

senses.d: To pay to the extent of claims or deserts; to give what is due to; as, to satisfy a creditor.
To answer or discharge, as a claim, debt, legal demand, or the like; to give compensation for; to pay off; to requite; as, to satisfy a claim or an execution.
To free from doubt, suspense, or uncertainty; to give assurance to; to set at rest the mind of; to convince; as, to satisfy one's self by inquiry.
q: The standing evidences of the truth of the gospel are in themselves most firm, solid, and satisfying.

Satisfy.syn: To satiate; sate; content; grafity; compensate. See Satiate.
Satisfy.etym: [OF. satisfier; L. satis enough + -ficare (in comp.) to make; cf. F. satisfaire, L. satisfacere. See Sad, a., and Fact.]

senses.d: To give satisfaction; to afford gratification; to leave nothing to be desired.
To make payment or atonement; to atone.
A sylvan deity or demigod, represented as part man and part goat, and characterized by riotous merriment and lasciviousness.
q: Rough Satyrs danced; and Fauns, with cloven heel, From the glad sound would not be absent long.

senses.d: Any one of many species of butterflies belonging to the family Nymphalidæ. Their colors are commonly brown and gray, often with ocelli on the wings. Called also meadow browns.
The orang-outang.
Soul.
Same as Sal, the tree.
The herb sage, or salvia.
To make safe; to procure the safety of; to preserve from injury, destruction, or evil of any kind; to rescue from impending danger; as, to save a house from the flames.
q: God save all this fair company.
He cried, saying, Lord, save me.
Thou hast . . . quitted all to save A world from utter loss.

senses.d: Specifically, to deliver from sin and its penalty; to rescue from a state of condemnation and spiritual death, and bring into a state of spiritual life.
q: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.

senses.d: To keep from being spent or lost; to secure from waste or expenditure; to lay up; to reserve.
q: Now save a nation, and now save a groat.

senses.d: To rescue from something undesirable or hurtful; to prevent from doing something; to spare.
q: I'll save you That labor, sir. All's now done.

senses.d: To hinder from doing, suffering, or happening; to obviate the necessity of; to prevent; to spare.
q: Will you not speak to save a lady's blush?

senses.d: To hold possession or use of; to escape loss of.
q: Just saving the tide, and putting in a stock of merit.

Save.syn: To preserve; rescue; deliver; protect; spare; reserve; prevent.
Save.etym: [OE. saven, sauven, salven, OF. salver, sauver, F. sauver, L. salvare, fr. salvus saved, safe. See Safe, a.]

senses.d: To avoid unnecessary expense or expenditure; to prevent waste; to be economical.
q: Brass ordnance saveth in the quantity of the material.

senses.d: Except; excepting; not including; leaving out; deducting; reserving; saving.
q: Five times received I forty stripes save one.

Save.etym: [F. sauf, properly adj., safe. See Safe, a.]

senses.d: Except; unless.
Preserving; rescuing.
q: He is the saving strength of his anointed.

senses.d: Avoiding unnecessary expense or waste; frugal; not lavish or wasteful; economical; as, a saving cook.
Bringing back in returns or in receipts the sum expended; incurring no loss, though not gainful; as, a saving bargain; the ship has made a saving voyage.
Making reservation or exception; as, a saving clause.
With the exception of; except; excepting; also, without disrespect to.
q: None of us put off our clothes, saving that every one put them off for washing.
And in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.

senses.d: Something kept from being expended or lost; that which is saved or laid up; as, the savings of years of economy.
Exception; reservation.
q: Contend not with those that are too strong for us, but still with a saving to honesty.

senses.d: Something said; speech; discourse.
A saying; a proverb; a maxim.
q: His champions are the prophets and apostles, His weapons holy saws of sacred writ.

senses.d: Dictate; command; decree.
q: rules the creatures by his powerful saw.

Saw.etym: [OE. sawe, AS. sagu; akin to secgan to say. See Say, v. t. and cf. Saga.]

senses.d: An instrument for cutting or dividing substances, as wood, iron, etc., consisting of a thin blade, or plate, of steel, with a series of sharp teeth on the edge, which remove successive portions of the material by cutting and tearing.

Saw.etym: [OE. sawe, AS. sage; akin to D. zaag, G. säge, OHG. sega, saga, Dan. sav, Sw. såg, Icel. sög, L. secare to cut, securis ax, secula sickle. Cf. Scythe, Sickle, Section, Sedge.]

senses.d: To cut with a saw; to separate with a saw; as, to saw timber or marble.
To form by cutting with a saw; as, to saw boards or planks, that is, to saw logs or timber into boards or planks; to saw shingles; to saw out a panel.
Also used figuratively; as, to saw the air.
To use a saw; to practice sawing; as, a man saws well.
To cut, as a saw; as, the saw or mill saws fast.
To be cut with a saw; as, the timber saws smoothly.
Saw.
Trial by sample; assay; sample; specimen; smack.
q: If those principal works of God . . . be but certain tastes and says, as it were, of that final benefit.
Thy tongue some say of breeding breathes.

senses.d: Tried quality; temper; proof.
q: He found a sword of better say.

senses.d: Essay; trial; attempt.
To try; to assay.
A kind of silk or satin.
q: Thou say, thou serge, nay, thou buckram lord!

senses.d: A delicate kind of serge, or woolen cloth.
q: His garment neither was of silk nor say.

Say.etym: [OE. saie, F. saie, fr. L. saga, equiv. to sagum, sagus, a coarse woolen mantle; cf. Gr. σάγοσ. See Sagum.]

senses.d: To utter or express in words; to tell; to speak; to declare; as, he said many wise things.
q: Arise, and say how thou camest here.

senses.d: To repeat; to rehearse; to recite; to pronounce; as, to say a lesson.
q: Of my instruction hast thou nothing bated In what thou hadst to say?
After which shall be said or sung the following hymn.

senses.d: To announce as a decision or opinion; to state positively; to assert; hence, to form an opinion upon; to be sure about; to be determined in mind as to.
q: But what it is, hard is to say.

senses.d: To mention or suggest as an estimate, hypothesis, or approximation; hence, to suppose; — in the imperative, followed sometimes by the subjunctive; as, he had, say fifty thousand dollars; the fox had run, say ten miles.
q: Say, for nonpayment that the debt should double, Is twenty hundred kisses such a trouble?

Say.etym: [OE. seggen, seyen, siggen, sayen, sayn, AS. secgan; akin to OS. seggian, D. zeggen, LG. seggen, OHG. sagēn, G. sagen, Icel. segja, Sw. säga, Dan. sige, Lith. sakyti; cf. OL. insece tell, relate, Gr. ἔννεπε (for εν̓-σεπε), ἔσπετε. Cf. Saga, Saw a saying.]

senses.d: To speak; to express an opinion; to make answer; to reply.
q: You have said; but whether wisely or no, let the forest judge.
To this argument we shall soon have said; for what concerns it us to hear a husband divulge his household privacies?

senses.d: A speech; something said; an expression of opinion; a current story; a maxim or proverb.
q: He no sooner said out his say, but up rises a cunning snap.
That strange palmer's boding say, That fell so ominous and drear Full on the object of his fear.

Say.etym: [From Say, v. t.; cf. Saw a saying.]

senses.d: That which is said; a declaration; a statement, especially a proverbial one; an aphorism; a proverb.
q: Many are the sayings of the wise, In ancient and in modern books enrolled.

Saying.syn: Declaration; speech; adage; maxim; aphorism; apothegm; saw; proverb; byword.

senses.d: An incrustation over a sore, wound, vesicle, or pustule, formed by the drying up of the discharge from the diseased part.
The itch in man; also, the scurvy.
The mange, esp. when it appears on sheep.
A disease of potatoes producing pits in their surface, caused by a minute fungus (Tiburcinia Scabies).
A slight irregular protuberance which defaces the surface of a casting, caused by the breaking away of a part of the mold.
A mean, dirty, paltry fellow.
A nickname for a workman who engages for lower wages than are fixed by the trades unions; also, for one who takes the place of a workman on a strike.

Scab.etym: [OE. scab, scabbe, shabbe; cf. AS. scæb, sceabb, scebb, Dan. & Sw. skab, and also L. scabies, fr. scabere to scratch, akin to E. shave. See Shave, and cf. Shab, Shabby.]

senses.d: To become covered with a scab; as, the wound scabbed over.
Any one of various more or less destructive fungus diseases attacking cultivated plants, and usually forming dark-colored crustlike spots.
The case in which the blade of a sword, dagger, etc., is kept; a sheath.
q: Nor in thy scabbard sheathe that famous blade.

Scabbard.etym: [OE. scaubert, scauberk, OF. escaubers, escauberz, pl., scabbards, probably of German or Scan. origin; cf. Icel. skālpr scabbard, and G. bergen to conceal. Cf. Hauberk.]

senses.d: To put in a scabbard.
Abounding with scabs; diseased with scabs.
Fig.: Mean; paltry; vile; worthless.
A temporary structure of timber, boards, etc., for various purposes, as for supporting workmen and materials in building, for exhibiting a spectacle upon, for holding the spectators at a show, etc.
q: Pardon, gentles all, The flat, unraised spirits that have dared On this unworthy scaffold to bring forth So great an object.

senses.d: Specifically, a stage or elevated platform for the execution of a criminal; as, to die on the scaffold.
q: That a scaffold of execution should grow a scaffold of coronation.

senses.d: An accumulation of adherent, partly fused material forming a shelf, or dome-shaped obstruction, above the tuyères in a blast furnace.

Scaffold.etym: [OF. eschafault, eschafaut, escafaut, escadafaut, F. échafaud; probably originally the same word as E. & F. catafalque, It. catafalco. See Catafalque.]

senses.d: To furnish or uphold with a scaffold.

The dish of a balance; hence, the balance itself; an instrument or machine for weighing; as, to turn the scale; — chiefly used in the plural when applied to the whole instrument or apparatus for weighing. Also used figuratively.
q: Long time in even scale The battle hung.
The scales are turned; her kindness weighs no more Now than my vows.

senses.d: The sign or constellation Libra.

Scale.etym: [AS. scāle; perhaps influenced by the kindred Icel. skāl balance, dish, akin also to D. schaal a scale, bowl, shell, G. schale, OHG. scāla, Dan. skaal drinking cup, bowl, dish, and perh. to E. scale of a fish. Cf. Scale of a fish, Skull the brain case.]

senses.d: To weigh or measure according to a scale; to measure; also, to grade or vary according to a scale or system.
q: Scaling his present bearing with his past.

senses.d: One of the small, thin, membranous, bony or horny pieces which form the covering of many fishes and reptiles, and some mammals, belonging to the dermal part of the skeleton, or dermoskeleton. See Cycloid, Ctenoid, and Ganoid.
q: Fish that, with their fins and shining scales, Glide under the green wave.

senses.d: Hence, any layer or leaf of metal or other material, resembling in size and thinness the scale of a fish; as, a scale of iron, of bone, etc.
One of the small scalelike structures covering parts of some invertebrates, as those on the wings of Lepidoptera and on the body of Thysanura; the elytra of certain annelids. See Lepidoptera.
A scale insect. (See below.)

A small appendage like a rudimentary leaf, resembling the scales of a fish in form, and often in arrangement; as, the scale of a bud, of a pine cone, and the like. The name is also given to the chaff on the stems of ferns.
The thin metallic side plate of the handle of a pocketknife. See Illust. of Pocketknife.
An incrustation deposit on the inside of a vessel in which water is heated, as a steam boiler.
The thin oxide which forms on the surface of iron forgings. It consists essentially of the magnetic oxide, Fe3O4. Also, a similar coating upon other metals.

Scale.etym: [Cf. AS. scealu, scalu, a shell, parings; akin to D. schaal, G. schale, OHG. scala, Dan. & Sw. skal a shell, Dan. skiæl a fish scale, Goth. skalja tile, and E. shale, shell, and perhaps also to scale of a balance; but perhaps rather fr. OF. escale, escaile, F. écaille scale of a fish, and écale shel

senses.d: To strip or clear of scale or scales; as, to scale a fish; to scale the inside of a boiler.
To take off in thin layers or scales, as tartar from the teeth; to pare off, as a surface.
To scatter; to spread.
To clean, as the inside of a cannon, by the explosion of a small quantity of powder.
To separate and come off in thin layers or laminæ; as, some sandstone scales by exposure.
q: Those that cast their shell are the lobster and crab; the old skins are found, but the old shells never; so it is likely that they scale off.

senses.d: To separate; to scatter.
A ladder; a series of steps; a means of ascending.
Hence, anything graduated, especially when employed as a measure or rule, or marked by lines at regular intervals.
Gradation; succession of ascending and descending steps and degrees; progressive series; scheme of comparative rank or order; as, a scale of being.
q: There is a certain scale of duties . . . which for want of studying in right order, all the world is in confusion.

senses.d: Relative dimensions, without difference in proportion of parts; size or degree of the parts or components in any complex thing, compared with other like things; especially, the relative proportion of the linear dimensions of the parts of a drawing, map, model, etc., to the dimensions of the corresponding parts of the object that is represented; as, a map on a scale of an inch to a mile.

Scale.etym: [L. scalae, pl., scala staircase, ladder; akin to scandere to climb. See Scan; cf. Escalade.]

senses.d: To climb by a ladder, or as if by a ladder; to ascend by steps or by climbing; to clamber up; as, to scale the wall of a fort.
q: Oft have I scaled the craggy oak.

Scale.etym: [Cf. It. scalare, fr. L. scalae, scala. See Scale a ladder.]

senses.d: To lead up by steps; to ascend.
q: Satan from hence, now on the lower stair, That scaled by steps of gold to heaven-gate, Looks down with wonder.

senses.d: A scurf or scabby disease, especially of the scalp.
q: It is a dry scall, even a leprosy upon the head.

Scall.etym: [Icel. skalli a bald head. Cf. Scald, a.]

senses.d: Scabby; scurfy.
A bed of oysters or mussels.
That part of the integument of the head which is usually covered with hair.
q: By the bare scalp of Robin Hodd's fat friar, This fellow were a king for our wild faction!

senses.d: A part of the skin of the head, with the hair attached, cut or torn off from an enemy by the Indian warriors of North America, as a token of victory.
Fig.: The top; the summit.

Scalp.etym: [Perhaps akin to D. schelp shell. Cf. Scallop.]

senses.d: To deprive of the scalp; to cut or tear the scalp from the head of.
To remove the skin of.
q: We must scalp the whole lid .

senses.d: To brush the hairs or fuzz from, as wheat grains, in the process of high milling.
To make a small, quick profit by slight fluctuations of the market; — said of brokers who operate in this way on their own account.

Not full, large, or plentiful; scarcely sufficient; less than is wanted for the purpose; scanty; meager; not enough; as, a scant allowance of provisions or water; a scant pattern of cloth for a garment.
q: His sermon was scant, in all, a quarter of an hour.

senses.d: Sparing; parsimonious; chary.
q: Be somewhat scanter of your maiden presence.

Scant.etym: [Icel. skamt, neuter of skamr, skammr, short; cf. skamta to dole out, to portion.]

senses.d: To limit; to straiten; to treat illiberally; to stint; as, to scant one in provisions; to scant ourselves in the use of necessaries.
q: Where a man hath a great living laid together and where he is scanted.
I am scanted in the pleasure of dwelling on your actions.

senses.d: To cut short; to make small, narrow, or scanty; to curtail.
To fail, or become less; to scantle; as, the wind scants.
In a scant manner; with difficulty; scarcely; hardly.
q: So weak that he was scant able to go down the stairs.

senses.d: Scantness; scarcity.
A goat upon whose head were symbolically placed the sins of the people, after which he was suffered to escape into the wilderness.
Hence, a person or thing that is made to bear blame for others.
A mark in the skin or flesh of an animal, made by a wound or ulcer, and remaining after the wound or ulcer is healed; a cicatrix; a mark left by a previous injury; a blemish; a disfigurement.
q: This earth had the beauty of youth, . . . and not a wrinkle, scar, or fracture on all its body.

senses.d: A mark left upon a stem or branch by the fall of a leaf, leaflet, or frond, or upon a seed by the separation of its support. See Illust.. under Axillary.

Scar.etym: [OF. escare, F. eschare an eschar, a dry slough (cf. It. & Sp. escara), L. eschara, fr. Gr. � hearth, fireplace, scab, eschar. Cf. Eschar.]

senses.d: To mark with a scar or scars.
q: Yet I'll not shed her blood; Nor scar that whiter skin of hers than snow.
His cheeks were deeply scarred.

senses.d: To form a scar.
An isolated or protruding rock; a steep, rocky eminence; a bare place on the side of a mountain or steep bank of earth.
q: O sweet and far, from cliff and scar, The horns of Elfland faintly blowing.

Scar.etym: [Scot. scar, scaur, Icel. sker a skerry, an isolated rock in the sea; akin to Dan. skiær, Sw. skär. Cf. Skerry.]

senses.d: A marine food fish, the scarus, or parrot fish.

Scar.etym: [L. scarus, a kind of fish, Gr. σκάροσ.]

senses.d: Not plentiful or abundant; in small quantity in proportion to the demand; not easily to be procured; rare; uncommon.
q: You tell him silver is scarcer now in England, and therefore risen one fifth in value.
The scarcest of all is a Pescennius Niger on a medallion well preserved.

senses.d: Scantily supplied (with); deficient (in); — with of.
Sparing; frugal; parsimonious; stingy.

Scarce.etym: [OE. scars, OF. escars, eschars, LL. scarpsus, excarpsus, for L. excerptus, p. p. of excerpere to pick out, and hence to contract, to shorten; ex (see Ex-) + carpere. See Carpet, and cf. Excerp.]

senses.d: With difficulty; hardly; scantly; barely; but just.
q: With a scarce well-lighted flame.
The eldest scarcely five year was of age.
Slowly she sails, and scarcely stems the tides.
He had scarcely finished, when the laborer arrived who had been sent for my ransom.

senses.d: Frugally; penuriously.

The quality or condition of being scarce; smallness of quantity in proportion to the wants or demands; deficiency; lack of plenty; short supply; penury; as, a scarcity of grain; a great scarcity of beauties.
q: A scarcity of snow would raise a mutiny at Naples.
Praise . . . owes its value to its scarcity.
The value of an advantage is enhanced by its scarceness.

Scarceness.syn: Deficiency; lack; want; penury; dearth; rareness; rarity; infrequency.

senses.d: To frighten; to strike with sudden fear; to alarm.
q: The noise of thy crossbow Will scare the herd, and so my shoot is lost.

Scare.syn: To alarm; frighten; startle; affright; terrify.
Scare.etym: [OE. skerren, skeren, Icel. skirra to bar, prevent, skirrask to shun , shrink from; or fr. OE. skerre, adj., scared, Icel. skjarr; both perhaps akin to E. sheer to turn.]

senses.d: Fright; esp., sudden fright produced by a trifling cause, or originating in mistake.
A deep bright red tinged with orange or yellow, — of many tints and shades; a vivid or bright red color.
Cloth of a scarlet color.
q: All her household are clothed with scarlet.

Scarlet.etym: [OE. scarlat, scarlet, OF. escarlate, F. écarlate (cf. Pr. escarlat, escarlata, Sp. & Pg. escarlata, It. scarlatto, LL. scarlatum), from Per. sakirlāt.]

senses.d: Of the color called scarlet; as, a scarlet cloth or thread.
To dye or tinge with scarlet.
q: The ashy paleness of my cheek Is scarleted in ruddy flakes of wrath.

senses.d: Go away; begone; away; — chiefly used in driving off a cat.
Tribute.
A shower of rain.
To strew about; to sprinkle around; to throw down loosely; to deposit or place here and there, esp. in an open or sparse order.
q: And some are scattered all the floor about.
Why should my muse enlarge on Libyan swains, Their scattered cottages, and ample plains?
Teach the glad hours to scatter, as they fly, Soft quiet, gentle love, and endless joy.

senses.d: To cause to separate in different directions; to reduce from a close or compact to a loose or broken order; to dissipate; to disperse.
q: Scatter and disperse the giddy Goths.

senses.d: Hence, to frustrate, disappoint, and overthrow; as, to scatter hopes, plans, or the like.
To be dispersed or dissipated; to disperse or separate; as, clouds scatter after a storm.
Dispersed; dissipated; sprinkled, or loosely spread.
Irregular in position; having no regular order; as, scattered leaves.
Going or falling in various directions; not united or aggregated; divided among many; as, scattering votes.
Act of strewing about; something scattered.
To perceive by the olfactory organs; to smell; as, to scent game, as a hound does.
q: Methinks I scent the morning air.

senses.d: To imbue or fill with odor; to perfume.
q: Balm from a silver box distilled around, Shall all bedew the roots, and scent the sacred ground.

Scent.etym: [Originally sent, fr. F. sentir to feel, to smell. See Sense.]

senses.d: To have a smell.
q: Thunderbolts . . . do scent strongly of brimstone.

senses.d: To hunt animals by means of the sense of smell.
That which, issuing from a body, affects the olfactory organs of animals; odor; smell; as, the scent of an orange, or of a rose; the scent of musk.
q: With lavish hand diffuses scents ambrosial.

senses.d: Specifically, the odor left by an animal on the ground in passing over it; as, dogs find or lose the scent; hence, course of pursuit; track of discovery.
q: He gained the observations of innumerable ages, and traveled upon the same scent into Ethiopia.

senses.d: The power of smelling; the sense of smell; as, a hound of nice scent; to divert the scent.

Division or separation; specifically (Eccl.), permanent division or separation in the Christian church; breach of unity among people of the same religious faith; the offense of seeking to produce division in a church without justifiable cause.
q: Set bounds to our passions by reason, to our errors by truth, and to our schisms by charity.

Schism.etym: [OE. scisme, OF. cisme, scisme, F. schisme, L. schisma, Gr. σχίσμα, fr. σχίζειν to split; akin to L. scindere, Skr. chid, and prob. to E. shed, v.t. (which see); cf. Rescind, Schedule, Zest.]

senses.d: One who attends a school; one who learns of a teacher; one under the tuition of a preceptor; a pupil; a disciple; a learner; a student.
q: I am no breeching scholar in the schools.

senses.d: One engaged in the pursuits of learning; a learned person; one versed in any branch, or in many branches, of knowledge; a person of high literary or scientific attainments; a savant.
A man of books.
In English universities, an undergraduate who belongs to the foundation of a college, and receives support in part from its revenues.

Scholar.etym: [OE. scoler, AS. scōlere, fr. L. scholaris belonging to a school, fr. schola a school. See School.]

senses.d: A shoal; a multitude; as, a school of fish.

School.etym: [For shoal a crowd; prob. confused with school for learning.]

senses.d: A place for learned intercourse and instruction; an institution for learning; an educational establishment; a place for acquiring knowledge and mental training; as, the school of the prophets.
q: Disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus.

senses.d: A place of primary instruction; an establishment for the instruction of children; as, a primary school; a common school; a grammar school.
q: As he sat in the school at his primer.

senses.d: A session of an institution of instruction.
q: How now, Sir Hugh! No school to-day?

senses.d: One of the seminaries for teaching logic, metaphysics, and theology, which were formed in the Middle Ages, and which were characterized by academical disputations and subtilties of reasoning.
q: At Cambridge the philosophy of Descartes was still dominant in the schools.

senses.d: The room or hall in English universities where the examinations for degrees and honors are held.
An assemblage of scholars; those who attend upon instruction in a school of any kind; a body of pupils.
q: What is the great community of Christians, but one of the innumerable schools in the vast plan which God has instituted for the education of various intelligences?

senses.d: The disciples or followers of a teacher; those who hold a common doctrine, or accept the same teachings; a sect or denomination in philosophy, theology, science, medicine, politics, etc.
q: Let no man be less confident in his faith . . . by reason of any difference in the several schools of Christians.

senses.d: The canons, precepts, or body of opinion or practice, sanctioned by the authority of a particular class or age; as, he was a gentleman of the old school.
q: His face pale but striking, though not handsome after the schools.

senses.d: Figuratively, any means of knowledge or discipline; as, the school of experience.

School.etym: [OE. scole, AS. sc�lu, L. schola, Gr. � leisure, that in which leisure is employed, disputation, lecture, a school, probably from the same root as �, the original sense being perhaps, a stopping, a resting. See Scheme.]

senses.d: To train in an institution of learning; to educate at a school; to teach.
q: He's gentle, never schooled, and yet learned.

senses.d: To tutor; to chide and admonish; to reprove; to subject to systematic discipline; to train.
q: It now remains for you to school your child, And ask why God's Anointed be reviled.
The mother, while loving her child with the intensity of a sole affection, had schooled herself to hope for little other return than the waywardness of an April breeze.

senses.d: The man who presides over and teaches a school; a male teacher of a school.
q: Let the soldier be abroad if he will; he can do nothing in this age. There is another personage abroad, — a person less imposing, — in the eyes of some, perhaps, insignificant. The schoolmaster is abroad; and I trust to him, armed with his primer, against the soldier in full military array.

senses.d: One who, or that which, disciplines and directs.
q: The law was our schoolmaster, to bring us unto Christ.

senses.d: Knowledge; knowledge of principles and causes; ascertained truth of facts.
q: If we conceive God's sight or science, before the creation, to be extended to all and every part of the world, seeing everything as it is, . . . his science or sight from all eternity lays no necessity on anything to come to pass.
Shakespeare's deep and accurate science in mental philosophy.

senses.d: Accumulated and established knowledge, which has been systematized and formulated with reference to the discovery of general truths or the operation of general laws; knowledge classified and made available in work, life, or the search for truth; comprehensive, profound, or philosophical knowledge.
q: All this new science that men lere .
Science is . . . a complement of cognitions, having, in point of form, the character of logical perfection, and in point of matter, the character of real truth.

senses.d: Especially, such knowledge when it relates to the physical world and its phenomena, the nature, constitution, and forces of matter, the qualities and functions of living tissues, etc.; — called also natural science, and physical science.
q: Voltaire hardly left a single corner of the field entirely unexplored in science, poetry, history, philosophy.

senses.d: Any branch or department of systematized knowledge considered as a distinct field of investigation or object of study; as, the science of astronomy, of chemistry, or of mind.
q: Good sense, which only is the gift of Heaven, And though no science, fairly worth the seven.

senses.d: Art, skill, or expertness, regarded as the result of knowledge of laws and principles.
q: His science, coolness, and great strength.

Science.etym: [F., fr. L. scientia, fr. sciens, -entis, p. pr. of scire to know. Cf. Conscience, Conscious, Nice.]

senses.d: To cause to become versed in science; to make skilled; to instruct.
Derision; ridicule; mockery; derisive or mocking expression of scorn, contempt, or reproach.
q: With scoffs, and scorns, and contumelious taunts.

senses.d: An object of scorn, mockery, or derision.
q: The scoff of withered age and beardless youth.

Scoff.etym: [OE. scof; akin to OFries. schof, OHG. scoph, Icel. skaup, and perh. to E. shove.]

senses.d: To show insolent ridicule or mockery; to manifest contempt by derisive acts or language; — often with at.
q: Truth from his lips prevailed with double sway, And fools who came to scoff, remained to pray.
God's better gift they scoff at and refuse.

Scoff.syn: To sneer; mock; gibe; jeer. See Sneer.
Scoff.etym: [Cf. Dan. skuffe to deceive, delude, Icel. skopa to scoff, OD. schoppen. See Scoff, n.]

senses.d: To treat or address with derision; to assail scornfully; to mock at.
q: To scoff religion is ridiculously proud and immodest.

senses.d: One who scoffs.
To burn superficially; to parch, or shrivel, the surface of, by heat; to subject to so much heat as changes color and texture without consuming; as, to scorch linen.
q: Summer drouth or singèd air Never scorch thy tresses fair.

senses.d: To affect painfully with heat, or as with heat; to dry up with heat; to affect as by heat.
q: Lashed by mad rage, and scorched by brutal fires.

senses.d: To burn; to destroy by, or as by, fire.
q: Power was given unto him to scorch men with fire.
The fire that scorches me to death.

Scorch.etym: [OE. scorchen, probably akin to scorcnen; cf. Norw. skrokken shrunk up, skrekka, skrökka, to shrink, to become wrinkled up, dial. Sw. skråkkla to wrinkle (see Shrug); but perhaps influenced by OF. escorchier to strip the bark from, to flay, to skin, F. écorcher, LL. excorticare; L. ex from + cortex,

senses.d: To be burnt on the surface; to be parched; to be dried up.
q: Scatter a little mungy straw or fern amongst your seedlings, to prevent the roots from scorching.

senses.d: To burn or be burnt.
q: He laid his long forefinger on the scarlet letter, which forthwith seemed to scorch into Hester's breast, as if it had been red hot.

senses.d: To ride or drive at great, usually at excessive, speed; — applied chiefly to automobilists and bicyclists.
Extreme and lofty contempt; haughty disregard; that disdain which springs from the opinion of the utter meanness and unworthiness of an object.
q: Scorn at first makes after love the more.
And wandered backward as in scorn, To wait an æon to be born.

senses.d: An act or expression of extreme contempt.
q: Every sullen frown and bitter scorn But fanned the fuel that too fast did burn.

senses.d: An object of extreme disdain, contempt, or derision.
q: Thou makest us a reproach to our neighbors, a scorn and a derision to them that are round about us.

Scorn.syn: Contempt; disdain; derision; contumely; despite; slight; dishonor; mockery.
Scorn.etym: [OE. scorn, scarn, scharn, OF. escarn, escharn, eschar, of German origin; cf. OHG. skern mockery, skernōn to mock; but cf. also OF. escorner to mock.]

senses.d: To hold in extreme contempt; to reject as unworthy of regard; to despise; to contemn; to disdain.
q: I scorn thy meat; 't would choke me.
This my long sufferance, and my day of grace, Those who neglect and scorn shall never taste.
We scorn what is in itself contemptible or disgraceful.

senses.d: To treat with extreme contempt; to make the object of insult; to mock; to scoff at; to deride.
q: His fellow, that lay by his bed's side, Gan for to laugh, and scorned him full fast.
To taunt and scorn you thus opprobriously.

Scorn.syn: To contemn; despise; disdain. See Contemn.
Scorn.etym: [OE. scornen, scarnen, schornen, OF. escarnir, escharnir. See Scorn, n.]

senses.d: To scoff; to mock; to show contumely, derision, or reproach; to act disdainfully.
q: He said mine eyes were black and my hair black, And, now I am remembered, scorned at me.

senses.d: One who scorns; a despiser; a contemner; specifically, a scoffer at religion.
q: Surely he scorneth the scorners: but he giveth grace unto the lowly.

senses.d: Full of scorn or contempt; contemptuous; disdainful.
q: Scornful of winter's frost and summer's sun.
Dart not scornful glances from those eyes.

senses.d: Treated with scorn; exciting scorn.
q: The scornful mark of every open eye.

senses.d: Any one of numerous species of pulmonate arachnids of the order Scorpiones, having a suctorial mouth, large claw-bearing palpi, and a caudal sting.
The pine or gray lizard (Sceloporus undulatus).
The scorpene.
A painful scourge.
q: My father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.

senses.d: A sign and constellation. See Scorpio.
An ancient military engine for hurling stones and other missiles.

Scorpion.etym: [F., fr. L. scorpio, scorpius, Gr. �, perhaps akin to E. sharp.]

senses.d: To rub hard with something rough, as sand or Bristol brick, especially for the purpose of cleaning; to clean by friction; to make clean or bright; to cleanse from grease, dirt, etc., as articles of dress.
To purge; as, to scour a horse.
To remove by rubbing or cleansing; to sweep along or off; to carry away or remove, as by a current of water; — often with off or away.
q: stain my favors in a bloody mask, Which, washed away, shall scour my shame with it.

senses.d: To pass swiftly over; to brush along; to traverse or search thoroughly; as, to scour the coast.
q: Not so when swift Camilla scours the plain.

Scour.etym: [Akin to LG. schüren, D. schuren, schueren, G. scheuern, Dan. skure; Sw. skura; all possibly fr. LL. escurare, fr. L. ex + curare to take care. Cf. Cure.]

senses.d: To clean anything by rubbing.
To cleanse anything.
q: Warm water is softer than cold, for it scoureth better.

senses.d: To be purged freely; to have a diarrhœa.
To run swiftly; to rove or range in pursuit or search of something; to scamper.
q: So four fierce coursers, starting to the race, Scour through the plain, and lengthen every pace.

senses.d: Diarrhœa or dysentery among cattle.
To cleanse or clear, as by a current of water; to flush.
q: If my neighbor ought to scour a ditch.

senses.d: The act of scouring.
A place scoured out by running water, as in the bed of a stream below a fall.
q: If you catch the two sole denizens of a particular scour, you will find another pair installed in their place to-morrow.

senses.d: A lash; a strap or cord; especially, a lash used to inflict pain or punishment; an instrument of punishment or discipline; a whip.
q: Up to coach then goes The observed maid, takes both the scourge and reins.

senses.d: Hence, a means of inflicting punishment, vengeance, or suffering; an infliction of affliction; a punishment.
q: Sharp scourges of adversity.
What scourge for perjury Can this dark monarchy afford false Clarence?

Scourge.etym: [F. escourgée, fr. L. excoriata (sc. scutica) a stripped off (lash or whip), fr. excoriare to strip, to skin. See Excoriate.]

senses.d: To whip severely; to lash.
q: Is it lawful for you to scourge a . . . Roman?

senses.d: To punish with severity; to chastise; to afflict, as for sins or faults, and with the purpose of correction.
q: Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.

senses.d: To harass or afflict severely.
q: To scourge and impoverish the people.

senses.d: To scrape, paw, or scratch with the hands; to proceed by clawing with the hands and feet; to scramble; as, to scrabble up a cliff or a tree.
q: Now after a while Little-faith came to himself, and getting up made shift to scrabble on his way.

senses.d: To make irregular, crooked, or unmeaning marks; to scribble; to scrawl.
q: David . . . scrabbled on the doors of the gate.

Scrabble.etym: [Freq. of scrape. Cf. Scramble, Scrawl, v. t.]

senses.d: To mark with irregular lines or letters; to scribble; as, to scrabble paper.
The act of scrabbling; a moving upon the hands and knees; a scramble; also, a scribble.
Something scraped off; hence, a small piece; a bit; a fragment; a detached, incomplete portion.
q: I have no materials — not a scrap.

senses.d: Specifically, a fragment of something written or printed; a brief excerpt; an unconnected extract.
The crisp substance that remains after drying out animal fat; as, pork scraps.
Same as Scrap iron, below.

Scrap.etym: [OE. scrappe, fr. Icel. skrap trifle, cracking. See Scrape, v. t.]

senses.d: To rub over the surface of (something) with a sharp or rough instrument; to rub over with something that roughens by removing portions of the surface; to grate harshly over; to abrade; to make even, or bring to a required condition or form, by moving the sharp edge of an instrument breadthwise over the surface with pressure, cutting away excesses and superfluous parts; to make smooth or clean; as, to scrape a bone with a knife; to scrape a metal plate to an even surface.
To remove by rubbing or scraping (in the sense above).
q: I will also scrape her dust from her, and make her like the top of a rock.

senses.d: To collect by, or as by, a process of scraping; to gather in small portions by laborious effort; hence, to acquire avariciously and save penuriously; — often followed by together or up; as, to scrape money together.
q: The prelatical party complained that, to swell a number the nonconformists did not choose, but scrape, subscribers.

senses.d: To express disapprobation of, as a play, or to silence, as a speaker, by drawing the feet back and forth upon the floor; — usually with down.
q: He tried to scrape acquaintance with her, but failed ignominiously.

Scrape.etym: [Icel. skrapa; akin to Sw. skrapa, Dan. skrabe, D. schrapen, schrabben, G. schrappen, and prob. to E. sharp.]

senses.d: To rub over the surface of anything with something which roughens or removes it, or which smooths or cleans it; to rub harshly and noisily along.
To occupy one's self with getting laboriously; as, he scraped and saved until he became rich.
To play awkwardly and inharmoniously on a violin or like instrument.
To draw back the right foot along the ground or floor when making a bow.
The act of scraping; also, the effect of scraping, as a scratch, or a harsh sound; as, a noisy scrape on the floor; a scrape of a pen.
A drawing back of the right foot when bowing; also, a bow made with that accompaniment.
A disagreeable and embarrassing predicament out of which one can not get without undergoing, as it were, a painful rubbing or scraping; a perplexity; a difficulty.
q: The too eager pursuit of this his old enemy through thick and thin has led him into many of these scrapes.

senses.d: To utter a harsh, shrill cry; to make a sharp outcry, as in terror or acute pain; to scream; to shriek.

Screech.etym: [Also formerly, scritch, OE. skriken, skrichen, schriken, of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. skrækja to shriek, to screech, skrīkja to titter, Sw. skrika to shriek, Dan. skrige; also Gael. sgreach, sgreuch, W. ysgrechio, Skr. kharj to creak. Cf. Shriek, v., Scream, v.]

senses.d: A harsh, shrill cry, as of one in acute pain or in fright; a shriek; a scream.
One who writes; a draughtsman; a writer for another; especially, an offical or public writer; an amanuensis or secretary; a notary; a copyist.
A writer and doctor of the law; one skilled in the law and traditions; one who read and explained the law to the people.

Scribe.etym: [L. scriba, fr. scribere to write; cf. Gr. σκάριφοσ a splinter, pencil, style (for writing), E. scarify. Cf. Ascribe, Describe, Script, Scrivener, Scrutoire.]

senses.d: To write, engrave, or mark upon; to inscribe.

To cut (anything) in such a way as to fit closely to a somewhat irregular surface, as a baseboard to a floor which is out of level, a board to the curves of a molding, or the like; — so called because the workman marks, or scribes, with the compasses the line that he afterwards cuts.
To score or mark with compasses or a scribing iron.
To make a mark.
q: With the separated points of a pair of spring dividers scribe around the edge of the templet.

senses.d: A small bag; a wallet; a satchel.
q: And in requital ope his leathern scrip.

Scrip.etym: [OE. scrippe, probably of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. & OSw. skreppa, and also LL. scrippum, OF. esquerpe, escrepe, F. écharpe scarf. Cf. Scrap, Scarf a piece of dress.]

senses.d: A small writing, certificate, or schedule; a piece of paper containing a writing.
q: Call them generally, man by man, according to the scrip.
Bills of exchange can not pay our debts abroad, till scrips of paper can be made current coin.

senses.d: A preliminary certificate of a subscription to the capital of a bank, railroad, or other company, or for a share of other joint property, or a loan, stating the amount of the subscription and the date of the payment of the installments; as, insurance scrip, consol scrip, etc. When all the installments are paid, the scrip is exchanged for a bond share certificate.
Paper fractional currency.
Anything written; a writing; a document; an inscription.
q: I have put it in scripture and in remembrance.
Then the Lord of Manny read the scripture on the tomb, the which was in Latin.

senses.d: The books of the Old and the New Testament, or of either of them; the Bible; — used by way of eminence or distinction, and chiefly in the plural.
q: There is not any action a man ought to do, or to forbear, but the Scripture will give him a clear precept or prohibition for it.
Compared with the knowledge which the Scriptures contain, every other subject of human inquiry is vanity.

senses.d: A passage from the Bible; a text.
q: The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose.
Hanging by the twined thread of one doubtful Scripture.

Scripture.etym: [L. scriptura, fr. scribere, scriptum, to write: cf. OF. escripture, escriture, F. écriture. See Scribe.]

senses.d: A roll of paper or parchment; a writing formed into a roll; a schedule; a list.
q: The heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll.
Here is the scroll of every man's name.

senses.d: An ornament formed of undulations giving off spirals or sprays, usually suggestive of plant form. Roman architectural ornament is largely of some scroll pattern.
A mark or flourish added to a person's signature, intended to represent a seal, and in some States allowed as a substitute for a seal.
Same as Skew surface. See under Skew.

Scroll.etym: [A dim. of OE. scroue, scrowe (whence E. escrow), OF. escroe, escroue, F. écrou entry in the jail book, LL. scroa scroll, probably of Teutonic origin; cf. OD. schroode a strip, shred, slip of paper, akin to E. shred. Cf. Shred, Escrow.]

senses.d: The extraneous matter or impurities which rise to the surface of liquids in boiling or fermentation, or which form on the surface by other means; also, the scoria of metals in a molten state; dross.
q: Some to remove the scum as it did rise.

senses.d: refuse; recrement; anything vile or worthless.
q: The great and innocent are insulted by the scum and refuse of the people.

Scum.etym: [Of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. & Sw. skum, Icel. skūm, LG. schum, D. schuim, OHG. scūm, G. schaum; probably from a root meaning, to cover. √158. Cf. Hide skin, Meerschaum, Skim, v., Sky.]

senses.d: To take the scum from; to clear off the impure matter from the surface of; to skim.
q: You that scum the molten lead.

senses.d: To sweep or range over the surface of.
q: Wandering up and down without certain seat, they lived by scumming those seas and shores as pirates.

senses.d: To form a scum; to become covered with scum. Also used figuratively.
q: Life, and the interest of life, have stagnated and scummed over.

senses.d: Covered or affected with scurf or scabs; scabby; scurfy; specifically, diseased with the scurvy.
Vile; mean; low; vulgar; contemptible.
q: That scurvy custom of taking tobacco.
spoke spoke such scurvy and provoking terms.

senses.d: A disease characterized by livid spots, especially about the thighs and legs, due to extravasation of blood, and by spongy gums, and bleeding from almost all the mucous membranes. It is accompanied by paleness, languor, depression, and general debility. It is occasioned by confinement, innutritious food, and hard labor, but especially by lack of fresh vegetable food, or confinement for a long time to a limited range of food, which is incapable of repairing the waste of the system. It was formerly prevalent among sailors and soldiers.

Scurvy.etym: [Probably from the same source as scorbute, but influenced by scurf, scurfy, scurvy, adj.; cf. D. scheurbuik scurvy, G. scharbock, LL. scorbutus. Cf. Scorbute.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Scythia (a name given to the northern part of Asia, and Europe adjoining to Asia), or its language or inhabitants.
A native or inhabitant of Scythia; specifically (Ethnol.), one of a Slavonic race which in early times occupied Eastern Europe.
The language of the Scythians.

One of the larger bodies of salt water, less than an ocean, found on the earth's surface; a body of salt water of second rank, generally forming part of, or connecting with, an ocean or a larger sea; as, the Mediterranean Sea; the Sea of Marmora; the North Sea; the Carribean Sea.
An inland body of water, esp. if large or if salt or brackish; as, the Caspian Sea; the Sea of Aral; sometimes, a small fresh-water lake; as, the Sea of Galilee.
The ocean; the whole body of the salt water which covers a large part of the globe.
q: I marvel how the fishes live in the sea.
Ambiguous between sea and land The river horse and scaly crocodile.

senses.d: The swell of the ocean or other body of water in a high wind; motion or agitation of the water's surface; also, a single wave; a billow; as, there was a high sea after the storm; the vessel shipped a sea.
A great brazen laver in the temple at Jerusalem; — so called from its size.
q: He made a molten sea of ten cubits from brim to brim, round in compass, and five cubits the height thereof.

senses.d: Fig.: Anything resembling the sea in vastness; as, a sea of glory.
q: All the space . . . was one sea of heads.

Sea.etym: [OE. see, AS. sǣ; akin to D. zee, OS. & OHG. sēo, G. see, OFries. se, Dan. sö, Sw. sjö, Icel. sær, Goth. saiws, and perhaps to L. saevus fierce, savage. √151a.]

senses.d: Following the business of a mariner; as, a seafaring man.
Any aquatic carnivorous mammal of the families Phocidæ and Otariidæ.

Seal.etym: [OE. sele, AS. seolh; akin to OHG. selah, Dan. sæl, Sw. själ, Icel. selr.]

senses.d: An engraved or inscribed stamp, used for marking an impression in wax or other soft substance, to be attached to a document, or otherwise used by way of authentication or security.
Wax, wafer, or other tenacious substance, set to an instrument, and impressed or stamped with a seal; as, to give a deed under hand and seal.
