q: Till thou canst rail the seal from off my bond Thou but offend'st thy lungs to speak so loud.

senses.d: That which seals or fastens; esp., the wax or wafer placed on a letter or other closed paper, etc., to fasten it.
That which confirms, ratifies, or makes stable; that which authenticates; that which secures; assurance.
q: Like a red seal is the setting sun On the good and the evil men have done.

senses.d: An arrangement for preventing the entrance or return of gas or air into a pipe, by which the open end of the pipe dips beneath the surface of water or other liquid, or a deep bend or sag in the pipe is filled with the liquid; a draintrap.

Seal.etym: [OE. seel, OF. seel, F. sceau, fr. L. sigillum a little figure or image, a seal, dim. of signum a mark, sign, figure, or image. See Sign, n., and cf. Sigil.]

senses.d: To set or affix a seal to; hence, to authenticate; to confirm; to ratify; to establish; as, to seal a deed.
q: And with my hand I seal my true heart's love.

senses.d: To mark with a stamp, as an evidence of standard exactness, legal size, or merchantable quality; as, to seal weights and measures; to seal silverware.
To fasten with a seal; to attach together with a wafer, wax, or other substance causing adhesion; as, to seal a letter.
Hence, to shut close; to keep close; to make fast; to keep secure or secret.
q: Seal up your lips, and give no words but “mum”.

senses.d: To fix, as a piece of iron in a wall, with cement, plaster, or the like.
To close by means of a seal; as, to seal a drainpipe with water. See 2d Seal, 5.
Among the Mormons, to confirm or set apart as a second or additional wife.
q: If a man once married desires a second helpmate . . . she is sealed to him under the solemn sanction of the church.

Seal.etym: [OE. selen; cf. OF. seeler, seieler, F. sceller, LL. sigillare. See Seal a stamp.]

senses.d: To affix one's seal, or a seal.
q: I will seal unto this bond.

senses.d: Grease; tallow; lard.
The fold or line formed by sewing together two pieces of cloth or leather.
Hence, a line of junction; a joint; a suture, as on a ship, a floor, or other structure; the line of union, or joint, of two boards, planks, metal plates, etc.
q: Precepts should be so finely wrought together . . . that no coarse seam may discover where they join.

senses.d: A thin layer or stratum; a narrow vein between two thicker strata; as, a seam of coal.
A line or depression left by a cut or wound; a scar; a cicatrix.

Seam.etym: [OE. seem, seam, AS. seám; akin to D. zoom, OHG. soum, G. saum, LG. soom, Icel. saumr, Sw. & Dan. söm, and E. sew. √ 156. See Sew to fasten with thread.]

senses.d: To form a seam upon or of; to join by sewing together; to unite.
To mark with something resembling a seam; to line; to scar.
q: Seamed o'er with wounds which his own saber gave.

senses.d: To make the appearance of a seam in, as in knitting a stocking; hence, to knit with a certain stitch, like that in such knitting.
To become ridgy; to crack open.
q: Later their lips began to parch and seam.

senses.d: A denomination of weight or measure.
The quantity of eight bushels of grain.
The quantity of 120 pounds of glass.

Seam.etym: [AS. seám, LL. sauma, L. sagma a packsaddle, fr. Gr. �. See Sumpter.]

senses.d: Dry; withered; no longer green; — applied to leaves.
q: I have lived long enough; my way of life Is fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf.

Sear.etym: [OE. seer, AS. seár (assumed) fr. seárian to wither; akin to D. zoor dry, LG. soor, OHG. sorēn to wither, Gr. αὕειν to parch, to dry, Skr. çush (for sush) to dry, to wither, Zend hush to dry. √152. Cf. Austere, Sorrel, a.]

senses.d: To wither; to dry up.

To burn (the surface of) to dryness and hardness; to cauterize; to expose to a degree of heat such as changes the color or the hardness and texture of the surface; to scorch; to make callous; as, to sear the skin or flesh. Also used figuratively.
q: I'm seared with burning steel.
It was in vain that the amiable divine tried to give salutary pain to that seared conscience.
The discipline of war, being a discipline in destruction of life, is a discipline in callousness. Whatever sympathies exist are seared.

Sear.etym: [OE. seeren, AS. seárian. See Sear, a.]

senses.d: The catch in a gunlock by which the hammer is held cocked or half cocked.

Sear.etym: [F. serre a grasp, pressing, fr. L. sera. See Serry.]

senses.d: To look over or through, for the purpose of finding something; to examine; to explore; as, to search the city.
q: They are come to search the house.
Search me, O God, and know my heart.

senses.d: To inquire after; to look for; to seek.
q: I will both search my sheep, and seek them out.
Enough is left besides to search and know.

senses.d: To examine or explore by feeling with an instrument; to probe; as, to search a wound.
To examine; to try; to put to the test.

Search.syn: To explore; examine; scrutinize; seek; investigate; pry into; inquire.
Search.etym: [OE. serchen, cerchen, OF. cerchier, F. chercher, L. circare to go about, fr. L. circum, circa, around. See Circle.]

senses.d: To seek; to look for something; to make inquiry, exploration, or examination; to hunt.
q: Once more search with me.
It sufficeth that they have once with care sifted the matter, and searched into all the particulars.

senses.d: The act of seeking or looking for something; quest; inquiry; pursuit for finding something; examination.
q: Thus the orb he roamed With narrow search, and with inspection deep Considered every creature.
Nor did my search of liberty begin Till my black hairs were changed upon my chin.

Search.syn: Scrutiny; examination; exploration; investigation; research; inquiry; quest; pursuit.
Search.etym: [Cf. OF. cerche. See Search, v. t.]

senses.d: Exploring thoroughly; scrutinizing; penetrating; trying; as, a searching discourse; a searching eye.
Scorched; cauterized; hence, figuratively, insensible; not susceptible to moral influences.
q: A seared conscience and a remorseless heart.

senses.d: One of the divisions of the year, marked by alterations in the length of day and night, or by distinct conditions of temperature, moisture, etc., caused mainly by the relative position of the earth with respect to the sun. In the north temperate zone, four seasons, namely, spring, summer, autumn, and winter, are generally recognized. Some parts of the world have three seasons, — the dry, the rainy, and the cold; other parts have but two, — the dry and the rainy.
q: The several seasons of the year in their beauty.

senses.d: Hence, a period of time, especially as regards its fitness for anything contemplated or done; a suitable or convenient time; proper conjuncture; as, the season for planting; the season for rest.
q: The season, prime for sweetest scents and airs.

senses.d: A period of time not very long; a while; a time.
q: Thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season.

senses.d: That which gives relish; seasoning.
q: You lack the season of all natures, sleep.

Season.etym: [OE. sesoun, F. saison, properly, the sowing time, fr. L. satio a sowing, a planting, fr. serere, satum, to sow, plant; akin to E. sow, v., to scatter, as seed.]

senses.d: To render suitable or appropriate; to prepare; to fit.
q: He is fit and seasoned for his passage.

senses.d: To fit for any use by time or habit; to habituate; to accustom; to inure; to ripen; to mature; as, to season one to a climate.
Hence, to prepare by drying or hardening, or removal of natural juices; as, to season timber.
To fit for taste; to render palatable; to give zest or relish to; to spice; as, to season food.
Hence, to fit for enjoyment; to render agreeable.
q: You season still with sports your serious hours.
The proper use of wit is to season conversation.

senses.d: To qualify by admixture; to moderate; to temper.
To imbue; to tinge or taint.
q: Season their younger years with prudent and pious principles.

senses.d: To copulate with; to impregnate.
To become mature; to grow fit for use; to become adapted to a climate.
To become dry and hard, by the escape of the natural juices, or by being penetrated with other substance; as, timber seasons in the sun.
To give token; to savor.
The place or thing upon which one sits; hence; anything made to be sat in or upon, as a chair, bench, stool, saddle, or the like.
q: And Jesus . . . overthrew the tables of the money changers, and the seats of them that sold doves.

senses.d: The place occupied by anything, or where any person or thing is situated, resides, or abides; a site; an abode, a station; a post; a situation.
q: Where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is.
He that builds a fair house upon an ill seat committeth himself to prison.
A seat of plenty, content, and tranquillity.

senses.d: That part of a thing on which a person sits; as, the seat of a chair or saddle; the seat of a pair of pantaloons.
A sitting; a right to sit; regular or appropriate place of sitting; as, a seat in a church; a seat for the season in the opera house.
Posture, or way of sitting, on horseback.
q: She had so good a seat and hand she might be trusted with any mount.

senses.d: A part or surface on which another part or surface rests; as, a valve seat.

Seat.etym: [OE. sete, Icel. sæti; akin to Sw. säte, Dan. sæde, MHG. sāze, AS. set, setl, and E. sit. √154. See Sit, and cf. Settle, n.]

senses.d: To place on a seat; to cause to sit down; as, to seat one's self.
q: The guests were no sooner seated but they entered into a warm debate.

senses.d: To cause to occupy a post, site, situation, or the like; to station; to establish; to fix; to settle.
q: Thus high . . . is King Richard seated.
They had seated themselves in New Guiana.

senses.d: To assign a seat to, or the seats of; to give a sitting to; as, to seat a church, or persons in a church.
To fix; to set firm.
q: From their foundations, loosening to and fro, They plucked the seated hills.

senses.d: To settle; to plant with inhabitants; as to seat a country.
To put a seat or bottom in; as, to seat a chair.
To rest; to lie down.
The eleventh month of the ancient Hebrew year, approximately corresponding with February.
Immediately following the first; next to the first in order of place or time; hence, occurring again; another; other.
q: And he slept and dreamed the second time.

senses.d: Next to the first in value, power, excellence, dignity, or rank; secondary; subordinate; inferior.
q: May the day when we become the second people upon earth . . . be the day of our utter extirpation.

senses.d: Being of the same kind as another that has preceded; another, like a prototype; as, a second Cato; a second Troy; a second deluge.
q: A Daniel, still say I, a second Daniel!

Second.etym: [F., fr. L. secundus second, properly, following, fr. sequi to follow. See Sue to follow, and cf. Secund.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, follows, or comes after; one next and inferior in place, time, rank, importance, excellence, or power.
q: Man An angel's second, nor his second long.

senses.d: One who follows or attends another for his support and aid; a backer; an assistant; specifically, one who acts as another's aid in a duel.
q: Being sure enough of seconds after the first onset.

senses.d: Aid; assistance; help.
q: Give second, and my love Is everlasting thine.

senses.d: An article of merchandise of a grade inferior to the best; esp., a coarse or inferior kind of flour.

The sixtieth part of a minute of time or of a minute of space, that is, the second regular subdivision of the degree; as, sound moves about 1,140 English feet in a second; five minutes and ten seconds north of this place.
In the duodecimal system of mensuration, the twelfth part of an inch or prime; a line. See Inch, and Prime, n., 8.
The interval between any tone and the tone which is represented on the degree of the staff next above it.
To follow in the next place; to succeed; to alternate.
q: In the method of nature, a low valley is immediately seconded with an ambitious hill.
Sin is seconded with sin.

senses.d: To follow or attend for the purpose of assisting; to support; to back; to act as the second of; to assist; to forward; to encourage.
q: We have supplies to second our attempt.
In human works though labored on with pain, A thousand movements scarce one purpose gain; In God's, one single can its end produce, Yet serves to second too some other use.

senses.d: Specifically, to support, as a motion or proposal, by adding one's voice to that of the mover or proposer.

Second.etym: [Cf. F. seconder, L. secundare, from secundus. See Second, a.]

senses.d: In a secondary manner or degree.
Secondly; in the second place.
q: God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers.

senses.d: Succeeding next in order to the first; of second place, origin, rank, etc.; not primary; subordinate; not of the first order or rate.
q: Wheresoever there is moral right on the one hand, no secondary right can discharge it.
Two are the radical differences; the secondary differences are as four.

senses.d: Acting by deputation or delegated authority; as, the work of secondary hands.
Possessing some quality, or having been subject to some operation (as substitution), in the second degree; as, a secondary salt, a secondary amine, etc. Cf. primary.

Subsequent in origin; — said of minerals produced by alteration or deposition subsequent to the formation of the original rock mass; also of characters of minerals (as secondary cleavage, etc.) developed by pressure or other causes.
Pertaining to the second joint of the wing of a bird.
Dependent or consequent upon another disease; as, Bright's disease is often secondary to scarlet fever.

Secondary.etym: [Cf. F. secondaire, L. secundaire. See Second, a.]

senses.d: One who occupies a subordinate, inferior, or auxiliary place; a delegate or deputy; one who is second or next to the chief officer; as, the secondary, or undersheriff of the city of London.
q: Old Escalus . . . is thy secondary.

senses.d: A secondary circle.
A secondary quill.
Hidden; concealed; as, secret treasure; secret plans; a secret vow.
q: The secret things belong unto the Lord our God; but those things which are revealed belong unto us.

senses.d: Withdrawn from general intercourse or notice; in retirement or secrecy; secluded.
q: There, secret in her sapphire cell, He with the Naïs wont to dwell.

senses.d: Faithful to a secret; not inclined to divulge or betray confidence; secretive.
q: Secret Romans, that have spoke the word, And will not palter.

senses.d: Separate; distinct.
q: They suppose two other divine hypostases superior thereunto, which were perfectly secret from matter.

Secret.syn: Hidden; concealed; secluded; retired; unseen; unknown; private; obscure; recondite; latent; covert; clandestine; privy. See Hidden.
Secret.etym: [F. secret (cf. Sp. & Pg. secreto, It. secreto, segreto), fr. L. secretus, p. p. of secernere to put apart, to separate. See Certain, and cf. Secrete, Secern.]

senses.d: Something studiously concealed; a thing kept from general knowledge; what is not revealed, or not to be revealed.
q: To tell our own secrets is often folly; to communicate those of others is treachery.

senses.d: A thing not discovered; what is unknown or unexplained; a mystery.
q: All secrets of the deep, all nature's works.

senses.d: The parts which modesty and propriety require to be concealed; the genital organs.
q: Bread eaten in secret is pleasant.

Secret.etym: [F. secret (cf. Pr. secret, Sp. & Pg. secreto, It. secreto, segreto), from L. secretum. See Secret, a.]

senses.d: To keep secret.
In a secret manner.
A cutting; a scion.

Those following a particular leader or authority, or attached to a certain opinion; a company or set having a common belief or allegiance distinct from others; in religion, the believers in a particular creed, or upholders of a particular practice; especially, in modern times, a party dissenting from an established church; a denomination; in philosophy, the disciples of a particular master; a school; in society and the state, an order, rank, class, or party.
q: He beareth the sign of poverty, And in that sect our Savior saved all mankind.
As of the sect of which that he was born, He kept his lay, to which that he was sworn.
The cursed sect of that detestable and false prophet Mohammed.
As concerning this sect , we know that everywhere it is spoken against.

Sect.etym: [F. secte, L. secta, fr. sequi to follow; often confused with L. secare, sectum, to cut. See Sue to follow, and cf. Sept, Suit, n.]

senses.d: Free from fear, care, or anxiety; easy in mind; not feeling suspicion or distrust; confident.
q: But thou, secure of soul, unbent with woes.

senses.d: Overconfident; incautious; careless; — in a bad sense.
Confident in opinion; not entertaining, or not having reason to entertain, doubt; certain; sure; — commonly with of; as, secure of a welcome.
q: Confidence then bore thee on, secure Either to meet no danger, or to find Matter of glorious trial.

senses.d: Not exposed to danger; safe; — applied to persons and things, and followed by against or from.

Secure.syn: Safe; undisturbed; easy; sure; certain; assured; confident; careless; heedless; inattentive.
Secure.etym: [L. securus; pref. se- without + cura care. See Cure care, and cf. Sure, a.]

senses.d: To make safe; to relieve from apprehensions of, or exposure to, danger; to guard; to protect.
q: I spread a cloud before the victor's sight, Sustained the vanquished, and secured his flight.

senses.d: To put beyond hazard of losing or of not receiving; to make certain; to assure; to insure; — frequently with against or from, rarely with of; as, to secure a creditor against loss; to secure a debt by a mortgage.
q: It secures its possessor of eternal happiness.

senses.d: To make fast; to close or confine effectually; to render incapable of getting loose or escaping; as, to secure a prisoner; to secure a door, or the hatches of a ship.
To get possession of; to make one's self secure of; to acquire certainly; as, to secure an estate.
In a secure manner; without fear or apprehension; without danger; safely.
q: His daring foe . . . securely him defied.

senses.d: The condition or quality of being secure; secureness.
q: His trembling hand had lost the ease, Which marks security to please.

senses.d: Hence, carelessness; negligence; heedlessness.
q: He means, my lord, that we are too remiss, Whilst Bolingbroke, through our security, Grows strong and great in substance and in power.

senses.d: Freedom from risk; safety.
q: Give up yourself merely to chance and hazard, From firm security.
Some . . . alleged that we should have no security for our trade.

senses.d: That which secures or makes safe; protection; guard; defense.
q: Those who lent him money lent it on no security but his bare word.

senses.d: One who becomes surety for another, or engages himself for the performance of another's obligation.
An evidence of debt or of property, as a bond, a certificate of stock, etc.; as, government securities.

Security.syn: Protection; defense; guard; shelter; safety; certainty; ease; assurance; carelessness; confidence; surety; pledge; bail.
Security.etym: [L. securitas: cf. F. sécurité. See Secure, and cf. Surety.]

senses.d: The raising of commotion in a state, not amounting to insurrection; conduct tending to treason, but without an overt act; excitement of discontent against the government, or of resistance to lawful authority.
q: In soothing them, we nourish 'gainst our senate The cockle of rebellion, insolence, sedition.
Noisy demagogues who had been accused of sedition.

senses.d: Dissension; division; schism.
q: Now the works of the flesh are manifest, . . . emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies.

Sedition.syn: Insurrection; tumult; uproar; riot; rebellion; revolt. See Insurrection.
Sedition.etym: [OE. sedicioun, OF. sedition, F. sédition, fr. L. seditio, originally, a going aside; hence, an insurrectionary separation; pref. se-, sed-, aside + itio a going, fr. ire, itum, to go. Cf. Issue.]

senses.d: To draw aside from the path of rectitude and duty in any manner; to entice to evil; to lead astray; to tempt and lead to iniquity; to corrupt.
q: For me, the gold of France did not seduce.

senses.d: Specifically, to induce to surrender chastity; to debauch by means of solicitation.

Seduce.syn: To allure; entice; tempt; attract; mislead; decoy; inveigle. See Allure.
Seduce.etym: [L. seducere, seductum; pref. se- aside + ducere to lead. See Duke.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, seduces; specifically, one who prevails over the chastity of a woman by enticements and persuasions.
q: He whose firm faith no reason could remove, Will melt before that soft seducer, love.

senses.d: Seductive.
A seat; a site; a place where sovereign power is exercised.
q: Jove laughed on Venus from his sovereign see.

senses.d: Specifically: (a) The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop; as, the see of New York. (b) The seat of an archbishop; a province or jurisdiction of an archbishop; as, an archiepiscopal see. (c) The seat, place, or office of the pope, or Roman pontiff; as, the papal see. (d) The pope or his court at Rome; as, to appeal to the see of Rome.

See.etym: [OE. se, see, OF. se, sed, sied, fr. L. sedes a seat, or the kindred sedere to sit. See Sit, and cf. Siege.]

senses.d: To perceive by the eye; to have knowledge of the existence and apparent qualities of by the organs of sight; to behold; to descry; to view.
q: I will now turn aside, and see this great sight.

senses.d: To perceive by mental vision; to form an idea or conception of; to note with the mind; to observe; to discern; to distinguish; to understand; to comprehend; to ascertain.
q: Go, I pray thee, see whether it be well with thy brethren.
Jesus saw that he answered discreetly.
Who's so gross That seeth not this palpable device?

senses.d: To follow with the eyes, or as with the eyes; to watch; to regard attentively; to look after.
q: I had a mind to see him out, and therefore did not care for contradicting him.

senses.d: To have an interview with; especially, to make a call upon; to visit; as, to go to see a friend.
q: And Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death.

senses.d: To fall in with; to meet or associate with; to have intercourse or communication with; hence, to have knowledge or experience of; as, to see military service.
q: Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, if a man keep my saying, he shall never see death.
Improvement in wisdom and prudence by seeing men.

senses.d: To accompany in person; to escort; to wait upon; as, to see one home; to see one aboard the cars.

See.etym: [OE. seen, sen, seon, AS. seón; akin to OFries. sīa, D. zien, OS. & OHG. sehan, G. sehen, Icel. sjā, Sw. se, Dan. see, Goth. saíhwan, and probably to L. sequi to follow (and so originally meaning, to follow with the eyes). Gr. ἕπεσθαι, Skr. sac. Cf. Sight, Sue to follow.]

senses.d: To have the power of sight, or of perceiving by the proper organs; to possess or employ the sense of vision; as, he sees distinctly.
q: Whereas I was blind, now I see.

senses.d: Figuratively: To have intellectual apprehension; to perceive; to know; to understand; to discern; — often followed by a preposition, as through, or into.
q: For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind.
Many sagacious persons will find us out, . . . and see through all our fine pretensions.

senses.d: To be attentive; to take care; to give heed; — generally with to; as, to see to the house.
q: See that ye fall not out by the way.
Cassio's a proper man, let me see now, - To get his place.

senses.d: In poker and similar games at cards, to meet (a bet), or to equal the bet of (a player), by staking the same sum.
A ripened ovule, consisting of an embryo with one or more integuments, or coverings; as, an apple seed; a currant seed. By germination it produces a new plant.
q: And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself.

senses.d: The generative fluid of the male; semen; sperm; — not used in the plural.
That from which anything springs; first principle; original; source; as, the seeds of virtue or vice.
The principle of production.
q: Praise of great acts he scatters as a seed, Which may the like in coming ages breed.

senses.d: Progeny; offspring; children; descendants; as, the seed of Abraham; the seed of David.
Race; generation; birth.
q: Of mortal seed they were not held.

Seed.etym: [OE. seed, sed, AS. sǣd, fr. sāwan to sow; akin to D. zaad seed, G. saat, Icel. sāð, sæði, Goth. manasēþs seed of men, world. See Sow to scatter seed, and cf. Colza.]

senses.d: To sow seed.
To shed the seed.
To grow to maturity, and produce seed.
q: Many interests have grown up, and seeded, and twisted their roots in the crevices of many wrongs.

senses.d: To sprinkle with seed; to plant seeds in; to sow; as, to seed a field.
To cover thinly with something scattered; to ornament with seedlike decorations.
q: A sable mantle seeded with waking eyes.

senses.d: The season proper for sowing.
q: While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night, shall not cease.

senses.d: In view of the fact (that); considering; taking into account (that); insmuch as; since; because; — followed by a dependent clause; as, he did well, seeing that he was so young.
q: Wherefore come ye to me, seeing ye hate me?

senses.d: Sick.
To go in search of; to look for; to search for; to try to find.
q: The man asked him, saying, What seekest thou? And he said, I seek my brethren.

senses.d: To inquire for; to ask for; to solicit; to beseech.
q: Others, tempting him, sought of him a sign.

senses.d: To try to acquire or gain; to strive after; to aim at; as, to seek wealth or fame; to seek one's life.
To try to reach or come to; to go to; to resort to.
q: Seek not Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal.
Since great Ulysses sought the Phrygian plains.

Seek.etym: [OE. seken, AS. sēcan, sēcean; akin to OS. sōkian, LG. söken, D. zoeken, OHG. suohhan, G. suchen, Icel. sækja, Sw. söka, Dan. söge, Goth. sōkjan, and E. sake. Cf. Beseech, Ransack, Sagacious, Sake, Soc.]

senses.d: To make search or inquiry; to endeavor to make discovery.
q: Seek ye out of the book of the Lord, and read.
To seek Upon a man and do his soul unrest.

senses.d: To appear, or to appear to be; to have a show or semblance; to present an appearance; to look; to strike one's apprehension or fancy as being; to be taken as.
q: Thou picture of what thou seem'st.
All seemed well pleased; all seemed, but were not all.
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man; but the end thereof are the ways of death.
A prince of Italy, it seems, entertained his mistress on a great lake.
Ham. Ay, madam, it is common. Queen. If it be, Why seems it so particular with thee? Ham. Seems, madam! Nay, it is; I know not “seems.”

Seem.etym: [OE. semen to seem, to become, befit, AS. sēman to satisfy, pacify; akin to Icel. sæma to honor, to bear with, conform to, sæmr becoming, fit, sōma to beseem, to befit, sama to beseem, semja to arrange, settle, put right, Goth. samjan to please, and to E. same. The sense is probably due to the adj.

senses.d: To befit; to beseem.
Suited to the object, occasion, purpose, or character; suitable; fit; becoming; comely; decorous.
q: He had a seemly nose.
I am a woman, lacking wit To make a seemly answer to such persons.
Suspense of judgment and exercise of charity were safer and seemlier for Christian men than the hot pursuit of these controversies.

Seemly.syn: Becoming; fit; suitable; proper; appropriate; congruous; meet; decent; decorous.
Seemly.etym: [Icel. s�miligr, fr. s�mr becoming, fit; akin to samr same, E. same; the sense being properly, the same or like, hence, fitting. See Seem, v. i.]

senses.d: In a decent or suitable manner; becomingly.
q: Suddenly a men before him stood, Not rustic as before, but seemlier clad, As one in city or court or place bred.

senses.d: Versed; skilled; accomplished.
q: Well seen in every science that mote be.
Noble Boyle, not less in nature seen, Than his great brother read in states and men.

senses.d: Sore; painful.
One who sees.
A person who foresees events; a prophet.
To decoct or prepare for food in hot liquid; to boil; as, to seethe flesh.
q: Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets.

Seethe.etym: [OE. sethen, AS. seó�an; akin to D. sieden, OHG. siodan, G. sieden, Icel. sj��a, Sw. sjuda, Dan. syde, Goth. saubs a burnt offering. Cf. Sod, n., Sodden, Suds.]

senses.d: To be a state of ebullition or violent commotion; to be hot; to boil.
q: A long Pointe, round which the Mississippi used to whirl, and seethe, and foam.

senses.d: To fall or rush upon suddenly and lay hold of; to gripe or grasp suddenly; to reach and grasp.
q: For by no means the high bank he could seize.
Seek you to seize and gripe into your hands The royalties and rights of banished Hereford?

senses.d: To take possession of by force.
q: At last they seize The scepter, and regard not David's sons.

senses.d: To invade suddenly; to take sudden hold of; to come upon suddenly; as, a fever seizes a patient.
q: Hope and deubt alternate seize her seul.

senses.d: To take possession of by virtue of a warrant or other legal authority; as, the sheriff seized the debtor's goods.
To fasten; to fix.
q: As when a bear hath seized her cruel claws Upon the carcass of some beast too weak.

senses.d: To grap with the mind; to comprehend fully and distinctly; as, to seize an idea.
To bind or fasten together with a lashing of small stuff, as yarn or marline; as, to seize ropes.

Seize.syn: To catch; grasp; clutch; snatch; apprehend; arrest; take; capture.
Seize.etym: [OE. seisen, saisen, OF. seisir, saisir, F. saisir, of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. set. The meaning is properly, to set, put, place, hence, to put in possession of. See Set, v. t.]

senses.d: A word of doubtful meaning, occuring frequently in the Psalms; by some, supposed to signify silence or a pause in the musical performance of the song.
q: Beyond the fact that Selah is a musical term, we know absolutely nothing about it.

senses.d: Same; particular; very; identical.
q: To shoot another arrow that self way Which you did shoot the first.
At that self moment enters Palamon.

Self.etym: [AS. self, seolf, sylf; akin to OS. self, OFries. self, D. zelf, G. selb, selber, selbst, Dan. selv. Sw. sjelf, Icel. sjālfr, Goth. silba. Cf. Selvage.]

senses.d: The individual as the object of his own reflective consciousness; the man viewed by his own cognition as the subject of all his mental phenomena, the agent in his own activities, the subject of his own feelings, and the possessor of capacities and character; a person as a distinct individual; a being regarded as having personality.
q: A man's self may be the worst fellow to converse with in the world.

The self, the I, is recognized in every act of intelligence as the subject to which that act belongs. It is I that perceive, I that imagine, I that remember, I that attend, I that compare, I that feel, I that will, I that am conscious.

senses.d: Hence, personal interest, or love of private interest; selfishness; as, self is his whole aim.
Personification; embodiment.
q: She was beauty's self.

senses.d: Having its own or a single nature or character, as in color, composition, etc., without addition or change; unmixed; as, a self bow, one made from a single piece of wood; self flower or plant, one which is wholly of one color; self-colored.
Precisely the same; the very same; identical.
q: His servant was healed in the selfsame hour.

senses.d: Self.
A sill.
A cell; a house.
A saddle for a horse.
q: He left his lofty steed with golden self.

senses.d: A throne or lofty seat.

Sell.etym: [F. selle, L. sella, akin to sedere to sit. See Sit.]

senses.d: To transfer to another for an equivalent; to give up for a valuable consideration; to dispose of in return for something, especially for money.
q: If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor.
I am changed; I'll go sell all my land.

senses.d: To make a matter of bargain and sale of; to accept a price or reward for, as for a breach of duty, trust, or the like; to betray.
q: You would have sold your king to slaughter.

senses.d: To impose upon; to trick; to deceive; to make a fool of; to cheat.

Sell.etym: [OE. sellen, sillen, AS. sellan, syllan, to give, to deliver; akin to OS. sellian, OFries. sella, OHG. sellen, Icel. selja to hand over, to sell, Sw. sälja to sell, Dan. s�lge, Goth. saljan to offer a sacrifice; all from a noun akin to E. sale. Cf. Sale.]

senses.d: To practice selling commodities.
q: I will buy with you, sell with you; . . . but I will not eat with you.

senses.d: To be sold; as, corn sells at a good price.
An imposition; a cheat; a hoax.
One who sells.
Self; same.
An assembly or council having the highest deliberative and legislative functions.
q: The senate was thus the medium through which all affairs of the whole government had to pass.

senses.d: The upper and less numerous branch of a legislature in various countries, as in France, in the United States, in most of the separate States of the United States, and in some Swiss cantons.
In general, a legislative body; a state council; the legislative department of government.
The governing body of the Universities of Cambridge and London.

In some American colleges, a council of elected students, presided over by the president of the college, to which are referred cases of discipline and matters of general concern affecting the students.

Senate.etym: [OE. senat, F. sénat, fr. L. senatus, fr. senex, gen. senis, old, an old man. See Senior, Sir.]

senses.d: A member of a senate.
q: The duke and senators of Venice greet you.

senses.d: A member of the king's council; a king's councilor.

Senator.etym: [OE. senatour, OF. senatour, F. sénateur, fr. L. senator.]

senses.d: To cause to go in any manner; to dispatch; to commission or direct to go; as, to send a messenger.
q: I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran.
I proceeded forth and came from God; neither came I of myself, but he sent me.
Servants, sent on messages, stay out somewhat longer than the message requires.

senses.d: To give motion to; to cause to be borne or carried; to procure the going, transmission, or delivery of; as, to send a message.
q: He . . . sent letters by posts on horseback.
O send out thy light an thy truth; let them lead me.

senses.d: To emit; to impel; to cast; to throw; to hurl; as, to send a ball, an arrow, or the like.
To cause to be or to happen; to bestow; to inflict; to grant; — sometimes followed by a dependent proposition.
q: The Lord shall send upon thee cursing, vexation, and rebuke.
And sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
God send your mission may bring back peace.

Send.etym: [AS. sendan; akin to OS. sendian, D. zenden, G. senden, OHG. senten, Icel. senda, Sw. sända, Dan. sende, Goth. sandjan, and to Goth. sinp a time (properly, a going), gasinpa companion, OHG. sind journey, AS. sī�, Icel. sinni a walk, journey, a time. W. hynt a way, journey, OIr. s�t. Cf. Sense.]

senses.d: To dispatch an agent or messenger to convey a message, or to do an errand.
q: See ye how this son of a murderer hath sent to take away my head?

senses.d: To pitch; as, the ship sends forward so violently as to endanger her masts.
The impulse of a wave by which a vessel is carried bodily.
Since.

A faculty, possessed by animals, of perceiving external objects by means of impressions made upon certain organs (sensory or sense organs) of the body, or of perceiving changes in the condition of the body; as, the senses of sight, smell, hearing, taste, and touch. See Muscular sense, under Muscular, and Temperature sense, under Temperature.
q: Let fancy still my sense in Lethe steep.
What surmounts the reach Of human sense I shall delineate.
The traitor Sense recalls The soaring soul from rest.

senses.d: Perception by the sensory organs of the body; sensation; sensibility; feeling.
q: In a living creature, though never so great, the sense and the affects of any one part of the body instantly make a transcursion through the whole.

senses.d: Perception through the intellect; apprehension; recognition; understanding; discernment; appreciation.
q: This Basilius, having the quick sense of a lover.
High disdain from sense of injured merit.

senses.d: Sound perception and reasoning; correct judgment; good mental capacity; understanding; also, that which is sound, true, or reasonable; rational meaning.
q: He raves; his words are loose As heaps of sand, and scattering wide from sense.

senses.d: That which is felt or is held as a sentiment, view, or opinion; judgment; notion; opinion.
q: I speak my private but impartial sense With freedom.
The municipal council of the city had ceased to speak the sense of the citizens.

senses.d: Meaning; import; signification; as, the true sense of words or phrases; the sense of a remark.
q: So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense.
I think 't was in another sense.

senses.d: Moral perception or appreciation.
q: Some are so hardened in wickedness as to have no sense of the most friendly offices.

senses.d: One of two opposite directions in which a line, surface, or volume, may be supposed to be described by the motion of a point, line, or surface.

Sense.etym: [L. sensus, from sentire, sensum, to perceive, to feel, from the same root as E. send; cf. OHG. sin sense, mind, sinnan to go, to journey, G. sinnen to meditate, to think: cf. F. sens. For the change of meaning cf. See, v. t. See Send, and cf. Assent, Consent, Scent, v. t., Sentence, Sentient.]

senses.d: To perceive by the senses; to recognize.
q: Is he sure that objects are not otherwise sensed by others than they are by him?

senses.d: Pertaining to, consisting in, or affecting, the sense, or bodily organs of perception; relating to, or concerning, the body, in distinction from the spirit.
q: Pleasing and sensual rites and ceremonies.
Far as creation's ample range extends, The scale of sensual, mental powers ascends.

senses.d: Hence, not spiritual or intellectual; carnal; fleshly; pertaining to, or consisting in, the gratification of the senses, or the indulgence of appetites; wordly.
q: These be they who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit.
The greatest part of men are such as prefer . . . that good which is sensual before whatsoever is most divine.

senses.d: Devoted to the pleasures of sense and appetite; luxurious; voluptuous; lewd; libidinous.
q: No small part of virtue consists in abstaining from that wherein sensual men place their felicity.

senses.d: Pertaining or peculiar to the philosophical doctrine of sensualism.

Sensual.etym: [L. sensualis, from sensus sense: cf. F. sensuel.]

senses.d: Sense; meaning; significance.
q: Tales of best sentence and most solace.
The discourse itself, voluble enough, and full of sentence.

senses.d: An opinion; a decision; a determination; a judgment, especially one of an unfavorable nature.
q: My sentence is for open war.
That by them we may pass sentence upon his doctrines.

senses.d: A philosophical or theological opinion; a dogma; as, Summary of the Sentences; Book of the Sentences.

In civil and admiralty law, the judgment of a court pronounced in a cause; in criminal and ecclesiastical courts, a judgment passed on a criminal by a court or judge; condemnation pronounced by a judicial tribunal; doom. In common law, the term is exclusively used to denote the judgment in criminal cases.
q: Received the sentence of the law.

senses.d: A short saying, usually containing moral instruction; a maxim; an axiom; a saw.
A combination of words which is complete as expressing a thought, and in writing is marked at the close by a period, or full point. See Proposition, 4.
q: He fills, he bounds, connects, and equals all.
A king . . . understanding dark sentences.

Sentence.etym: [F., from L. sententia, for sentientia, from sentire to discern by the senses and the mind, to feel, to think. See Sense, n., and cf. Sentiensi.]

senses.d: To pass or pronounce judgment upon; to doom; to condemn to punishment; to prescribe the punishment of.
q: Nature herself is sentenced in your doom.

senses.d: To decree or announce as a sentence.
To utter sententiously.
To disunite; to divide; to disconnect; to sever; to part in any manner.
q: From the fine gold I separate the alloy.
Separate thyself, I pray thee, from me.
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?

senses.d: To come between; to keep apart by occupying the space between; to lie between; as, the Mediterranean Sea separates Europe and Africa.
To set apart; to select from among others, as for a special use or service.
q: Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called thaem.

Separate.etym: [L. separatus, p. p. of separare to separate; pfref. se- aside + parare to make ready, prepare. See Parade, and cf. Sever.]

senses.d: To part; to become disunited; to be disconnected; to withdraw from one another; as, the family separated.
Divided from another or others; disjoined; disconnected; separated; — said of things once connected.
q: Him that was separate from his brethren.

senses.d: Unconnected; not united or associated; distinct; — said of things that have not been connected.
q: For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinnere.

senses.d: Disunited from the body; disembodied; as, a separate spirit; the separate state of souls.
Designed or employed to separate.
The act of separating, or the state of being separated, or separate.
Chemical analysis.
Divorce.
The operation of removing water from steam.
The Hebrew plural of Seraph. Cf. Cherubim.
Dry; withered. Same as Sear.
q: But with its sound it shook the sails That were so thin and sere.

senses.d: Claw; talon.
Any reptile of the order Ophidia; a snake, especially a large snake. See Illust. under Ophidia.
Fig.: A subtle, treacherous, malicious person.
A species of firework having a serpentine motion as it passess through the air or along the ground.
The constellation Serpens.
A bass wind instrument, of a loud and coarse tone, formerly much used in military bands, and sometimes introduced into the orchestra; — so called from its form.

Serpent.etym: [F., fr. L. serpens, -entis (sc. bestia), fr. serpens, p. pr. of serpere to creep; akin to Gr. ���, Skr. sarp, and perhaps to L. repere, E. reptile. Cf. Herpes.]

senses.d: To wind like a serpent; to crook about; to meander.
To wind; to encircle.

One who serves, or does services, voluntarily or on compulsion; a person who is employed by another for menial offices, or for other labor, and is subject to his command; a person who labors or exerts himself for the benefit of another, his master or employer; a subordinate helper.
q: Men in office have begun to think themselves mere agents and servants of the appointing power, and not agents of the government or the country.

senses.d: One in a state of subjection or bondage.
q: Thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt.

senses.d: A professed lover or suitor; a gallant.
q: In my time a servant was I one.
Our betters tell us they are our humble servants, but understand us to be their slaves.

Servant.etym: [OE. servant, servaunt, F. servant, a & p. pr. of servir to serve, L. servire. See Serve, and cf. Sergeant.]

senses.d: To subject.

To work for; to labor in behalf of; to exert one's self continuously or statedly for the benefit of; to do service for; to be in the employment of, as an inferior, domestic, serf, slave, hired assistant, official helper, etc.; specifically, in a religious sense, to obey and worship.
q: God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit.
Jacob loved Rachel; and said, I will serve thee seven years for Rachel thy younger daughter.
No man can serve two masters.
Had I but served my God with half the zeal I served my king, he would not in mine age Have left me naked to mine enemies.

senses.d: To be subordinate to; to act a secondary part under; to appear as the inferior of; to minister to.
q: Bodies bright and greater should not serve The less not bright.

senses.d: To be suitor to; to profess love to.
q: To serve a lady in his beste wise.

senses.d: To wait upon; to supply the wants of; to attend; specifically, to wait upon at table; to attend at meals; to supply with food; as, to serve customers in a shop.
q: Others, pampered in their shameless pride, Are served in plate and in their chariots ride.

senses.d: Hence, to bring forward, arrange, deal, or distribute, as a portion of anything, especially of food prepared for eating; — often with up; formerly with in.
q: Bid them cover the table, serve in the meat, and we will come in to dinner.
Some part he roasts, then serves it up so dressed.

senses.d: To perform the duties belonging to, or required in or for; hence, to be of use to; as, a curate may serve two churches; to serve one's country.
To contribute or conduce to; to promote; to be sufficient for; to satisfy; as, to serve one's turn.
q: Turn it into some advantage, by observing where it can serve another end.

senses.d: To answer or be (in the place of something) to; as, a sofa serves one for a seat and a couch.
To treat; to behave one's self to; to requite; to act toward; as, he served me very ill.
To work; to operate; as, to serve the guns.
To bring to notice, deliver, or execute, either actually or constructively, in such manner as the law requires; as, to serve a summons.
To pass or spend, as time, esp. time of punishment; as, to serve a term in prison.

Serve.syn: To obey; minister to; subserve; promote; aid; help; assist; benefit; succor.
Serve.etym: [OE. serven, servien, OF. & F. servir, fr. L. servire; akin to servus a servant or slave, servare to protect, preserve, observe; cf. Zend har to protect, haurva protecting. Cf. Conserve, Desert merit, Dessert, Observe, Serf, Sergeant.]

senses.d: To be a servant or a slave; to be employed in labor or other business for another; to be in subjection or bondage; to render menial service.
q: The Lord shall give thee rest . . . from the hard bondage wherein thou wast made to serve.

senses.d: To perform domestic offices; to be occupied with household affairs; to prepare and dish up food, etc.
q: But Martha . . . said, Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone?

senses.d: To be in service; to do duty; to discharge the requirements of an office or employment. Specifically, to act in the public service, as a soldier, seaman. etc.
q: Many . . . who had before been great commanders, but now served as private gentlemen without pay.

senses.d: To be of use; to answer a purpose; to suffice; to suit; to be convenient or favorable.
q: This little brand will serve to light your fire.
As occasion serves, this noble queen And prince shall follow with a fresh supply.

senses.d: To lead off in delivering the ball.

A name given to several trees and shrubs of the genus Pyrus, as Pyrus domestica and P. torminalis of Europe, the various species of mountain ash or rowan tree, and the American shad bush (see Shad bush, under Shad). They have clusters of small, edible, applelike berries.

Service.etym: [Properly, the tree which bears serve, OE. serves, pl., service berries, AS. syrfe service tree; akin to L. sorbus.]

senses.d: The act of serving; the occupation of a servant; the performance of labor for the benefit of another, or at another's command; attendance of an inferior, hired helper, slave, etc., on a superior, employer, master, or the like; also, spiritual obedience and love.
q: Madam, I entreat true peace of you, Which I will purchase with my duteous service.
God requires no man's service upon hard and unreasonable terms.

senses.d: The deed of one who serves; labor performed for another; duty done or required; office.
q: I have served him from the hour of my nativity, . . . and have nothing at his hands for my service but blows.
This poem was the last piece of service I did for my master, King Charles.
To go on the forlorn hope is a service of peril; who will understake it if it be not also a service of honor?

senses.d: Office of devotion; official religious duty performed; religious rites appropriate to any event or ceremonial; as, a burial service.
q: The outward service of ancient religion, the rites, ceremonies, and ceremonial vestments of the old law.

senses.d: Hence, a musical composition for use in churches.
Duty performed in, or appropriate to, any office or charge; official function; hence, specifically, military or naval duty; performance of the duties of a soldier.
q: When he cometh to experience of service abroad . . . ne maketh a worthy soldier.

senses.d: Useful office; advantage conferred; that which promotes interest or happiness; benefit; avail.
q: The stork's plea, when taken in a net, was the service she did in picking up venomous creatures.

senses.d: Profession of respect; acknowledgment of duty owed.

The act and manner of bringing food to the persons who eat it; order of dishes at table; also, a set or number of vessels ordinarily used at table; as, the service was tardy and awkward; a service of plate or glass.
q: There was no extraordinary service seen on the board.

senses.d: The act of bringing to notice, either actually or constructively, in such manner as is prescribed by law; as, the service of a subpœna or an attachment.
The materials used for serving a rope, etc., as spun yarn, small lines, etc.
The act of serving the ball.
Act of serving or covering. See Serve, v. t., 13.

Service.etym: [OE. servise, OF. servise, service, F. service, from L. servitium. See Serve.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a servant or slave; befitting a servant or a slave; proceeding from dependence; hence, meanly submissive; slavish; mean; cringing; fawning; as, servile flattery; servile fear; servile obedience.
q: She must bend the servile knee.
Fearing dying pays death servile breath.

senses.d: Held in subjection; dependent; enslaved.
q: Even fortune rules no more, O servile land!

senses.d: Not belonging to the original root; as, a servile letter.

Servile.etym: [L. servile, fr. servus a servant or slave: cf. F. servile. See Serve.]

senses.d: An element which forms no part of the original root; — opposed to radical.
One who serves; a servant; an attendant; one who acts under another; a follower or adherent.
q: Your trusty and most valiant servitor.

senses.d: An undergraduate, partly supported by the college funds, whose duty it formerly was to wait at table. A servitor corresponded to a sizar in Cambridge and Dublin universities.

Servitor.etym: [L., fr. servire to serve: cf. F. serviteur.]

senses.d: The state of voluntary or compulsory subjection to a master; the condition of being bound to service; the condition of a slave; slavery; bondage; hence, a state of slavish dependence.
q: You would have sold your king to slaughter, His princes and his peers to servitude.
A splendid servitude; . . . for he that rises up early, and goe� to bed late, only to receive addresses, is really as much abridged in his freedom as he that waits to present one.

senses.d: Servants, collectively.
q: After him a cumbrous train Of herds and flocks, and numerous servitude.

senses.d: A right whereby one thing is subject to another thing or person for use or convenience, contrary to the common right.

To cause to sit; to make to assume a specified position or attitude; to give site or place to; to place; to put; to fix; as, to set a house on a stone foundation; to set a book on a shelf; to set a dish on a table; to set a chest or trunk on its bottom or on end.
q: I do set my bow in the cloud.

senses.d: Hence, to attach or affix (something) to something else, or in or upon a certain place.
q: Set your affection on things above.
The Lord set a mark upon Cain.

senses.d: To make to assume specified place, condition, or occupation; to put in a certain condition or state (described by the accompanying words); to cause to be.
q: The Lord thy God will set thee on high.
I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother.
Every incident sets him thinking.

senses.d: To fix firmly; to make fast, permanent, or stable; to render motionless; to give an unchanging place, form, or condition to.
To cause to stop or stick; to obstruct; to fasten to a spot; hence, to occasion difficulty to; to embarrass; as, to set a coach in the mud.
q: They show how hard they are set in this particular.

senses.d: To fix beforehand; to determine; hence, to make unyielding or obstinate; to render stiff, unpliant, or rigid; as, to set one's countenance.
q: His eyes were set by reason of his age.
On these three objects his heart was set.
Make my heart as a millstone, set my face as a flint.

senses.d: To fix in the ground, as a post or a tree; to plant; as, to set pear trees in an orchard.
To fix, as a precious stone, in a border of metal; to place in a setting; hence, to place in or amid something which serves as a setting; as, to set glass in a sash.
q: And him too rich a jewel to be set In vulgar metal for a vulgar use.

senses.d: To render stiff or solid; especially, to convert into curd; to curdle; as, to set milk for cheese.
To put into a desired position or condition; to adjust; to regulate; to adapt.
To put in order in a particular manner; to prepare; as, to set (that is, to hone) a razor; to set a saw.
q: Tables for to sette, and beddes make.

senses.d: To extend and bring into position; to spread; as, to set the sails of a ship.

Set.etym: [OE. setten, AS. setton; akin to OS. settian, OFries. setta, D. zetten, OHG. sezzen, G. setzen, Icel. setja, Sw. sätta, Dan. s�tte, Goth. satjan; causative from the root of E. sit. √154. See Sit, and cf. Seize.]

senses.d: To pass below the horizon; to go down; to decline; to sink out of sight; to come to an end.
q: Ere the weary sun set in the west.
Thus this century sets with little mirth, and the next is likely to arise with more mourning.

senses.d: To fit music to words.
To place plants or shoots in the ground; to plant.
To be fixed for growth; to strike root; to begin to germinate or form; as, cuttings set well; the fruit has set well (i.e., not blasted in the blossom).
To become fixed or rigid; to be fastened.
q: A gathering and serring of the spirits together to resist, maketh the teeth to set hard one against another.

senses.d: To congeal; to concrete; to solidify.
q: That fluid substance in a few minutes begins to set.

senses.d: To have a certain direction in motion; to flow; to move on; to tend; as, the current sets to the north; the tide sets to the windward.
To begin to move; to go out or forth; to start; — now followed by out.
q: The king is set from London.

senses.d: To indicate the position of game; — said of a dog; as, the dog sets well; also, to hunt game by the aid of a setter.
To apply one's self; to undertake earnestly; — now followed by out.
q: If he sets industriously and sincerely to perform the commands of Christ, he can have no ground of doubting but it shall prove successful to him.

senses.d: To fit or suit one; to sit; as, the coat sets well.
Fixed in position; immovable; rigid; as, a set line; a set countenance.
Firm; unchanging; obstinate; as, set opinions or prejudices.
Regular; uniform; formal; as, a set discourse; a set battle.
Established; prescribed; as, set forms of prayer.
Adjusted; arranged; formed; adapted.
The act of setting, as of the sun or other heavenly body; descent; hence, the close; termination.
q: The weary sun hath made a golden set.

senses.d: That which is set, placed, or fixed.
q: We will in France, by God's grace, play a set Shall strike his father's crown into the hazard.
That was but civil war, an equal set.

senses.d: Permanent change of figure in consequence of excessive strain, as from compression, tension, bending, twisting, etc.; as, the set of a spring.
A kind of punch used for bending, indenting, or giving shape to, metal; as, a saw set.
A piece placed temporarily upon the head of a pile when the latter cannot be reached by the weight, or hammer, except by means of such an intervening piece.
A short steel spike used for driving the head of a nail below the surface.

A number of things of the same kind, ordinarily used or classed together; a collection of articles which naturally complement each other, and usually go together; an assortment; a suit; as, a set of chairs, of china, of surgical or mathematical instruments, of books, etc.
A number of persons associated by custom, office, common opinion, quality, or the like; a division; a group; a clique.
q: This falls into different divisions, or sets, of nations connected under particular religions.

senses.d: Direction or course; as, the set of the wind, or of a current.
In dancing, the number of persons necessary to execute a quadrille; also, the series of figures or movements executed.
The deflection of a tooth, or of the teeth, of a saw, which causes the the saw to cut a kerf, or make an opening, wider than the blade.
A young oyster when first attached.

Any of various standards of measurement of the fineness of cloth; specif., the number of reeds in one inch and the number of threads in each reed. The exact meaning varies according to the location where it is used. Sometimes written sett.
A stone, commonly of granite, shaped like a short brick and usually somewhat larger than one, used for street paving. Commonly written sett.
Camber of a curved roofing tile.
The manner, state, or quality of setting or fitting; fit; as, the set of a coat.
One who, or that which, sets; — used mostly in composition with a noun, as typesetter; or in combination with an adverb, as a setter on (or inciter), a setter up, a setter forth.

A hunting dog of a special breed originally derived from a cross between the spaniel and the pointer. Modern setters are usually trained to indicate the position of game birds by standing in a fixed position, but originally they indicated it by sitting or crouching.
One who hunts victims for sharpers.
One who adapts words to music in composition.
An adornment; a decoration; — with off.
q: They come as . . . setters off of thy graces.

senses.d: A shallow seggar for porcelain.
To cut the dewlap (of a cow or an ox), and to insert a seton, so as to cause an issue.
The act of one who, or that which, sets; as, the setting of type, or of gems; the setting of the sun; the setting (hardening) of moist plaster of Paris; the setting (set) of a current.
The act of marking the position of game, as a setter does; also, hunting with a setter.
Something set in, or inserted.
q: Thou shalt set in it settings of stones.

senses.d: That in which something, as a gem, is set; as, the gold setting of a jeweled pin.
A seat of any kind.
A bench; especially, a bench with a high back.
A place made lower than the rest; a wide step or platform lower than some other part.
q: And from the bottom upon the ground, even to the lower settle, shall be two cubits, and the breadth one cubit.

Settle.etym: [OE. setel, setil, a seat, AS. setl: akin to OHG. sezzal, G. sessel, Goth. sitls, and E. sit. √154. See Sit.]

senses.d: To place in a fixed or permanent condition; to make firm, steady, or stable; to establish; to fix; esp., to establish in life; to fix in business, in a home, or the like.
q: And he settled his countenance steadfastly upon him, until he was ashamed.
The father thought the time drew on Of setting in the world his only son.

senses.d: To establish in the pastoral office; to ordain or install as pastor or rector of a church, society, or parish; as, to settle a minister.
To cause to be no longer in a disturbed condition; to render quiet; to still; to calm; to compose.
q: God settled then the huge whale-bearing lake.
Hoping that sleep might settle his brains.

senses.d: To clear of dregs and impurities by causing them to sink; to render pure or clear; — said of a liquid; as, to settle coffee, or the grounds of coffee.
To restore or bring to a smooth, dry, or passable condition; — said of the ground, of roads, and the like; as, clear weather settles the roads.
To cause to sink; to lower; to depress; hence, also, to render close or compact; as, to settle the contents of a barrel or bag by shaking it.

To determine, as something which is exposed to doubt or question; to free from unscertainty or wavering; to make sure, firm, or constant; to establish; to compose; to quiet; as, to settle the mind when agitated; to settle questions of law; to settle the succession to a throne; to settle an allowance.
q: It will settle the wavering, and confirm the doubtful.

senses.d: To adjust, as something in discussion; to make up; to compose; to pacify; as, to settle a quarrel.
To adjust, as accounts; to liquidate; to balance; as, to settle an account.
Hence, to pay; as, to settle a bill.
To plant with inhabitants; to colonize; to people; as, the French first settled Canada; the Puritans settled New England; Plymouth was settled in 1620.

Settle.syn: To fix; establish; regulate; arrange; compose; adjust; determine; decide.
Settle.etym: [OE. setlen, AS. setlan. √154. See Settle, n. In senses 7, 8, and 9 perhaps confused with OE. sahtlen to reconcile, AS. sahtlian, fr. saht reconciliation, sacon to contend, dispute. Cf. Sake.]

senses.d: To become fixed or permanent; to become stationary; to establish one's self or itself; to assume a lasting form, condition, direction, or the like, in place of a temporary or changing state.
q: The wind came about and settled in the west.
Chyle . . . runs through all the intermediate colors until it settles in an intense red.

senses.d: To fix one's residence; to establish a dwelling place or home; as, the Saxons who settled in Britain.
To enter into the married state, or the state of a householder.
q: As people marry now and settle.

senses.d: To be established in an employment or profession; as, to settle in the practice of law.
To become firm, dry, and hard, as the ground after the effects of rain or frost have disappeared; as, the roads settled late in the spring.
To become clear after being turbid or obscure; to clarify by depositing matter held in suspension; as, the weather settled; wine settles by standing.
q: A government, on such occasions, is always thick before it settles.

senses.d: To sink to the bottom; to fall to the bottom, as dregs of a liquid, or the sediment of a reserveir.
To sink gradually to a lower level; to subside, as the foundation of a house, etc.
To become calm; to cease from agitation.
q: Till the fury of his highness settle, Come not before him.

senses.d: To adjust differences or accounts; to come to an agreement; as, he has settled with his creditors.
To make a jointure for a wife.
q: He sighs with most success that settles well.

senses.d: One more than six; six and one added; as, seven days make one week.

Seven.etym: [OE. seven, seoven, seofen, AS. seofon, seofan, seofen; akin to D. zeven, OS., Goth., & OHG. sibun, G. sieben, Icel. sjau, sjö, Sw. sju, Dan. syv, Lith. septyni, Russ. seme, W. saith, Gael. seachd, Ir. seacht, L. septem, Gr. ���, Skr. saptan. √305. Cf. Hebdomad, Heptagon, September.]

senses.d: The number greater by one than six; seven units or objects.
q: Of every beast, and bird, and insect small, Game sevens and pairs.

senses.d: A symbol representing seven units, as 7, or vii.
Repeated seven times; having seven thicknesses; increased to seven times the size or amount.
Seven times as much or as often.
q: Whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold.

senses.d: One more than sixteen; ten and seven added; as, seventeen years.

Seventeen.etym: [OE. seventene, AS. seofontȳne, i.e., seven-ten. Cf. Seventy.]

senses.d: The number greater by one than sixteen; the sum of ten and seven; seventeen units or objects.
A symbol denoting seventeen units, as 17, or xvii.
Next in order after the sixteenth; coming after sixteen others.
q: In . . . the seventeenth day of the month . . . were all the fountains of the great deep broken up.

senses.d: Constituting or being one of seventeen equal parts into which anything is divided.
The next in order after the sixteenth; one coming after sixteen others.
The quotient of a unit divided by seventeen; one of seventeen equal parts or divisions of one whole.
An interval of two octaves and a third.
Next in order after the sixth;; coming after six others.
q: On the seventh day, God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.

senses.d: Constituting or being one of seven equal parts into which anything is divided; as, the seventh part.
One next in order after the sixth; one coming after six others.
The quotient of a unit divided by seven; one of seven equal parts into which anything is divided.
An interval embracing seven diatonic degrees of the scale.
Seven times ten; one more than sixty-nine.

Seventy.etym: [AS. hund-seofontig. See Seven, and Ten, and cf. Seventeen, Sixty.]

senses.d: The sum of seven times ten; seventy units or objects.
A symbol representing seventy units, as 70, or lxx.
To separate, as one from another; to cut off from something; to divide; to part in any way, especially by violence, as by cutting, rending, etc.; as, to sever the head from the body.
q: The angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just.

senses.d: To cut or break open or apart; to divide into parts; to cut through; to disjoin; as, to sever the arm or leg.
q: Our state can not be severed; we are one.

senses.d: To keep distinct or apart; to except; to exempt.
q: I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there.

senses.d: To disunite; to disconnect; to terminate; as, to sever an estate in joint tenancy.

Sever.etym: [OF. sevrer, severer, to separate, F. sevrer to wean, fr. L. separare. See Separate, and cf. Several.]

senses.d: To suffer disjunction; to be parted, or rent asunder; to be separated; to part; to separate.
To make a separation or distinction; to distinguish.
q: The Lord shall sever between the cattle of Israel and the cattle of Egypt.
They claimed the right of severing in their challenge.

senses.d: Separate; distinct; particular; single.
q: Each several ship a victory did gain.
Each might his several province well command, Would all but stoop to what they understand.

senses.d: Diverse; different; various.
q: Habits and faculties, several, and to be distinguished.
Four several armies to the field are led.

senses.d: Consisting of a number more than two, but not very many; divers; sundry; as, several persons were present when the event took place.

Several.etym: [OF., fr. LL. separalis, fr. L. separ separate, different. See Sever, Separate.]

senses.d: By itself; severally.
q: Every kind of thing is laid up several in barns or storehoudses.

senses.d: Each particular taken singly; an item; a detail; an individual.
q: There was not time enough to hear . . . The severals.

senses.d: Persons oe objects, more than two, but not very many.
q: Several of them neither rose from any conspicuous family, nor left any behind them.

senses.d: An inclosed or separate place; inclosure.
q: They had their several for heathen nations, their several for the people of their own nation.

senses.d: Separately; distinctly; apart from others; individually.
q: There must be an auditor to check and revise each severally by itself.

senses.d: Serious in feeling or manner; sedate; grave; austere; not light, lively, or cheerful.
q: Your looks alter, as your subject does, From kind to fierce, from wanton to severe.

senses.d: Very strict in judgment, discipline, or government; harsh; not mild or indulgent; rigorous; as, severe criticism; severe punishment.
q: Come! you are too severe a moraler.
Let your zeal, if it must be expressed in anger, be always more severe against thyself than against others.

senses.d: Rigidly methodical, or adherent to rule or principle; exactly conformed to a standard; not allowing or employing unneccessary ornament, amplification, etc.; strict; — said of style, argument, etc.
q: The Latin, a most severe and compendious language.

senses.d: Sharp; afflictive; distressing; violent; extreme; as, severe pain, anguish, fortune; severe cold.
Difficult to be endured; exact; critical; rigorous; as, a severe test.

Severe.syn: Strict; grave; austere; stern; morose; rigid; exact; rigorous; hard; rough; harsh; censorious; tart; acrimonious; sarcastic; satirical; cutting; biting; keen; bitter; cruel. See Strict.
Severe.etym: [L. severus; perhaps akin to Gr. ��� awe, ��� revered, holy, solemn, Goth. swikns innocent, chaste: cf. F. sévère. Cf. Asseverate, Persevere.]

senses.d: The quality or state of being severe.
Gravity or austerity; extreme strictness; rigor; harshness; as, the severity of a reprimand or a reproof; severity of discipline or government; severity of penalties.
The quality or power of distressing or paining; extreme degree; extremity; intensity; inclemency; as, the severity of pain or anguish; the severity of cold or heat; the severity of the winter.
Harshness; cruel treatment; sharpness of punishment; as, severity practiced on prisoners of war.
Exactness; rigorousness; strictness; as, the severity of a test.

senses.d: Juice; gravy; a seasoned dish; a delicacy.

senses.d: To follow; to pursue; to sue.

senses.d: To close or stop by ssewing; — often with up; as, to sew up a rip.
To inclose by sewing; — sometimes with up; as, to sew money in a bag.

senses.d: To practice sewing; to work with needle and thread.
To drain, as a pond, for taking the fish.
To perform the duties of a sewer. See 3d Sewer.
Comparative obscurity owing to interception or interruption of the rays of light; partial darkness caused by the intervention of something between the space contemplated and the source of light.
Darkness; obscurity; — often in the plural.

senses.d: An obscure place; a spot not exposed to light; hence, a secluded retreat.
q: Let us seek out some desolate shade, and there Weep our sad bosoms empty.

senses.d: That which intercepts, or shelters from, light or the direct rays of the sun; hence, also, that which protects from heat or currents of air; a screen; protection; shelter; cover; as, a lamp shade.

Sleep under a fresh tree's shade.
Let the arched knife well sharpened now assail the spreading shades of vegetables.

senses.d: Shadow.

senses.d: The soul after its separation from the body; — so called because the ancients it to be perceptible to the sight, though not to the touch; a spirit; a ghost; as, the shades of departed heroes.

Degree or variation of color, as darker or lighter, stronger or paler; as, a delicate shade of pink.
q: White, red, yellow, blue, with their several degrees, or shades and mixtures, as green only in by the eyes.

q: New shades and combinations of thought.
Every shade of religious and political opinion has its own headquarters.

Shade.etym: [OE. shade, shadewe, schadewe, AS. sceadu, scead; akin to OS. skado, D. schaduw, OHG. scato, (gen. scatewes), G. schatten, Goth. skadus, Ir. & Gael. sgath, and probably to Gr. σκότοσ darkness. √162. Cf. Shadow, Shed a hat.]

senses.d: To obscure; to dim the brightness of.

Darkness; shade; obscurity.

An imperfect and faint representation; adumbration; indistinct image; dim bodying forth; hence, mystical representation; type.

and shadows of that destined seed.

senses.d: To protect; to shelter from danger; to shroud.

Abounding in shade or shades; overspread with shade; causing shade.

And Amaryllis fills the shady groves.

A column, an obelisk, or other spire-shaped or columnar monument.

'Tis our fast intent To shake all cares and business from our age.

Our salutations were very hearty on both sides, consisting of many kind shakes of the hand.

A fissure in rock or earth.
A rapid alternation of a principal tone with another represented on the next degree of the staff above or below it; a trill.
One of the staves of a hogshead or barrel taken apart.
A shook of staves and headings.
The redshank; — so called from the nodding of its head while on the ground.

Cracked or checked; split. See Shake, n., 2.
q: Nor is the wood shaken or twisted.

As an auxiliary, shall indicates a duty or necessity whose obligation is derived from the person speaking; as, you shall go; he shall go; that is, I order or promise your going. It thus ordinarily expresses, in the second and third persons, a command, a threat, or a promise. If the auxillary be emphasized, the command is made more imperative, the promise or that more positive and sure. It is also employed in the language of prophecy; as, “the day shall come when . . . , ” since a promise or threat and an authoritative prophecy nearly coincide in significance. In shall with the first person, the necessity of the action is sometimes implied as residing elsewhere than in the speaker; as, I shall suffer; we shall see; and there is always a less distinct and positive assertion of his volition than is indicated by will. “I shall go” implies nearly a simple futurity; more exactly, a foretelling or an expectation of my going, in which, naturally enough, a certain degree of plan or intention may be included; emphasize the shall, and the event is described as certain to occur, and the expression approximates in meaning to our emphatic “I will go.” In a question, the relation of speaker and source of obligation is of course transferred to the person addressed; as, “Shall you go?” (answer, “I shall go”); “Shall he go?” i.e., “Do you require or promise his going?” (answer, “He shall go”.) The same relation is transferred to either second or third person in such phrases as “You say, or think, you shall go;” “He says, or thinks, he shall go.” After a conditional conjunction (as if, whether) shall is used in all persons to express futurity simply; as, if I, you, or he shall say they are right. Should is everywhere used in the same connection and the same senses as shall, as its imperfect. It also expresses duty or moral obligation; as, he should do it whether he will or not. In the early English, and hence in our English Bible, shall is the auxiliary mainly used, in all the persons, to express simple futurity. (Cf. Will, v. t.) Shall may be used elliptically; thus, with an adverb or other word expressive of motion go may be omitted.

senses.d: That which deceives expectation; any trick, fraud, or device that deludes and disappoints; a make-believe; delusion; imposture; humbug.
q: Believe who will the solemn sham, not I.

senses.d: A false front, or removable ornamental covering.

senses.d: False; counterfeit; pretended; feigned; unreal; as, a sham fight.
q: They scorned the sham independence proffered to them by the Athenians.

senses.d: To trick; to cheat; to deceive or delude with false pretenses.
q: Fooled and shammed into a conviction.

senses.d: To obtrude by fraud or imposition.
q: We must have a care that we do not . . . sham fallacies upon the world for current reason.

senses.d: To assume the manner and character of; to imitate; to ape; to feign.
To make false pretenses; to deceive; to feign; to impose.
q: Wondering . . . whether those who lectured him were such fools as they professed to be, or were only shamming.

senses.d: A saxicoline singing bird (Kittacincla macroura) of India, noted for the sweetness and power of its song. One of a succession of niches or platforms, one above another, to hold ore which is thrown successively from platform to platform, and thus raised to a higher level.
A place where butcher's meat is sold.
q: As summer flies are in the shambles.

senses.d: A place for slaughtering animals for meat.
q: To make a shambles of the parliament house.

Shamble.etym: [OE. schamel a bench, stool, AS. scamel, sceamol, a bench, form, stool, fr. L. scamellum, dim. of scamnum a bench, stool.]

senses.d: To walk awkwardly and unsteadily, as if the knees were weak; to shuffle along.

Shamble.etym: [Cf. OD. schampelen to slip, schampen to slip away, escape. Cf. Scamble, Scamper.]

senses.d: A painful sensation excited by a consciousness of guilt or impropriety, or of having done something which injures reputation, or of the exposure of that which nature or modesty prompts us to conceal.
q: HIde, for shame, Romans, your grandsires' images, That blush at their degenerate progeny.
Have you no modesty, no maiden shame?

senses.d: Reproach incurred or suffered; dishonor; ignominy; derision; contempt.
q: Ye have borne the shame of the heathen.
Honor and shame from no condition rise.
And every woe a tear can claim Except an erring sister's shame.

senses.d: The cause or reason of shame; that which brings reproach, and degrades a person in the estimation of others; disgrace.
q: O C�sar, what a wounding shame is this!
Guides who are the shame of religion.

senses.d: The parts which modesty requires to be covered; the private parts.

Shame.etym: [OE. shame, schame, AS. scamu, sceamu; akin to OS. & OHG. scama, G. scham, Icel. skömm, shkamm, Sw. & Dan. skam, D. & G. schande, Goth. skanda shame, skaman sik to be ashamed; perhaps from a root skam meaning to cover, and akin to the root (kam) of G. hemd shirt, E. chemise. Cf. Sham.]

senses.d: To make ashamed; to excite in (a person) a comsciousness of guilt or impropriety, or of conduct derogatory to reputation; to put to shame.
q: Were there but one righteous in the world, he would . . . shame the world, and not the world him.

senses.d: To cover with reproach or ignominy; to dishonor; to disgrace.
q: And with foul cowardice his carcass shame.

senses.d: To mock at; to deride.
q: Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor.

senses.d: To be ashamed; to feel shame.
q: I do shame To think of what a noble strain you are.

senses.d: Easily confused or put out of countenance; diffident; bashful; modest.
q: Your shamefaced virtue shunned the people's prise.

Shamefaced.etym: [For shamefast; AS. scamfæst. See Shame, n., and Fast firm.]

senses.d: Bringing shame or disgrace; injurious to reputation; disgraceful.
q: His naval preparations were not more surprising than his quick and shameful retreat.

senses.d: Exciting the feeling of shame in others; indecent; as, a shameful picture; a shameful sight.

Shameful.syn: Disgraceful; reproachful; indecent; unbecoming; degrading; scandalous; ignominious; infamous.

senses.d: Destitute of shame; wanting modesty; brazen-faced; insensible to disgrace.
q: Shame enough to shame thee, wert thou not shameless.

senses.d: Indicating want of modesty, or sensibility to disgrace; indecent; as, a shameless picture or poem.

Shameless.syn: Impudent; unblushing; audacious; immodest; indecent; indelicate.

senses.d: One who, or that which, disgraces, or makes ashamed.
To form or create; especially, to mold or make into a particular form; to give proper form or figure to.
q: I was shapen in iniquity.
Grace shaped her limbs, and beauty decked her face.

senses.d: To adapt to a purpose; to regulate; to adjust; to direct; as, to shape the course of a vessel.
q: To the stream, when neither friends, nor force, Nor speed nor art avail, he shapes his course.
Charmed by their eyes, their manners I acquire, And shape my foolishness to their desire.

senses.d: To image; to conceive; to body forth.
q: Oft my jealousy Shapes faults that are not.

senses.d: To design; to prepare; to plan; to arrange.
q: When shapen was all this conspiracy, From point to point.
I will early shape me therefor.
