Shape.etym: [OE. shapen, schapen, AS. sceapian. The p. p. shapen is from the strong verb, AS. scieppan, scyppan, sceppan, p. p. sceapen. See Shape, n.]

senses.d: To suit; to be adjusted or conformable.
Character or construction of a thing as determining its external appearance; outward aspect; make; figure; form; guise; as, the shape of a tree; the shape of the head; an elegant shape.
q: He beat me grievously, in the shape of a woman.

senses.d: That which has form or figure; a figure; an appearance; a being.
q: Before the gates three sat, On either side, a formidable shape.

senses.d: A model; a pattern; a mold.
Form of embodiment, as in words; form, as of thought or conception; concrete embodiment or example, as of some quality.
Dress for disguise; guise.
q: Look better on this virgin, and consider This Persian shape laid by, and she appearing In a Greekish dress.

senses.d: A rolled or hammered piece, as a bar, beam, angle iron, etc., having a cross section different from merchant bar.

Shape.etym: [OE. shap, schap, AS. sceap in gesceap creation, creature, fr. the root of scieppan, scyppan, sceppan, to shape, to do, to effect; akin to OS. giskeppian, OFries. skeppa, D. scheppen, G. schaffen, OHG. scaffan, scepfen, skeffen, Icer. skapa, skepja, Dan. skabe, skaffe, Sw. skapa, skaffa, Goth. gaska

senses.d: The part (usually an iron or steel plate) of a plow which cuts the ground at the bottom of a furrow; a plowshare.
The part which opens the ground for the reception of the seed, in a machine for sowing seed.

Share.etym: [OE. schar, AS. scear; akin to OHG. scaro, G. schar, pflugshar, and E. shear, v. See Shear.]

senses.d: A certain quantity; a portion; a part; a division; as, a small share of prudence.
Especially, the part allotted or belonging to one, of any property or interest owned by a number; a portion among others; an apportioned lot; an allotment; a dividend.
Hence, one of a certain number of equal portions into which any property or invested capital is divided; as, a ship owned in ten shares.
The pubes; the sharebone.

Share.etym: [OE. share, AS. scearu, scaru, fr. sceran to shear, cut. See Shear, v.]

senses.d: To part among two or more; to distribute in portions; to divide.
q: Suppose I share my fortune equally between my children and a stranger.

senses.d: To partake of, use, or experience, with others; to have a portion of; to take and possess in common; as, to share a shelter with another.
q: While avarice and rapine share the land.

senses.d: To cut; to shear; to cleave; to divide.
q: The shared visage hangs on equal sides.

senses.d: To have part; to receive a portion; to partake, enjoy, or suffer with others.
q: A right of inheritance gave every one a title to share in the goods of his father.

senses.d: Having a very thin edge or fine point; of a nature to cut or pierce easily; not blunt or dull; keen.
q: He dies upon my scimeter's sharp point.

senses.d: Terminating in a point or edge; not obtuse or rounded; somewhat pointed or edged; peaked or ridged; as, a sharp hill; sharp features.

Affecting the sense as if pointed or cutting, keen, penetrating, acute: to the taste or smell, pungent, acid, sour, as ammonia has a sharp taste and odor; to the hearing, piercing, shrill, as a sharp sound or voice; to the eye, instantaneously brilliant, dazzling, as a sharp flash.
High in pitch; acute; as, a sharp note or tone.
Very trying to the feelings; piercing; keen; severe; painful; distressing; as, sharp pain, weather; a sharp and frosty air.
q: Sharp misery had worn him to the bones.
The morning sharp and clear.
In sharpest perils faithful proved.

senses.d: Cutting in language or import; biting; sarcastic; cruel; harsh; rigorous; severe; as, a sharp rebuke.
q: To that place the sharp Athenian law Can not pursue us.
Be thy words severe, Sharp as merits but the sword forbear.

senses.d: Of keen perception; quick to discern or distinguish; having nice discrimination; acute; penetrating; sagacious; clever; as, a sharp eye; sharp sight, hearing, or judgment.
q: Nothing makes men sharper . . . than want.
Many other things belong to the material world, wherein the sharpest philosophers have never ye� arrived at clear and distinct ideas.

senses.d: Eager in pursuit; keen in quest; impatient for gratification; keen; as, a sharp appetite.
Fierce; ardent; fiery; violent; impetuous.
q: A sharp assault already is begun.

senses.d: Keenly or unduly attentive to one's own interest; close and exact in dealing; shrewd; as, a sharp dealer; a sharp customer.
q: The necessity of being so sharp and exacting.

senses.d: Composed of hard, angular grains; gritty; as, sharp sand.
Steep; precipitous; abrupt; as, a sharp ascent or descent; a sharp turn or curve.

Sharp.syn: Keen; acute; piercing; penetrating; quick; sagacious; discerning; shrewd; witty; ingenious; sour; acid; tart; pungent; acrid; severe; poignant; biting; acrimonious; sarcastic; cutting; bitter; painful; afflictive; violent; harsh; fierce; ardent; fiery.
Sharp.etym: [OE. sharp, scharp, scarp, AS. scearp; akin to OS. skarp, LG. scharp, D. scherp, G. scharf, Dan. & Sw. skarp, Icel. skarpr. Cf. Escarp, Scrape, Scorpion.]

senses.d: To a point or edge; piercingly; eagerly; sharply.
q: The head full sharp yground.
You bite so sharp at reasons.

senses.d: Precisely; exactly; as, we shall start at ten o'clock sharp.
A sharp tool or weapon.
q: If butchers had but the manners to go to sharps, gentlemen would be contented with a rubber at cuffs.

senses.d: The character used to indicate that the note before which it is placed is to be raised a half step, or semitone, in pitch.
A portion of a stream where the water runs very rapidly.
A sewing needle having a very slender point; a needle of the most pointed of the three grades, blunts, betweens, and sharps.
Same as Middlings, 1.
An expert.
To sharpen.
To raise above the proper pitch; to elevate the tone of; especially, to raise a half step, or semitone, above the natural tone.
To play tricks in bargaining; to act the sharper.
To sing above the proper pitch.
To make sharp.
To give a keen edge or fine point to; to make sharper; as, to sharpen an ax, or the teeth of a saw.
To render more quick or acute in perception; to make more ready or ingenious.
q: The air . . . sharpened his visual ray To objects distant far.
He that wrestles with us strengthens our nerves and sharpens our skill.

senses.d: To make more eager; as, to sharpen men's desires.
q: Epicurean cooks Sharpen with cloyless sauce his appetite.

senses.d: To make more pungent and intense; as, to sharpen a pain or disease.
To make biting, sarcastic, or severe.
To render more shrill or piercing.
q: Inclosures not only preserve sound, but increase and sharpen it.

senses.d: To make more tart or acid; to make sour; as, the rays of the sun sharpen vinegar.
To raise, as a sound, by means of a sharp; to apply a sharp to.
To grow or become sharp.
A person who bargains closely, especially, one who cheats in bargains; a swinder; also, a cheating gamester.
q: Sharpers, as pikes, prey upon their own kind.

Sharper.syn: Swindler; cheat; deceiver; trickster; rogue. See Swindler.

senses.d: In a sharp manner,; keenly; acutely.
q: They are more sharply to be chastised and reformed than the rude Irish.
The soldiers were sharply assailed with wants.
You contract your eye when you would see sharply.

senses.d: The quality or condition of being sharp; keenness; acuteness.
To cut or pare off from the surface of a body with a razor or other edged instrument; to cut off closely, as with a razor; as, to shave the beard.

To make bare or smooth by cutting off closely the surface, or surface covering, of; especially, to remove the hair from with a razor or other sharp instrument; to take off the beard or hair of; as, to shave the face or the crown of the head; he shaved himself.
q: I'll shave your crown for this.
The laborer with the bending scythe is seen Shaving the surface of the waving green.

senses.d: To cut off thin slices from; to cut in thin slices.
q: Plants bruised or shaven in leaf or root.

senses.d: To skim along or near the surface of; to pass close to, or touch lightly, in passing.
q: Now shaves with level wing the deep.

senses.d: To strip; to plunder; to fleece.

Shave.etym: [OE. shaven, schaven, AS. scafan, sceafan; akin to D. schaven, G. schaben, Icel. skafa, Sw. skafva, Dan. skave, Goth. scaban, Russ. kopate to dig, Gr. ����, and probably to L. scabere to scratch, to scrape. Cf. Scab, Shaft, Shape.]

senses.d: To use a razor for removing the beard; to cut closely; hence, to be hard and severe in a bargain; to practice extortion; to cheat.
A thin slice; a shaving.
A cutting of the beard; the operation of shaving.
An exorbitant discount on a note.
A hand tool consisting of a sharp blade with a handle at each end; a drawing knife; a spokeshave.
The act of passing very near to, so as almost to graze; as, the bullet missed by a close shave.

Shave.etym: [AS. scafa, sceafa, a sort of knife. See Shave, v. t.]

senses.d: This or that female; the woman understood or referred to; the animal of the female sex, or object personified as feminine, which was spoken of.
q: She loved her children best in every wise.
Then Sarah denied, . . . for she was afraid.

senses.d: A woman; a female; — used substantively.
q: Lady, you are the cruelest she alive.

She.etym: [OE. she, sche, scheo, scho, AS. seó, fem. of the definite article, originally a demonstrative pronoun; cf. OS. siu, D. zij, G. sie, OHG. siu, sī, si, Icel. sū, sjā, Goth. si she, sō, fem. article, Russ. siia, fem., this, Gr. �, fem. article, Skr. sā, syā. The possessive her or hers, and the objecti

senses.d: A sheave.
A quantity of the stalks and ears of wheat, rye, or other grain, bound together; a bundle of grain or straw.
q: The reaper fills his greedy hands, And binds the golden sheaves in brittle bands.

senses.d: Any collection of things bound together; a bundle; specifically, a bundle of arrows sufficient to fill a quiver, or the allowance of each archer, — usually twenty-four.
q: The sheaf of arrows shook and rattled in the case.

Sheaf.etym: [OE. sheef, shef, schef, AS. sceáf; akin to D. schoof, OHG. scoub, G. schaub, Icel. skauf a fox's brush, and E. shove. See Shove.]

senses.d: To gather and bind into a sheaf; to make into sheaves; as, to sheaf wheat.
To collect and bind cut grain, or the like; to make sheaves.
q: They that reap must sheaf and bind.

senses.d: Same as Sheeling.
To put under a sheal or shelter.
To take the husks or pods off from; to shell; to empty of its contents, as a husk or a pod.
q: That's a shealed peascod.

senses.d: A shell or pod.
To cut, clip, or sever anything from with shears or a like instrument; as, to shear sheep; to shear cloth.
To separate or sever with shears or a similar instrument; to cut off; to clip (something) from a surface; as, to shear a fleece.
q: Before the golden tresses . . . were shorn away.

senses.d: To reap, as grain.
Fig.: To deprive of property; to fleece.
To produce a change of shape in by a shear. See Shear, n., 4.

Shear.etym: [OE. sheren, scheren, to shear, cut, shave, AS. sceran, scieran, scyran; akin to D. & G. scheren, Icel. skera, Dan. ski�re, Gr. ���. Cf. Jeer, Score, Shard, Share, Sheer to turn aside.]

senses.d: A pair of shears; — now always used in the plural, but formerly also in the singular. See Shears.
q: On his head came razor none, nor shear.
Short of the wool, and naked from the shear.

senses.d: A shearing; — used in designating the age of sheep.
q: After the second shearing, he is a two-shear ram; . . . at the expiration of another year, he is a three-shear ram; the name always taking its date from the time of shearing.

senses.d: An action, resulting from applied forces, which tends to cause two contiguous parts of a body to slide relatively to each other in a direction parallel to their plane of contact; — also called shearing stress, and tangential stress.
A strain, or change of shape, of an elastic body, consisting of an extension in one direction, an equal compression in a perpendicular direction, with an unchanged magnitude in the third direction.
To deviate. See Sheer.
To become more or less completely divided, as a body under the action of forces, by the sliding of two contiguous parts relatively to each other in a direction parallel to their plane of contact.
One who shears.
q: Like a lamb dumb before his shearer.

senses.d: A reaper.
The act or operation of clipping with shears or a shearing machine, as the wool from sheep, or the nap from cloth.
The product of the act or operation of clipping with shears or a shearing machine; as, the whole shearing of a flock; the shearings from cloth.
Same as Shearling.
The act or operation of reaping.
The act or operation of dividing with shears; as, the shearing of metal plates.
The process of preparing shear steel; tilting.
The process of making a vertical side cutting in working into a face of coal.
A case for the reception of a sword, hunting knife, or other long and slender instrument; a scabbard.
q: The dead knight's sword out of his sheath he drew.

senses.d: Any sheathlike covering, organ, or part.

Sheath.etym: [OE. schethe, AS. scǣð, sceáð, scēð; akin to OS. skēðia, D. scheede, G. scheide, OHG. sceida, Sw. skida, Dan. skede, Icel. skeiðir, pl., and to E. shed, v.t., originally meaning, to separate, to part. See Shed.]

senses.d: A wheel having a groove in the rim for a rope to work in, and set in a block, mast, or the like; the wheel of a pulley.

Sheave.etym: [Akin to OD. schijve orb, disk, wheel, D. schiff, G. scheibe, Icel. skīfa a shaving, slice; cf. Gr. ��� a staff. Cf. Shift, v., Shive.]

senses.d: To gather and bind into a sheaf or sheaves; hence, to collect.
A slight or temporary structure built to shade or shelter something; a structure usually open in front; an outbuilding; a hut; as, a wagon shed; a wood shed.
q: The first Aletes born in lowly shed.
Sheds of reeds which summer's heat repel.

Shed.etym: [The same word as shade. See Shade.]

senses.d: To separate; to divide.

To part with; to throw off or give forth from one's self; to emit; to diffuse; to cause to emanate or flow; to pour forth or out; to spill; as, the sun sheds light; she shed tears; the clouds shed rain.
q: Did Romeo's hand shed Tybalt's blood?
Twice seven consenting years have shed Their utmost bounty on thy head.

senses.d: To let fall; to throw off, as a natural covering of hair, feathers, shell; to cast; as, fowls shed their feathers; serpents shed their skins; trees shed leaves.
To cause to flow off without penetrating; as, a tight roof, or covering of oiled cloth, sheeds water.
To sprinkle; to intersperse; to cover.
To divide, as the warp threads, so as to form a shed, or passageway, for the shuttle.

Shed.etym: [OE. scheden, sch�den, to pour, to part, AS. scādan, sceádan, to pert, to separate; akin to OS. sk��an, OFries. sk�tha, G. scheiden, OHG. sceidan, Goth. skaidan, and probably to Lith. skëdu I part, separate, L. scindere to cleave, to split, Gr. ���, Skr. chid, and perch. also to L. caedere to cut. √

senses.d: To fall in drops; to pour.
q: Such a rain down from the welkin shadde.

senses.d: To let fall the parts, as seeds or fruit; to throw off a covering or envelope.
q: White oats are apt to shed most as they lie, and black as they stand.

senses.d: A parting; a separation; a division.
q: They say also that the manner of making the shed of newwedded wives' hair with the iron head of a javelin came up then likewise.

senses.d: The act of shedding or spilling; — used only in composition, as in bloodshed.
That which parts, divides, or sheds; — used in composition, as in watershed.
The passageway between the threads of the warp through which the shuttle is thrown, having a sloping top and bottom made by raising and lowering the alternate threads.
A covered structure for housing aircraft; a hangar.
One who, or that which, sheds; as, a shedder of blood; a shedder of tears.
A crab in the act of casting its shell, or immediately afterwards while still soft; — applied especially to the edible crabs, which are most prized while in this state.
The act of shedding, separating, or casting off or out; as, the shedding of blood.
That which is shed, or cast off.
Any one of several species of ruminants of the genus Ovis, native of the higher mountains of both hemispheres, but most numerous in Asia.
A weak, bashful, silly fellow.
Fig.: The people of God, as being under the government and protection of Christ, the great Shepherd.

Sheep.etym: [OE. shep, scheep, AS. sc�p, sceáp; akin to OFries. sk�p, LG. & D. schaap, G. schaf, OHG. scāf, Skr. chāga. √295. Cf. Sheepherd.]

senses.d: A small inclosure for sheep; a pen; a fold.
A fold or pen for sheep; a place where sheep are collected or confined.
A keeper or feeder of sheep; also, an owner of sheep.
The skin of a sheep; or, leather prepared from it.
A diploma; — so called because usually written or printed on parchment prepared from the skin of the sheep.
In general, a large, broad piece of anything thin, as paper, cloth, etc.; a broad, thin portion of any substance; an expanded superficies.
A broad piece of cloth, usually linen or cotton, used for wrapping the body or for a covering; especially, one used as an article of bedding next to the body.
q: He fell into a trance, and saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners.
If I do die before thee, prithee, shroud me In one of those same sheets.

senses.d: A broad piece of paper, whether folded or unfolded, whether blank or written or printed upon; hence, a letter; a newspaper, etc.
A single signature of a book or a pamphlet;
the book itself.
q: To this the following sheets are intended for a full and distinct answer.

senses.d: A broad, thinly expanded portion of metal or other substance; as, a sheet of copper, of glass, or the like; a plate; a leaf.
A broad expanse of water, or the like.
A sail.
An extensive bed of an eruptive rock intruded between, or overlying, other strata.
A rope or chain which regulates the angle of adjustment of a sail in relation in relation to the wind; — usually attached to the lower corner of a sail, or to a yard or a boom.

Sheet.etym: [OE. shete, schete, AS. scēte, scȳte, fr. sceát a projecting corner, a fold in a garment (akin to D. schoot sheet, bosom, lap, G. schoss bosom, lap, flap of a coat, Icel. skaut, Goth. skauts the hem of a garment); originally, that which shoots out, from the root of AS. sceótan to shoot. √159. See Sh

senses.d: To furnish with a sheet or sheets; to wrap in, or cover with, a sheet, or as with a sheet.
To expand, as a sheet.
q: The star shot flew from the welkin blue, As it fell from the sheeted sky.

senses.d: An ancient weight and coin used by the Jews and by other nations of the same stock.
A jocose term for money.
That which covers or defends from injury or annoyance; a protection; a screen.
q: The sick and weak the healing plant shall aid, From storms a shelter, and from heat a shade.

senses.d: One who protects; a guardian; a defender.
q: Thou hast been a shelter for me.

senses.d: The state of being covered and protected; protection; security.
q: Who into shelter takes their tender bloom.

Shelter.syn: Asylum; refuge; retreat; covert; sanctuary; protection; defense; security.
Shelter.etym: [Cf. OE. scheltrun, shiltroun, schelltrome, scheldtrome, a guard, squadron, AS. scildtruma a troop of men with shields; scild shield + truma a band of men. See Shield, n.]

senses.d: To be a shelter for; to provide with a shelter; to cover from injury or annoyance; to shield; to protect.
q: Those ruins sheltered once his sacred head.
You have no convents . . . in which such persons may be received and sheltered.

senses.d: To screen or cover from notice; to disguise.
q: In vain I strove to cheek my growing flame, Or shelter passion under friendship's name.

senses.d: To betake to cover, or to a safe place; — used reflexively.
q: They sheltered themselves under a rock.

senses.d: To take shelter.
q: There oft the Indian herdsman, shunning heat, Shelters in cool.

senses.d: A descendant of Shem.
A man employed in tending, feeding, and guarding sheep, esp. a flock grazing at large.
The pastor of a church; one with the religious guidance of others.

Shepherd.etym: [OE. schepherde, schephirde, AS. sceáphyrde; sceáp sheep + hyrde, hirde, heorde, a herd, a guardian. See Sheep, and Herd.]

senses.d: To tend as a shepherd; to guard, herd, lead, or drive, as a shepherd.
q: White, fleecy clouds . . .
Shepherded by the slow, unwilling wind.

senses.d: A fragment; — now used only in composition, as in potsherd. See Shard.
q: The thigh . . . which all in sherds it drove.

senses.d: The chief officer of a shire or county, to whom is intrusted the execution of the laws, the serving of judicial writs and processes, and the preservation of the peace.

Sheriff.etym: [OE. shereve, AS. scīr-ger�fa; scīr a shire + ger�fa a reeve. See Shire, and Reeve, and cf. Shrievalty.]

senses.d: The part of a plow which projects downward beneath the beam, for holding the share and other working parts; — also called standard, or post.
Show.
A word which was made the criterion by which to distinguish the Ephraimites from the Gileadites. The Ephraimites, not being able to pronounce sh, called the word sibboleth. See Judges xii.
q: Without reprieve, adjudged to death, For want of well pronouncing shibboleth.

senses.d: Also in an extended sense.
q: The th, with its twofold value, is . . . the shibboleth of foreigners.

senses.d: Hence, the criterion, test, or watchword of a party; a party cry or pet phrase.

Shibboleth.etym: [Heb. shibbōleth an ear of corn, or a stream, a flood.]

senses.d: A broad piece of defensive armor, carried on the arm, — formerly in general use in war, for the protection of the body. See Buckler.
q: Now put your shields before your hearts and fight, With hearts more proof than shields.

senses.d: Anything which protects or defends; defense; shelter; protection.
Figuratively, one who protects or defends.
q: Fear not, Abram; I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.

senses.d: In lichens, a Hardened cup or disk surrounded by a rim and containing the fructification, or asci.
The escutcheon or field on which are placed the bearings in coats of arms. Cf. Lozenge. See Illust. of Escutcheon.
A framework used to protect workmen in making an adit under ground, and capable of being pushed along as excavation progresses.
A spot resembling, or having the form of, a shield.
A coin, the old French crown, or écu, having on one side the figure of a shield.

Shield.etym: [OE. sheld, scheld, AS. scield, scild, sceld, scyld; akin to OS. scild, OFries. skeld, D. & G. schild, OHG. scilt, Icel. skjöldr, Sw. sköld, Dan. skiold, Goth. skildus; of uncertain origin. Cf. Sheldrake.]

senses.d: To cover with, or as with, a shield; to cover from danger; to defend; to protect from assault or injury.
q: Shouts of applause ran ringing through the field, To see the son the vanquished father shield.
A woman's shape doth shield thee.

senses.d: To ward off; to keep off or out.
q: They brought with them their usual weeds, fit to shield the cold to which they had been inured.

senses.d: To avert, as a misfortune; hence, as a supplicatory exclamation, forbid!
q: God shield that it should so befall.
God shield I should disturb devotion!

senses.d: A word used by Jacob on his deathbed, and interpreted variously, as “the Messiah,” or as the city “Shiloh,” or as “Rest.”

Shiloh.etym: [Heb. shīlōh, literally, quiet, rest, fr. shālāh to rest.]

senses.d: The front part of the leg below the knee; the front edge of the shin bone; the lower part of the leg; the shank.
A fish plate for rails.

Shin.etym: [OE. shine, schine, AS. scina; akin to D. scheen, OHG. scina, G. schiene, schienbein, Dan. skinnebeen, Sw. skenben. Cf. Chine.]

senses.d: To climb a mast, tree, rope, or the like, by embracing it alternately with the arms and legs, without help of steps, spurs, or the like; — used with up; as, to shin up a mast.
To run about borrowing money hastily and temporarily, as for the payment of one's notes at the bank.
To climb (a pole, etc.) by shinning up.
To emit rays of light; to give light; to beam with steady radiance; to exhibit brightness or splendor; as, the sun shines by day; the moon shines by night.
q: Hyperion's quickening fire doth shine.
God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Cghrist.
Let thine eyes shine forth in their full luster.

senses.d: To be bright by reflection of light; to gleam; to be glossy; as, to shine like polished silver.
To be effulgent in splendor or beauty.
q: Once brightest shined this child of heat and air.

senses.d: To be eminent, conspicuous, or distinguished; to exhibit brilliant intellectual powers; as, to shine in courts; to shine in conversation.
q: Few are qualified to shine in company; but it in most men's power to be agreeable.

Shine.etym: [OE. shinen, schinen, AS. scīnan; akin to D. schijnen, OFries. skīna, OS. & OHG. scīnan, G. scheinen, Icel. skīna, Sw. skina, Dan. skinne, Goth. skeinan, and perh. to Gr. ��� shadow. √157. Cf. Sheer pure, and Shimmer.]

senses.d: To cause to shine, as a light.
q: He doth not rain wealth, nor shine honor and virtues, upon men equally.

senses.d: To make bright; to cause to shine by reflected light; as, in hunting, to shine the eyes of a deer at night by throwing a light on them.
The quality or state of shining; brightness; luster, gloss; polish; sheen.
q: Now sits not girt with taper's holy shine.
Fair opening to some court's propitious shine.
The distant shine of the celestial city.

senses.d: Sunshine; fair weather.
q: Be it fair or foul, or rain or shine.

senses.d: A liking for a person; a fancy.
Caper; antic; row.
Shining; sheen.
Emitting light, esp. in a continuous manner; radiant; as, shining lamps; also, bright by the reflection of light; as, shining armor.
Splendid; illustrious; brilliant; distinguished; conspicious; as, a shining example of charity.
Having the surface smooth and polished; — said of leaves, the surfaces of shells, etc.
q: True paradise . . . inclosed with shining rock.
Some in a brilliant buckle bind her waist, Some round her neck a circling light display.
His sparkling blade about his head he blest.

Shining.syn: Glistening; bright; radiant; resplendent; effulgent; lustrous; brilliant; glittering; splendid; illustrious.

senses.d: Emission or reflection of light.
Pay; reward.
q: In withholding or abridging of the ship or the hire or the wages of servants.

senses.d: Any large seagoing vessel.
q: Like a stately ship . . . With all her bravery on, and tackle trim, Sails filled, and streamers waving.
Thou, too, sail on, O Ship of State!

senses.d: Specifically, a vessel furnished with a bowsprit and three masts (a mainmast, a foremast, and a mizzenmast), each of which is composed of a lower mast, a topmast, and a topgallant mast, and square-rigged on all masts. See Illustation in Appendix.
A dish or utensil (originally fashioned like the hull of a ship) used to hold incense.

Ship.etym: [OE. ship, schip, AS. scip; akin to OFries. skip, OS. scip, D. schip, G. schiff, OHG. scif, Dan. skib, Sw. skeep, Icel. & Goth. skip; of unknown origin. Cf. Equip, Skiff, Skipper.]

senses.d: To put on board of a ship, or vessel of any kind, for transportation; to send by water.
q: The timber was . . . shipped in the bay of Attalia, from whence it was by sea transported to Pelusium.

senses.d: By extension, in commercial usage, to commit to any conveyance for transportation to a distance; as, to ship freight by railroad.
Hence, to send away; to get rid of.
To engage or secure for service on board of a ship; as, to ship seamen.
To receive on board ship; as, to ship a sea.
To put in its place; as, to ship the tiller or rudder.
To engage to serve on board of a vessel; as, to ship on a man-of-war.
To embark on a ship.
The captain, master, or commander of a ship.
Relating to ships, their ownership, transfer, or employment; as, shiping concerns.
Relating to, or concerned in, the forwarding of goods; as, a shipping clerk.
The act of one who, or of that which, ships; as, the shipping of flour to Liverpool.
The collective body of ships in one place, or belonging to one port, country, etc.; vessels, generally; tonnage.
Navigation.
The breaking in pieces, or shattering, of a ship or other vessel by being cast ashore or driven against rocks, shoals, etc., by the violence of the winds and waves.
A ship wrecked or destroyed upon the water, or the parts of such a ship; wreckage.
Fig.: Destruction; ruin; irretrievable loss.
q: Holding faith and a good conscience, which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck.
It was upon an Indian bill that the late ministry had made shipwreck.

senses.d: To destroy, as a ship at sea, by running ashore or on rocks or sandbanks, or by the force of wind and waves in a tempest.
q: Shipwrecking storms and direful thunders break.

senses.d: To cause to experience shipwreck, as sailors or passengers. Hence, to cause to suffer some disaster or loss; to destroy or ruin, as if by shipwreck; to wreck; as, to shipwreck a business.

A tree that furnished the precious wood of which the ark, tables, altars, boards, etc., of the Jewish tabernacle were made; — now believed to have been the wood of the Acacia Seyal, which is hard, fine grained, and yellowish brown in color.
The wood of the shittah tree.
One of the small pieces, or splinters, into which a brittle thing is broken by sudden violence; — generally used in the plural.
A thin slice; a shive.
q: Of your soft bread, not but a shiver.

senses.d: A variety of blue slate.
A sheave or small wheel in a pulley.
A small wedge, as for fastening the bolt of a window shutter.
A spindle.

Shiver.etym: [OE. schivere, fr. shive; cf. G. schifer a splinter, slate, OHG. scivere a splinter, Dan. & Sw. skifer a slate. See Shive, and cf. Skever.]

senses.d: To break into many small pieces, or splinters; to shatter; to dash to pieces by a blow; as, to shiver a glass goblet.
q: All the ground With shivered armor strown.

Shiver.etym: [OE. schiveren, scheveren; cf. OD. scheveren. See Shiver a fragment.]

senses.d: To separate suddenly into many small pieces or parts; to be shattered.
q: There shiver shafts upon shields thick.
The natural world, should gravity once cease, . . . would instantly shiver into millions of atoms.

senses.d: To tremble; to vibrate; to quiver; to shake, as from cold or fear.
q: Prometheus is laid On icy Caucasus to shiver.
The man that shivered on the brink of sin, Thus steeled and hardened, ventures boldly in.

Shiver.etym: [OE. chiveren, cheveren; of uncertain origin. This word seems to have been confused with shiver to shatter.]

senses.d: To cause to shake or tremble, as a sail, by steering close to the wind.
The act of shivering or trembling.
A pile or assemblage of sheaves of grain, as wheat, rye, or the like, set up in a field, the sheaves varying in number from twelve to sixteen; a stook.
q: And cause it on shocks to be by and by set.
Behind the master walks, builds up the shocks.

senses.d: A lot consisting of sixty pieces; — a term applied in some Baltic ports to loose goods.

Shock.etym: [OE. schokke; cf. OD schocke, G. schock a heap, quantity, threescore, MHG. schoc, Sw. skok, and also G. hocke a heap of hay, Lith. kugis.]

senses.d: To collect, or make up, into a shock or shocks; to stook; as, to shock rye.
To be occupied with making shocks.
q: Reap well, scatter not, gather clean that is shorn, Bind fast, shock apace.

senses.d: A quivering or shaking which is the effect of a blow, collision, or violent impulse; a blow, impact, or collision; a concussion; a sudden violent impulse or onset.
q: These strong, unshaken mounds resist the shocks Of tides and seas tempestuous.
He stood the shock of a whole host of foes.

senses.d: A sudden agitation of the mind or feelings; a sensation of pleasure or pain caused by something unexpected or overpowering; also, a sudden agitating or overpowering event.

A sudden depression of the vital forces of the entire body, or of a port of it, marking some profound impression produced upon the nervous system, as by severe injury, overpowering emotion, or the like.
The sudden convulsion or contraction of the muscles, with the feeling of a concussion, caused by the discharge, through the animal system, of electricity from a charged body.

Shock.etym: [Cf. D. schok a bounce, jolt, or leap, OHG. scoc a swing, MHG. schoc, Icel. skykkjun tremuously, F. choc a shock, collision, a dashing or striking against, Sp. choque, It. ciocco a log. √161. Cf. Shock to shake.]

senses.d: To give a shock to; to cause to shake or waver; hence, to strike against suddenly; to encounter with violence.
q: Come the three corners of the world in arms, And we shall shock them.
I shall never forget the force with which he shocked De Vipont.

senses.d: To strike with surprise, terror, horror, or disgust; to cause to recoil; as, his violence shocked his associates.
q: Advise him not to shock a father's will.

Shock.etym: [OE. schokken; cf. D. schokken, F. choquer, Sp. chocar. √161. Cf. Chuck to strike, Jog, Shake, Shock a striking, Shog, n. & v.]

senses.d: To meet with a shock; to meet in violent encounter.
A dog with long hair or shag; — called also shockdog.
A thick mass of bushy hair; as, a head covered with a shock of sandy hair.
Bushy; shaggy; as, a shock hair.
q: His red shock peruke . . . was laid aside.

senses.d: To subject to the action of an electrical discharge so as to cause a more or less violent depression or commotion of the nervous system.
f Shoe.
A covering for the human foot, usually made of leather, having a thick and somewhat stiff sole and a lighter top. It differs from a boot on not extending so far up the leg.
q: Your hose should be ungartered, . . . yourshoe untied.
Spare none but such as go in clouted shoon.

senses.d: Anything resembling a shoe in form, position, or use.

Shoe.etym: [OE. sho, scho, AS. sc�h, sceóh; akin to OFries. sk�, OS. sk�h, D. schoe, schoen, G. schuh, OHG. scuoh, Icel. sk�r, Dan. & Sw. sko, Goth. sk�hs; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: To furnish with a shoe or shoes; to put a shoe or shoes on; as, to shoe a horse, a sled, an anchor.
To protect or ornament with something which serves the purpose of a shoe; to tip.
q: The sharp and small end of the billiard stick, which is shod with brass or silver.

senses.d: The outer cover or tread of a pneumatic tire, esp. for an automobile.
A set of staves and headings sufficient in number for one hogshead, cask, barrel, or the like, trimmed, and bound together in compact form.
A set of boards for a sugar box.
The parts of a piece of house furniture, as a bedstead, packed together.
To pack, as staves, in a shook.

An inclined plane, either artificial or natural, down which timber, coal, etc., are caused to slide; also, a narrow passage, either natural or artificial, in a stream, where the water rushes rapidly; esp., a channel, having a swift current, connecting the ends of a bend in the stream, so as to shorten the course.

Shoot.etym: [F. chute. See Chute. Confused with shoot to let fly.]

senses.d: To let fly, or cause to be driven, with force, as an arrow or a bullet; — followed by a word denoting the missile, as an object.
q: If you please To shoot an arrow that self way.

senses.d: To discharge, causing a missile to be driven forth; — followed by a word denoting the weapon or instrument, as an object; — often with off; as, to shoot a gun.
q: The two ends od a bow, shot off, fly from one another.

senses.d: To strike with anything shot; to hit with a missile; often, to kill or wound with a firearm; — followed by a word denoting the person or thing hit, as an object.
q: When Roger shot the hawk hovering over his master's dove house.

senses.d: To send out or forth, especially with a rapid or sudden motion; to cast with the hand; to hurl; to discharge; to emit.
q: An honest weaver as ever shot shuttle.
A pit into which the dead carts had nightly shot corpses by scores.

senses.d: To push or thrust forward; to project; to protrude; — often with out; as, a plant shoots out a bud.
q: They shoot out the lip, they shake the head.
Beware the secret snake that shoots a sting.

senses.d: To plane straight; to fit by planing.
q: Two pieces of wood that are shot, that is, planed or else pared with a paring chisel.

senses.d: To pass rapidly through, over, or under; as, to shoot a rapid or a bridge; to shoot a sand bar.
q: She . . . shoots the Stygian sound.

senses.d: To variegate as if by sprinkling or intermingling; to color in spots or patches.
q: The tangled water courses slept, Shot over with purple, and green, and yellow.

Shoot.etym: [OE. shotien, schotien, AS. scotian, v. i., sceótan; akin to D. schieten, G. schie�en, OHG. sciozan, Icel. skj�ta, Sw. skjuta, Dan. skyde; cf. Skr. skund to jump. √159. Cf. Scot a contribution, Scout to reject, Scud, Scuttle, v. i., Shot, Sheet, Shut, Shuttle, Skittish, Skittles.]

senses.d: To cause an engine or weapon to discharge a missile; — said of a person or an agent; as, they shot at a target; he shoots better than he rides.
q: The archers have . . . shot at him.

senses.d: To discharge a missile; — said of an engine or instrument; as, the gun shoots well.
To be shot or propelled forcibly; — said of a missile; to be emitted or driven; to move or extend swiftly, as if propelled; as, a shooting star.
q: There shot a streaming lamp along the sky.

senses.d: To penetrate, as a missile; to dart with a piercing sensation; as, shooting pains.
q: Thy words shoot through my heart.

senses.d: To feel a quick, darting pain; to throb in pain.
q: These preachers make His head to shoot and ache.

senses.d: To germinate; to bud; to sprout.
q: Onions, as they hang, will shoot forth.
But the wild olive shoots, and shades the ungrateful plain.

senses.d: To grow; to advance; as, to shoot up rapidly.
q: Well shot in years he seemed.
Delightful task! to rear the tender thought, To teach the young idea how to shoot.

senses.d: To change form suddenly; especially, to solidify.
q: If the menstruum be overcharged, metals will shoot into crystals.

senses.d: To protrude; to jut; to project; to extend; as, the land shoots into a promontory.
q: There shot up against the dark sky, tall, gaunt, straggling houses.

senses.d: To move ahead by force of momentum, as a sailing vessel when the helm is put hard alee.
The act of shooting; the discharge of a missile; a shot; as, the shoot of a shuttle.
q: The Turkish bow giveth a very forcible shoot.
One underneath his horse to get a shoot doth stalk.

senses.d: A young branch or growth.
q: Superfluous branches and shoots of this second spring.

senses.d: A rush of water; a rapid.
A vein of ore running in the same general direction as the lode.
A weft thread shot through the shed by the shuttle; a pick.
A shoat; a young hog.
One who shoots, as an archer or a gunner.
That which shoots.
The act of one who, or that which, shoots; as, the shooting of an archery club; the shooting of rays of light.
A wounding or killing with a firearm; specifically (Sporting), the killing of game; as, a week of shooting.
A sensation of darting pain; as, a shooting in one's head.
Of or pertaining to shooting; for shooting; darting.
A sewer.
A prop, as a timber, placed as a brace or support against the side of a building or other structure; a prop placed beneath anything, as a beam, to prevent it from sinking or sagging.

Shore.etym: [OE. schore; akin to LG. schore, D. schoor, OD. schoore, Icel. skor�a, and perhaps to E. shear, as being a piece cut off.]

senses.d: To support by a shore or shores; to prop; — usually with up; as, to shore up a building.
The coast or land adjacent to a large body of water, as an ocean, lake, or large river.
q: Michael Cassio, Lieutenant to the warlike Moor Othello, Is come shore.
The fruitful shore of muddy Nile.

Shore.etym: [OE. schore, AS. score, probably fr. scieran, and so meaning properly, that which is shorn off, edge; akin to OD. schoore, schoor. See Shear, v. t.]

senses.d: To set on shore.
Not long; having brief length or linear extension; as, a short distance; a short piece of timber; a short flight.
q: The bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it.

senses.d: Not extended in time; having very limited duration; not protracted; as, short breath.
q: The life so short, the craft so long to learn.
To short absense I could yield.

senses.d: Limited in quantity; inadequate; insufficient; scanty; as, a short supply of provisions, or of water.
Insufficiently provided; inadequately supplied; scantily furnished; lacking; not coming up to a resonable, or the ordinary, standard; — usually with of; as, to be short of money.
q: We shall be short in our provision.

senses.d: Deficient; defective; imperfect; not coming up, as to a measure or standard; as, an account which is short of the trith.
Not distant in time; near at hand.
q: Marinell was sore offended That his departure thence should be so short.
He commanded those who were appointed to attend him to be ready by a short day.

senses.d: Limited in intellectual power or grasp; not comprehensive; narrow; not tenacious, as memory.
q: Their own short understandings reach No farther than the present.

senses.d: Less important, efficaceous, or powerful; not equal or equivalent; less (than); — with of.
q: Hardly anything short of an invasion could rouse them again to war.

senses.d: Abrupt; brief; pointed; petulant; as, he gave a short answer to the question.
Breaking or crumbling readily in the mouth; crisp; as, short pastry.
Brittle.
Engaging or engaged to deliver what is not possessed; as, short contracts; to be short of stock. See The shorts, under Short, n., and To sell short, under Short, adv.

Short.etym: [OE. short, schort, AS. scort, sceort; akin to OHG. scurz, Icel. skorta to be short of, to lack, and perhaps to E. shear, v. t. Cf. Shirt.]

senses.d: A summary account.
q: The short and the long is, our play is preferred.

senses.d: The part of milled grain sifted out which is next finer than the bran.
q: The first remove above bran is shorts.

senses.d: Short, inferior hemp.
Breeches; shortclothes.
A short sound, syllable, or vowel.
q: If we compare the nearest conventional shorts and longs in English, as in “bit” and “beat,” “not” and “naught,” we find that the short vowels are generally wide, the long narrow, besides being generally diphthongic as well. Hence, originally short vowels can be lengthened and yet kept quite distinct from the original longs.

senses.d: In a short manner; briefly; limitedly; abruptly; quickly; as, to stop short in one's course; to turn short.
q: He was taken up very short, and adjudged corrigible for such presumptuous language.

senses.d: To shorten.
To fail; to decrease.
To make short or shorter in measure, extent, or time; as, to shorten distance; to shorten a road; to shorten days of calamity.
To reduce or diminish in amount, quantity, or extent; to lessen; to abridge; to curtail; to contract; as, to shorten work, an allowance of food, etc.
q: Here, where the subject is so fruitful, I am shortened by my chain.

senses.d: To make deficient (as to); to deprive; — with of.
q: Spoiled of his nose, and shortened of his ears.

senses.d: To make short or friable, as pastry, with butter, lard, pot liquor, or the like.
To become short or shorter; as, the day shortens in northern latitudes from June to December; a metallic rod shortens by cold.
In a short or brief time or manner; soon; quickly.
q: I shall grow jealous of you shortly.
The armies came shortly in view of each other.

senses.d: In few words; briefly; abruptly; curtly; as, to express ideas more shortly in verse than in prose.
Woven in such a way as to produce an effect of variegation, of changeable tints, or of being figured; as, shot silks. See Shoot, v. t., 8.
A share or proportion; a reckoning; a scot.
q: Here no shots are where all shares be.
A man is never . . . welcome to a place till some certain shot be paid and the hostess say “Welcome.”

Shot.etym: [AS. scot, sceot, fr. sceótan to shoot; akin to D. sschot, Icel. skot. √159. See Scot a share, Shoot, v. t., and cf. Shot a shooting.]

senses.d: The act of shooting; discharge of a firearm or other weapon which throws a missile.
q: He caused twenty shot of his greatest cannon to be made at the king's army.

senses.d: A missile weapon, particularly a ball or bullet; specifically, whatever is discharged as a projectile from firearms or cannon by the force of an explosive.
Small globular masses of lead, of various sizes, — used chiefly for killing game; as, bird shot; buckshot.
The flight of a missile, or the distance which it is, or can be, thrown; as, the vessel was distant more than a cannon shot.
A marksman; one who practices shooting; as, an exellent shot.

Shot.etym: [OE. shot, schot, AS. gesceot a missile; akin to D. schot a shot, shoot, G. schuss, geschoss a missile, Icel. skot a throwing, a javelin, and E. shoot, v.t. √159. See Shoot, and cf. Shot a share.]

senses.d: To load with shot, as a gun.
A cast of a net.
A spherical weight, to be put, or thrown, in competition for distance.
A stroke or propulsive action in certain games, as in billiards, hockey, curling, etc.; also, a move, as in chess.
A guess; conjecture; also, an attempt.

Used as an auxiliary verb, to express a conditional or contingent act or state, or as a supposition of an actual fact; also, to express moral obligation (see Shall); e. g.: they should have come last week; if I should go; I should think you could go.

Should.etym: [OE. sholde, shulde, scholde, schulde, AS. scolde, sceolde. See Shall.]

senses.d: The joint, or the region of the joint, by which the fore limb is connected with the body or with the shoulder girdle; the projection formed by the bones and muscles about that joint.
The flesh and muscles connected with the shoulder joint; the upper part of the back; that part of the human frame on which it is most easy to carry a heavy burden; — often used in the plural.
q: Then by main force pulled up, and on his shoulders bore The gates of Azza.
Adown her shoulders fell her length of hair.

senses.d: Fig.: That which supports or sustains; support.
q: In thy shoulder do I build my seat.

senses.d: That which resembles a human shoulder, as any protuberance or projection from the body of a thing.
q: The north western shoulder of the mountain.

senses.d: The upper joint of the fore leg and adjacent parts of an animal, dressed for market; as, a shoulder of mutton.
The angle of a bastion included between the face and flank. See Illust. of Bastion.

An abrupt projection which forms an abutment on an object, or limits motion, etc., as the projection around a tenon at the end of a piece of timber, the part of the top of a type which projects beyond the base of the raised character, etc.

Shoulder.etym: [OE. shulder, shuldre, schutder, AS. sculdor; akin to D. schoulder, G. schulter, OHG. scultarra, Dan. skulder, Sw. skuldra.]

senses.d: To push or thrust with the shoulder; to push with violence; to jostle.
q: As they the earth would shoulder from her seat.
Around her numberless the rabble flowed, Shouldering each other, crowding for a view.

senses.d: To take upon the shoulder or shoulders; as, to shoulder a basket; hence, to assume the burden or responsibility of; as, to shoulder blame; to shoulder a debt.
q: As if Hercules Or burly Atlas shouldered up their state.

senses.d: To push with the shoulder; to make one's way, as through a crowd, by using the shoulders; to move swaying the shoulders from side to side.
q: A yoke of the great sulky white bullocks . . . came shouldering along together.

senses.d: To utter a sudden and loud outcry, as in joy, triumph, or exultation, or to attract attention, to animate soldiers, etc.
q: Shouting of the men and women eke.
They shouted thrice: what was the last cry for?

Shout.etym: [OE. shouten, of unknown origin; perhaps akin to shoot; cf. Icel. skūta, skūti, a taunt.]

senses.d: To utter with a shout; to cry; — sometimes with out; as, to shout, or to shout out, a man's name.
To treat with shouts or clamor.
A loud burst of voice or voices; a vehement and sudden outcry, especially of a multitudes expressing joy, triumph, exultation, or animated courage.
q: The Rhodians, seeing the enemy turn their backs, gave a great shout in derision.

senses.d: To entertain with refreshments or the like gratuitously; to treat.
To treat (one) to something; also, to give (something) by way of treating.
A gratuitous entertainment, with refreshments or the like; a treat.
An implement consisting of a broad scoop, or more or less hollow blade, with a handle, used for lifting and throwing earth, coal, grain, or other loose substances.

Shovel.etym: [OE. shovele, schovele, AS. scoft, sceoft; akin to D. schoffel, G. schaufel, OHG. sc�vala, Dan. skovl, Sw. skofvel, skyffel, and to E. shove. √160. See Shove, v. t.]

senses.d: To take up and throw with a shovel; as, to shovel earth into a heap, or into a cart, or out of a pit.
To gather up as with a shovel.

To exhibit or present to view; to place in sight; to display; — the thing exhibited being the object, and often with an indirect object denoting the person or thing seeing or beholding; as, to show a house; show your colors; shopkeepers show customers goods (show goods to customers).
q: Go thy way, shew thyself to the priest.
Nor want we skill or art from whence to raise Magnificence; and what can heaven show more?

senses.d: To exhibit to the mental view; to tell; to disclose; to reveal; to make known; as, to show one's designs.
q: Shew them the way wherein they must walk.
If it please my father to do thee evil, then I will shew it thee, and send thee away.

senses.d: Specifically, to make known the way to (a person); hence, to direct; to guide; to asher; to conduct; as, to show a person into a parlor; to show one to the door.
To make apparent or clear, as by evidence, testimony, or reasoning; to prove; to explain; also, to manifest; to evince; as, to show the truth of a statement; to show the causes of an event.
q: I 'll show my duty by my timely care.

senses.d: To bestow; to confer; to afford; as, to show favor.
q: Shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me.

Show.etym: [OE. schowen, shewen, schewen, shawen, AS. sceáwian, to look, see, view; akin to OS. scaw�n, OFries. skawia, D. schouwen, OHG. scouw�n, G. schauen, Dan. skue, Sw. sk�da, Icel. sko�a, Goth. usskawjan to waken, skuggwa a mirror, Icel. skuggy shade, shadow, L. cavere to be on one's guard, Gr. ��� to ma

senses.d: To exhibit or manifest one's self or itself; to appear; to look; to be in appearance; to seem.
q: Just such she shows before a rising storm.
All round a hedge upshoots, and shows At distance like a little wood.

senses.d: To have a certain appearance, as well or ill, fit or unfit; to become or suit; to appear.
q: My lord of York, it better showed with you.

senses.d: The act of showing, or bringing to view; exposure to sight; exhibition.
That which os shown, or brought to view; that which is arranged to be seen; a spectacle; an exhibition; as, a traveling show; a cattle show.
q: As for triumphs, masks, feasts, and such shows.

senses.d: Proud or ostentatious display; parade; pomp.
q: I envy none their pageantry and show.

senses.d: Semblance; likeness; appearance.
q: He through the midst unmarked, In show plebeian angel militant Of lowest order, passed.

senses.d: False semblance; deceitful appearance; pretense.
q: Beware of the scribes, . . . which devour widows' houses, and for a shew make long prayers.

senses.d: A discharge, from the vagina, of mucus streaked with blood, occuring a short time before labor.
A pale blue flame, at the top of a candle flame, indicating the presence of fire damp.
One who shows or exhibits.
That which shows; a mirror.
A fall or rain or hail of short duration; sometimes, but rarely, a like fall of snow.
q: In drought or else showers.
Or wet the thirsty earth with falling showers.

senses.d: That which resembles a shower in falling or passing through the air copiously and rapidly.
q: With showers of stones he drives them far away.

senses.d: A copious supply bestowed.
q: He and myself Have travail'd in the great shower of your gifts.

Shower.etym: [OE. shour, schour, AS. se�r; akin to D. schoer, G. schauer, OHG. sc�r, Icel. sk�r, Sw. skur, Goth. sk�ra windis a storm of wind; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To water with a shower; to ��t copiously with rain.
q: Lest it again dissolve and shower the earth.

senses.d: To bestow liberally; to destribute or scatter in �undance; to rain.
q: C�sar's favor, That showers down greatness on his friends.

senses.d: To rain in showers; to fall, as in a hower or showers.
A long, narrow piece cut or torn off; a strip.
In general, a fragment; a piece; a particle.

Shred.etym: [OE. shrede, schrede, AS. screáde; akin to OD. schroode, G. schrot a piece cut off, Icel. skrjoðr a shred, and to E. shroud. Cf. Screed, Scroll, Scrutiny.]

senses.d: To cut or tear into small pieces, particularly narrow and long pieces, as of cloth or leather.
To lop; to prune; to trim.

Shred.etym: [OE. shreden, schreden, AS. screádian; akin to OD. schrooden, OHG. scr�tan, G. schroten. See Shred, n.]

senses.d: A case, box, or receptacle, especially one in which are deposited sacred relics, as the bones of a saint.
Any sacred place, as an altar, tromb, or the like.
q: Too weak the sacred shrine guard.

senses.d: A place or object hallowed from its history or associations; as, a shrine of art.

Shrine.etym: [OE. schrin, AS. scrīn, from L. scrinium a case, chest, box.]

senses.d: To enshrine; to place reverently, as in a shrine.

Short for Ancient Arabic Order of Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, a secret order professedly originated by one Kalif Alu, a son-in-law of Mohammed, at Mecca, in the year of the Hegira 25 (about 646 a. d.) In the modern order, established in the United States in 1872, only Knights Templars or thirty-second degree Masons are eligible for admission, though the order itself is not Masonic.
That which clothes, covers, conceals, or protects; a garment.
q: Swaddled, as new born, in sable shrouds.

senses.d: Especially, the dress for the dead; a winding sheet.
That which covers or shelters like a shroud.
q: Jura answers through her misty shroud.

senses.d: A covered place used as a retreat or shelter, as a cave or den; also, a vault or crypt.
q: The shroud to which he won His fair-eyed oxen.
A vault, or shroud, as under a church.

senses.d: The branching top of a tree; foliage.
q: The Assyrian wad a cedar in Lebanon, with fair branches and with a shadowing shroad.

senses.d: A set of ropes serving as stays to support the masts. The lower shrouds are secured to the sides of vessels by heavy iron bolts and are passed around the head of the lower masts.
One of the two annular plates at the periphery of a water wheel, which form the sides of the buckets; a shroud plate.

Shroud.etym: [OE. shroud, shrud, schrud, AS. scrūd a garment, clothing; akin to Icel. skruð the shrouds of a ship, furniture of a church, a kind of stuff, Sw. skrud dress, attire, and E. shred. See Shred, and cf. Shrood.]

senses.d: To cover with a shroud; especially, to inclose in a winding sheet; to dress for the grave.
q: The ancient Egyptian mummies were shrouded in a number of folds of linen besmeared with gums.

senses.d: To cover, as with a shroud; to protect completely; to cover so as to conceal; to hide; to veil.
q: One of these trees, with all his young ones, may shroud four hundred horsemen.
Some tempest rise, And blow out all the stars that light the skies, To shroud my shame.

senses.d: To take shelter or harbor.
q: If your stray attendance be yet lodged, Or shroud within these limits.

senses.d: To lop. See Shrood.
A liquor composed of vegetable acid, especially lemon juice, and sugar, with spirit to preserve it.

Shrub.etym: [Ar. shirb, shurb, a drink, beverage, fr. shariba to drink. Cf. Sirup, Sherbet.]

senses.d: A woody plant of less size than a tree, and usually with several stems from the same root.

Shrub.etym: [OE. schrob, AS. scrob, scrobb; akin to Norw. skrubba the dwarf cornel tree.]

senses.d: To lop; to prune.
To avoid; to keep clear of; to get out of the way of; to escape from; to eschew; as, to shun rocks, shoals, vice.
q: I am pure from the blood of all men. For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Scarcity and want shall shun you.

Shun.etym: [OE. shunien, schunien, schonien, AS. scunian, sceonian; cf. D. schuinen to slepe, schuin oblique, sloping, Icel. skunda, skynda, to hasten. Cf. Schooner, Scoundrel, Shunt.]

senses.d: To close so as to hinder ingress or egress; as, to shut a door or a gate; to shut one's eyes or mouth.
To forbid entrance into; to prohibit; to bar; as, to shut the ports of a country by a blockade.
q: Shall that be shut to man which to the beast Is open?

senses.d: To preclude; to exclude; to bar out.
To fold together; to close over, as the fingers; to close by bringing the parts together; as, to shut the hand; to shut a book.

Shut.etym: [OE. shutten, schutten, shetten, schitten, AS. scyttan to shut or lock up (akin to D. schutten, G. schützen to protect), properly, to fasten with a bolt or bar shot across, fr. AS. sceótan to shoot. √159. See Shoot.]

senses.d: To close itself; to become closed; as, the door shuts; it shuts hard.
Closed or fastened; as, a shut door.
Rid; clear; free; as, to get shut of a person.
Formed by complete closure of the mouth passage, and with the nose passage remaining closed; stopped, as are the mute consonants, p, t, k, b, d, and hard g.
The act or time of shutting; close; as, the shut of a door.
q: Just then returned at shut of evening flowers.

senses.d: A door or cover; a shutter.
The line or place where two pieces of metal are united by welding.
An instrument used in weaving for passing or shooting the thread of the woof from one side of the cloth to the other between the threads of the warp.
q: Like shuttles through the loom, so swiftly glide My feathered hours.

senses.d: The sliding thread holder in a sewing machine, which carries the lower thread through a loop of the upper thread, to make a lock stitch.
A shutter, as for a channel for molten metal.

Shuttle.etym: [Also shittle, OE. schitel, scytyl, schetyl; cf. OE. schitel a bolt of a door, AS. scyttes; all from AS. sceótan to shoot; akin to Dan. skyttel, skytte, shuttle, dial. Sw. skyttel, sköttel. √159. See Shoot, and cf. Shittle, Skittles.]

senses.d: To move backwards and forwards, like a shuttle.
q: I had to fly far and wide, shutting athwart the big Babel, wherever his calls and pauses had to be.

senses.d: A syllable applied, in solmization, to the note B; more recently, to the seventh tone of any major diatonic scale. It was added to Guido's scale by Le Maire about the end of the 17th century.
Affected with disease of any kind; ill; indisposed; not in health. See the Synonym under Illness.
q: Simon's wife's mother lay sick of a fever.
Behold them that are sick with famine.

senses.d: Affected with, or attended by, nausea; inclined to vomit; as, sick at the stomach; a sick headache.
Having a strong dislike; disgusted; surfeited; — with of; as, to be sick of flattery.
q: He was not so sick of his master as of his work.

senses.d: Corrupted; imperfect; impaired; weakned.
q: So great is his antipathy against episcopacy, that, if a seraphim himself should be a bishop, he would either find or make some sick feathers in his wings.

Sick.syn: Diseased; ill; disordered; distempered; indisposed; weak; ailing; feeble; morbid.
Sick.etym: [OE. sek, sik, ill, AS. seóc; akin to OS. siok, seoc, OFries. siak, D. ziek, G. siech, OHG. sioh, Icel. sj�kr, Sw. sjuk, Dan. syg, Goth. siuks ill, siukan to be ill.]

senses.d: Sickness.
To fall sick; to sicken.

A reaping instrument consisting of a steel blade curved into the form of a hook, and having a handle fitted on a tang. The sickle has one side of the blade notched, so as always to sharpen with a serrated edge. Cf. Reaping hook, under Reap.
q: When corn has once felt the sickle, it has no more benefit from the sunshine.

senses.d: A group of stars in the constellation Leo. See Illust. of Leo.

Sickle.etym: [OE. sikel, AS. sicol; akin to D. sikkel, G. sichel, OHG. sihhila, Dan. segel, segl, L. secula, fr. secare to cut; or perhaps from L. secula. See Saw a cutting instrument.]

senses.d: Somewhat sick; disposed to illness; attended with disease; as, a sickly body.
q: This physic but prolongs thy sickly days.

senses.d: Producing, or tending to, disease; as, a sickly autumn; a sickly climate.
Appearing as if sick; weak; languid; pale.
q: The moon grows sickly at the sight of day.
Nor torrid summer's sickly smile.

senses.d: Tending to produce nausea; sickening; as, a sickly smell; sickly sentimentality.

Sickly.syn: Diseased; ailing; infirm; weakly; unhealthy; healthless; weak; feeble; languid; faint.

senses.d: In a sick manner or condition; ill.
q: My people sickly beareth our marriage.

senses.d: To make sick or sickly; — with over, and probably only in the past participle.
q: Sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought.
Sentiments sicklied over . . . with that cloying heaviness into which unvaried sweetness is too apt to subside.

senses.d: The quality or state of being sick or diseased; illness; sisease or malady.
q: I do lament the sickness of the king.
Trust not too much your now resistless charms; Those, age or sickness soon or late disarms.

senses.d: Nausea; qualmishness; as, sickness of stomach.

The margin, edge, verge, or border of a surface; especially (when the thing spoken of is somewhat oblong in shape), one of the longer edges as distinguished from the shorter edges, called ends; a bounding line of a geometrical figure; as, the side of a field, of a square or triangle, of a river, of a road, etc.

Any outer portion of a thing considered apart from, and yet in relation to, the rest; as, the upper side of a sphere; also, any part or position viewed as opposite to or contrasted with another; as, this or that side.
q: Looking round on every side beheld A pathless desert.

senses.d: One of the halves of the body, of an animals or man, on either side of the mesial plane; or that which pertains to such a half; as, a side of beef; a side of sole leather.
q: One of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side.

senses.d: A slope or declivity, as of a hill, considered as opposed to another slope over the ridge.
q: Along the side of yon small hill.

senses.d: The position of a person or party regarded as opposed to another person or party, whether as a rival or a foe; a body of advocates or partisans; a party; hence, the interest or cause which one maintains against another; a doctrine or view opposed to another.
q: God on our side, doubt not of victory.
We have not always been of the . . . same side in politics.
Sets the passions on the side of truth.

senses.d: A line of descent traced through one parent as distinguished from that traced through another.
q: To sit upon thy father David's throne, By mother's side thy father.

senses.d: Fig.: Aspect or part regarded as contrasted with some other; as, the bright side of poverty.

Side.etym: [AS. sīde; akin to D. zijde, G. seite, OHG. sīta, Icel. sī�a, Dan. side, Sw. sida; cf. AS. sīd large, spacious, Icel. sī�r long, hanging.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a side, or the sides; being on the side, or toward the side; lateral.
q: One mighty squadron with a side wind sped.

senses.d: Hence, indirect; oblique; collateral; incidental; as, a side issue; a side view or remark.
q: The law hath no side respect to their persons.

senses.d: Long; large; extensive.
q: His gown had side sleeves down to mid leg.

senses.d: To lean on one side.
To embrace the opinions of one party, or engage in its interest, in opposition to another party; to take sides; as, to side with the ministerial party.
q: All side in parties, and begin the attack.

senses.d: To be or stand at the side of; to be on the side toward.
q: His blind eye that sided Paridell.

senses.d: To suit; to pair; to match.
To work (a timber or rib) to a certain thickness by trimming the sides.
To furnish with a siding; as, to side a house.
A seat; especially, a royal seat; a throne.
q: A stately siege of sovereign majesty, And thereon sat a woman gorgeous gay.
In our great hall there stood a vacant chair . . . And Merlin called it “The siege perilous.”

senses.d: Hence, place or situation; seat.
q: Ah! traitorous eyes, come out of your shameless siege forever.

senses.d: Rank; grade; station; estimation.
q: I fetch my life and being From men of royal siege.

senses.d: Passage of excrements; stool; fecal matter.
q: The siege of this mooncalf.

senses.d: The sitting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender; the surrounding or investing of a place by an army, and approaching it by passages and advanced works, which cover the besiegers from the enemy's fire. See the Note under Blockade.
Hence, a continued attempt to gain possession.
q: Love stood the siege, and would not yield his breast.

senses.d: The floor of a glass-furnace.
A workman's bench.

Siege.etym: [OE. sege, OF. siege, F. siège a seat, a siege; cf. It. seggia, seggio, zedio, a seat, asseggio, assedio, a siege, F. assiéger to besiege, It. & LL. assediare, L. obsidium a siege, besieging; all ultimately fr. L. sedere to sit. See Sit, and cf. See, n.]

senses.d: To besiege; to beset.
q: Through all the dangers that can siege The life of man.

senses.d: A utensil for separating the finer and coarser parts of a pulverized or granulated substance from each other. It consist of a vessel, usually shallow, with the bottom perforated, or made of hair, wire, or the like, woven in meshes.
A kind of coarse basket.

Sieve.etym: [OE. sive, AS. sife; akin to D. zeef, zift, OHG. sib, G. sieb. √151a. Cf. Sift.]

senses.d: To separate with a sieve, as the fine part of a substance from the coarse; as, to sift meal or flour; to sift powder; to sift sand or lime.
To separate or part as if with a sieve.
q: When yellow sands are sifted from below, The glittering billows give a golden show.

senses.d: To examine critically or minutely; to scrutinize.
q: Sifting the very utmost sentence and syllable.
Opportunity I here have had To try thee, sift thee.
Let him but narrowly sift his ideas.

Sift.etym: [AS. siftan, from sife sieve. √151a. See Sieve.]

senses.d: To inhale a larger quantity of air than usual, and immediately expel it; to make a deep single audible respiration, especially as the result or involuntary expression of fatigue, exhaustion, grief, sorrow, or the like.
Hence, to lament; to grieve.
q: He sighed deeply in his spirit.

senses.d: To make a sound like sighing.
q: And the coming wind did roar more loud, And the sails did sigh like sedge.
The winter winds are wearily sighing.

Sigh.etym: [OE. sighen, si�en; cf. also OE. siken, AS. sīcan, and OE. sighten, si�ten, sichten, AS. siccettan; all, perhaps, of imitative origin.]

senses.d: To exhale (the breath) in sighs.
q: Never man sighed truer breath.

senses.d: To utter sighs over; to lament or mourn over.
q: Ages to come, and men unborn, Shall bless her name, and sigh her fate.

senses.d: To express by sighs; to utter in or with sighs.
q: They . . . sighed forth proverbs.
The gentle swain . . . sighs back her grief.

senses.d: A deep and prolonged audible inspiration or respiration of air, as when fatigued or grieved; the act of sighing.
q: I could drive the boat with my sighs.

senses.d: Figuratively, a manifestation of grief; a lan�ent.
q: With their sighs the air Frequenting, sent from hearts contrite.

Sigh.etym: [OE. sigh; cf. OE. sik. See Sigh, v. i.]

senses.d: Uttering sighs; grieving; lamenting.
The act of seeing; perception of objects by the eye; view; as, to gain sight of land.
q: A cloud received him out of their sight.

senses.d: The power of seeing; the faculty of vision, or of perceiving objects by the instrumentality of the eyes.
q: Thy sight is young, And thou shalt read when mine begin to dazzle.
O loss of sight, of thee I most complain!

senses.d: The state of admitting unobstructed vision; visibility; open view; region which the eye at one time surveys; space through which the power of vision extends; as, an object within sight.
A spectacle; a view; a show; something worth seeing.
q: Moses said, I will now turn aside and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt.
They never saw a sight so fair.

senses.d: The instrument of seeing; the eye.
q: Why cloud they not their sights?

senses.d: Inspection; examination; as, a letter intended for the sight of only one person.
Mental view; opinion; judgment; as, in their sight it was harmless.
q: That which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God.

senses.d: A small aperture through which objects are to be seen, and by which their direction is settled or ascertained; as, the sight of a quadrant.
q: Thier eyes of fire sparking through sights of steel.

senses.d: A small piece of metal, fixed or movable, on the breech, muzzle, center, or trunnion of a gun, or on the breech and the muzzle of a rifle, pistol, etc., by means of which the eye is guided in aiming.
In a drawing, picture, etc., that part of the surface, as of paper or canvas, which is within the frame or the border or margin. In a frame or the like, the open space, the opening.
A great number, quantity, or sum; as, a sight of money.
q: A wonder sight of flowers.

Sight.syn: Vision; view; show; spectacle; representation; exhibition.
Sight.etym: [OE. sight, si�t, siht, AS. siht, gesiht, gesih�, gesieh�, gesyh�; akin to D. gezicht, G. sicht, gesicht, Dan. sigte, Sw. sigt, from the root of E. see. See See, v. t.]

senses.d: To get sight of; to see; as, to sight land; to sight a wreck.
To look at through a sight; to see accurately; as, to sight an object, as a star.
To apply sights to; to adjust the sights of; also, to give the proper elevation and direction to by means of a sight; as, to sight a rifle or a cannon.
To take aim by a sight.
That by which anything is made known or represented; that which furnishes evidence; a mark; a token; an indication; a proof.
A remarkable event, considered by the ancients as indicating the will of some deity; a prodigy; an omen.
An event considered by the Jews as indicating the divine will, or as manifesting an interposition of the divine power for some special end; a miracle; a wonder.
q: Through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God.
It shall come to pass, if they will not believe thee, neither hearken to the voice of the first sign, that they will believe the voice of the latter sign.

senses.d: Something serving to indicate the existence, or preserve the memory, of a thing; a token; a memorial; a monument.
q: What time the fire devoured two hundred and fifty men, and they became a sign.

senses.d: Any symbol or emblem which prefigures, typifles, or represents, an idea; a type; hence, sometimes, a picture.
q: The holy symbols, or signs, are not barely significative; but what they represent is as certainly delivered to us as the symbols themselves.
Saint George of Merry England, the sign of victory.

senses.d: A word or a character regarded as the outward manifestation of thought; as, words are the sign of ideas.
A motion, an action, or a gesture by which a thought is expressed, or a command or a wish made known.
q: They made signs to his father, how he would have him called.

senses.d: Hence, one of the gestures of pantomime, or of a language of a signs such as those used by the North American Indians, or those used by the deaf and dumb.
A military emblem carried on a banner or a standard.

A lettered board, or other conspicuous notice, placed upon or before a building, room, shop, or office to advertise the business there transacted, or the name of the person or firm carrying it on; a publicly displayed token or notice.
q: The shops were, therefore, distinguished by painted signs, which gave a gay and grotesque aspect to the streets.

senses.d: The twelfth part of the ecliptic or zodiac.
A character indicating the relation of quantities, or an operation performed upon them; as, the sign + (plus); the sign — (minus); the sign of division ÷, and the like.

Sign.syn: Token; mark; note; symptom; indication; signal; symbol; type; omen; prognostic; presage; manifestation. See Emblem.
Sign.etym: [F. signe, L. signum; cf. AS. segen, segn, a sign, standard, banner, also fr. L. signum. Cf. Ensign, Resign, Seal a stamp, Signal, Signet.]

senses.d: To represent by a sign; to make known in a typical or emblematic manner, in distinction from speech; to signify.
q: I signed to Browne to make his retreat.

senses.d: To make a sign upon; to mark with a sign.
q: We receive this child into the congregation of Christ's flock, and do sign him with the sign of the cross.

senses.d: To affix a signature to; to ratify by hand or seal; to subscribe in one's own handwriting.
q: Inquire the Jew's house out, give him this deed, And let him sign it.

senses.d: To assign or convey formally; — used with away.
To mark; to make distinguishable.

Sign.etym: [OE. seinen to bless, originally, to make the sign of the cross over; in this sense fr. ASS. segnian (from segn, n.), or OF. seignier, F. signer, to mark, to sign (in sense 3), fr. L. signare to mark, set a mark upon, from signum. See Sign, n.]

senses.d: To be a sign or omen.
To make a sign or signal; to communicate directions or intelligence by signs.
To write one's name, esp. as a token of assent, responsibility, or obligation.
A seal; especially, in England, the seal used by the sovereign in sealing private letters and grants that pass by bill under the sign manual; — called also privy signet.
q: I had my father's signet in my purse.

Signet.etym: [OF. signet a signet, F., a bookmark, dim. of signe. See Sign, n., and cf. Sennet.]

senses.d: The act of signifying; a making known by signs or other means.
q: A signification of being pleased.
All speaking or signification of one's mind implies an act or addres of one man to another.

senses.d: That which is signified or made known; that meaning which a sign, character, or token is intended to convey; as, the signification of words.
To show by a sign; to communicate by any conventional token, as words, gestures, signals, or the like; to announce; to make known; to declare; to express; as, a signified his desire to be present.
q: I 'll to the king; and signify to him That thus I have resign'd my charge to you.
The government should signify to the Protestants of Ireland that want of silver is not to be remedied.

senses.d: To mean; to import; to denote; to betoken.
q: He bade her tell him what it signified.
A tale Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, Signifying nothing.

Signify.syn: To express; manifest; declare; utter; intimate; betoken; denote; imply; mean.
Signify.etym: [F. signifier, L. significare; signum a sign + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Sign, n., and -fy.]

senses.d: The state of being silent; entire absence of sound or noise; absolute stillness.
q: I saw and heared; for such a numerous host Fled not in silence through the frighted deep.

senses.d: Forbearance from, or absence of, speech; taciturnity; muteness.
Secrecy; as, these things were transacted in silence.
q: The administration itself keeps a profound silence.

senses.d: The cessation of rage, agitation, or tumilt; calmness; quiest; as, the elements were reduced to silence.
Absence of mention; oblivion.
q: And what most merits fame, in silence hid.

senses.d: Be silent; — used elliptically for let there be silence, or keep silence.
To compel to silence; to cause to be still; to still; to hush.
q: Silence that dreadful bell; it frights the isle.

senses.d: To put to rest; to quiet.
q: This would silence all further opposition.
These would have silenced their scruples.

senses.d: To restrain from the exercise of any function, privilege of instruction, or the like, especially from the act of preaching; as, to silence a minister of the gospel.
q: The Rev. Thomas Hooker of Chelmsford, in Essex, was silenced for nonconformity.

senses.d: To cause to cease firing, as by a vigorous cannonade; as, to silence the batteries of an enemy.
Free from sound or noise; absolutely still; perfectly quiet.
q: How silent is this town!

senses.d: Not speaking; indisposed to talk; speechless; mute; taciturn; not loquacious; not talkative.
q: Ulysses, adds he, was the most eloquent and most silent of men.
This new-created world, whereof in hell Fame is not silent.

senses.d: Keeping at rest; inactive; calm; undisturbed; as, the wind is silent.
Not pronounced; having no sound; quiescent; as, e is silent in “fable.”
Having no effect; not operating; inefficient.
q: Cause . . . silent, virtueless, and dead.

Silent.syn: Mute; taciturn; dumb; speechless; quiet; still. See Mute, and Taciturn.
Silent.etym: [L. silens, -entis, p. pr. of silere to be silent; akin to Goth. ana-silan.]

senses.d: That which is silent; a time of silence.
The fine, soft thread produced by various species of caterpillars in forming the cocoons within which the worm is inclosed during the pupa state, especially that produced by the larvæ of Bombyx mori.
Hence, thread spun, or cloth woven, from the above-named material.
That which resembles silk, as the filiform styles of the female flower of maize.

Silk.etym: [OE. silk, selk, AS. seolc, seoloc; akin to Icel. silki, SW. & Dan. silke; prob. through Slavic from an Oriental source; cf. Lith. szilkai, Russ. shelk', and also L. sericum Seric stuff, silk. Cf. Sericeous. Serge a woolen stuff.]

senses.d: Happy; fortunate; blessed.
Harmless; innocent; inoffensive.
q: The silly virgin strove him to withstand.
A silly, innocent hare murdered of a dog.

senses.d: Weak; helpless; frail.
q: After long storms . . . With which my silly bark was tossed sore.
The silly buckets on the deck.

senses.d: Rustic; plain; simple; humble.
q: A fourth man, in a sillyhabit.
All that did their silly thoughts so busy keep.

senses.d: Weak in intellect; destitute of ordinary strength of mind; foolish; witless; simple; as, a silly woman.
Proceeding from want of understanding or common judgment; characterized by weakness or folly; unwise; absurd; stupid; as, silly conduct; a silly question.

Silly.syn: Simple; brainless; witless; shallow; foolish; unwise; indiscreet. See Simple.
Silly.etym: [OE. seely, sely, AS. s�lig, ges�lig, happy, good, fr. s�l, s�l, good, happy, s�l good fortune, happines; akin to OS. sālig, a, good, happy, D. zalig blessed, G. selig, OHG. sālīg, Icel. s�l, Sw. säll, Dan. salig, Goth. s�ls good, kind, and perh. also to L. sollus whole, entire, Gr. ���, Skr. sarva.

senses.d: A soft white metallic element, sonorous, ductile, very malleable, and capable of a high degree of polish. It is found native, and also combined with sulphur, arsenic, antimony, chlorine, etc., in the minerals argentite, proustite, pyrargyrite, ceragyrite, etc. Silver is one of the “noble” metals, so-called, not being easily oxidized, and is used for coin, jewelry, plate, and a great variety of articles. Symbol Ag (Argentum). Atomic weight 107.7. Specific gravity 10.5.
Coin made of silver; silver money.
Anything having the luster or appearance of silver.
The color of silver.
