Silver.etym: [OE. silver, selver, seolver, AS. seolfor, siolfur, siolufr, silofr, sylofr; akin to OS. silubar, OFries. selover, D. zilver, LG. sulver, OHG. silabar, silbar, G. silber, Icel. silfr, Sw. silfver, Dan. sölv, Goth. silubr, Russ. serebro, Lith. sidabras; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to silver; made of silver; as, silver leaf; a silver cup.
Resembling silver.
q: Others, on silver lakes and rivers, bathed Their downy breast.

senses.d: Precious; costly.
Giving a clear, ringing sound soft and clear.
Sweet; gentle; peaceful.
To cover with silver; to give a silvery appearance to by applying a metal of a silvery color; as, to silver a pin; to silver a glass mirror plate with an amalgam of tin and mercury.
To polish like silver; to impart a brightness to, like that of silver.
q: And smiling calmness silvered o'er the deep.

senses.d: To make hoary, or white, like silver.
q: His head was silvered o'er with age.

senses.d: To acquire a silvery color.
q: The eastern sky began to silver and shine.

senses.d: A small silver coin.
q: A thousand vines at a thousand silverings.

senses.d: One whose occupation is to manufacture utensils, ornaments, etc., of silver; a worker in silver.
The quality or state of being similar or like; resemblance; likeness; similarity; as, similitude of substance.
q: Let us make now man in our image, man In our similitude.
If fate some future bard shall join In sad similitude of griefs to mine.

senses.d: The act of likening, or that which likens, one thing to another; fanciful or imaginative comparison; a simile.
q: Tasso, in his similitudes, never departed from the woods; that is, all his comparisons were taken from the country.

senses.d: That which is like or similar; a representation, semblance, or copy; a facsimile.
q: Man should wed his similitude.

Similitude.etym: [F. similitude, L. similitudo, from similis similar. See Similar.]

senses.d: Single; not complex; not infolded or entangled; uncombined; not compounded; not blended with something else; not complicated; as, a simple substance; a simple idea; a simple sound; a simple machine; a simple problem; simple tasks.
Plain; unadorned; as, simple dress.
Mere; not other than; being only.
q: A medicine . . . whose simple touch Is powerful to araise King Pepin.

senses.d: Not given to artifice, stratagem, or duplicity; undesigning; sincere; true.
q: Full many fine men go upon my score, as simple as I stand here, and I trust them.
Must thou trust Tradition's simple tongue?
To be simple is to be great.

senses.d: Artless in manner; unaffected; unconstrained; natural; inartificial;; straightforward.
q: In simple manners all the secret lies.

senses.d: Direct; clear; intelligible; not abstruse or enigmatical; as, a simple statement; simple language.
Weak in intellect; not wise or sagacious; of but moderate understanding or attainments; hence, foolish; silly.
q: The simple believeth every word; but the prudent man looketh well to his going.

senses.d: Not luxurious; without much variety; plain; as, a simple diet; a simple way of living.
q: Thy simple fare and all thy plain delights.

senses.d: Humble; lowly; undistinguished.
q: A simple husbandman in garments gray.
Clergy and laity, male and female, gentle and simple made the fuel of the same fire.

senses.d: Without subdivisions; entire; as, a simple stem; a simple leaf.
Not capable of being decomposed into anything more simple or ultimate by any means at present known; elementary; thus, atoms are regarded as simple bodies. Cf. Ultimate, a.
Homogenous.

Simple.syn: Single; uncompounded; unmingled; unmixed; mere; uncombined; elementary; plain; artless; sincere; harmless; undesigning; frank; open; unaffected; inartificial; unadorned; credulous; silly; foolish; shallow; unwise.
Simple.etym: [F., fr. L. simplus, or simplex, gen. simplicis. The first part of the Latin words is probably akin to E. same, and the sense, one, one and the same; cf. L. semel once, singuli one to each, single. Cg. Single, a., Same, a., and for the last part of the word cf. Double, Complex.]

senses.d: Something not mixed or compounded.
A medicinal plant; — so called because each vegetable was supposed to possess its particular virtue, and therefore to constitute a simple remedy.
q: What virtue is in this remedy lies in the naked simple itself as it comes over from the Indies.

senses.d: A drawloom.
A feast which is not a double or a semidouble.
To gather simples, or medicinal plants.
q: As simpling on the flowery hills she strayed.

senses.d: The quality or state of being simple, unmixed, or uncompounded; as, the simplicity of metals or of earths.
The quality or state of being not complex, or of consisting of few parts; as, the simplicity of a machine.
Artlessness of mind; freedom from cunning or duplicity; lack of acuteness and sagacity.
q: Marquis Dorset, a man, for his harmless simplicity neither misliked nor much regarded.
In wit a man; simplicity a child.

senses.d: Freedom from artificial ornament, pretentious style, or luxury; plainness; as, simplicity of dress, of style, or of language; simplicity of diet; simplicity of life.
Freedom from subtlety or abstruseness; clearness; as, the simplicity of a doctrine; the simplicity of an explanation or a demonstration.
Weakness of intellect; silliness; folly.
q: How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning?

senses.d: Old form of Since.
q: Sin that his lord was twenty year of age.

senses.d: Transgression of the law of God; disobedience of the divine command; any violation of God's will, either in purpose or conduct; moral deficiency in the character; iniquity; as, sins of omission and sins of commission.
q: Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.
Sin is the transgression of the law.
I think 't no sin. To cozen him that would unjustly win.
Enthralled By sin to foul, exorbitant desires.

senses.d: An offense, in general; a violation of propriety; a misdemeanor; as, a sin against good manners.
q: I grant that poetry's a crying sin.

senses.d: A sin offering; a sacrifice for sin.
q: He hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin.

senses.d: An embodiment of sin; a very wicked person.
q: Thy ambition, Thou scarlet sin, robbed this bewailing land Of noble Buckingham.

Sin.etym: [OE. sinne, AS. synn, syn; akin to D. zonde, OS. sundia, OHG. sunta, G. sünde, Icel., Dan. & Sw. synd, L. sons, sontis, guilty, perhaps originally from the p. pr. of the verb signifying, to be, and meaning, the one who it is. Cf. Authentic, Sooth.]

senses.d: To depart voluntarily from the path of duty prescribed by God to man; to violate the divine law in any particular, by actual transgression or by the neglect or nonobservance of its injunctions; to violate any known rule of duty; — often followed by against.
q: Against thee, thee only, have I sinned.
All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.

senses.d: To violate human rights, law, or propriety; to commit an offense; to trespass; to transgress.
q: I am a man More sinned against than sinning.
Who but wishes to invert the laws Of order, sins against the eternal cause.

Sin.etym: [OE. sinnen, singen, sinegen, AS. syngian. See Sin, n.]

senses.d: From a definite past time until now; as, he went a month ago, and I have not seen him since.
q: We since become the slaves to one man's lust.

senses.d: In the time past, counting backward from the present; before this or now; ago.
q: How many ages since has Virgil writ?
About two years since, it so fell out, that he was brought to a great lady's house.

senses.d: When or that.
q: Do you remember since we lay all night in the windmill in St. George's field?

Since.etym: [For sins, contr. fr. OE. sithens, sithenes, formed by an adverbial ending (cf. Besides) from OE. sithen, also shortened into sithe, sin, AS. siððan, syððan, seoððan, afterward, then, since, after; properly, after that; fr. sīð after, later, adv. and prep. (originally a comparative adv., akin to OS.

senses.d: From the time of; in or during the time subsequent to; subsequently to; after; — usually with a past event or time for the object.
q: The Lord hath blessed thee, since my coming.
I have a model by which he build a nobler poem than any extant since the ancients.

senses.d: Seeing that; because; considering; — formerly followed by that.
q: Since that my penitence comes after all, Imploring pardon.
Since truth and constancy are vain, Since neither love, nor sense of pain, Nor force of reason, can persuade, Then let example be obeyed.

Since.syn: Because; for; as; inasmuch as; considering. See Because.

senses.d: Pure; unmixed; unadulterated.
q: There is no sincere acid in any animal juice.
A joy which never was sincere till now.

senses.d: Whole; perfect; unhurt; uninjured.
q: The inviolable body stood sincere.

senses.d: Being in reality what it appears to be; having a character which corresponds with the appearance; not falsely assumed; genuine; true; real; as, a sincere desire for knowledge; a sincere contempt for meanness.
q: A sincere intention of pleasing God in all our actions.

senses.d: Honest; free from hypocrisy or dissimulation; as, a sincere friend; a sincere person.
q: The more sincere you are, the better it will fare with you at the great day of account.

Sincere.syn: Honest; unfeigned; unvarnished; real; true; unaffected; inartificial; frank; upright. See Hearty.
Sincere.etym: [L. sincerus, of uncertain origin; the first part perhaps akin to sin- in singuli (see Single), and the second to cernere to separate (cf. Discern): cf. F. sincère.]

senses.d: In a sincere manner.
Purely; without alloy.
Honestly; unfeignedly; without dissimulation; as, to speak one's mind sincerely; to love virtue sincerely.
The quality or state of being sincere; honesty of mind or intention; freedom from simulation, hypocrisy, disguise, or false pretense; sincereness.
q: I protest, in the sincerity of love.
Sincerity is a duty no less plain than important.

senses.d: A tendon or tendonous tissue. See Tendon.
Muscle; nerve.
Fig.: That which supplies strength or power.
q: The portion and sinew of her fortune, her marriage dowry.
The bodies of men, munition, and money, may justly be called the sinews of war.

Sinew.etym: [OE. sinewe, senewe, AS. sinu, seonu; akin to D. zenuw, OHG. senawa, G. sehne, Icel. sin, Sw. sena, Dan. sene; cf. Skr. snāva. √290.]

senses.d: To knit together, or make strong with, or as with, sinews.
q: Wretches, now stuck up for long tortures . . . might, if properly treated, serve to sinew the state in time of danger.

senses.d: Tainted with, or full of, sin; wicked; iniquitous; criminal; unholy; as, sinful men; sinful thoughts.
q: Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity.

senses.d: To utter sounds with musical inflections or melodious modulations of voice, as fancy may dictate, or according to the notes of a song or tune, or of a given part (as alto, tenor, etc.) in a chorus or concerted piece.
q: The noise of them that sing do I hear.

senses.d: To utter sweet melodious sounds, as birds do.
q: On every bough the briddes heard I sing.
Singing birds, in silver cages hung.

senses.d: To make a small, shrill sound; as, the air sings in passing through a crevice.
q: O'er his head the flying spear Sang innocent, and spent its force in air.

senses.d: To tell or relate something in numbers or verse; to celebrate something in poetry.
q: Bid her . . . sing Of human hope by cross event destroyed.

senses.d: To cry out; to complain.
q: They should sing if thet they were bent.

Sing.etym: [AS. singan; akin to D. zingen, OS. & OHG. singan, G. singen, Icel. syngja, Sw. sjunga, Dan. synge, Goth. siggwan, and perhaps to E. say, v.t., or cf. Gr. ��� voice. Cf. Singe, Song.]

senses.d: To utter with musical inflections or modulations of voice.
q: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.
And in the darkness sing your carol of high praise.

senses.d: To celebrate is song; to give praises to in verse; to relate or rehearse in numbers, verse, or poetry.
q: Arms and the man I sing.
The last, the happiest British king, Whom thou shalt paint or I shall sing.

senses.d: To influence by singing; to lull by singing; as, to sing a child to sleep.
To accompany, or attend on, with singing.
q: I heard them singing home the bride.

senses.d: To burn slightly or superficially; to burn the surface of; to burn the ends or outside of; as, to singe the hair or the skin.
q: You sulphurous and thought-executing fires, . . . Singe my white head!
I singed the toes of an ape through a burning glass.

senses.d: To remove the nap of (cloth), by passing it rapidly over a red-hot bar, or over a flame, preliminary to dyeing it.

Singe.etym: [OE. sengen, AS. sengan in besengan (akin to D. zengen, G. sengen), originally, to cause to sing, fr. AS. singan to sing, in allusion to the singing or hissing sound often produced when a substance is singed, or slightly burned. See Sing.]

senses.d: A burning of the surface; a slight burn.
One who, or that which, singes.
One employed to singe cloth.
A machine for singeing cloth.
One who sings; especially, one whose profession is to sing.
One only, as distinguished from more than one; consisting of one alone; individual; separate; as, a single star.
q: No single man is born with a right of controlling the opinions of all the rest.

senses.d: Alone; having no companion.
q: Who single hast maintained, Against revolted multitudes, the cause Of truth.

senses.d: Hence, unmarried; as, a single man or woman.
q: Grows, lives, and dies in single blessedness.
Single chose to live, and shunned to wed.

senses.d: Not doubled, twisted together, or combined with others; as, a single thread; a single strand of a rope.
Performed by one person, or one on each side; as, a single combat.
q: These shifts refuted, answer thy appellant, . . . Who now defles thee thrice ti single fight.

senses.d: Uncompounded; pure; unmixed.
q: Simple ideas are opposed to complex, and single to compound.

senses.d: Not deceitful or artful; honest; sincere.
q: I speak it with a single heart.

senses.d: Simple; not wise; weak; silly.
q: He utters such single matter in so infantly a voice.

Single.etym: [L. singulus, a dim. from the root in simplex simple; cf. OE. & OF. sengle, fr. L. singulus. See Simple, and cf. Singular.]

senses.d: To select, as an individual person or thing, from among a number; to choose out from others; to separate.
q: Dogs who hereby can single out their master in the dark.
His blood! she faintly screamed her mind Still singling one from all mankind.

senses.d: To sequester; to withdraw; to retire.
q: An agent singling itself from consorts.

senses.d: To take alone, or one by one.
q: Men . . . commendable when they are singled.

senses.d: To take the irrregular gait called single-foot;- said of a horse. See Single-foot.
q: Many very fleet horses, when overdriven, adopt a disagreeable gait, which seems to be a cross between a pace and a trot, in which the two legs of one side are raised almost but not quite, simultaneously. Such horses are said to single, or to be single-footed.

senses.d: A unit; one; as, to score a single.
The reeled filaments of silk, twisted without doubling to give them firmness.
A handful of gleaned grain.
A game with but one player on each side; — usually in the plural.
A hit by a batter which enables him to reach first base only.
The quality or state of being single, or separate from all others; the opposite of doubleness, complication, or multiplicity.
Freedom from duplicity, or secondary and selfish ends; purity of mind or purpose; simplicity; sincerity; as, singleness of purpose; singleness of heart.
Separate or apart from others; single; distinct.
q: And God forbid that all a company Should rue a singular man's folly.

senses.d: Engaged in by only one on a side; single.
q: To try the matter thus together in a singular combat.

senses.d: Existing by itself; single; individual.
q: The idea which represents one . . . determinate thing, is called a singular idea, whether simple, complex, or compound.

senses.d: Each; individual; as, to convey several parcels of land, all and singular.
Denoting one person or thing; as, the singular number; — opposed to dual and plural.
Standing by itself; out of the ordinary course; unusual; uncommon; strange; as, a singular phenomenon.
q: So singular a sadness Must have a cause as strange as the effect.

senses.d: Distinguished as existing in a very high degree; rarely equaled; eminent; extraordinary; exceptional; as, a man of singular gravity or attainments.
Departing from general usage or expectations; odd; whimsical; — often implying disapproval or censure.
q: His zeal None seconded, as out of season judged, Or singular and rash.
To be singular in anything that is wise and worthy, is not a disparagement, but a praise.

senses.d: Being alone; belonging to, or being, that of which there is but one; unique.
q: These busts of the emperors and empresses are all very scarce, and some of them almost singular in their kind.

Singular.syn: Unexampled; unprecedented; eminent; extraordinary; remarkable; uncommon; rare; unusual; peculiar; strange; odd; eccentric; fantastic.
Singular.etym: [OE. singuler, F. singulier, fr. L. singularius, singularis, fr. singulus single. See Single, a.]

senses.d: An individual instance; a particular.
The singular number, or the number denoting one person or thing; a word in the singular number.
To fall by, or as by, the force of gravity; to descend lower and lower; to decline gradually; to subside; as, a stone sinks in water; waves rise and sink; the sun sinks in the west.
q: I sink in deep mire.

senses.d: To enter deeply; to fall or retire beneath or below the surface; to penetrate.
q: The stone sunk into his forehead.

senses.d: Hence, to enter so as to make an abiding impression; to enter completely.
q: Let these sayings sink down into your ears.

senses.d: To be overwhelmed or depressed; to fall slowly, as so the ground, from weakness or from an overburden; to fail in strength; to decline; to decay; to decrease.
q: I think our country sinks beneath the yoke.
He sunk down in his chariot.
Let not the fire sink or slacken.

senses.d: To decrease in volume, as a river; to subside; to become diminished in volume or in apparent height.
q: The Alps and Pyreneans sink before him.

Sink.syn: To fall; subside; drop; droop; lower; decline; decay; decrease; lessen.
Sink.etym: [OE. sinken, AS. sincan; akin to D. zinken, OS. sincan, G. sinken, Icel. sökkva, Dan. synke, Sw. sjunka, Goth. siggan, and probably to E. silt. Cf. Silt.]

senses.d: To cause to sink; to put under water; to immerse or submerge in a fluid; as, to sink a ship.
q: fell upon the wings and sank a single ship.

senses.d: Figuratively: To cause to decline; to depress; to degrade; hence, to ruin irretrievably; to destroy, as by drowping; as, to sink one's reputation.
q: I raise of sink, imprison or set free.
If I have a conscience, let it sink me.
Thy cruel and unnatural lust of power Has sunk thy father more than all his years.

senses.d: To make (a depression) by digging, delving, or cutting, etc.; as, to sink a pit or a well; to sink a die.
To bring low; to reduce in quantity; to waste.
q: You sunk the river repeated draughts.

senses.d: To conseal and appropriate.
q: If sent with ready money to buy anything, and you happen to be out of pocket, sink the money, and take up the goods on account.

senses.d: To keep out of sight; to suppress; to ignore.
q: A courtly willingness to sink obnoxious truths.

senses.d: To reduce or extinguish by payment; as, to sink the national debt.
A drain to carry off filthy water; a jakes.
A shallow box or vessel of wood, stone, iron, or other material, connected with a drain, and used for receiving filthy water, etc., as in a kitchen.
A hole or low place in land or rock, where waters sink and are lost; — called also sink hole.
The lowest part of a natural hollow or closed basin whence the water of one or more streams escapes by evaporation; as, the sink of the Humboldt River.
One who has sinned; especially, one who has sinned without repenting; hence, a persistent and incorrigible transgressor; one condemned by the law of God.
To act as a sinner.
q: Whether the charmer sinner it or saint it.

senses.d: A man of social authority and dignity; a lord; a master; a gentleman; — in this sense usually spelled sire.
q: He was crowned lord and sire.
In the election of a sir so rare.

senses.d: A title prefixed to the Christian name of a knight or a baronet.
q: Sir Horace Vere, his brother, was the principal in the active part.

senses.d: An English rendering of the LAtin Dominus, the academical title of a bachelor of arts; — formerly colloquially, and sometimes contemptuously, applied to the clergy.
q: Instead of a faithful and painful teacher, they hire a Sir John, which hath better skill in playing at tables, or in keeping of a garden, than in God's word.

senses.d: A respectful title, used in addressing a man, without being prefixed to his name; — used especially in speaking to elders or superiors; sometimes, also, used in the way of emphatic formality.

Sir.etym: [OE. sire, F. sire, contr. from the nominative L. senior an elder, elderly person, compar. of senex,senis, an aged person; akin to Gr. ��� old, Skr. sana, Goth. sineigs old, sinista eldest, Ir. & Gael. sean old, W. hen. Cf. Seignior, Senate, Seneschal, Senior, Senor, Signor, Sire, Sirrah.]

senses.d: To stay, as judicial proceedings; to delay or suspend; to stop.
To cause to take a place, as at the bar of a court; hence, to cite; to summon; to bring into court.
q: Some, however, have preposterously sisted nature as the first or generative principle.

Sist.etym: [L. sistere to bring to a stand, to stop.]

senses.d: A stay or suspension of proceedings; an order for a stay of proceedings.
A female who has the same parents with another person, or who has one of them only. In the latter case, she is more definitely called a half sister. The correlative of brother.
q: I am the sister of one Claudio.

senses.d: A woman who is closely allied to, or assocciated with, another person, as in the sdame faith, society, order, or community.
One of the same kind, or of the same condition; — generally used adjectively; as, sister fruits.

Sister.etym: [OE. sister, fr. Icel. systir; also suster, from AS. sweostor, sweoster, swuster, akin to OFries. sweester, suster, LG. süster, suster, D. zuster, OS. & OHG. swestar, G. schwester, Icel. systir, Sw. syster, Dan. söster, Goth. swistar, Lith. ses�, Russ. sestra, Pol. siostra, L. soror, Skr. svasr. √29

senses.d: To be sister to; to resemble closely.
To rest upon the haunches, or the lower extremity of the trunk of the body; — said of human beings, and sometimes of other animals; as, to sit on a sofa, on a chair, or on the ground.
q: And he came and took the book put of the right hand of him that sate upon the seat.
I pray you, jest, sir, as you sit at dinner.

senses.d: To perch; to rest with the feet drawn up, as birds do on a branch, pole, etc.
To remain in a state of repose; to rest; to abide; to rest in any position or condition.
q: And Moses said to . . . the children of Reuben, Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here?
Like a demigod here sit I in the sky.

senses.d: To lie, rest, or bear; to press or weigh; — with on; as, a weight or burden sits lightly upon him.
q: The calamity sits heavy on us.

senses.d: To be adjusted; to fit; as, a coat sits well or ill.
q: This new and gorgeous garment, majesty, Sits not so easy on me as you think.

senses.d: To suit one well or ill, as an act; to become; to befit; — used impersonally.
To cover and warm eggs for hatching, as a fowl; to brood; to incubate.
q: As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not.

senses.d: To have position, as at the point blown from; to hold a relative position; to have direction.
q: Like a good miller that knows how to grind, which way soever the wind sits.
Sits the wind in that quarter?

senses.d: To occupy a place or seat as a member of an official body; as, to sit in Congress.
To hold a session; to be in session for official business; — said of legislative assemblies, courts, etc.; as, the court sits in January; the aldermen sit to-night.
To take a position for the purpose of having some artistic representation of one's self made, as a picture or a bust; as, to sit to a painter.

Sit.etym: [OE. sitten, AS. sittan; akin to OS. sittian, OFries. sitta, D. zitten, G. sitzen, OHG. sizzen, Icel. sitja, SW. sitta, Dan. sidde, Goth. sitan, Russ. sidiete, L. sedere, Gr. ἔζεσθαι, Skr. sad. √154. Cf. Assess,Assize, Cathedral, Chair, Dissident, Excise, Insidious, Possess, Reside, Sanhedrim, Séanc

senses.d: To sit upon; to keep one's seat upon; as, he sits a horse well.
q: Hardly the muse can sit the headstrong horse.

senses.d: To cause to be seated or in a sitting posture; to furnish a seat to; — used reflexively.
q: They sat them down to weep.
Sit you down, father; rest you.

senses.d: To suit (well or ill); to become.
Since; afterwards; seeing that.
q: We need not fear them, sith Christ is with us.
Sith thou art rightful judge.

senses.d: Time.
q: And humbly thanked him a thousand sithes.

senses.d: Being in the state, or the position, of one who, or that which, sits.
The state or act of one who sits; the posture of one who occupies a seat.
A seat, or the space occupied by or allotted for a person, in a church, theater, etc.; as, the hall has 800 sittings.
The act or time of sitting, as to a portrait painter, photographer, etc.
The actual presence or meeting of any body of men in their seats, clothed with authority to transact business; a session; as, a sitting of the judges of the King's Bench, or of a commission.
q: The sitting closed in great agitation.

senses.d: The time during which one sits while doing something, as reading a book, playing a game, etc.
q: For the understanding of any one of St. Paul's Epistles I read it all through at one sitting.

senses.d: A brooding over eggs for hatching, as by fowls.
q: The male bird . . . amuses her with his songs during the whole time of her sitting.

senses.d: Having a site, situation, or location; being in a relative position; permanently fixed; placed; located; as, a town situated, or situate, on a hill or on the seashore.
Placed; residing.
q: Pleasure situate in hill and dale.

Situate.etym: [LL. situatus, from situare to place, fr. L. situs situation, site. See Site.]

senses.d: To place.
Manner in which an object is placed; location, esp. as related to something else; position; locality site; as, a house in a pleasant situation.
Position, as regards the conditions and circumstances of the case.
q: A situation of the greatest ease and tranquillity.

senses.d: Relative position; circumstances; temporary state or relation at a moment of action which excites interest, as of persons in a dramatic scene.
q: There's situation for you! there's an heroic group!

senses.d: Permanent position or employment; place; office; as, a situation in a store; a situation under government.

Situation.syn: State; position; seat; site; station; post; place; office; condition; case; plight. See State.

senses.d: The third month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year; — supposed to correspond nearly with our month of June.
One more than five; twice three; as, six yards.

Six.etym: [AS. six, seox, siex; akin to OFries. sex, D. zes, OS. & OHG. sehs, G. sechs, Icel., Sw., & Dan. sex, Goth. saíhs, Lith. szeszi, Russ. sheste, Gael. & Ir. se, W. chwech, L. sex, Gr. ��, Per. shesh, Skr. shash. √304. Cf. Hexagon, Hexameter, Samite, Senary, Sextant, Sice.]

senses.d: The number greater by a unit than five; the sum of three and three; six units or objects.
A symbol representing six units, as 6, vi., or VI.
Six times twenty; one hundred and twenty.
Six and ten; consisting of six and ten; fifteen and one more.

Sixteen.etym: [AS. sixt�ne, sixt�ne. See Six, and Ten, and cf. Sixty.]

senses.d: The number greater by a unit than fifteen; the sum of ten and six; sixteen units or objects.
A symbol representing sixteen units, as 16, or xvi.
Sixth after the tenth; next in order after the fifteenth.
Constituting or being one of sixteen equal parts into which anything is divided.
The quotient of a unit divided by sixteen; one of sixteen equal parts of one whole.
The next in order after the fifteenth; the sixth after the tenth.
An interval comprising two octaves and a second.
First after the fifth; next in order after the fifth.
Constituting or being one of six equal parts into which anything is divided.
The quotient of a unit divided by six; one of six equal parts which form a whole.
The next in order after the fifth.
The interval embracing six diatonic degrees of the scale.
Six times ten; fifty-nine and one more; threescore.

Sixty.etym: [AS. siextig; akin to G. sechzig, Goth. saíhs tigjus. See Six, Ten, and cf. Sixteen.]

senses.d: The sum of six times ten; sixty units or objects.
A symbol representing sixty units, as 60, lx., or LX.
Six.
A thin, weak glue used in various trades, as in painting, bookbinding, paper making, etc.
Any viscous substance, as gilder's varnish.

Size.etym: [OIt. sisa glue used by painters, shortened fr. assisa, fr. assidere, p. p. assiso, to make to sit, to seat, to place, L. assidere to sit down; ad + sidere to sit down, akin to sedere to sit. See Sit, v. i., and cf. Assize, Size bulk.]

senses.d: To cover with size; to prepare with size.
A settled quantity or allowance. See Assize.
An allowance of food and drink from the buttery, aside from the regular dinner at commons; — corresponding to battel at Oxford.
Extent of superficies or volume; bulk; bigness; magnitude; as, the size of a tree or of a mast; the size of a ship or of a rock.
Figurative bulk; condition as to rank, ability, character, etc.; as, the office demands a man of larger size.
q: Men of a less size and quality.
The middling or lower size of people.

senses.d: A conventional relative measure of dimension, as for shoes, gloves, and other articles made up for sale.
An instrument consisting of a number of perforated gauges fastened together at one end by a rivet, — used for ascertaining the size of pearls.

Size.etym: [Abbrev. from assize. See Assize, and cf. Size glue.]

senses.d: To fix the standard of.
To adjust or arrange according to size or bulk.
To swell; to increase the bulk of.
To bring or adjust anything exactly to a required dimension, as by cutting.
To take greater size; to increase in size.
q: Our desires give them fashion, and so, As they wax lesser, fall, as they size, grow.

senses.d: To order food or drink from the buttery; hence, to enter a score, as upon the buttery book.
Discrimination; judgment; propriety; reason; cause.
q: For great skill is, he prove that he wrought.

senses.d: Knowledge; understanding.
q: That by his fellowship he color might Both his estate and love from skill of any wight.
Nor want we skill or art.

senses.d: The familiar knowledge of any art or science, united with readiness and dexterity in execution or performance, or in the application of the art or science to practical purposes; power to discern and execute; ability to perceive and perform; expertness; aptitude; as, the skill of a mathematician, physician, surgeon, mechanic, etc.
q: Phocion, . . . by his great wisdom and skill at negotiations, diverted Alexander from the conquest of Athens.
Where patience her sweet skill imparts.

senses.d: Display of art; exercise of ability; contrivance; address.
q: Richard . . . by a thousand princely skills, gathering so much corn as if he meant not to return.

senses.d: Any particular art.
q: Learned in one skill, and in another kind of learning unskillful.

Skill.syn: Dexterity; adroitness; expertness; art; aptitude; ability.
Skill.etym: [Icel. skil a distinction, discernment; akin to skilja to separate, divide, distinguish, Sw. skilja,. skille to separate, skiel reason, right, justice, Sw. skäl reason, Lith. skelli to cleave. Cf. Shell, Shoal, a multitude.]

senses.d: To know; to understand.
q: To skill the arts of expressing our mind.

senses.d: To be knowing; to have understanding; to be dexterous in performance.
q: I can not skill of these thy ways.

senses.d: To make a difference; to signify; to matter; — used impersonally.
q: What skills it, if a bag of stones or gold About thy neck do drown thee?
It skills not talking of it.

senses.d: The external membranous integument of an animal.
The hide of an animal, separated from the body, whether green, dry, or tanned; especially, that of a small animal, as a calf, sheep, or goat.
A vessel made of skin, used for holding liquids. See Bottle, 1.
The bark or husk of a plant or fruit; the exterior coat of fruits and plants.
That part of a sail, when furled, which remains on the outside and covers the whole.

Skin.etym: [Icel. skinn; akin to Sw. skinn, Dan. skind, AS. scinn, G. schined to skin.]

senses.d: To strip off the skin or hide of; to flay; to peel; as, to skin an animal.
To cover with skin, or as with skin; hence, to cover superficially.
q: It will but skin and film the ulcerous place.

senses.d: To strip of money or property; to cheat.
To become covered with skin; as, a wound skins over.
To produce, in recitation, examination, etc., the work of another for one's own, or to use in such exercise cribs, memeoranda, etc., which are prohibited.
A basket. See Skep.
A basket on wheels, used in cotton factories.
An iron bucket, which slides between guides, for hoisting mineral and rock.
A charge of sirup in the pans.
A beehive; a skep.
To leap lightly; to move in leaps and hounds; — commonly implying a sportive spirit.
q: The lamb thy riot dooms to bleed to-day, Had he thy reason, would he skip and play?
So she drew her mother away skipping, dancing, and frisking fantastically.

senses.d: Fig.: To leave matters unnoticed, as in reading, speaking, or writing; to pass by, or overlook, portions of a thing; — often followed by over.

Skip.etym: [OE. skippen, of uncertain origin; cf. Icel. skopa run, skoppa to spin like a top, OSw. & dial. Sw. skimmpa to run, skimpa, skompa, to hop, skip; or Ir. sgiob to snatch, Gael. sgiab to start or move suddenly, to snatch, W. ysgipio to snatch.]

senses.d: To leap lightly over; as, to skip the rope.
To pass over or by without notice; to omit; to miss; as, to skip a line in reading; to skip a lesson.
q: They who have a mind to see the issue may skip these two chapters.

senses.d: To cause to skip; as, to skip a stone.
A light leap or bound.
The act of passing over an interval from one thing to another; an omission of a part.
A passage from one sound to another by more than a degree at once.
The lower and loose part of a coat, dress, or other like garment; the part below the waist; as, the skirt of a coat, a dress, or a mantle.
A loose edging to any part of a dress.
q: A narrow lace, or a small skirt of ruffled linen, which runs along the upper part of the stays before, and crosses the breast, being a part of the tucker, is called the modesty piece.

senses.d: Border; edge; margin; extreme part of anything
A petticoat.
The diaphragm, or midriff, in animals.

Skirt.etym: [OE. skyrt, of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. skyrta a shirt, Sw. skört a skirt, skjorta a shirt. See Shirt.]

senses.d: To cover with a skirt; to surround.
q: Skirted his loins and thighs with downy gold.

senses.d: To border; to form the border or edge of; to run along the edge of; as, the plain was skirted by rows of trees.
To be on the border; to live near the border, or extremity.
q: Savages . . . who skirt along our western frontiers.

senses.d: A school, company, or shoal.
q: A knavish skull of boys and girls did pelt at him.
These fishes enter in great flotes and skulls.

senses.d: The skeleton of the head of a vertebrate animal, including the brain case, or cranium, and the bones and cartilages of the face and mouth. See Illusts. of Carnivora, of Facial angles under Facial, and of Skeleton, in Appendix.
The head or brain; the seat of intelligence; mind.
q: Skulls that can not teach, and will not learn.

senses.d: A covering for the head; a skullcap.
q: Let me put on my skull first.

senses.d: A sort of oar. See Scull.

Skull.etym: [OE. skulle, sculle, scolle; akin to Scot. skull, skoll, a bowl, Sw. skalle skull, skal a shell, and E. scale; cf. G. hirnschale, Dan. hierneskal. Cf. Scale of a balance.]

senses.d: A cloud.
q: that blew so hideously and high, That it ne lefte not a sky In all the welkin long and broad.

senses.d: Hence, a shadow.
q: She passeth as it were a sky.

senses.d: The apparent arch, or vault, of heaven, which in a clear day is of a blue color; the heavens; the firmament; — sometimes in the plural.
q: The Norweyan banners flout the sky.

senses.d: The wheather; the climate.
q: Thou wert better in thy grave than to answer with thy uncovered body this extremity of the skies.

Sky.etym: [OE. skie a cloud, Icel. skȳ; akin to Sw. & Dan. sky; cf. AS. scūa, scūwa, shadow, Icel. skuggi; probably from the same root as E. scum. √158. See Scum, and cf. Hide skin, Obscure.]

senses.d: To hang (a picture on exhibition) near the top of a wall, where it can not be well seen.
q: Brother Academicians who skied his pictures.

senses.d: To throw towards the sky; as, to sky a ball at cricket.
Small coal; also, coal dust; culm.
A valley, or small, shallow dell.

Slack.etym: [Icel. slakki a slope on a mountain edge.]

senses.d: Lax; not tense; not hard drawn; not firmly extended; as, a slack rope.
Weak; not holding fast; as, a slack hand.
Remiss; backward; not using due diligence or care; not earnest or eager; as, slack in duty or service.
q: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness.

senses.d: Not violent, rapid, or pressing; slow; moderate; easy; as, business is slack.
q: C�sar . . . about sunset, hoisting sail with a slack southwest, at midnight was becalmed.

Slack.syn: Loose; relaxed; weak; remiss; backward; abated; diminished; inactive; slow; tardy; dull.
Slack.etym: [OE. slak, AS. sleac; akin to OS. slak, OHG. slah, Prov. G. schlack, Icel. slakr, Sw. slak; cf. Skr. sṛj to let loose, to throw. Cf. Slake.]

senses.d: Slackly; as, slack dried hops.
The part of anything that hangs loose, having no strain upon it; as, the slack of a rope or of a sail.
To become slack; to be made less tense, firm, or rigid; to decrease in tension; as, a wet cord slackens in dry weather.
To be remiss or backward; to be negligent.
To lose cohesion or solidity by a chemical combination with water; to slake; as, lime slacks.
To abate; to become less violent.
q: Whence these raging fires Will slacken, if his breath stir not their flames.

senses.d: To lose rapidity; to become more slow; as, a current of water slackens.
To languish; to fail; to flag.
To end; to cease; to desist; to slake.
q: That through your death your lineage should slack.
They will not of that firste purpose slack.

senses.d: To render slack; to make less tense or firm; as, to slack a rope; to slacken a bandage.
To neglect; to be remiss in.
q: Slack not the pressage.

senses.d: To deprive of cohesion by combining chemically with water; to slake; as, to slack lime.
To cause to become less eager; to repress; to make slow or less rapid; to retard; as, to slacken pursuit; to slacken industry.
q: I should be grieved, young prince, to think my presence Unbent your thoughts, and slackened 'em to arms.
In this business of growing rich, poor men should slack their pace.
With such delay Well plased, they slack their course.

senses.d: To cause to become less intense; to mitigate; to abate; to ease.
q: To respite, or deceive, or slack thy pain Of this ill mansion.

senses.d: The quality or state of being slack.

A false tale or report maliciously uttered, tending to injure the reputation of another; the malicious utterance of defamatory reports; the dissemination of malicious tales or suggestions to the injury of another.
q: Whether we speak evil of a man to his face or behind his back; the former way, indeed, seems to be the most generous, but yet is a great fault, and that which we call “reviling;” the latter is more mean and base, and that which we properly call “slander”, or “Backbiting.”
make the careful magistrate The mark of slander.

senses.d: Disgrace; reproach; dishonor; opprobrium.
q: Thou slander of thy mother's heavy womb.

senses.d: Formerly, defamation generally, whether oral or written; in modern usage, defamation by words spoken; utterance of false, malicious, and defamatory words, tending to the damage and derogation of another; calumny. See the Note under Defamation.

Slander.etym: [OE. sclandere, OF. esclandre, esclandle, escandre, F. esclandre, fr. L. scandalum, Gr. ��� a snare, stumbling block, offense, scandal; probably originally, the spring of a trap, and akin to Skr. skand to spring, leap. See Scan, and cf. Scandal.]

senses.d: To defame; to injure by maliciously uttering a false report; to tarnish or impair the reputation of by false tales maliciously told or propagated; to calumniate.
q: O, do not slander him, for he is kind.

senses.d: To bring discredit or shame upon by one's acts.
q: Tax not so bad a voice To slander music any more than once.

Slander.syn: To asperse; defame; calumniate; vilify; malign; belie; scandalize; reproach. See Asperse.

senses.d: One who slanders; a defamer; a calumniator.
Given or disposed to slander; uttering slander.
Embodying or containing slander; calumnious; as, slanderous words, speeches, or reports.
Any long, narrow piece of land; a promontory.
A fetter worn on the leg by a convict.

Low, vulgar, unauthorized language; a popular but unauthorized word, phrase, or mode of expression; also, the jargon of some particular calling or class in society; low popular cant; as, the slang of the theater, of college, of sailors, etc.

Slang.etym: [Said to be of Gypsy origin; but probably from Scand., and akin to E. sling; cf. Norw. sleng a slinging, an invention, device, slengja to sling, to cast, slengja kjeften (literally, to sling the jaw) to use abusive language, to use slang, slenjeord (ord = word) an insulting word, a new word that has

senses.d: To address with slang or ribaldry; to insult with vulgar language.
q: Every gentleman abused by a cabman or slanged by a bargee was bound there and then to take off his coat and challenge him to fisticuffs.

senses.d: The act of killing.
The extensive, violent, bloody, or wanton destruction of life; carnage.
q: On war and mutual slaughter bent.

senses.d: The act of killing cattle or other beasts for market.

Slaughter.etym: [OE. slautir, slaughter, slaghter, Icel. slātr slain flesh, modified by OE. slaught, slaht, slaughter, fr. AS. sleaht a stroke, blow; both from the root of E. slay. See Slay, v. t., and cf. Onslaught.]

senses.d: To visit with great destruction of life; to kill; to slay in battle.
q: Your castle is surprised; your wife and babes Savagely slaughtered.

senses.d: To butcher; to kill for the market, as beasts.
One of a race of people occupying a large part of Eastern and Northern Europe, including the Russians, Bulgarians, Roumanians, Servo-Croats, Slovenes, Poles, Czechs, Wends or Sorbs, Slovaks, etc.

Slav.etym: [A word originally meaning, intelligible, and used to contrast the people so called with foreigners who spoke languages unintelligible to the Slavs; akin to OSlav. slovo a word, slava fame, Skr. çru to hear. Cf. Loud.]

senses.d: A person who is held in bondage to another; one who is wholly subject to the will of another; one who is held as a chattel; one who has no freedom of action, but whose person and services are wholly under the control of another.
q: Art thou our slave, Our captive, at the public mill our drudge?

senses.d: One who has lost the power of resistance; one who surrenders himself to any power whatever; as, a slave to passion, to lust, to strong drink, to ambition.
A drudge; one who labors like a slave.
An abject person; a wretch.

Slave.syn: Bond servant; bondman; bondslave; captive; henchman; vassal; dependent; drudge. See Serf.
Slave.etym: [Cf. F. esclave, D. slaaf, Dan. slave, sclave, Sw. slaf, all fr. G. sklave, MHG. also slave, from the national name of the Slavonians, or Sclavonians (in LL. Slavi or Sclavi), who were frequently made slaves by the Germans. See Slav.]

senses.d: To drudge; to toil; to labor as a slave.
To enslave.
To put to death with a weapon, or by violence; hence, to kill; to put an end to; to destroy.
q: With this sword then will I slay you both.
I will slay the last of them with the sword.
I'll slay more gazers than the basilisk.

Slay.etym: [OE. slan, sl�n, sleen, slee, AS. sleán to strike, beat, slay; akin to OFries. slā, D. slaan, OS. & OHG. slahan, G. schlagen, Icel. slā, Dan. slaae, Sw. sl�, Goth. slahan; perhaps akin to L. lacerare to tear to pieces, Gr. ����, E. lacerate. Cf. Slaughter, Sledge a hammer, Sley.]

senses.d: One who slays; a killer; a murderer; a destroyer of life.
To slay.
To take rest by a suspension of the voluntary exercise of the powers of the body and mind, and an apathy of the organs of sense; to slumber.
q: Watching at the head of these that sleep.

senses.d: To be careless, inattentive, or uncouncerned; not to be vigilant; to live thoughtlessly.
q: We sleep over our happiness.

senses.d: To be dead; to lie in the grave.
q: Them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him.

senses.d: To be, or appear to be, in repose; to be quiet; to be unemployed, unused, or unagitated; to rest; to lie dormant; as, a question sleeps for the present; the law sleeps.
q: How sweet the moonlight sleep upon this bank!

Sleep.etym: [OE. slepen, AS. sl�pan; akin to OFries. sl�pa, OS. slāpan, D. slapen, OHG. slāfan, G. schlafen, Goth. sl�pan, and G. schlaff slack, loose, and L. labi to glide, slide, labare to totter. Cf. Lapse.]

senses.d: To be slumbering in; — followed by a cognate object; as, to sleep a dreamless sleep.
To give sleep to; to furnish with accomodations for sleeping; to lodge.

A natural and healthy, but temporary and periodical, suspension of the functions of the organs of sense, as well as of those of the voluntary and rational soul; that state of the animal in which there is a lessened acuteness of sensory perception, a confusion of ideas, and a loss of mental control, followed by a more or less unconscious state.
q: O sleep, thou ape of death.

Sleep.syn: Slumber; repose; rest; nap; doze; drowse.
Sleep.etym: [AS. slǣp; akin to OFries. slēp, OS. slāp, D. slaap, OHG. slāf, G. schlaf, Goth. slēps. See Sleep, v. i.]

senses.d: One who sleeps; a slumberer; hence, a drone, or lazy person.
That which lies dormant, as a law.
A sleeping car.
An animal that hibernates, as the bear.
A large fresh-water gobioid fish (Eleotris dormatrix).
Something lying in a reclining posture or position.

One of the pieces of timber, stone, or iron, on or near the level of the ground, for the support of some superstructure, to steady framework, to keep in place the rails of a railway, etc.; a stringpiece.
One of the joists, or roughly shaped timbers, laid directly upon the ground, to receive the flooring of the ground story.
One of the knees which connect the transoms to the after timbers on the ship's quarter.
The lowest, or bottom, tier of casks.

Sleeper.etym: [Cf. Norw. sleip a sleeper (a timber), as adj., slippery, smooth. See Slape.]

senses.d: Cunning; craft; artful practice.
An artful trick; sly artifice; a feat so dexterous that the manner of performance escapes observation.
q: The world hath many subtle sleights.

senses.d: Dexterous practice; dexterity; skill.

Sleight.etym: [OE. sleighte, sleihte, sleithe, Icel. sl�g� (for sl�g�) slyness, cunning, fr. sl�gr (for sl�gr) sly, cunning. See Sly.]

senses.d: To move along the surface of any body by slipping, or without walking or rolling; to slip; to glide; as, snow slides down the mountain's side.
Especially, to move over snow or ice with a smooth, uninterrupted motion, as on a sled moving by the force of gravity, or on the feet.
q: They bathe in summer, and in winter slide.

senses.d: To pass inadvertently.
q: Beware thou slide not by it.

senses.d: To pass along smoothly or unobservedly; to move gently onward without friction or hindrance; as, a ship or boat slides through the water.
q: Ages shall slide away without perceiving.
Parts answering parts shall slide into a whole.

senses.d: To slip when walking or standing; to fall.
q: Their foot shall slide in due time.

senses.d: To pass from one note to another with no perceptible cassation of sound.
To pass out of one's thought as not being of any consequence.
q: With good hope let he sorrow slide.
With a calm carelessness letting everything slide.

Slide.etym: [OE. sliden, AS. slīdan; akin to MHG. slīten, also to AS. slidor slippery, E. sled, Lith. slidus slippery. Cf. Sled.]

senses.d: To cause to slide; to thrust along; as, to slide one piece of timber along another.
To pass or put imperceptibly; to slip; as, to slide in a word to vary the sense of a question.
The act of sliding; as, a slide on the ice.
Smooth, even passage or progress.
q: A better slide into their business.

senses.d: That on which anything moves by sliding.
That which operates by sliding.
A plate or slip of glass on which is a picture or delineation to be exhibited by means of a magic lantern, stereopticon, or the like; a plate on which is an object to be examined with a microscope.
The descent of a mass of earth, rock, or snow down a hill or mountain side; as, a land slide, or a snow slide; also, the track of bare rock left by a land slide.
A small dislocation in beds of rock along a line of fissure.
A grace consisting of two or more small notes moving by conjoint degrees, and leading to a principal note either above or below.
A sound which, by a gradual change in the position of the vocal organs, passes imperceptibly into another sound.
Same as Guide bar, under Guide.
Sleight.
To overthrow; to demolish.
To make even or level.
To throw heedlessly.
q: The rogue slighted me into the river.

Slight.etym: [Cf. D. slechten to level, to demolish.]

senses.d: Not decidedly marked; not forcible; inconsiderable; unimportant; insignificant; not severe; weak; gentle; — applied in a great variety of circumstances; as, a slight (i.e., feeble) effort; a slight (i.e., perishable) structure; a slight (i.e., not deep) impression; a slight (i.e., not convincing) argument; a slight (i.e., not thorough) examination; slight (i.e., not severe) pain, and the like.
q: Slight is the subject, but not so the praise.
Some firmly embrace doctrines upon slight grounds.

senses.d: Not stout or heavy; slender.
q: His own figure, which was formerly so slight.

senses.d: Foolish; silly; weak in intellect.

Slight.etym: [OE. sli�t, sleght, probably from OD. slicht, slecht, simple, plain, D. slecht; akin to OFries. sliucht, G. schlecht, schlicht, OHG. sleht smooth, simple, Icel. sl�ttr smooth, Sw. slät, Goth. slaíhts; or uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To disregard, as of little value and unworthy of notice; to make light of; as, to slight the divine commands.
q: The wretch who slights the bounty of the skies.
Beware . . . lest the like befall . . . If they transgress and slight that sole command.
This my long-sufferance, and my day of grace, Those who neglect and scorn shall never taste.

senses.d: The act of slighting; the manifestation of a moderate degree of contempt, as by neglect or oversight; neglect; indignity.

Slight.syn: Neglect; disregard; inattention; contempt; disdain; scorn; disgrace; indignity; disparagement.

senses.d: Slightly.
q: Think not so slight of glory.

senses.d: In a slight manner.
Slightingly; negligently.
Soft, moist earth or clay, having an adhesive quality; viscous mud.
q: As it ebbs, the seedsman Upon the slime and ooze scatters his grain.

senses.d: Any mucilaginous substance; any substance of a dirty nature, that is moist, soft, and adhesive.
Bitumen.
q: Slime had they for mortar.

senses.d: Mud containing metallic ore, obtained in the preparatory dressing.
A mucuslike substance which exudes from the bodies of certain animals.

Slime.etym: [OE. slim, AS. slīm; akin to D. slijm, G. schleim, MHG. slīmen to make smooth, Icel. slīm slime, Dan. sliim; cf. L. limare to file, polish, levis smooth, Gr. ���; or cf. L. limus mud.]

senses.d: To smear with slime.

An instrument for throwing stones or other missiles, consisting of a short strap with two strings fastened to its ends, or with a string fastened to one end and a light stick to the other. The missile being lodged in a hole in the strap, the ends of the string are taken in the hand, and the whole whirled rapidly round until, by loosing one end, the missile is let fly with centrifugal force.
The act or motion of hurling as with a sling; a throw; figuratively, a stroke.
q: The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune.
At one sling Of thy victorius arm, well-pleasing Son.

senses.d: A contrivance for sustaining anything by suspension

Sling.etym: [OE. slinge; akin to OD. slinge, D. slinger, OHG. slinga; cf. OF. eslingue, of German origin. See Sling, v. t.]

senses.d: To throw with a sling.
To throw; to hurl; to cast.
To hang so as to swing; as, to sling a pack.
To pass a rope round, as a cask, gun, etc., preparatory to attaching a hoisting or lowering tackle.

Sling.etym: [AS. slingan; akin to D. slingeren, G. schlingen, to wind, to twist, to creep, OHG. slingan to wind, to twist, to move to and fro, Icel. slyngva, slöngva, to sling, Sw. slunga, Dan. slynge, Lith. slinkti to creep.]

senses.d: A drink composed of spirit (usually gin) and water sweetened.
One who slings, or uses a sling.
To move along the surface of a thing without bounding, rolling, or stepping; to slide; to glide.
To slide; to lose one's footing or one's hold; not to tread firmly; as, it is necessary to walk carefully lest the foot should slip.
To move or fly (out of place); to shoot; — often with out, off, etc.; as, a bone may slip out of its place.
To depart, withdraw, enter, appear, intrude, or escape as if by sliding; to go or come in a quiet, furtive manner; as, some errors slipped into the work.
q: Thus one tradesman slips away, To give his partner fairer play.
Thrice the flitting shadow slipped away.

senses.d: To err; to fall into error or fault.
q: There is one that slippeth in his speech, but not from his heart.
Cry, “Havoc,” and let slip the dogs of war.

Slip.etym: [OE. slippen; akin to LG. & D. slippen, MHG. slipfen (cf. Dan. slippe, Sw. slippa, Icel. sleppa), and fr. OE. slipen, AS. slīpan (in comp.), akin to G. schleifen to slide, glide, drag, whet, OHG. slīfan to slide, glide, make smooth, Icel. slīpa to whet; cf. also AS. sl�pan, Goth. sliupan, OS. slopia

senses.d: To cause to move smoothly and quickly; to slide; to convey gently or secretly.
q: He tried to slip a powder into her drink.

senses.d: To omit; to loose by negligence.
q: And slip no advantage That my secure you.

senses.d: To cut slips from; to cut; to take off; to make a slip or slips of; as, to slip a piece of cloth or paper.
q: The branches also may be slipped and planted.

senses.d: To let loose in pursuit of game, as a greyhound.
q: Lucento slipped me like his greyhound.

senses.d: To cause to slip or slide off, or out of place; as, a horse slips his bridle; a dog slips his collar.
To bring forth (young) prematurely; to slink.
The act of slipping; as, a slip on the ice.
An unintentional error or fault; a false step.
q: This good man's slip mended his pace to martyrdom.

senses.d: A twig separated from the main stock; a cutting; a scion; hence, a descendant; as, a slip from a vine.
q: A native slip to us from foreign seeds.
The girlish slip of a Sicilian bride.

senses.d: A slender piece; a strip; as, a slip of paper.
q: Moonlit slips of silver cloud.
A thin slip of a girl, like a new moon Sure to be rounded into beauty soon.

senses.d: A leash or string by which a dog is held; — so called from its being made in such a manner as to slip, or become loose, by relaxation of the hand.
q: We stalked over the extensive plains with Killbuck and Lena in the slips, in search of deer.

senses.d: An escape; a secret or unexpected desertion; as, to give one the slip.
A portion of the columns of a newspaper or other work struck off by itself; a proof from a column of type when set up and in the galley.
Any covering easily slipped on.
A counterfeit piece of money, being brass covered with silver.
Matter found in troughs of grindstones after the grinding of edge tools.
Potter's clay in a very liquid state, used for the decoration of ceramic ware, and also as a cement for handles and other applied parts.
A particular quantity of yarn.
The retrograde movement on a pulley of a belt as it slips.
The difference between the actual and synchronous speed of an induction motor.
A memorandum of the particulars of a risk for which a policy is to be executed. It usually bears the broker's name and is initiated by the underwrites.
Having the quality opposite to adhesiveness; allowing or causing anything to slip or move smoothly, rapidly, and easily upon the surface; smooth; glib; as, oily substances render things slippery.
Not affording firm ground for confidence; as, a slippery promise.
q: The slippery tops of human state.

senses.d: Not easily held; liable or apt to slip away.
q: The slippery god will try to loose his hold.

senses.d: Liable to slip; not standing firm.
Unstable; changeable; mutable; uncertain; inconstant; fickle.
Uncertain in effect.
Wanton; unchaste; loose in morals.
Addicted to sloth; inactive; sluggish; lazy; indolent; idle.
q: He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster.

senses.d: Slew.
Moving a short space in a relatively long time; not swift; not quick in motion; not rapid; moderate; deliberate; as, a slow stream; a slow motion.
Not happening in a short time; gradual; late.
q: These changes in the heavens, though slow, produced Like change on sea and land, sidereal blast.

senses.d: Not ready; not prompt or quick; dilatory; sluggish; as, slow of speech, and slow of tongue.
q: Fixed on defense, the Trojans are not slow To guard their shore from an expected foe.

senses.d: Not hasty; not precipitate; acting with deliberation; tardy; inactive.
q: He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding.

senses.d: Behind in time; indicating a time earlier than the true time; as, the clock or watch is slow.
Not advancing or improving rapidly; as, the slow growth of arts and sciences.
Heavy in wit; not alert, prompt, or spirited; wearisome; dull.

Slow.syn: Dilatory; late; lingering; tardy; sluggish; dull; inactive.
Slow.etym: [OE. slow, slaw, AS. slāw; akin to OS. slēu blunt, dull, D. sleeuw, slee, sour, OHG. slēo blunt, dull, Icel. slōr, slær, Dan. slöv, Sw. slö. Cf. Sloe, and Sloth.]

senses.d: Slowly.
q: Let him have time to mark how slow time goes In time of sorrow.

senses.d: To render slow; to slacken the speed of; to retard; to delay; as, to slow a steamer.
To go slower; — often with up; as, the train slowed up before crossing the bridge.
A moth.
In a slow manner; moderately; not rapidly; not early; not rashly; not readly; tardly.
A person habitually lazy, idle, and inactive; a drone.
q: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.

senses.d: Sluggish; lazy.
An artifical passage for water, fitted with a valve or gate, as in a mill stream, for stopping or regulating the flow; also, a water gate or flood gate.
Hence, an opening or channel through which anything flows; a source of supply.
q: Each sluice of affluent fortune opened soon.
This home familiarity . . . opens the sluices of sensibility.

senses.d: The stream flowing through a flood gate.
A long box or trough through which water flows, — used for washing auriferous earth.

Sluice.etym: [OF. escluse, F. écluse, LL. exclusa, sclusa, from L. excludere, exclusum, to shut out: cf. D. sluis sluice, from the Old French. See Exclude.]

senses.d: To emit by, or as by, flood gates.
To wet copiously, as by opening a sluice; as, to sluice meadows.
q: He dried his neck and face, which he had been sluicing with cold water.

senses.d: To wash with, or in, a stream of water running through a sluice; as, to sluice eart or gold dust in mining.
To sleep; especially, to sleep lightly; to doze.
q: He that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.

senses.d: To be in a state of negligence, sloth, supineness, or inactivity.

Slumber.etym: [OE. slombren, slumberen, slumeren, AS. slumerian, fr. sluma slumber; akin to D. sluimeren to slumber, MHG. slummern, slumen, G. schlummern, Dan. slumre, Sw. slumra, Goth. slawan to be silent.]

senses.d: To lay to sleep.
To stun; to stupefy.
Sleep; especially, light sleep; sleep that is not deep or sound; repose.
q: He at last fell into a slumber, and thence into a fast sleep, which detained him in that place until it was almost night.
Fast asleep? It is no matter; Enjoy the honey-heavy dew of slumber.
Rest to my soul, and slumber to my eyes.

senses.d: Having little size, compared with other things of the same kind; little in quantity or degree; diminutive; not large or extended in dimension; not great; not much; inconsiderable; as, a small man; a small river.
q: To compare Great things with small.

senses.d: Being of slight consequence; feeble in influence or importance; unimportant; trivial; insignificant; as, a small fault; a small business.
Envincing little worth or ability; not large-minded; — sometimes, in reproach, paltry; mean.
q: A true delineation of the smallest man is capable of interesting the greatest man.

senses.d: Not prolonged in duration; not extended in time; short; as, after a small space.
Weak; slender; fine; gentle; soft; not loud.

Small.etym: [OE. small, AS. smæl; akin to D. smal narrow, OS. & OHG. smal small, G. schmal narrow, Dan. & Sw. smal, Goth. smals small, Icel. smali small cattle, sheep, or goats; cf. Gr. μη̑λον a sheep or goat.]

senses.d: In or to small extent, quantity, or degree; little; slightly.
Not loudly; faintly; timidly.
q: You may speak as small as you will.

senses.d: The small or slender part of a thing; as, the small of the leg or of the back.
Smallclothes.
Same as Little go. See under Little, a.
To make little or less.
To feel a lively, pungent local pain; — said of some part of the body as the seat of irritation; as, my finger smarts; these wounds smart.
To feel a pungent pain of mind; to feel sharp pain or grief; to suffer; to feel the sting of evil.
q: No creature smarts so little as a fool.
He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it.

Smart.etym: [OE. smarten, AS. smeortan; akin to D. smarten, smerten, G. schmerzen, OHG. smerzan, Dan. smerte, SW. smärta, D. smart, smert, a pain, G. schmerz, Ohg. smerzo, and probably to L. mordere to bite; cf. Gr. ����, �����, terrible, fearful, Skr. m�d to rub, crush. Cf. Morsel.]

senses.d: To cause a smart in.
Quick, pungent, lively pain; a pricking local pain, as the pain from puncture by nettles.
Severe, pungent pain of mind; pungent grief; as, the smart of affliction.
q: To stand 'twixt us and our deserved smart.
Counsel mitigates the greatest smart.

senses.d: A fellow who affects smartness, briskness, and vivacity; a dandy.
Smart money (see below).
Causing a smart; pungent; pricking; as, a smart stroke or taste.
q: How smart lash that speech doth give my conscience.

senses.d: Keen; severe; poignant; as, smart pain.
Vigorous; sharp; severe.
Accomplishing, or able to accomplish, results quickly; active; sharp; clever.
Efficient; vigorous; brilliant.
Marked by acuteness or shrewdness; quick in suggestion or reply; vivacious; witty; as, a smart reply; a smart saying.
q: Who, for the poor renown of being smart Would leave a sting within a brother's heart?
A sentence or two, . . . which I thought very smart.

senses.d: Pretentious; showy; spruce; as, a smart gown.
Brisk; fresh; as, a smart breeze.

Smart.syn: Pungent; poignant; sharp; tart; acute; quick; lively; brisk; witty; clever; keen; dashy; showy.

senses.d: To perceive by the olfactory nerves, or organs of smell; to have a sensation of, excited through the nasal organs when affected by the appropriate materials or qualities; to obtain the scent of; as, to smell a rose; to smell perfumes.
To detect or perceive, as if by the sense of smell; to scent out; — often with out.
q: Can you smell him out by that?

senses.d: To give heed to.
q: From that time forward I began to smellthe Word of God, and forsook the school doctors.

Smell.etym: [OE. smellen, smillen, smullen; cf. LG. smellen, smelen, smölen, schmelen, to smoke, to reek, D. smeulen to smolder, and E. smolder. Cf. Smell, n.]

senses.d: To affect the olfactory nerves; to have an odor or scent; — often followed by of; as, to smell of smoke, or of musk.
To have a particular tincture or smack of any quality; to savor; as, a report smells of calumny.
q: Praises in an enemy are superfluous, or smell of craft.

senses.d: To exercise the sense of smell.
To exercise sagacity.
The sense or faculty by which certain qualities of bodies are perceived through the instrumentally of the olfactory nerves. See Sense.
The quality of any thing or substance, or emanation therefrom, which affects the olfactory organs; odor; scent; fragrance; perfume; as, the smell of mint.
q: Breathing the smell of field and grove.
That which, above all others, yields the sweetest smell in the air, is the violent.

Smell.etym: [OE. smel, smil, smul, smeol. See Smell, v. t.]

senses.d: The act of one who smells.
The sense by which odors are perceived; the sense of smell.
To strike; to inflict a blow upon with the hand, or with any instrument held in the hand, or with a missile thrown by the hand; as, to smite with the fist, with a rod, sword, spear, or stone.
q: Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
And David . . . took thence a stone, and slang it, and smote the Philistine in his forehead.

senses.d: To cause to strike; to use as an instrument in striking or hurling.
q: Prophesy, and smite thine hands together.
Saul . . . smote the javelin into the wall.

senses.d: To destroy the life of by beating, or by weapons of any kind; to slay by a blow; to kill; as, to smite one with the sword, or with an arrow or other instrument.
To put to rout in battle; to overthrow by war.
To blast; to destroy the life or vigor of, as by a stroke or by some visitation.
q: The flax and the barly was smitten.

senses.d: To afflict; to chasten; to punish.
q: Let us not mistake God's goodness, nor imagine, because he smites us, that we are forsaken by him.

senses.d: To strike or affect with passion, as love or fear.
q: The charms that smite the simple heart.
Smit with the love of sister arts we came.

Smite.etym: [AS. smītan to smite, to soil, pollute; akin to OFries. smīta to smite, LG. smiten, D. smijten, G. schmeissen, OHG. smīzan to smear, stroke, OSw. & dial. Sw. smita to smite, Dan. smide to throw, Goth. bismeitan, to anoint, besmear; cf. Skr. mēd to be fat. The original sense seems to have been, to da

senses.d: To strike; to collide; to beat.
q: The heart melteth, and the knees smite together.

senses.d: The act of smiting; a blow.
One who smites.
q: I give my back to the smiters.

senses.d: One who forges with the hammer; one who works in metals; as, a blacksmith, goldsmith, silversmith, and the like.
q: Nor yet the smith hath learned to form a sword.

senses.d: One who makes or effects anything.

Smith.etym: [AS. smið; akin to D. smid, G. schmied, OHG. smid, Icel. smiðr, Dan. & Sw. smed, Goth. smiþa (in comp.); cf. Gr. σμίλη a sort of knife, σμινύη a hoe, mattock.]

senses.d: To beat into shape; to forge.
q: What smith that any smitheth.

senses.d: The visible exhalation, vapor, or substance that escapes, or expelled, from a burning body, especially from burning vegetable matter, as wood, coal, peat, or the like.
That which resembles smoke; a vapor; a mist.
Anything unsubstantial, as idle talk.
The act of smoking, esp. of smoking tobacco; as, to have a smoke.

Smoke.etym: [AS. smoca, fr. smeócan to smoke; akin to LG. & D. smook smoke, Dan. smög, G. schmauch, and perh. to Gr. ��� to burn in a smoldering fire; cf. Lith. smaugti to choke.]

senses.d: To emit smoke; to throw off volatile matter in the form of vapor or exhalation; to reek.
q: Hard by a cottage chimney smokes.

senses.d: Hence, to burn; to be kindled; to rage.
q: The anger of the Lord and his jealousy shall smoke agains. that man.

senses.d: To raise a dust or smoke by rapid motion.
q: Proud of his steeds, he smokes along the field.

senses.d: To draw into the mouth the smoke of tobacco burning in a pipe or in the form of a cigar, cigarette, etc.; to habitually use tobacco in this manner.
To suffer severely; to be punished.
q: Some of you shall smoke for it in Rome.

Smoke.etym: [AS. smocian; akin to D. smoken, G. schmauchen, Dan. smöge. See Smoke, n.]

senses.d: To apply smoke to; to hang in smoke; to disinfect, to cure, etc., by smoke; as, to smoke or fumigate infected clothing; to smoke beef or hams for preservation.
To fill or scent with smoke; hence, to fill with incense; to perfume.
To smell out; to hunt out; to find out; to detect.
q: I alone Smoked his true person, talked with him.
He was first smoked by the old Lord Lafeu.
Upon that . . . I began to smoke that they were a parcel of mummers.

senses.d: To ridicule to the face; to quiz.
To inhale and puff out the smoke of, as tobacco; to burn or use in smoking; as, to smoke a pipe or a cigar.
To subject to the operation of smoke, for the purpose of annoying or driving out; — often with out; as, to smoke a woodchuck out of his burrow.
Having an even surface, or a surface so even that no roughness or points can be perceived by the touch; not rough; as, smooth glass; smooth porcelain.
q: The outlines must be smooth, imperceptible to the touch, and even, without eminence or cavities.

senses.d: Evenly spread or arranged; sleek; as, smooth hair.
Gently flowing; moving equably; not ruffled or obstructed; as, a smooth stream.
Flowing or uttered without check, obstruction, or hesitation; not harsh; voluble; even; fluent.
q: The only smooth poet of those times.
Waller was smooth; but Dryden taught to join The varying verse, the full-resounding line.
When sage Minerva rose, From her sweet lips smooth elocution flows.

senses.d: Bland; mild; smoothing; fattering.
q: This smooth discourse and mild behavior oft Conceal a traitor.

senses.d: Causing no resistance to a body sliding along its surface; frictionless.

Smooth.syn: Even; plain; level; flat; polished; glossy; sleek; soft; bland; mild; soothing; voluble; flattering; adulatory; deceptive.
Smooth.etym: [OE. smothe, smethe, AS. smēðe, smœðe, where ē, œ, come from an older ō; cf. LG. smöde, smöe, smödig; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: Smoothly.
q: Smooth runs the water where the brook is deep.

senses.d: The act of making smooth; a stroke which smooths.
That which is smooth; the smooth part of anything.
To make smooth; to make even on the surface by any means; as, to smooth a board with a plane; to smooth cloth with an iron.
To free from obstruction; to make easy.
q: Thou, Abelard! the last sad office pay, And smooth my passage to the realms of day.

senses.d: To free from harshness; to make flowing.
q: In their motions harmony divine So smooths her charming tones that God's own ear Listens delighted.

senses.d: To palliate; to gloze; as, to smooth over a fault.
To give a smooth or calm appearance to.
q: Each perturbation smoothed with outward calm.

senses.d: To ease; to regulate.

Smooth.etym: [OE. smothen, smethen, AS. smēðian; cf. LG. smöden. See Smooth, a.]

senses.d: To flatter; to use blandishment.
q: Because I can not flatter and speak fair, Smile in men's faces, smooth, deceive and cog.

senses.d: One who, or that which, smooths.

Any one of numerous species of terrestrial air-breathing gastropods belonging to the genus Helix and many allied genera of the family Helicidæ. They are abundant in nearly all parts of the world except the arctic regions, and feed almost entirely on vegetation; a land snail.
Hence, a drone; a slow-moving person or thing.
A spiral cam, or a flat piece of metal of spirally curved outline, used for giving motion to, or changing the position of, another part, as the hammer tail of a striking clock.
A tortoise; in ancient warfare, a movable roof or shed to protect besiegers; a testudo.
q: They had also all manner of gynes . . . that needful is taking or sieging of castle or of city, as snails, that was naught else but hollow pavises and targets, under the which men, when they fought, were heled , . . . as the snail is in his house; therefore they cleped them snails.

senses.d: The pod of the sanil clover.

Snail.etym: [OE. snaile, AS. snægel, snegel, snægl; akin to G. schnecke, OHG. snecko, Dan. snegl, Icel. snigill.]

senses.d: To snarl.

Snar.etym: [Akin to LG. & OD. snarren, G. schnarren, E. snore. See Snore, and cf. Snarl to growl.]

senses.d: A contrivance, often consisting of a noose of cord, or the like, by which a bird or other animal may be entangled and caught; a trap; a gin.
Hence, anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.
q: If thou retire, the Dauphin, well appointed, Stands with the snares of war to tangle thee.

senses.d: The gut or string stretched across the lower head of a drum.
An instrument, consisting usually of a wireloop or noose, for removing tumors, etc., by avulsion.

Snare.etym: [AS. sneara cord, a string; akin to D. snoer, G. schnur, OHG. snour a cord, snarahha a noose, Dan. snare, Sw. & Icel. snara, Goth. sn�rj� a basket; and probably also to E. needle. See Needle, and cf. Snarl to entangle.]

senses.d: To catch with a snare; to insnare; to entangle; hence, to bring into unexpected evil, perplexity, or danger.
q: Lest that too heavenly form . . . snare them.
The mournful crocodile With sorrow snares relenting passengers.

senses.d: To take or seize hastily, abruptly, or without permission or ceremony; as, to snatch a loaf or a kiss.
q: When half our knowledge we must snatch, not take.

senses.d: To seize and transport away; to rap.

Snatch.syn: To twitch; pluck; grab; catch; grasp; gripe.
Snatch.etym: [OE. snachen, snechen; akin to D. snakken to gasp, to long (for), to desire. Cf. Snack, n., Sneck.]

senses.d: To attempt to seize something suddenly; to catch; — often with at; as, to snatch at a rope.
A hasty catching or seizing; a grab; a catching at, or attempt to seize, suddenly.
A short period of vigorous action; as, a snatch at weeding after a shower.
q: They move by fits and snatches.

senses.d: A small piece, fragment, or quantity; a broken part; a scrap.
q: We have often little snatches of sunshine.
Leave me your snatches, and yield me a direct answer.

senses.d: To emit air, chiefly through the nose, audibly and violently, by a kind of involuntary convulsive force, occasioned by irritation of the inner membrane of the nose.

Sneeze.etym: [OE. snesen; of uncertain origin; cf. D. snuse to sniff, E. neese, and AS. fneósan.]

senses.d: A sudden and violent ejection of air with an audible sound, chiefly through the nose.
To force the air with violence through the nose, so as to make a noise, as do high-spirited horsed in prancing and play.
To snore.
To laugh out loudly.

Snort.etym: [OE. snorten; akin to snoren. See Snore.]

senses.d: The act of snorting; the sound produced in snorting.
To expel throught the nostrils with a snort; to utter with a snort.
The long, projecting nose of a beast, as of swine.
The nose of a man; — in contempt.
The nozzle of a pipe, hose, etc.
The anterior prolongation of the head of a gastropod; — called also rostrum.

Snout.etym: [OE. snoute, probably of Scand, or Low German origin; cf. LG. snute, D. snuit, G. schnauze, Sw. snut, snyte, Dan. snude, Icel. sn�ta to blow the nose; probably akin to E. snuff, v.t. Cf. Snite, Snot, Snuff.]

senses.d: To furnish with a nozzle or point.
A square-rigged vessel, differing from a brig only in that she has a trysail mast close abaft the mainmast, on which a large trysail is hoisted.

Snow.etym: [LG. snaue, or D. snaauw, from LG. snau a snout, a beak.]

senses.d: Watery particles congealed into white or transparent crystals or flakes in the air, and falling to the earth, exhibiting a great variety of very beautiful and perfect forms.
Fig.: Something white like snow, as the white color (argent) in heraldry; something which falls in, or as in, flakes.
q: The field of snow with eagle of black therein.

Snow.etym: [OE. snow, snaw, AS. snāw; akin to D. sneeuw, OS. & OHG. snēo, G. schnee, Icel. snær, snjōr, snajār, Sw. snö, Dan. snee, Goth. snaiws, Lith. snëgas, Russ. snieg', Ir. & Gael. sneachd, W. nyf, L. nix, nivis, Gr. acc. νίφα, also AS. snīwan to snow, G. schneien, OHG. snīwan, Lith. snigti, L. ningit it

senses.d: To fall in or as snow; — chiefly used impersonally; as, it snows; it snowed yesterday.
To scatter like snow; to cover with, or as with, snow.
White like snow.
Abounding with snow; covered with snow.
Fig.: Pure; unblemished; unstained; spotless.
q: There did he lose his snowy innocence.

senses.d: The part of a candle wick charred by the flame, whether burning or not.
q: If the burning snuff happens to get out of the snuffers, you have a chance that it may fall into a dish of soup.

Snuff.etym: [Cf. G. schnuppe candle snuff, schnuppen to snuff a candle (see Snuff, v. t., to snuff a candle), or cf. Snub, v. t.]

senses.d: To crop the snuff of, as a candle; to take off the end of the snuff of.

Snuff.etym: [OE. snuffen. See Snuff of a candle Snuff to sniff.]

senses.d: To draw in, or to inhale, forcibly through the nose; to sniff.
q: He snuffs the wind, his heels the sand excite.

senses.d: To perceive by the nose; to scent; to smell.

Snuff.etym: [Akin to D. snuffen, G. schnupfen, schnuppen, to snuff, schnupfen a cold in the head, schnuppen to snuff (air), also, to snuff (a candle). Cf. Sniff, Snout, Snub, v. i.]

senses.d: To inhale air through the nose with violence or with noise, as do dogs and horses.
To turn up the nose and inhale air, as an expression of contempt; hence, to take offense.
q: Do the enemies of the church rage and snuff?

senses.d: The act of snuffing; perception by snuffing; a sniff.
Pulverized tobacco, etc., prepared to be taken into the nose; also, the amount taken at once.
Resentment, displeasure, or contempt, expressed by a snuffing of the nose.
One who snuffs.
The common porpoise.
An instrument for cropping and holding the snuff of a candle.
In that manner or degree; as, indicated (in any way), or as implied, or as supposed to be known.
q: Why is his chariot so long in coming?

senses.d: In like manner or degree; in the same way; thus; for like reason; whith equal reason; — used correlatively, following as, to denote comparison or resemblance; sometimes, also, following inasmuch as.
q: As a war should be undertaken upon a just motive, so a prince ought to consider the condition he is in.

senses.d: In such manner; to such degree; — used correlatively with as or that following; as, he was so fortunate as to escape.
q: I viewed in may mind, so far as I was able, the beginning and progress of a rising world.
He is very much in Sir Roger's esteem, so that he lives in the family rather as a relation than dependent.

senses.d: Very; in a high degree; that is, in such a degree as can not well be expressed; as, he is so good; he planned so wisely.

In the same manner; as has been stated or suggested; in this or that condition or state; under these circumstances; in this way; — with reflex reference to something just asserted or implied; used also with the verb to be, as a predicate.
q: Use him with great respect yourself, and cause all your family to do so too.
