It concerns every man, with the greatest seriousness, to inquire into those matters, whether they be so or not.
He is Sir Robert's son, and so art thou.

senses.d: The case being such; therefore; on this account; for this reason; on these terms; — used both as an adverb and a conjuction.
q: God makes him in his own image an intellectual creature, and so capable of dominion.
Here, then, exchange we mutually forgiveness; So may the guilt of all my broken vows, My perjuries to thee, be all forgotten.

senses.d: It is well; let it be as it is, or let it come to pass; — used to express assent.
q: And when 't is writ, for my sake read it over, And if it please you, so; if not, why, so.
There is Percy; if your father will do me any honor, so; if not, let him kill the next Percy himself.

senses.d: Well; the fact being as stated; — used as an expletive; as, so the work is done, is it?
Is it thus? do you mean what you say? — with an upward tone; as, do you say he refuses? So?
About the number, time, or quantity specified; thereabouts; more or less; as, I will spend a week or so in the country; I have read only a page or so.
q: A week or so will probably reconcile us.

So.etym: [OE. so, sa, swa, AS. swā; akin to OFries, sā, s�, D. zoo, OS. & OHG. s�, G. so, Icel. svā, sv�, svo, so, Sw. s�, Dan. saa, Goth. swa so, sw� as; cf. L. suus one's own, Skr. sva one's own, one's self. √192. Cf. As, Custom, Ethic, Idiom, Such.]

senses.d: Provided that; on condition that; in case that; if.
q: Though all the winds of doctrine were let loose play upon the earth, so truth be in the field, we do injuriously, by licensing and prohibiting, to misdoubt her strength.

senses.d: Be as you are; stand still; stop; that will do; right as you are; — a word used esp. to cows; also used by sailors.

To cause or suffer to lie in a fluid till the substance has imbibed what it can contain; to macerate in water or other liquid; to steep, as for the purpose of softening or freshening; as, to soak cloth; to soak bread; to soak salt meat, salt fish, or the like.
To drench; to wet thoroughly.
q: Their land shall be soaked with blood.

senses.d: To draw in by the pores, or through small passages; as, a sponge soaks up water; the skin soaks in moisture.
To make (its way) by entering pores or interstices; — often with through.
q: The rivulet beneath soaked its way obscurely through wreaths of snow.

senses.d: Fig.: To absorb; to drain.

Soak.etym: [OE. soken, AS. socian to sioak, steep, fr. s�can, s�gan, to suck. See Suck.]

senses.d: To lie steeping in water or other liquid; to become sturated; as, let the cloth lie and soak.
To enter (into something) by pores or interstices; as, water soaks into the earth or other porous matter.
To drink intemperately or gluttonously.

A substance which dissolves in water, thus forming a lather, and is used as a cleansing agent. Soap is produced by combining fats or oils with alkalies or alkaline earths, usually by boiling, and consists of salts of sodium, potassium, etc., with the fatty acids (oleic, stearic, palmitic, etc.). See the Note below, and cf. Saponification. By extension, any compound of similar composition or properties, whether used as a cleaning agent or not.
q: The purifying action of soap depends upon the fact that it is decomposed by a large quantity of water into free alkali and an insoluble acid salt. The first of these takes away the fatty dirt on washing, and the latter forms the soap lather which envelops the greasy matter and thus tends to remove it.

Soap.etym: [OE. sope, AS. sāpe; akin to D. zeep, G. seife, OHG. seifa, Icel. sāpa, Sw. s�pa, Dan. s�be, and perhaps to AS. sīpan to drip, MHG. sīfen, and L. sebum tallow. Cf. Saponaceous.]

senses.d: To rub or wash over with soap.
To flatter; to wheedle.
To soak.
To sigh with a sudden heaving of the breast, or with a kind of convulsive motion; to sigh with tears, and with a convulsive drawing in of the breath.
q: Sobbing is the same thing , stronger.
She sighed, she sobbed, and, furious with despair. She rent her garments, and she tore her hair.

Sob.etym: [OE. sobben; akin to AS. seófian, siófian, to complain, bewail, seófung, siófung, sobbing, lamentation; cf. OHG. s�ftön, s�ft�n, to sigh, MHG. siuften, siufzen, G. seufzen, MHG. s�ft a sigh, properly, a drawing in of breath, from s�fen to drink, OHG. s�fan. Cf. Sup.]

senses.d: The act of sobbing; a convulsive sigh, or inspiration of the breath, as in sorrow.
q: Break, heart, or choke with sobs my hated breath.

senses.d: Any sorrowful cry or sound.
q: The tremulous sob of the complaining owl.

senses.d: Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; habitually temperate; as, a sober man.
q: That we may hereafter live a godly, righteous, and sober life, to the glory of Thy holy name.

senses.d: Not intoxicated or excited by spirituous liquors; as, the sot may at times be sober.
Not mad or insane; not wild, visionary, or heated with passion; exercising cool, dispassionate reason; self-controlled; self-possessed.
q: There was not a sober person to be had; all was tempestuous and blustering.
No sober man would put himself into danger for the applause of escaping without breaking his neck.

senses.d: Not proceeding from, or attended with, passion; calm; as, sober judgment; a man in his sober senses.
Serious or subdued in demeanor, habit, appearance, or color; solemn; grave; sedate.
q: What parts gay France from sober Spain?
See her sober over a sampler, or gay over a jointed baby.
Twilight gray Had in her sober livery all things clad.

Sober.syn: Grave; temperate; abstinent; abstemious; moderate; regular; steady; calm; quiet; cool; collected; dispassionate; unimpassioned; sedate; staid; serious; solemn; somber. See Grave.
Sober.etym: [OE. sobre, F. sobre, from L. sobrius, probably from a prefix so- expressing separation + ebrius drunken. Cf. Ebriety.]

senses.d: To make sober.
q: There shallow draughts intoxicate the brain, And drinking largely sobers us again.

senses.d: To become sober; — often with down.
q: Vance gradually sobered down.

senses.d: In a sober manner; temperately; cooly; calmly; gravely; seriously.
Grave; serious; solemn; sad.
q: looked hollow and thereto soberly.

senses.d: The quality or state of being sober.
Habitual soberness or temperance as to the use of spirituous liquors; as, a man of sobriety.
q: Public sobriety is a relative duty.

senses.d: Habitual freedom from enthusiasm, inordinate passion, or overheated imagination; calmness; coolness; gravity; seriousness; as, the sobriety of riper years.
q: Mirth makes them not mad, Nor sobriety sad.

Sobriety.syn: Soberness; temperance; abstinence; abstemiousness; moderation; regularity; steadness; calmness; coolness; sober-mindeness; sedateness; staidness; gravity; seriousness; solemnity.
Sobriety.etym: [L. sobrietas: cf. F. sobriété. See Sober.]

senses.d: An opening into which anything is fitted; any hollow thing or place which receives and holds something else; as, the sockets of the teeth.
q: His eyeballs in their hollow sockets sink.

senses.d: Especially, the hollow tube or place in which a candle is fixed in the candlestick.
q: And in the sockets oily bubbles dance.

Socket.etym: [OE. soket, a dim. through OF. fr. L. soccus. See Sock a covering for the foot.]

senses.d: The rock dove.
That stratum of the surface of the soil which is filled with the roots of grass, or any portion of that surface; turf; sward.
q: She there shall dress a sweeter sod Than Fancy's feet have ever trod.

Sod.etym: [Akin to LG. sode, D. zode, OD. sode, soode, OFries. satha, and E. seethe. So named from its sodden state in wet weather. See Seethe.]

senses.d: To cover with sod; to turf.
Boiled; seethed; also, soaked; heavy with moisture; saturated; as, sodden beef; sodden bread; sodden fields.
To be seethed; to become sodden.
To soak; to make heavy with water.
An inhabitant of Sodom.
One guilty of sodomy.

A word compounded of so and ever, used in composition with who, what, where, when, how, etc., and indicating any out of all possible or supposable persons, things, places, times, ways, etc. It is sometimes used separate from the pronoun or adverb.
q: For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
What great thing soever a man proposed to do in his life, he should think of achieving it by fifty.

senses.d: Easily yielding to pressure; easily impressed, molded, or cut; not firm in resisting; impressible; yielding; also, malleable; — opposed to hard; as, a soft bed; a soft peach; soft earth; soft wood or metal.
Not rough, rugged, or harsh to the touch; smooth; delicate; fine; as, soft silk; a soft skin.
q: They that wear soft clothing are in king's houses.

senses.d: Hence, agreeable to feel, taste, or inhale; not irritating to the tissues; as, a soft liniment; soft wines.
Not harsh or offensive to the sight; not glaring; pleasing to the eye; not exciting by intensity of color or violent contrast; as, soft hues or tints.
q: The sun, shining upon the upper part of the clouds . . . made the softest lights imaginable.

senses.d: Not harsh or rough in sound; gentle and pleasing to the ear; flowing; as, soft whispers of music.
q: Her voice was ever soft, Gentle, and low, — an excellent thing in woman.
Soft were my numbers; who could take offense?

senses.d: Easily yielding; susceptible to influence; flexible; gentle; kind.
q: I would to God my heart were flint, like Edward's; Or Edward's soft and pitiful, like mine.
The meek or soft shall inherit the earth.

senses.d: Expressing gentleness, tenderness, or the like; mild; conciliatory; courteous; kind; as, soft eyes.
q: A soft answer turneth away wrath.
A face with gladness overspread, Soft smiles, by human kindness bred.

senses.d: Effeminate; not courageous or manly, weak.
q: A longing after sensual pleasures is a dissolution of the spirit of a man, and makes it loose, soft, and wandering.

senses.d: Gentle in action or motion; easy.
q: On her soft axle, white she paces even, And bears thee soft with the smooth air along.

senses.d: Weak in character; impressible.
q: The deceiver soon found this soft place of Adam's.

senses.d: Somewhat weak in intellect.
q: He made soft fellows stark noddies, and such as were foolish quite mad.

senses.d: Quiet; undisturbed; paceful; as, soft slumbers.

Soft.etym: [OE. softe, AS. s�fte, properly adv. of s�fte, adj.; akin to OS. sāfto, adv., D. zacht, OHG. samfto, adv., semfti, adj., G. sanft, LG. sacht; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: A soft or foolish person; an idiot.
Softly; without roughness or harshness; gently; quietly.
q: A knight soft riding toward them.

senses.d: Be quiet; hold; stop; not so fast.
q: Soft, you; a word or two before you go.

senses.d: In a soft manner.

To feed, as cattle or horses, in the barn or an inclosure, with fresh grass or green food cut for them, instead of sending them out to pasture; hence (such food having the effect of purging them), to purge by feeding on green food; as, to soil a horse.

Soil.etym: [OF. saoler, saouler, to satiate, F. soûler, L. satullare, fr. satullus, dim. of satur sated. See Satire.]

senses.d: The upper stratum of the earth; the mold, or that compound substance which furnishes nutriment to plants, or which is particularly adapted to support and nourish them.
Land; country.
q: Must I thus leave thee, Paradise? thus leave Thee, native soil?

senses.d: Dung; fæces; compost; manure; as, night soil.
q: Improve land by dung and other sort of soils.

Soil.etym: [OE. soile, F. sol, fr. L. solum bottom, soil; but the word has probably been influenced in form by soil a miry place. Cf. Saloon, Soil a miry place, Sole of the foot.]

senses.d: To enrich with soil or muck; to manure.
q: Men . . . soil their ground, not that they love the dirt, but that they expect a crop.

senses.d: A marshy or miry place to which a hunted boar resorts for refuge; hence, a wet place, stream, or tract of water, sought for by other game, as deer.
q: As deer, being stuck, fly through many soils, Yet still the shaft sticks fast.
O, sir, have you taken soil here? It is well a man may reach you after three hours' running.

Soil.etym: [OF. soil, souil, F. souille, from OF. soillier, F. souiller. See Soil to make dirty.]

senses.d: To make dirty or unclean on the surface; to foul; to dirty; to defile; as, to soil a garment with dust.
q: Our wonted ornaments now soiled and stained.

senses.d: To stain or mar, as with infamy or disgrace; to tarnish; to sully.

Soil.syn: To foul; dirt; dirty; begrime; bemire; bespatter; besmear; daub; bedaub; stain; tarnish; sully; defile; pollute.
Soil.etym: [OE. soilen, OF. soillier, F. souiller, (assumed) LL. suculare, fr. L. sucula a little pig, dim. of sus a swine. See Sow, n.]

senses.d: To become soiled; as, light colors soil sooner than dark ones.
That which soils or pollutes; a soiled place; spot; stain.
q: A lady's honor . . . will not bear a soil.

Soil.etym: [See Soil to make dirty, Soil a miry place.]

senses.d: To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporary resident or as a stranger, not considering the place as a permanent habitation; to delay; to tarry.
q: Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there.
Home he goeth, he might not longer sojourn.
The soldiers first assembled at Newcastle, and there sojourned three days.

Sojourn.etym: [OE. sojornen, sojournen, OF. sojorner, sejorner, F. séjourner, fr. L. sub under, about + diurnus belonging to the day. See Journal, Diurnal.]

senses.d: A temporary residence, as that of a traveler in a foreign land.
q: Though long detained In that obscure sojourn.

Sojourn.etym: [Cf. OF. sujurn, sujur, sejor, F. séjour. See Sojourn, v. i.]

senses.d: One who sojourns.
q: We are strangers before thee, and sojourners.

senses.d: The act or state of one who sojourns.
The sun.
Gold; — so called from its brilliancy, color, and value.
A syllable applied in solmization to the note G, or to the fifth tone of any diatonic scale.
The tone itself.
A sou.
A silver and gold coin of Peru. The silver sol is the unit of value, and is worth about 68 cents.
A fluid mixture of a colloid and a liquid; a liquid colloidal solution or suspension.

Sol.etym: [From hydrosol an aqueous colloidal solution, confused with G. sole, soole, salt water from which salt is obtained.]

senses.d: Comfort in grief; alleviation of grief or anxiety; also, that which relieves in distress; that which cheers or consoles; relief.
q: In business of mirth and of solace.
The proper solaces of age are not music and compliments, but wisdom and devotion.

senses.d: Rest; relaxation; ease.
q: To make his steed some solace.

Solace.etym: [OF. solas, ssoulaz, L. solacium, solatium, fr. solari to comfort, console. Cf. Console, v. t.]

senses.d: To cheer in grief or under calamity; to comfort; to relieve in affliction, solitude, or discomfort; to console; — applied to persons; as, to solace one with the hope of future reward.
To allay; to assuage; to soothe; as, to solace grief.

Solace.syn: To comfort; assuage; allay. See Comfort.
Solace.etym: [OF. solacier, soulacier, F. solacier, LL. solatiare. See Solace, n.]

senses.d: To take comfort; to be cheered.
Solary; military pay.

Sold.etym: [F. solde. See Soldier, and cf. Sou.]

senses.d: One who is engaged in military service as an officer or a private; one who serves in an army; one of an organized body of combatants.
q: I am a soldier and unapt to weep.

senses.d: Especially, a private in military service, as distinguished from an officer.
q: It were meet that any one, before he came to be a captain, should have been a soldier.

senses.d: A brave warrior; a man of military experience and skill, or a man of distinguished valor; — used by way of emphasis or distinction.
The red or cuckoo gurnard (Trigla pini.)
One of the asexual polymorphic forms of white ants, or termites, in which the head and jaws are very large and strong. The soldiers serve to defend the nest. See Termite.

Soldier.etym: [OE. souldier, soudiour, souder, OF. soldier, soldoier, soldeier, sodoier, soudoier, soudier, fr. L. solidus a piece of money (hence applied to the pay of a soldier), fr. solidus solid. See Solid, and cf. Sold, n.]

senses.d: To serve as a soldier.
To make a pretense of doing something, or of performing any task.
q: It needs an opera glass to discover whether the leaders are pulling, or only soldiering.

senses.d: Any one of several species of flatfishes of the genus Solea and allied genera of the family Soleidæ, especially the common European species (Solea vulgaris), which is a valuable food fish.

Any one of several American flounders somewhat resembling the true sole in form or quality, as the California sole (Lepidopsetta bilineata), the long-finned sole (Glyptocephalus zachirus), and other species.

Sole.etym: [F. sole, L. solea; — so named from its flat shape. See Sole of the foot.]

senses.d: The bottom of the foot; hence, also, rarely, the foot itself.
q: The dove found no rest for the sole of her foot.
Hast wandered through the world now long a day, Yet ceasest not thy weary soles to lead.

senses.d: The bottom of a shoe or boot, or the piece of leather which constitutes the bottom.
q: The “caliga” was a military shoe, with a very thick sole, tied above the instep.

senses.d: The bottom or lower part of anything, or that on which anything rests in standing.

Sole.etym: [AS. sole, fr. L. soolea (or rather an assumed L. sola), akin to solumround, soil, sole of the foot. Cf. Exile, Saloon, Soil earth, Sole the fish.]

senses.d: To furnish with a sole; as, to sole a shoe.
Being or acting without another; single; individual; only.
q: He, be sure . . . first and last will reign Sole king.

senses.d: Single; unmarried; as, a feme sole.

Sole.etym: [L. solus, or OF. sol, F. seul (fr. L. solus; cf. L. sollus whole, entire. Cf. Desolate, Solemn, Solo, Sullen.]

senses.d: Marked with religious rites and pomps; enjoined by, or connected with, religion; sacred.
q: His holy rites and solemn feasts profaned.
The worship of this image was advanced, and a solemn supplication observed everry year.

senses.d: Pertaining to a festival; festive; festal.
Stately; ceremonious; grand.
q: His feast so solemn and so rich.
To-night we hold a splemn supper.

senses.d: Fitted to awaken or express serious reflections; marked by seriousness; serious; grave; devout; as, a solemn promise; solemn earnestness.
q: Nor wanting power to mitigate and swage With solemn touches troubled thoughts.
There reigned a solemn silence over all.

senses.d: Real; earnest; downright.
q: Frederick, the emperor, . . . has spared no expense in strengthening this city; since which time we find no solemn taking it by the Turks.

senses.d: Affectedly grave or serious; as, to put on a solemn face.
Made in form; ceremonious; as, solemn war; conforming with all legal requirements; as, probate in solemn form.

Solemn.syn: Grave; formal; ritual; ceremonial; sober; serious; reverential; devotional; devout. See Grave.
Solemn.etym: [OE. solempne, OF. solempne, L. solemnis, solennis, sollemnis, sollennis; sollus all, entire + annus a year; properly, that takes place every year; — used especially of religious solemnities. Cf. Silly, Annual.]

senses.d: A rite or ceremony performed with religious reverence; religious or ritual ceremony; as, the solemnity of a funeral, a sacrament.
q: Great was the cause; our old solemnities From no blind zeal or fond tradition rise, But saved from death, our Argives yearly pay These grateful honors to the god of day.

senses.d: ceremony adapted to impress with awe.
q: The forms and solemnities of the last judgment.

senses.d: Ceremoniousness; impressiveness; seriousness; grave earnestness; formal dignity; gravity.
q: With much glory and great solemnity.
The statelines and gravity of the Spaniards shows itself in the solemnity of their language.
These promises were often made with great solemnity and confirmed with an oath.

senses.d: Hence, affected gravity or seriousness.
q: Solemnity 's a cover for a sot.

senses.d: Solemn state or feeling; awe or reverence; also, that which produces such a feeling; as, the solemnity of an audience; the solemnity of Westminster Abbey.
A solemn or formal observance; proceeding according to due form; the formality which is necessary to render a thing done valid.

Solemnity.etym: [L. solemnitas, solennitas: cf. F. solennité, solemnité, OF. also sollempnité.]

senses.d: In a solemn manner; with gravity; seriously; formally.
q: There in deaf murmurs solemnly are wise.
I do solemnly assure the reader.

senses.d: In a solitary manner; in solitude; alone.
Living or being by one's self; having no companion present; being without associates; single; alone; lonely.
q: Those rare and solitary, these in flocks.
Hie home unto my chamber, Where thou shalt find me, sad and solitary.

senses.d: Performed, passed, or endured alone; as, a solitary journey; a solitary life.
q: Satan . . . explores his solitary flight.

senses.d: Not much visited or frequented; remote from society; retired; lonely; as, a solitary residence or place.
Not inhabited or occupied; without signs of inhabitants or occupation; desolate; deserted; silent; still; hence, gloomy; dismal; as, the solitary desert.
q: How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people.
Let that night be solitary; let no joyful voice come therein.

senses.d: Single; individual; sole; as, a solitary instance of vengeance; a solitary example.
Not associated with others of the same kind.

Solitary.etym: [L. solitarius, fr. solus alone: cf. F. solitaire. See Sole, a., and cf. Solitaire.]

senses.d: One who lives alone, or in solitude; an anchoret; a hermit; a recluse.
One of the kings of Israel, noted for his superior wisdom and magnificent reign; hence, a very wise man.

Consisting of a greater or less portion or sum; composed of a quantity or number which is not stated; — used to express an indefinite quantity or number; as, some wine; some water; some persons. Used also pronominally; as, I have some.
q: Some theoretical writers allege that there was a time when there was no such thing as society.

senses.d: A certain; one; — indicating a person, thing, event, etc., as not known individually, or designated more specifically; as, some man, that is, some one man.
q: Some man praiseth his neighbor by a wicked intent.
Most gentlemen of property, at some period or other of their lives, are ambitious of representing their county in Parliament.

senses.d: Not much; a little; moderate; as, the censure was to some extent just.

About; near; more or less; — used commonly with numerals, but formerly also with a singular substantive of time or distance; as, a village of some eighty houses; some two or three persons; some hour hence.
q: The number slain on the rebel's part were some two thousand.

senses.d: Considerable in number or quantity.
q: On its outer point, some miles away. The lighthouse lifts its massive masonry.

senses.d: Certain; those of one part or portion; — in distinction from other or others; as, some men believe one thing, and others another.
q: Some fell among thorns; . . . but other fell into good ground.

senses.d: A part; a portion; — used pronominally, and followed sometimes by of; as, some of our provisions.
q: Your edicts some reclaim from sins, But most your life and blest example wins.
Some to the shores do fly, Some to the woods, or whither fear advised.
Some in his bed, some in the deep sea.

Some.etym: [OE. som, sum, AS. sum; akin to OS., OFries., & OHG. sum, OD. som, D. sommig, Icel. sumr, Dan. somme (pl.), Sw. somlige (pl.), Goth. sums, and E. same. √191. See Same, a., and cf. -some.]

senses.d: A person unknown or uncertain; a person indeterminate; some person.
q: Jesus said, Somebody hath touched me.
We must draw in somebody that may stand 'Twixt us and danger.

senses.d: A person of consideration or importance.
q: Before these days rose up Theudas, boasting himself to be somebody.

senses.d: Anything unknown, undetermined, or not specifically designated; a certain indefinite thing; an indeterminate or unknown event; an unspecified task, work, or thing.
q: There is something in the wind.
The whole world has something to do, something to talk of, something to wish for, and something to be employed about.
Something attemped, something done, Has earned a night's repose.

senses.d: A part; a portion, more or less; an indefinite quantity or degree; a little.
q: Something yet of doubt remains.
Something of it arises from our infant state.

senses.d: A person or thing importance.
q: If a man thinketh himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.

senses.d: In some degree; somewhat; to some extent; at some distance.
q: I something fear my father's wrath.
We have something fairer play than a reasoner could have expected formerly.
My sense of touch is something coarse.
It must be done to-night, And something from the palace.

senses.d: At a past time indefinitely referred to; once; formerly.
q: Did they not sometime cry “All hail” to me?

senses.d: At a time undefined; once in a while; now and then; sometimes.
q: Sometime we see a cloud that's dragonish, A vapor sometime like a bear or lion.

senses.d: At one time or other hereafter; as, I will do it sometime.
Having been formerly; former; late; whilom.
q: Our sometime sister, now our queen.
Ion, our sometime darling, whom we prized.

senses.d: Formerly; sometime.
q: That fair and warlike form In which the majesty of buried Denmark Did sometimes march.

senses.d: At times; at intervals; not always; now and then; occasionally.
q: It is good that we sometimes be contradicted.

senses.d: Former; sometime.
q: Thy sometimes brother's wife.

senses.d: More or less; a certain quantity or degree; a part, more or less; something.
q: These salts have somewhat of a nitrous taste.
Somewhat of his good sense will suffer, in this transfusion, and much of the beauty of his thoughts will be lost.

senses.d: A person or thing of importance; a somebody.
q: Here come those that worship me. They think that I am somewhat.

senses.d: In some degree or measure; a little.
q: His giantship is gone, somewhat crestfallen.
Somewhat back from the village street.

senses.d: A male child; the male issue, or offspring, of a parent, father or mother.
q: Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son.

senses.d: A male descendant, however distant; hence, in the plural, descendants in general.
q: I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings.
I am the Lord, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.

senses.d: Any young male person spoken of as a child; an adopted male child; a pupil, ward, or any other young male dependent.
q: The child grew, and she brought him unto Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son.
Be plain, good son, and homely in thy drift.

senses.d: A native or inhabitant of some specified place; as, sons of Albion; sons of New England.
The produce of anything.
q: Earth's tall sons, the cedar, oak, and pine.

senses.d: Jesus Christ, the Savior; — called the Son of God, and the Son of man.
q: We . . . do testify that the Father sent the Son to be the Savior of the world.
Who gave His Son sure all has given.

Son.etym: [OE. sone, sune, AS. sunu; akin to D. zoon, OS., OFries., & OHG. sunu, G. sohn, Icel. sonr, Sw. son, Dan. sön, Goth. sunus, Lith. sunus, Russ. suin', Skr. sūnu (from sū to beget, to bear), and Gr. � son. √293. Cf. Sow, n.]

senses.d: That which is sung or uttered with musical modulations of the voice, whether of a human being or of a bird, insect, etc.
A lyrical poem adapted to vocal music; a ballad.
More generally, any poetical strain; a poem.
q: The bard that first adorned our native tongue Tuned to his British lyre this ancient song.

senses.d: Poetical composition; poetry; verse.
q: This subject for heroic song.

senses.d: An object of derision; a laughingstock.
q: And now am I their song, yea, I am their byword.

senses.d: A trifle.

Song.syn: Sonnet; ballad; canticle; carol; canzonet; ditty; hymn; descant; lay; strain; poesy; verse.
Song.etym: [AS. song, sang, fr. singan to sing; akin to D. zang, G. sang, Icel. söngr, Goth. saggws. See Sing.]

senses.d: In a short time; shortly after any time specified or supposed; as, soon after sunrise.
q: She finished, and the subtle fiend his lore Soon learned.

senses.d: Without the usual delay; before any time supposed; early.
q: How is it that ye are come so soon to-day?

senses.d: Promptly; quickly; easily.
q: Small lights are soon blown out, huge fires abide.

senses.d: Readily; willingly; — in this sense used with would, or some other word expressing will.
q: I would as soon see a river winding through woods or in meadows, as when it is tossed up in so many whimsical figures at Versailles.

Soon.etym: [OE. sone, AS. s�na; cf. OFries. s�n, OS. sāna, sāno, OHG. sār, Goth. suns.]

senses.d: Speedy; quick.
To foretell; to predict.

Soothsay.etym: [Sooth + say; properly to say truth, tell the truth.]

senses.d: A true saying; a proverb; a prophecy.
Omen; portent. Having
q: God turn the same to good soothsay.

senses.d: One who foretells events by the art of soothsaying; a prognosticator.
A mantis.
A true saying; truth.
The act of one who soothsays; the foretelling of events; the art or practice of making predictions.
q: A damsel, possessed with a spirit of divination . . . which brought her masters much gain by soothsaying.

senses.d: A prediction; a prophecy; a prognostication.
q: Divinations and soothsayings and dreams are vain.

senses.d: Anything steeped, or dipped and softened, in any liquid; especially, something dipped in broth or liquid food, and intended to be eaten.
q: He it is to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped it.
Sops in wine, quantity, inebriate more than wine itself.
The bounded waters Should lift their bosoms higher than the shores, And make a sop of all this solid globe.

senses.d: Anything given to pacify; — so called from the sop given to Cerberus, as related in mythology.
q: All nature is cured with a sop.

senses.d: A thing of little or no value.

Sop.etym: [OE. sop, soppe; akin to AS. s�pan to sup, to sip, to drink, D. sop sop, G. suppe soup, Icel. soppa sop. See Sup, v. t., and cf. Soup.]

senses.d: To steep or dip in any liquid.
A conjurer; an enchanter; a magician.
q: Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers.

senses.d: A female sorcerer.
Divination by the assistance, or supposed assistance, of evil spirits, or the power of commanding evil spirits; magic; necromancy; witchcraft; enchantment.
q: Adder's wisdom I have learned, To fence my ear against thy sorceries.

Sorcery.etym: [OE. sorcerie, OF. sorcerie, fr. OF. & F. sorcier a sorcerer, LL. sortiarius, fr. L. sors, sortis, a lot, decision by lot, fate, destiny. See Sort, n.]

senses.d: Reddish brown; sorrel.

Sore.etym: [F. saure, sore, sor; faucon sor a sore falcon. See Sorrel, n.]

senses.d: A young hawk or falcon in the first year.
A young buck in the fourth year. See the Note under Buck.
Tender to the touch; susceptible of pain from pressure; inflamed; painful; — said of the body or its parts; as, a sore hand.
Fig.: Sensitive; tender; easily pained, grieved, or vexed; very susceptible of irritation.
q: Malice and hatred are very fretting and vexatious, and apt to make our minds sore and uneasy.

senses.d: Severe; afflictive; distressing; as, a sore disease; sore evil or calamity.
Criminal; wrong; evil.

Sore.etym: [OE. sor, sar, AS. sār; akin to D. zeer, OS. & OHG. s�r, G. sehr very, Icel. sārr, Sw. sår, Goth. sair pain. Cf. Sorry.]

senses.d: A place in an animal body where the skin and flesh are ruptured or bruised, so as to be tender or painful; a painful or diseased place, such as an ulcer or a boil.
q: The dogs came and licked his sores.

senses.d: Fig.: Grief; affliction; trouble; difficulty.
q: I see plainly where his sore lies.

Sore.etym: [OE. sor, sar, AS. sār. See Sore, a.]

senses.d: In a sore manner; with pain; grievously.
q: Thy hand presseth me sore.

senses.d: Greatly; violently; deeply.
q: prayed unto the Lord and wept sore.
Sore sighed the knight, who this long sermon heard.

senses.d: In a sore manner; grievously; painfully; as, to be sorely afflicted.

The uneasiness or pain of mind which is produced by the loss of any good, real or supposed, or by diseappointment in the expectation of good; grief at having suffered or occasioned evil; regret; unhappiness; sadness.
q: How great a sorrow suffereth now Arcite!
The safe and general antidote against sorrow is employment.

Sorrow.syn: Grief; unhappiness; regret; sadness; heaviness; mourning; affliction. See Affliction, and Grief.
Sorrow.etym: [OE. sorwe, sorewe, sor�e, AS. sorg, sorh; akin to D. zorg care, anxiety, OS. sorga, OHG. sorga, soraga, suorga, G. sorge, Icel., Sw., & Dan. sorg, Goth. saúrga; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: To feel pain of mind in consequence of evil experienced, feared, or done; to grieve; to be sad; to be sorry.
q: Sorrowing most of all . . . that they should see his face no more.
I desire no man to sorrow for me.

Sorrow.etym: [OE. sorowen, sorwen, sorhen, AS. sorgian; akin to Goth. saúrgan. See Sorrow, n.]

senses.d: Accompanied with sorrow; sorrowful.
Full of sorrow; exhibiting sorrow; sad; dejected; distressed.
q: My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.

senses.d: Producing sorrow; exciting grief; mournful; lamentable; grievous; as, a sorrowful accident.

Sorrowful.syn: Sad; mournful; dismal; disconsolate; drear; dreary; grievous; lamentable; doleful; distressing.

senses.d: Grieved for the loss of some good; pained for some evil; feeling regret; — now generally used to express light grief or affliction, but formerly often used to express deeper feeling.
q: Ye were made sorry after a godly manner.
I am sorry for thee, friend; 't is the duke's pleasure.
She entered, were he lief or sorry.

senses.d: Melancholy; dismal; gloomy; mournful.
q: All full of chirking was this sorry place.

senses.d: Poor; mean; worthless; as, a sorry excuse.
q: Cheeks of sorry grain will serve.
Good fruit will sometimes grow on a sorry tree.

Sorry.syn: Hurt; afflicted; mortified; vexed; chagrined; melancholy; dismal; poor; mean; pitiful.
Sorry.etym: [OE. sory, sary, AS. sārig, fr. sār, n., sore. See Sore, n. & a. The original sense was, painful; hence, miserable, sad.]

senses.d: Chance; lot; destiny.
q: By aventure, or sort, or cas .
Let blockish Ajax draw The sort to fight with Hector.

Sort.etym: [F. sorl, L. sors, sortis. See Sort kind.]

senses.d: A kind or species; any number or collection of individual persons or things characterized by the same or like qualities; a class or order; as, a sort of men; a sort of horses; a sort of trees; a sort of poems.
Manner; form of being or acting.
q: Which for my part I covet to perform, In sort as through the world I did proclaim.
Flowers, in such sort worn, can neither be smelt nor seen well by those that wear them.
I'll deceive you in another sort.
To Adam in what sort Shall I appear?
I shall not be wholly without praise, if in some sort I have copied his style.

senses.d: Condition above the vulgar; rank.
A chance group; a company of persons who happen to be together; a troop; also, an assemblage of animals.
q: A boy, a child, and we a sort of us, Vowed against his voyage.

senses.d: A pair; a set; a suit.
Letters, figures, points, marks, spaces, or quadrats, belonging to a case, separately considered.
q: As when the total kind Of birds, in orderly array on wing, Came summoned over Eden to receive Their names of there.
None of noble sort Would so offend a virgin.

Sort.etym: [F. sorie (cf. It. sorta, sorte), from L. sors, sorti, a lot, part, probably akin to serere to connect. See Series, and cf. Assort, Consort, Resort, Sorcery, Sort lot.]

senses.d: To separate, and place in distinct classes or divisions, as things having different qualities; as, to sort cloths according to their colors; to sort wool or thread according to its fineness.
q: Rays which differ in refrangibility may be parted and sorted from one another.

senses.d: To reduce to order from a confused state.
To conjoin; to put together in distribution; to class.
q: Shellfish have been, by some of the ancients, compared and sorted with insects.
She sorts things present with things past.

senses.d: To choose from a number; to select; to cull.
q: That he may sort out a worthy spouse.
I'll sort some other time to visit you.

senses.d: To conform; to adapt; to accommodate.
q: I pray thee, sort thy heart to patience.

senses.d: To join or associate with others, esp. with others of the same kind or species; to agree.
q: Nor do metals only sort and herd with metals in the earth, and minerals with minerals.
The illiberality of parents towards children makes them base, and sort with any company.

senses.d: To suit; to fit; to be in accord; to harmonize.
q: They are happy whose natures sort with their vocations.
Things sort not to my will.
I can not tell you precisely how they sorted.

senses.d: Like a sot; doltish; very foolish; drunken.
q: How ignorant are sottish pretenders to astrology!

senses.d: An old French copper coin, equivalent in value to, and now displaced by, the five-centime piece (⅟₂₀ of a franc), which is popularly called a sou.

Sou.etym: [F. sou, OF. sol, from L. solidus a gold coin, in LL., a coin of less value. See Sold, n., Solid, and and cf. Sol, Soldo.]

senses.d: Sole.
Sole.
To afford suitable sustenance.

Soul.etym: [F. soûler to satiate. See Soil to feed.]

senses.d: The spiritual, rational, and immortal part in man; that part of man which enables him to think, and which renders him a subject of moral government; — sometimes, in distinction from the higher nature, or spirit, of man, the so-called animal soul, that is, the seat of life, the sensitive affections and phantasy, exclusive of the voluntary and rational powers; — sometimes, in distinction from the mind, the moral and emotional part of man's nature, the seat of feeling, in distinction from intellect; — sometimes, the intellect only; the understanding; the seat of knowledge, as distinguished from feeling. In a more general sense, “an animating, separable, surviving entity, the vehicle of individual personal existence.”
q: The eyes of our souls only then begin to see, when our bodily eyes are closing.

senses.d: The seat of real life or vitality; the source of action; the animating or essential part.
q: Thou sun, of this great world both eye and soul.

senses.d: The leader; the inspirer; the moving spirit; the heart; as, the soul of an enterprise; an able general is the soul of his army.
q: He is the very soul of bounty!

senses.d: Energy; courage; spirit; fervor; affection, or any other noble manifestation of the heart or moral nature; inherent power or goodness.
q: That he wants algebra he must confess; But not a soul to give our arms success.

senses.d: A human being; a person; — a familiar appellation, usually with a qualifying epithet; as, poor soul.
q: As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
God forbid so many simple souls Should perish by the aword!
Now mistress Gilpin (careful soul).

senses.d: A pure or disembodied spirit.
q: That to his only Son . . . every soul in heaven Shall bend the knee.

Soul.etym: [OE. soule, saule, AS. sāwel, sāwl; akin to OFries. s�le, OS. s�ola, D. ziel, G. seele, OHG. s�la, s�ula, Icel. sāla, Sw. själ, Dan. siæl, Goth. saiwala; of uncertain origin, perhaps akin to L. saeculum a lifetime, age (cf. Secular.)]

senses.d: To indue with a soul; to furnish with a soul or mind.
The air bladder of a fish; as, cod sounds are an esteemed article of food.

Sound.etym: [AS. sund a swimming, akin to E. swim. See Swim.]

senses.d: A cuttlefish.
Whole; unbroken; unharmed; free from flaw, defect, or decay; perfect of the kind; as, sound timber; sound fruit; a sound tooth; a sound ship.
Healthy; not diseased; not being in a morbid state; — said of body or mind; as, a sound body; a sound constitution; a sound understanding.
Firm; strong; safe.
q: The brasswork here, how rich it is in beams, And how, besides, it makes the whole house sound.

senses.d: Free from error; correct; right; honest; true; faithful; orthodox; — said of persons; as, a sound lawyer; a sound thinker.
q: Do not I know you a favorer Of this new seat? Ye are nor sound.

senses.d: Founded in truth or right; supported by justice; not to be overthrown on refuted; not fallacious; as, sound argument or reasoning; a sound objection; sound doctrine; sound principles.
q: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me.

senses.d: heavy; laid on with force; as, a sound beating.
Undisturbed; deep; profound; as, sound sleep.
Founded in law; legal; valid; not defective; as, a sound title to land.

Sound.etym: [OE. sound, AS. sund; akin to D. gezond, G. gesund, OHG. gisunt, Dan. & Sw. sund, and perhaps to L. sanus. Cf. Sane.]

senses.d: Soundly.
q: So sound he slept that naught might him awake.

senses.d: A narrow passage of water, or a strait between the mainland and an island; also, a strait connecting two seas, or connecting a sea or lake with the ocean; as, the Sound between the Baltic and the german Ocean; Long Island Sound.
q: The Sound of Denmark, where ships pay toll.

Sound.etym: [AS. sund a narrow sea or strait; akin to Icel., Sw., Dan. & G. sund, probably so named because it could be swum across. See Swim.]

senses.d: To measure the depth of; to fathom; especially, to ascertain the depth of by means of a line and plummet.
Fig.: To ascertain, or try to ascertain, the thoughts, motives, and purposes of (a person); to examine; to try; to test; to probe.
q: I was in jest, And by that offer meant to sound your breast.
I've sounded my Numidians man by man.

senses.d: To explore, as the bladder or urethra, with a sound; to examine with a sound; also, to examine by auscultation or percussion; as, to sound a patient.

Sound.etym: [F. sonder; cf. AS. sundgyrd a sounding rod, sundline a sounding line (see Sound a narrow passage of water).]

senses.d: To ascertain the depth of water with a sounding line or other device.
q: I sound as a shipman soundeth in the sea with his plummet to know the depth of sea.

senses.d: Any elongated instrument or probe, usually metallic, by which cavities of the body are sounded or explored, especially the bladder for stone, or the urethra for a stricture.

The peceived object occasioned by the impulse or vibration of a material substance affecting the ear; a sensation or perception of the mind received through the ear, and produced by the impulse or vibration of the air or other medium with which the ear is in contact; the effect of an impression made on the organs of hearing by an impulse or vibration of the air caused by a collision of bodies, or by other means; noise; report; as, the sound of a drum; the sound of the human voice; a horrid sound; a charming sound; a sharp, high, or shrill sound.
q: The warlike sound Of trumpets loud and clarions.

senses.d: The occasion of sound; the impulse or vibration which would occasion sound to a percipient if present with unimpaired; hence, the theory of vibrations in elastic media such cause sound; as, a treatise on sound.
Noise without signification; empty noise; noise and nothing else.
q: Sense and not sound . . . must be the principle.

Sound.etym: [OE. soun, OF. son, sun, F. son, fr. L. sonus akin to Skr. svana sound, svan to sound, and perh. to E. swan. Cf. Assonant, Consonant, Person, Sonata, Sonnet, Sonorous, Swan.]

senses.d: To make a noise; to utter a voice; to make an impulse of the air that shall strike the organs of hearing with a perceptible effect.
q: How silver-sweet sound lovers' tongues!

senses.d: To be conveyed in sound; to be spread or published; to convey intelligence by sound.
q: From you sounded out the word of the Lord.

senses.d: To make or convey a certain impression, or to have a certain import, when heard; hence, to seem; to appear; as, this reproof sounds harsh; the story sounds like an invention.
q: Good sir, why do you start, and seem to fear Things that do sound so fair?

Sound.etym: [OE. sounen, sownen, OF. soner, suner, F. sonner, from L. sonare. See Sound a noise.]

senses.d: To causse to make a noise; to play on; as, to sound a trumpet or a horn.
q: A bagpipe well could he play and soun.

senses.d: To cause to exit as a sound; as, to sound a note with the voice, or on an instrument.
To order, direct, indicate, or proclain by a sound, or sounds; to give a signal for by a certain sound; as, to sound a retreat; to sound a parley.
q: The clock sounded the hour of noon.

senses.d: To celebrate or honor by sounds; to cause to be reported; to publish or proclaim; as, to sound the praises of fame of a great man or a great exploit.
To examine the condition of (anything) by causing the same to emit sounds and noting their character; as, to sound a piece of timber; to sound a vase; to sound the lungs of a patient.
To signify; to import; to denote.
q: Soun[d]ing alway the increase of his winning.

senses.d: Making or emitting sound; hence, sonorous; as, sounding words.
The act of one who, or that which, sounds (in any of the senses of the several verbs).
measurement by sounding; also, the depth so ascertained.
The quality or state of being sound; as, the soundness of timber, of fruit, of the teeth, etc.; the soundness of reasoning or argument; soundness of faith.

Soundness.syn: Firmness; strength; solidity; healthiness; truth; rectitude.

senses.d: Having an acid or sharp, biting taste, like vinegar, and the juices of most unripe fruits; acid; tart.
q: All sour things, as vinegar, provoke appetite.

senses.d: Changed, as by keeping, so as to be acid, rancid, or musty, turned.
Disagreeable; unpleasant; hence; cross; crabbed; peevish; morose; as, a man of a sour temper; a sour reply.
q: He was a scholar . . . Lofty and sour to them that loved him not, But to those men that sought him sweet as summer.

senses.d: Afflictive; painful.
Cold and unproductive; as, sour land; a sour marsh.

Sour.syn: Acid; sharp; tart; acetous; acetose; harsh; acrimonious; crabbed; currish; peevish.
Sour.etym: [OE. sour, sur, AS. s�r; akin to D. zuur, G. sauer, OHG. s�r, Icel. s�rr, Sw. sur, Dan. suur, Lith. suras salt, Russ. surovui harsh, rough. Cf. Sorrel, the plant.]

senses.d: A sour or acid substance; whatever produces a painful effect.
To cause to become sour; to cause to turn from sweet to sour; as, exposure to the air sours many substances.
q: So the sun's heat, with different powers, Ripens the grape, the liquor sours.

senses.d: To make cold and unproductive, as soil.
To make unhappy, uneasy, or less agreeable.
q: To sour your happiness I must report, The queen is dead.

senses.d: To cause or permit to become harsh or unkindly.
q: Pride had not sour'd nor wrath debased my heart.

senses.d: To macerate, and render fit for plaster or mortar; as, to sour lime for business purposes.

Sour.etym: [AS. s�rian to sour, to become sour.]

senses.d: To become sour; to turn from sweet to sour; as, milk soon sours in hot weather; a kind temper sometimes sours in adversity.
q: They keep out melancholy from the virtuous, and hinder the hatred of vice from souring into severity.

senses.d: That one of the four cardinal points directly opposite to the north; the region or direction to the right or direction to the right of a person who faces the east.
A country, region, or place situated farther to the south than another; the southern section of a country.
Specifically: That part of the United States which is south of Mason and Dixon's line. See under Line.
The wind from the south.

South.etym: [OE. south, suþ, AS. sūð for sunð; akin to D. zuid, OHG. sund, G. süd, süden, Icel. suðr, sunnr, Dan. syd, sönden, Sw. syd, söder, sunnan; all probably akin to E. sun, meaning, the side towards the sun. √297. See Sun.]

senses.d: Lying toward the south; situated at the south, or in a southern direction from the point of observation or reckoning; proceeding toward the south, or coming from the south; blowing from the south; southern; as, the south pole.
Toward the south; southward.
From the south; as, the wind blows south.
To turn or move toward the south; to veer toward the south.
To come to the meridian; to cross the north and south line; — said chiefly of the moon; as, the moon souths at nine.
Toward the south, or toward a point nearer the south than the east or west point; as, to go southward.
Toward the south.
The southern regions or countries; the south.
To sew. See Sew.
The female of swine, or of the hog kind.
A sow bug.
A channel or runner which receives the rows of molds in the pig bed.
A kind of covered shed, formerly used by besiegers in filling up and passing the ditch of a besieged place, sapping and mining the wall, or the like.

Sow.etym: [OE. sowe, suwe, AS. sugu, akin to sū, D. zog, zeug, OHG. sū, G. sau, Icel. sȳr, Dan. so, Sw. sugga, so, L. sus. Gr. ὑ̑σ, συ̑σ, Zend. hu boar; probably from the root seen in Skr. sū to beget, to bear; the animal being named in allusion to its fecundity. √294. Cf. Hyena, Soil to stain, Son, Swine.]

senses.d: To scatter, as seed, upon the earth; to plant by strewing; as, to sow wheat. Also used figuratively: To spread abroad; to propagate.
q: A sower went forth to sow; and when he sowed, some seeds fell by the wayside.
And sow dissension in the hearts of brothers.

senses.d: To scatter seed upon, in, or over; to supply or stock, as land, with seeds. Also used figuratively: To scatter over; to besprinkle.
q: The intellectual faculty is a goodly field, . . . and it is the worst husbandry in the world to sow it with trifles.
sowed with stars the heaven.
Now morn . . . sowed the earth with orient pearl.

Sow.etym: [OE. sowen, sawen, AS. sāwan; akin to OFries. s�a, D. zaaijen, OS. & HG. sājan, G. säen, Icel. sā, Sw. så, Dan. saae, Goth. saian, Lith. sēti, Russ. sieiate, L. serere, sevi. Cf. Saturday, Season, Seed, Seminary.]

senses.d: To scatter seed for growth and the production of a crop; — literally or figuratively.
q: They that sow in tears shall reap in joi.

senses.d: One who, or that which, sows.
Extension, considered independently of anything which it may contain; that which makes extended objects conceivable and possible.
q: Pure space is capable neither of resistance nor motion.

senses.d: Place, having more or less extension; room.
q: They gave him chase, and hunted him as hare; Long had he no space to dwell .
While I have time and space.

senses.d: A quantity or portion of extension; distance from one thing to another; an interval between any two or more objects; as, the space between two stars or two hills; the sound was heard for the space of a mile.
q: Put a space betwixt drove and drove.

senses.d: Quantity of time; an interval between two points of time; duration; time.
q: Nine times the space that measures day and night.
God may defer his judgments for a time, and give a people a longer space of repentance.

senses.d: A short time; a while.
Walk; track; path; course.
q: This ilke monk let old things pace, And held after the new world the space.

senses.d: A small piece of metal cast lower than a face type, so as not to receive the ink in printing, — used to separate words or letters.
One of the intervals, or open places, between the lines of the staff.

Space.etym: [OE. space, F. espace, from L. spatium space; cf. Gr. σπα̑ν to draw, to tear; perh. akin to E. span. Cf. Expatiate.]

senses.d: To walk; to rove; to roam.
q: And loved in forests wild to space.

Space.etym: [Cf. OF. espacier, L. spatiari. See Space, n.]

senses.d: To arrange or adjust the spaces in or between; as, to space words, lines, or letters.
The space from the thumb to the end of the little finger when extended; nine inches; eighth of a fathom.
Hence, a small space or a brief portion of time.
q: Yet not to earth's contracted span Thy goodness let me bound.
Life's but a span; I'll every inch enjoy.

senses.d: The spread or extent of an arch between its abutments, or of a beam, girder, truss, roof, bridge, or the like, between its supports.
A rope having its ends made fast so that a purchase can be hooked to the bight; also, a rope made fast in the center so that both ends can be used.
A pair of horses or other animals driven together; usually, such a pair of horses when similar in color, form, and action.

Span.etym: [AS. spann; akin to D. span, OHG. spanna, G. spanne, Icel. spönn. √170. See Span, v. t. ]

senses.d: To measure by the span of the hand with the fingers extended, or with the fingers encompassing the object; as, to span a space or distance; to span a cylinder.
q: My right hand hath spanned the heavens.

senses.d: To reach from one side of to the order; to stretch over as an arch.
q: The rivers were spanned by arches of solid masonry.

senses.d: To fetter, as a horse; to hobble.

Span.etym: [AS. pannan; akin to D. & G. spannen, OHG. spannan, Sw. spänna, Dan. spænde, Icel. spenna, and perh. to Gr. � to draw, to drag, L. spatium space. √170. Cf. Spin, v. t., Space, Spasm.]

senses.d: To be matched, as horses.

An old name for a nonmetallic mineral, usually cleavable and somewhat lustrous; as, calc spar, or calcite, fluor spar, etc. It was especially used in the case of the gangue minerals of a metalliferous vein.

Spar.etym: [AS. spær in spærstān chalkstone; akin to MHG. spar, G. sparkalk plaster.]

senses.d: A general term any round piece of timber used as a mast, yard, boom, or gaff.
Formerly, a piece of timber, in a general sense; — still applied locally to rafters.
The bar of a gate or door.

Spar.etym: [OE. sparre; akin to D. spar, G. sparren, OHG. sparro, Dan. & Sw. sparre, Icel. sparri; of uncertain origin. � 171. Cf. Spar, v. t. ]

senses.d: To bolt; to bar.
To To supply or equip with spars, as a vessel.

Spar.etym: [OE. sparren, AS. sparrian; akin to G. sperren, Icel. sperra; from the noun. √171. See Spara beam, bar.]

senses.d: To strike with the feet or spurs, as cocks do.
To use the fists and arms scientifically in attack or defense; to contend or combat with the fists, as for exercise or amusement; to box.
q: Made believe to spar at Paul with great science.

senses.d: To contest in words; to wrangle.

Spar.etym: [Of uncertain origin; cf. OF. esparer to kick, F. éparer, or Icel. sperra to stretch out the legs, to struggle.]

senses.d: A contest at sparring or boxing.
A movement of offense or defense in boxing.
To use frugally or stintingly, as that which is scarce or valuable; to retain or keep unused; to save.
q: thy Father's dreadful thunder didst not spare.
He that hath knowledge, spareth his words.

senses.d: To keep to one's self; to forbear to impart or give.
q: Be pleased your plitics to spare.
Spare my sight the pain Of seeing what a world of tears it costs you.

senses.d: To preserve from danger or punishment; to forbear to punish, injure, or harm; to show mercy to.
q: Spare us, good Lord.
Dim sadness did not spare That time celestial visages.
Man alone can whom he conquers spare.

senses.d: To save or gain, as by frugality; to reserve, as from some occupation, use, or duty.
q: All the time he could spare from the necessary cares of his weighty charge, he �estowed on . . . serving of God.

senses.d: To deprive one's self of, as by being frugal; to do without; to dispense with; to give up; to part with.
q: Where angry Jove did never spare One breath of kind and temperate air.
I could have better spared a better man.

Spare.etym: [AS. sparian, fr. spær spare, sparing, saving; akin to D. & G. sparen, OHG. spar�n, Icel. & Sw. spara, Dan. spare See Spare, a.]

senses.d: To be frugal; not to be profuse; to live frugally; to be parsimonious.
q: I, who at some times spend, at others spare, Divided between carelessness and care.

senses.d: To refrain from inflicting harm; to use mercy or forbearance.
q: He will not spare in the day of vengeance.

senses.d: To desist; to stop; to refrain.
Scanty; not abundant or plentiful; as, a spare diet.
Sparing; frugal; parsimonious; chary.
q: He was spare, but discreet of speech.

senses.d: Being over and above what is necessary, or what must be used or reserved; not wanted, or not used; superfluous; as, I have no spare time.
q: If that no spare clothes he had to give.

senses.d: Held in reserve, to be used in an emergency; as, a spare anchor; a spare bed or room.
Lean; wanting flesh; meager; thin; gaunt.
q: O, give me the spare men, and spare me the great ones.

senses.d: Slow.

Spare.etym: [AS. spær sparing. Cf. Spare, v. t. ]

senses.d: The act of sparing; moderation; restraint.
q: Killing for sacrifice, without any spare.

senses.d: Parsimony; frugal use.
q: Poured out their plenty without spite or spare.

senses.d: An opening in a petticoat or gown; a placket.
That which has not been used or expended.

The right of bowling again at a full set of pins, after having knocked all the pins down in less than three bowls. If all the pins are knocked down in one bowl it is a double spare; in two bowls, a single spare.
Spare; saving; frugal; merciful.
A small particle of fire or ignited substance which is emitted by a body in combustion.
q: Man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward.

senses.d: A small, shining body, or transient light; a sparkle.
That which, like a spark, may be kindled into a flame, or into action; a feeble germ; an elementary principle.
q: We have here and there a little clear light, some sparks of bright knowledge.
Bright gem instinct with music, vocal spark.

Spark.etym: [OE. sparke, AS. spearca; akin to D. spark, sperk; cf. Icel. spraka to crackle, Lith. spragëti, Gr. � a bursting with a noise, Skr. sph�rj to crackle, to thunder. Cf. Speak.]

senses.d: A brisk, showy, gay man.
q: The finest sparks and cleanest beaux.

senses.d: A lover; a gallant; a beau.
To sparkle.
To play the spark, beau, or lover.
q: A sure sign that his master was courting, or, as it is termed, sparking, within.

senses.d: To produce, or give off, sparks, as a dynamo at the commutator when revolving under the collecting brushes.
A little spark; a scintillation.
q: As fire is wont to quicken and go From a sparkle sprungen amiss, Till a city brent up is.
The shock was sufficiently strong to strike out some sparkles of his fiery temper.

senses.d: Brilliancy; luster; as, the sparkle of a diamond.

To emit sparks; to throw off ignited or incandescent particles; to shine as if throwing off sparks; to emit flashes of light; to scintillate; to twinkle; as, the blazing wood sparkles; the stars sparkle.
q: A mantelet upon his shoulder hanging Bretful of rubies red, as fire sparkling.

senses.d: To manifest itself by, or as if by, emitting sparks; to glisten; to flash.
q: I see bright honor sparkle through your eyes.

senses.d: To emit little bubbles, as certain kinds of liquors; to effervesce; as, sparkling wine.

Sparkle.syn: To shine; glisten; scintillate; radiate; coruscate; glitter; twinkle.

senses.d: To emit in the form or likeness of sparks.
To disperse.
q: The Landgrave hath sparkled his army without any further enterprise.

senses.d: To scatter on or over.

One of many species of small singing birds of the family Fringilligæ, having conical bills, and feeding chiefly on seeds. Many sparrows are called also finches, and buntings. The common sparrow, or house sparrow, of Europe (Passer domesticus) is noted for its familiarity, its voracity, its attachment to its young, and its fecundity. See House sparrow, under House.
Any one of several small singing birds somewhat resembling the true sparrows in form or habits, as the European hedge sparrow. See under Hedge.
q: He that doth the ravens feed, Yea, providently caters for the sparrow, Be comfort to my age!

Sparrow.etym: [OE. sparwe, AS. spearwa; akin to OHG. sparo, G. sperling, Icel. spörr, Dan. spurv, spurre, Sw. sparf, Goth. sparwa; — originally, probably, the quiverer or flutterer, and akin to E. spurn. See Spurn, and cf. Spavin.]

senses.d: A young oyster or other bivalve mollusk, both before and after it first becomes adherent, or such young, collectively.

Spat.etym: [From the root of spit; hence, literally, that which is ejected.]

senses.d: To emit spawn; to emit, as spawn.
A light blow with something flat.
Hence, a petty combat, esp. a verbal one; a little quarrel, dispute, or dissension.
To dispute.
To slap, as with the open hand; to clap together; as the hands.
q: Little Isabel leaped up and down, spatting her hands.

senses.d: A legging; a gaiter.
A kind of short cloth or leather gaiter worn over the upper part of the shoe and fastened beneath the instep; — chiefly in pl.
To utter words or articulate sounds, as human beings; to express thoughts by words; as, the organs may be so obstructed that a man may not be able to speak.
q: Till at the last spake in this manner.
Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth.

senses.d: To express opinions; to say; to talk; to converse.
q: That fluid substance in a few minutes begins to set, as the tradesmen speak.
An honest man, is able to speak for himself, when a knave is not.
During the century and a half which followed the Conquest, there is, to speak strictly, no English history.

senses.d: To utter a speech, discourse, or harangue; to adress a public assembly formally.
q: Many of the nobility made themselves popular by speaking in Parliament against those things which were most grateful to his majesty.

senses.d: To discourse; to make mention; to tell.
q: Lycan speaks of a part of Cæsar's army that came to him from the Leman Lake.

senses.d: To give sound; to sound.
q: Make all our trumpets speak.

senses.d: To convey sentiments, ideas, or intelligence as if by utterance; as, features that speak of self-will.
q: Thine eye begins to speak.

Speak.syn: To say; tell; talk; converse; discourse; articulate; pronounce; utter.
Speak.etym: [OE. speken, AS. specan, sprecan; akin to OF.ries. spreka, D. spreken, OS. spreken, G. sprechen, OHG. sprehhan, and perhaps to Skr. sphūrj to crackle, to thunder. Cf. Spark of fire, Speech.]

senses.d: To utter with the mouth; to pronounce; to utter articulately, as human beings.
q: They sat down with him upn ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him.

senses.d: To utter in a word or words; to say; to tell; to declare orally; as, to speak the truth; to speak sense.
To declare; to proclaim; to publish; to make known; to exhibit; to express in any way.
q: It is my father;s muste To speak your deeds.
Speaking a still good morrow with her eyes.
And for the heaven's wide circuit, let it speak The maker's high magnificence.
Report speaks you a bonny monk.

senses.d: To talk or converse in; to utter or pronounce, as in conversation; as, to speak Latin.
q: And French she spake full fair and fetisely.

senses.d: To address; to accost; to speak to.
q: thee in hope; he will speak thee fair.
each village senior paused to scan And speak the lovely caravan.

senses.d: One who speaks.
A book of selections for declamation.
Uttering speech; used for conveying speech; as, man is a speaking animal; a speaking tube.
Seeming to be capable of speech; hence, lifelike; as, a speaking likeness.
The act of uttering words.
Public declamation; oratory.
A long, pointed weapon, used in war and hunting, by thrusting or throwing; a weapon with a long shaft and a sharp head or blade; a lance.
q: They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks.

senses.d: Fig.: A spearman.
A sharp-pointed instrument with barbs, used for stabbing fish and other animals.
A shoot, as of grass; a spire.
The feather of a horse. See Feather, n., 4.
The rod to which the bucket, or plunger, of a pump is attached; a pump rod.

Spear.etym: [OE. spere, AS. spere; akin to D. & G. speer, OS. & OHS. sper, Icel. spjör, pl., Dan. spær, L. sparus.]

senses.d: To pierce with a spear; to kill with a spear; as, to spear a fish.
To shoot into a long stem, as some plants. See Spire.
Of or pertaining to a species; constituting a species or sort.
q: A special is called by the schools a “species”.

senses.d: Particular; peculiar; different from others; extraordinary; uncommon.
q: Our Savior is represented everywhere in Scripture as the special patron of the poor and the afficted.
To this special evil an improvement of style would apply a special redress.

senses.d: Appropriate; designed for a particular purpose, occasion, or person; as, a special act of Parliament or of Congress; a special sermon.
Limited in range; confined to a definite field of action, investigation, or discussion; as, a special dictionary of commercial terms; a special branch of study.
Chief in excellence.
q: The king hath drawn The special head of all the land together.

Special.syn: Peculiar; appropriate; specific; dictinctive; particular; exceptional; singular. See Peculiar.
Special.etym: [L. specialis, fr. species a particular sort, kind, or quality: cf. F. spécial. See Species, and cf. Especial.]

senses.d: A particular.
One appointed for a special service or occasion.
In a special manner; particularly; especially.
For a particular purpose; as, a meeting of the legislature is specially summoned.
A little or spot in or anything, of a different substance or color from that of the thing itself.
q: An huge great serpent, all with speckles pied.

senses.d: To mark with small spots of a different color from that of the rest of the surface; to variegate with spots of a different color from the ground or surface.
Marked or variegated with small spots of a different color from that of the rest of the surface.
Something exhibited to view; usually, something presented to view as extraordinary, or as unusual and worthy of special notice; a remarkable or noteworthy sight; a show; a pageant; a gazingstock.
q: O, piteous spectacle? O, bloody times!

senses.d: A spy-glass; a looking-glass.
q: Poverty a spectacle is, as thinketh me, Through which he may his very friends see.

senses.d: An optical instrument consisting of two lenses set in a light frame, and worn to assist sight, to obviate some defect in the organs of vision, or to shield the eyes from bright light.
Fig.: An aid to the intellectual sight.
q: Shakespeare . . . needed not the spectacles of books to read nature.

Spectacle.etym: [F., fr. L. spectaculum, fr. spectare to look at, to behold, v. intens. fr. specere. See Spy.]

senses.d: The faculty of uttering articulate sounds or words; the faculty of expressing thoughts by words or articulate sounds; the power of speaking.
q: There is none comparable to the variety of instructive expressions by speech, wherewith man alone is endowed for the communication of his thoughts.

senses.d: he act of speaking; that which is spoken; words, as expressing ideas; language; conversation.
q: O goode God! how gentle and how kind Ye seemed by your speech and your visage The day that maked was our marriage.
The acts of God . . . to human ears Can nort without process of speech be told.

senses.d: A particular language, as distinct from others; a tongue; a dialect.
q: People of a strange speech and of an hard language.

senses.d: Talk; mention; common saying.
q: The duke . . . did of me demand What was the speech among the Londoners Concerning the French journey.

senses.d: formal discourse in public; oration; harangue.
q: The constant design of these orators, in all their speeches, was to drive some one particular point.

senses.d: ny declaration of thoughts.
q: I. with leave of speech implored, . . . replied.

Speech.syn: Syn. Harangue; language; address; oration. See Harangue, and Language.
Speech.etym: [OE. speche, AS. sp�c, spr�, fr. specan, sprecan, to speak; akin to D. spraak speech, OHG. sprāhha, G. sprache, Sw. spr�k, Dan. sprog. See Speak.]

senses.d: To make a speech; to harangue.
Destitute or deprived of the faculty of speech.
Not speaking for a time; dumb; mute; silent.
q: Speechless with wonder, and half dead with fear.

senses.d: Prosperity in an undertaking; favorable issue; success.
q: O Lord God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day.

senses.d: The act or state of moving swiftly; swiftness; velocity; rapidly; rate of motion; dispatch; as, the speed a horse or a vessel.
q: Speed, to describe whose swiftness number fails.

senses.d: One who, or that which, causes or promotes speed or success.

Speed.syn: Haste; swiftness; celerity; quickness; dispatch; expedition; hurry; acceleration. See Haste.
Speed.etym: [AS. sp�d success, swiftness, from sp�wan to succeed; akin to D. spoedd, OHG. spuot success, spuot to succees, Skr. sphā to increase, grow fat. √170b.]

senses.d: To go; to fare.
q: To warn him now he is too farre sped.

senses.d: To experience in going; to have any condition, good or ill; to fare.
q: Ships heretofore in seas like fishes sped; The mightiest still upon the smallest fed.

senses.d: To fare well; to have success; to prosper.
q: Save London, and send true lawyers their meed! For whoso wants money with them shall not speed!
I told ye then he should prevail, and speed On his bad errand.

senses.d: To make haste; to move with celerity.
q: I have speeded hither with the very extremest inch of possibility.

senses.d: To be expedient.

Speed.etym: [AS. spēdan, fr. spēd, n.; akin to D. spoeden, G. sich sputen. See Speed, n.]

senses.d: To cause to be successful, or to prosper; hence, to aid; to favor.
q: With rising gales that speed their happy flight.

senses.d: To cause to make haste; to dispatch with celerity; to drive at full speed; hence, to hasten; to hurry.
q: He sped him thence home to his habitation.

senses.d: To hasten to a conclusion; to expedite.
q: Judicial acts . . . are sped in open court at the instance of one or both of the parties.

senses.d: To hurry to destruction; to put an end to; to ruin; to undo.
q: A dire dilemma! either way I 'm sped. If foes, they write, if friends, they read, me dead.

senses.d: To wish success or god fortune to, in any undertaking, especially in setting out upon a journey.
q: Welcome the coming, speed the parting guest.

Speed.syn: To dispatch; hasten; expedite; accelerate; hurry.

senses.d: In a speedy manner.
Not dilatory or slow; quick; swift; nimble; hasty; rapid in motion or performance; as, a speedy flight; on speedy foot.
q: I will wish her speedy strength.
Darts, which not the good could shun, The speedy ould outfly.

senses.d: To weigh or lay out; to dispose of; to part with; as, to spend money for clothing.
q: Spend thou that in the town.
Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?

senses.d: To bestow; to employ; — often with on or upon.
q: I . . . am never loath To spend my judgment.

senses.d: To consume; to waste; to squander; to exhaust; as, to spend an estate in gaming or other vices.
To pass, as time; to suffer to pass away; as, to spend a day idly; to spend winter abroad.
q: We spend our years as a tale that is told.

senses.d: To exhaust of force or strength; to waste; to wear away; as, the violence of the waves was spent.
q: Their bodies spent with long labor and thirst.

Spend.etym: [AS. spendan (in comp.), fr. L. expendere or dispendere to weigh out, to expend, dispense. See Pendant, and cf. Dispend, Expend, Spence, Spencer.]

senses.d: To expend money or any other possession; to consume, use, waste, or part with, anything; as, he who gets easily spends freely.
q: He spends as a person who knows that he must come to a reckoning.

senses.d: To waste or wear away; to be consumed; to lose force or strength; to vanish; as, energy spends in the using of it.
q: The sound spendeth and is dissipated in the open air.

senses.d: To be diffused; to spread.
q: The vines that they use for wine are so often cut, that their sap spendeth into the grapes.

senses.d: To break ground; to continue working.
Exhausted; worn out; having lost energy or motive force.
q: Now thou seest me Spent, overpowered, despairing of success.
Heaps of spent arrows fall and strew the ground.

senses.d: Exhausted of spawn or sperm; — said especially of fishes.
To eject from the stomach; to vomit.
To cast forth with abhorrence or disgust; to eject.
q: Because thou art lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spew thee out of my mouth.

Spew.etym: [OE. spewen, speowen, AS. spīwan;n to D. spuwen to spit. OS & OHG. spīwan, G. speien, Icel. sp�ja to spew, Sw. spy, Dan. spye, Goth. spiewan, th. spjauti, L. spuere to split, Gr. ���, Skr. shtiv, shthīv. Cf. Pyke, Spit.]

senses.d: To vomit.
To eject seed, as wet land swollen with frost.
That which is vomited; vomit.
Species; kind.
q: The spices of penance ben three.
Abstain you from all evil spice.
Justice, although it be but one entire virtue, yet is described in two kinds of spices. The one is named justice distributive, the other is called commutative.

senses.d: A vegetable production of many kinds, fragrant or aromatic and pungent to the taste, as pepper, cinnamon, nutmeg, mace, allspice, ginger, cloves, etc., which are used in cookery and to flavor sauces, pickles, etc.
q: Hast thou aught in thy purse any hot spices?

senses.d: Figuratively, that which enriches or alters the quality of a thing in a small degree, as spice alters the taste of food; that which gives zest or pungency; a slight flavoring; a relish; hence, a small quantity or admixture; a sprinkling; as, a spice of mischief.
q: So much of the will, with a spice of the willful.

Spice.etym: [OE. spice, spece, spice, species, OF. espice, espece, F. épice spice, espèce species, fr. L. species particular sort or kind, a species, a sight, appearance, show, LL., spices, drugs, etc., of the same sort, fr. L. specere to look. See Spy, and cf. Species.]

senses.d: To season with spice, or as with spice; to mix aromatic or pungent substances with; to flavor; to season; as, to spice wine; to spice one's words with wit.
q: She 'll receive thee, but will spice thy bread With flowery poisons.

senses.d: To fill or impregnate with the odor of spices.
q: In the spiced Indian air, by night.

senses.d: To render nice or dainty; hence, to render scrupulous.
Spices, in general.
A repository of spices.

Any one of numerous species of arachnids comprising the order Araneina. Spiders have the mandibles converted into poison fangs, or falcers. The abdomen is large and not segmented, with two or three pairs of spinnerets near the end, by means of which they spin threads of silk to form cocoons, or nests, to protect their eggs and young. Many species spin also complex webs to entrap the insects upon which they prey. The eyes are usually eight in number (rarely six), and are situated on the back of the cephalothorax. See Illust. under Araneina.
Any one of various other arachnids resembling the true spiders, especially certain mites, as the red spider (see under Red).
An iron pan with a long handle, used as a kitchen utensil in frying food. Originally, it had long legs, and was used over coals on the hearth.
A trevet to support pans or pots over a fire.

A skeleton, or frame, having radiating arms or members, often connected by crosspieces; as, a casting forming the hub and spokes to which the rim of a fly wheel or large gear is bolted; the body of a piston head; a frame for strengthening a core or mold for a casting, etc.

Spider.etym: [OE. spiþre, fr. AS. spinnan to spin; — so named from spinning its web; cf. D. spin a spider, G. spinne, Sw. spindel. See Spin.]

senses.d: An aromatic plant. In the United States it is the Aralia racemosa, often called spignet, and used as a medicine. The spikenard of the ancients is the Nardostachys Jatamansi, a native of the Himalayan region. From its blackish roots a perfume for the hair is still prepared in India.
A fragrant essential oil, as that from the Nardostachys Jatamansi.

Spikenard.etym: [For spiked nard; cf. G. spieknarde, NL. spica nardi. See Spike an ear, and Nard.]

senses.d: A bit of wood split off; a splinter.
A slender piece of anything.
A peg or pin for plugging a hole, as in a cask; a spile.
A metallic rod or pin.
A small roll of paper, or slip of wood, used as a lamplighter, etc.
One of the thick laths or poles driven horizontally ahead of the main timbering in advancing a level in loose ground.
A little sum of money.
To cover or decorate with slender pieces of wood, metal, ivory, etc.; to inlay.
To destroy; to kill; to put an end to.
q: And gave him to the queen, all at her will To choose whether she would him save or spill.
Greater glory think to save than spill.

senses.d: To mar; to injure; to deface; hence, to destroy by misuse; to waste.
q: They disfigure the stuff and spill the whole workmanship.
Spill not the morning, the quintessence of day, in recreations.

senses.d: To suffer to fall or run out of a vessel; to lose, or suffer to be scattered; — applied to fluids and to substances whose particles are small and loose; as, to spill water from a pail; to spill quicksilver from a vessel; to spill powder from a paper; to spill sand or flour.
To cause to flow out and be lost or wasted; to shed, or suffer to be shed, as in battle or in manslaughter; as, a man spills another's blood, or his own blood.
q: And to revenge his blood so justly spilt.

senses.d: To relieve a sail from the pressure of the wind, so that it can be more easily reefed or furled, or to lessen the strain.

Spill.etym: [OE. spillen, usually, to destroy, AS. spillan, spildan, to destroy; akin to Icel. spilla to destroy, Sw. spilla to spill, Dan. spilde, LG. & D. spillen to squander, OHG. spildan.]

senses.d: To be destroyed, ruined, or wasted; to come to ruin; to perish; to waste.
q: That thou wilt suffer innocents to spill.

senses.d: To be shed; to run over; to fall out, and be lost or wasted.
To draw out, and twist into threads, either by the hand or machinery; as, to spin wool, cotton, or flax; to spin goat's hair; to produce by drawing out and twisting a fibrous material.
q: All the yarn she spun in Ulysses' absence did but fill Ithaca full of moths.

senses.d: To draw out tediously; to form by a slow process, or by degrees; to extend to a great length; — with out; as, to spin out large volumes on a subject.
q: Do you mean that story is tediously spun out?

senses.d: To protract; to spend by delays; as, to spin out the day in idleness.
q: By one delay after another they spin out their whole lives.

senses.d: To cause to turn round rapidly; to whirl; to twirl; as, to spin a top.

To form (a web, a cocoon, silk, or the like) from threads produced by the extrusion of a viscid, transparent liquid, which hardens on coming into contact with the air; — said of the spider, the silkworm, etc.
To shape, as malleable sheet metal, into a hollow form, by bending or buckling it by pressing against it with a smooth hand tool or roller while the metal revolves, as in a lathe.

Spin.etym: [AS. spinnan; akin to D. & G. spinnen, Icel. & Sw. spinna, Dan. spinde, Goth. spinnan, and probably to E. span. √170. Cf. Span, v. t., Spider.]

senses.d: To practice spinning; to work at drawing and twisting threads; to make yarn or thread from fiber; as, the woman knows how to spin; a machine or jenny spins with great exactness.
q: They neither know to spin, nor care to toll.

senses.d: To move round rapidly; to whirl; to revolve, as a top or a spindle, about its axis.
q: Round about him spun the landscape, Sky and forest reeled together.
With a whirligig of jubilant mosquitoes spinning about each head.

senses.d: To stream or issue in a thread or a small current or jet; as, blood spinsfrom a vein.
To move swifty; as, to spin along the road in a carriage, on a bicycle, etc.
The act of spinning; as, the spin of a top; a spin a bicycle.
Velocity of rotation about some specified axis.

The long, round, slender rod or pin in spinning wheels by which the thread is twisted, and on which, when twisted, it is wound; also, the pin on which the bobbin is held in a spinning machine, or in the shuttle of a loom.
