A slender rod or pin on which anything turns; an axis; as, the spindle of a vane.
The shaft, mandrel, or arbor, in a machine tool, as a lathe or drilling machine, etc., which causes the work to revolve, or carries a tool or center, etc.
The vertical rod on which the runner of a grinding mill turns.
A shaft or pipe on which a core of sand is formed.
The fusee of a watch.
A long and slender stalk resembling a spindle.
A yarn measure containing, in cotton yarn, 15,120 yards; in linen yarn, 14,400 yards.
A solid generated by the revolution of a curved line about its base or double ordinate or chord.
Any marine univalve shell of the genus Rostellaria; — called also spindle stromb.

Spindle.etym: [AS. spinal, fr. spinnan to spin; akin to D. spil, G. spille, spindel, OHG. spinnala. √170. See Spin.]

senses.d: To shoot or grow into a long, slender stalk or body; to become disproportionately tall and slender.
q: It has begun to spindle into overintellectuality.

senses.d: Air set in motion by breathing; breath; hence, sometimes, life itself.
q: The mild air, with season moderate, Gently attempered, and disposed eo well, That still it breathed foorth sweet spirit.

senses.d: A rough breathing; an aspirate, as the letter h; also, a mark to denote aspiration; a breathing.
q: Be it a letter or spirit, we have great use for it.

senses.d: Life, or living substance, considered independently of corporeal existence; an intelligence conceived of apart from any physical organization or embodiment; vital essence, force, or energy, as distinct from matter.
The intelligent, immaterial and immortal part of man; the soul, in distinction from the body in which it resides; the agent or subject of vital and spiritual functions, whether spiritual or material.
q: There is a spirit in man; and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding.
As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.
Spirit is a substance wherein thinking, knowing, doubting, and a power of moving, do subsist.

senses.d: Specifically, a disembodied soul; the human soul after it has left the body.
q: Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was, and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
Ye gentle spirits far away, With whom we shared the cup of grace.

senses.d: Any supernatural being, good or bad; an apparition; a specter; a ghost; also, sometimes, a sprite,; a fairy; an elf.
q: Whilst young, preserve his tender mind from all impressions of spirits and goblins in the dark.

senses.d: Energy, vivacity, ardor, enthusiasm, courage, etc.
q: “Write it then, quickly,” replied Bede; and summoning all his spirits together, like the last blaze of a candle going out, he indited it, and expired.

senses.d: One who is vivacious or lively; one who evinces great activity or peculiar characteristics of mind or temper; as, a ruling spirit; a schismatic spirit.
q: Such spirits as he desired to please, such would I choose for my judges.

senses.d: Temper or disposition of mind; mental condition or disposition; intellectual or moral state; — often in the plural; as, to be cheerful, or in good spirits; to be downhearted, or in bad spirits.
q: God has . . . made a spirit of building succeed a spirit of pulling down.
A perfect judge will read each work of wit With the same spirit that its author writ.

senses.d: Intent; real meaning; — opposed to the letter, or to formal statement; also, characteristic quality, especially such as is derived from the individual genius or the personal character; as, the spirit of an enterprise, of a document, or the like.
Tenuous, volatile, airy, or vapory substance, possessed of active qualities.
q: All bodies have spirits . . . within them.

senses.d: Any liquid produced by distillation; especially, alcohol, the spirits, or spirit, of wine (it having been first distilled from wine): — often in the plural.

Spirit.syn: Life; ardor; energy; fire; courage; animatioon; cheerfulness; vivacity; enterprise.
Spirit.etym: [OF. espirit, esperit, F. esprit, L. spiritus, from spirare to breathe, to blow. Cf. Conspire, Expire, Esprit, Sprite.]

senses.d: To animate with vigor; to excite; to encourage; to inspirit; as, civil dissensions often spirit the ambition of private men; — sometimes followed by up.
q: Many officers and private men spirit up and assist those obstinate people to continue in their rebellion.

senses.d: To convey rapidly and secretly, or mysteriously, as if by the agency of a spirit; to kidnap; — often with away, or off.
q: The ministry had him spirited away, and carried abroad as a dangerous person.
I felt as if I had been spirited into some castle of antiquity.

senses.d: Consisting of spirit; not material; incorporeal; as, a spiritual substance or being.
q: It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the intellectual and higher endowments of the mind; mental; intellectual.
Of or pertaining to the moral feelings or states of the soul, as distinguished from the external actions; reaching and affecting the spirits.
q: God's law is spiritual; it is a transcript of the divine nature, and extends its authority to the acts of the soul of man.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the soul or its affections as influenced by the Spirit; controlled and inspired by the divine Spirit; proceeding from the Holy Spirit; pure; holy; divine; heavenly-minded; — opposed to carnal.
q: That I may impart unto you some spiritual gift.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings.
If a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one.

senses.d: Not lay or temporal; relating to sacred things; ecclesiastical; as, the spiritual functions of the clergy; lords spiritual and temporal; a spiritual corporation.

Spiritual.etym: [L. spiritualis: cf. F. spirituel. See Spirit.]

senses.d: A spiritual function, office, or affair. See Spirituality, 2.
q: He assigns supremacy to the pope in spirituals, and to the emperor in temporals.

senses.d: In a spiritual manner; with purity of spirit; like a spirit.
A long, slender, pointed rod, usually of iron, for holding meat while roasting.
A small point of land running into the sea, or a long, narrow shoal extending from the shore into the sea; as, a spit of sand.
The depth to which a spade goes in digging; a spade; a spadeful.

Spit.etym: [OE. spite, AS. spitu; akin to D. spit, G. spiess, OHG. spiz, Dan. spid. Sw. spett, and to G. spitz pointed. √170.]

senses.d: To thrust a spit through; to fix upon a spit; hence, to thrust through or impale; as, to spit a loin of veal.
To spade; to dig.
To attend to a spit; to use a spit.
q: She's spitting in the kitchen.

senses.d: To eject from the mouth; to throw out, as saliva or other matter, from the mouth.
To eject; to throw out; to belch.

Spit.etym: [AS. spittan; akin to G. spützen, Dan. spytte, Sw. spotta,Icel. sp�ta, and prob. E. spew. The past tense spat is due to AS. sp�tte, from sp�tan to spit. Cf. Spat, n., Spew, Spawl, Spot, n.]

senses.d: The secretion formed by the glands of the mouth; spitle; saliva; sputum.
To throw out saliva from the mouth.
To rain or snow slightly, or with sprinkles.
q: It had been spitting with rain.

senses.d: Ill-will or hatred toward another, accompanied with the disposition to irritate, annoy, or thwart; petty malice; grudge; rancor; despite.
q: This is the deadly spite that angers.

senses.d: Vexation; chargrin; mortification.
To be angry at; to hate.
q: The Danes, then . . . pagans, spited places of religion.

senses.d: To treat maliciously; to try to injure or thwart.
To fill with spite; to offend; to vex.
q: Darius, spited at the Magi, endeavored to abolish not only their learning, but their language.

senses.d: Filled with, or showing, spite; having a desire to vex, annoy, or injure; malignant; malicious; as, a spiteful person or act.
Put upon a spit; pierced as if by a spit.
Shot out long; — said of antlers.
To dig or stir with a small spade.
A small sort of spade.
The thick, moist matter which is secreted by the salivary glands; saliva; spit.

Spittle.etym: [From Spit to eject from the mouth: cf. Spattle, and AS. spātl.]

senses.d: To plunder; to strip by violence; to pillage; to rob; — with of before the name of the thing taken; as, to spoil one of his goods or possessions.
q: My sons their old, unhappy sire despise, Spoiled of his kingdom, and deprived of eyes.

senses.d: To seize by violence; to take by force; to plunder.
q: No man can enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he will first bind the strong man.

senses.d: To cause to decay and perish; to corrupt; to violate; to mar.
q: Spiritual pride spoils many graces.

senses.d: To render useless by injury; to injure fatally; to ruin; to destroy; as, to spoil paper; to have the crops spoiled by insects; to spoil the eyes by reading.

Spoil.etym: [F. spolier, OF. espoillier, fr. L. spoliare, fr. spolium spoil. Cf. Despoil, Spoliation.]

senses.d: To practice plunder or robbery.
q: Outlaws, which, lurking in woods, used to break forth to rob and spoil.

senses.d: To lose the valuable qualities; to be corrupted; to decay; as, fruit will soon spoil in warm weather.
That which is taken from another by violence; especially, the plunder taken from an enemy; pillage; booty.
q: Gentle gales, Fanning their odoriferous wings, dispense Native perfumes, and whisper whence they stole Those balmy spoils.

senses.d: Public offices and their emoluments regarded as the peculiar property of a successful party or faction, to be bestowed for its own advantage; — commonly in the plural; as, to the victor belong the spoils.
q: From a principle of gratitude I adhered to the coalition; my vote was counted in the day of battle, but I was overlooked in the division of the spoil.

senses.d: That which is gained by strength or effort.
q: Each science and each art his spoil.

senses.d: The act or practice of plundering; robbery; waste.
q: The man that hath no music in himself, Nor is not moved with concord of sweet sounds, Is fit for treason, stratagems, and spoils.

senses.d: Corruption; cause of corruption.
q: Villainous company hath been the spoil of me.

senses.d: The slough, or cast skin, of a serpent or other animal.
One who spoils; a plunderer; a pillager; a robber; a despoiler.
One who corrupts, mars, or renders useless.
The radius or ray of a wheel; one of the small bars which are inserted in the hub, or nave, and which serve to support the rim or felly.
A projecting handle of a steering wheel.
A rung, or round, of a ladder.
A contrivance for fastening the wheel of a vehicle, to prevent it from turning in going down a hill.

Spoke.etym: [OE. spoke, spake, AS. spāca; akin to D. speek, LG. speke, OHG. speihha, G. speiche. √170. Cf. Spike a nail.]

senses.d: To furnish with spokes, as a wheel.
Uttered in speech; delivered by word of mouth; oral; as, a spoken narrative; the spoken word.
Characterized by a certain manner or style in speaking; — often in composition; as, a pleasant-spoken man.
q: Methinks you 're better spoken.

senses.d: One who speaks for another.
q: He shall be thy spokesman unto the people.

senses.d: An implement consisting of a small bowl (usually a shallow oval) with a handle, used especially in preparing or eating food.
q: “Therefore behoveth him a full long spoon That shall eat with a fiend,” thus heard I say.
He must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil.

senses.d: Anything which resembles a spoon in shape; esp. (Fishing), a spoon bait.
Fig.: A simpleton; a spooney.

Spoon.etym: [OE. spon, AS. spōn, a chip; akin to D. spaan, G. span, Dan. spaan, Sw. spån, Icel. spánn, spónn, a chip, a spoon. √170. Cf. Span-new.]

senses.d: To take up in, or as in, a spoon.
To act with demonstrative or foolish fondness, as one in love.
A wooden club with a lofted face.
To catch by fishing with a spoon bait.
q: He had with him all the tackle necessary for spooning pike.

senses.d: In croquet, golf, etc., to push or shove (a ball) with a lifting motion, instead of striking with an audible knock.
To fish with a spoon bait.
In croquet, golf, etc., to spoon a ball.
That which diverts, and makes mirth; pastime; amusement.
q: It is as sport to a fool to do mischief.
Her sports were such as carried riches of knowledge upon the stream of delight.
Think it but a minute spent in sport.

senses.d: Mock; mockery; contemptuous mirth; derision.
q: Then make sport at me; then let me be your jest.

senses.d: That with which one plays, or which is driven about in play; a toy; a plaything; an object of mockery.
q: Flitting leaves, the sport of every wind.
Never does man appear to greater disadvantage than when he is the sport of his own ungoverned passions.

senses.d: Play; idle jingle.
q: An author who should introduce such a sport of words upon our stage would meet with small applause.

senses.d: Diversion of the field, as fowling, hunting, fishing, racing, games, and the like, esp. when money is staked.
A plant or an animal, or part of a plant or animal, which has some peculiarity not usually seen in the species; an abnormal variety or growth. See Sporting plant, under Sporting.
A sportsman; a gambler.

Sport.syn: Play; game; diversion; frolic; mirth; mock; mockery; jeer.

senses.d: To play; to frolic; to wanton.
q: , sporting with quick glance, Show to the sun their waved coats dropt with gold.

senses.d: To practice the diversions of the field or the turf; to be given to betting, as upon races.
To trifle.
To assume suddenly a new and different character from the rest of the plant or from the type of the species; — said of a bud, shoot, plant, or animal. See Sport, n., 6.
To divert; to amuse; to make merry; — used with the reciprocal pronoun.
q: Against whom do ye sport yourselves?

senses.d: To represent by any kind of play.
q: Now sporting on thy lyre the loves of youth.

senses.d: To exhibit, or bring out, in public; to use or wear; as, to sport a new equipage.
To give utterance to in a sportive manner; to throw out in an easy and copious manner; — with off; as, to sport off epigrams.
Of, pertaining to, or engaging in, sport or sports; exhibiting the character or conduct of one who, or that which, sports.
A mark on a substance or body made by foreign matter; a blot; a place discolored.
q: Out, damned spot! Out, I say!

senses.d: A stain on character or reputation; something that soils purity; disgrace; reproach; fault; blemish.
q: Yet Chloe, sure, was formed without a spot.

senses.d: A small part of a different color from the main part, or from the ground upon which it is; as, the spots of a leopard; the spots on a playing card.
A small extent of space; a place; any particular place.
q: That spot to which I point is Paradise.
“A jolly place,” said he, “in times of old! But something ails it now: the spot is cursed.”

senses.d: A variety of the common domestic pigeon, so called from a spot on its head just above its beak.

A sciænoid food fish (Liostomus xanthurus) of the Atlantic coast of the United States. It has a black spot behind the shoulders and fifteen oblique dark bars on the sides. Called also goody, Lafayette, masooka, and old wife.
Commodities, as merchandise and cotton, sold for immediate delivery.

Spot.syn: Stain; flaw; speck; blot; disgrace; reproach; fault; blemish; place; site; locality.
Spot.etym: [Cf. Scot. & D. spat, Dan. spette, Sw. spott spittle, slaver; from the root of E. spit. See Spit to eject from the mouth, and cf. Spatter.]

senses.d: To make visible marks upon with some foreign matter; to discolor in or with spots; to stain; to cover with spots or figures; as, to spot a garment; to spot paper.
To mark or note so as to insure recognition; to recognize; to detect; as, to spot a criminal.
To stain; to blemish; to taint; to disgrace; to tarnish, as reputation; to asperse.
q: My virgin life no spotted thoughts shall stain.
If ever I shall close these eyes but once, May I live spotted for my perjury.

senses.d: To become stained with spots.
Lit., being on the spot, or place;
on hand for immediate delivery after sale; — said of commodities; as, spot wheat.
Marked with spots; as, a spotted garment or character.
A man or woman engaged or joined in wedlock; a married person, husband or wife.
q: At last such grace I found, and means I wrought, That I that lady to my spouse had won.

senses.d: A married man, in distinction from a spousess or married woman; a bridegroom or husband.
q: At which marriage was no persons present but the spouse, the spousess, the Duchess of Bedford her mother, the priest, two gentlewomen, and a young man.

Spouse.etym: [OF. espous, espos, fem. espouse, F. époux, épouse, fr. L. sponsus, sponsa, prop. p. p. of spondere, sponsum, to promise solemnly, to engage one's self. Cf. Despond, Espouse, Respond, Sponsor.]

senses.d: To wed; to espouse.
q: This markis hath her spoused with a ring.
Though spoused, yet wanting wedlock's solemnize.
She was found again, and spoused to Marinell.

senses.d: To extend in length and breadth, or in breadth only; to stretch or expand to a broad or broader surface or extent; to open; to unfurl; as, to spread a carpet; to spread a tent or a sail.
q: He bought a parcel of a field where he had spread his tent.
Here the Rhone Hath spread himself a couch.

senses.d: To extend so as to cover something; to extend to a great or greater extent in every direction; to cause to fill or cover a wide or wider space.
q: Rose, as in a dance, the stately trees, and spread Their branches hung with copious fruit.

senses.d: To divulge; to publish, as news or fame; to cause to be more extensively known; to disseminate; to make known fully; as, to spread a report; — often accompanied by abroad.
q: They, when they were departed, spread abroad his fame in all that country.

senses.d: To propagate; to cause to affect great numbers; as, to spread a disease.
To diffuse, as emanations or effluvia; to emit; as, odoriferous plants spread their fragrance.
To strew; to scatter over a surface; as, to spread manure; to spread lime on the ground.
To prepare; to set and furnish with provisions; as, to spread a table.
q: Boiled the flesh, and spread the board.

Spread.syn: To diffuse; propagate; disperse; publish; distribute; scatter; circulate; disseminate; dispense.
Spread.etym: [OE. spreden, AS. sprædan; akin to D. spreiden, spreijen, LG. spreden, spreen, spreien, G. spreiten, Dan. sprede, Sw. sprida. Cf. Spray water flying in drops.]

senses.d: To extend in length and breadth in all directions, or in breadth only; to be extended or stretched; to expand.
q: Plants, if they spread much, are seldom tall.
Governor Winthrop, and his associates at Charlestown, had for a church a large, spreading tree.

senses.d: To be extended by drawing or beating; as, some metals spread with difficulty.
To be made known more extensively, as news.
To be propagated from one to another; as, the disease spread into all parts of the city.
Extent; compass.
q: I have got a fine spread of improvable land.

senses.d: Expansion of parts.
q: No flower hath spread like that of the woodbine.

senses.d: A cloth used as a cover for a table or a bed.
A table, as spread or furnished with a meal; hence, an entertainment of food; a feast.
A privilege which one person buys of another, of demanding certain shares of stock at a certain price, or of delivering the same shares of stock at another price, within a time agreed upon.
An unlimited expanse of discontinuous points.

An arbitrage transaction operated by buying and selling simultaneously in two separate markets, as Chicago and New York, when there is an abnormal difference in price between the two markets. It is called a back spreadwhen the difference in price is less than the normal one.
Surface in proportion to the depth of a cut stone.
A small shoot or twig of a tree or other plant; a spray; as, a sprig of laurel or of parsley.
A youth; a lad; — used humorously or in slight disparagement.
q: A sprig whom I remember, with a whey-face and a satchel, not so many years ago.

senses.d: A brad, or nail without a head.
A small eyebolt ragged or barbed at the point.

Sprig.etym: [AS. sprec; akin to Icel. sprek a stick. Cf. Spray a branch.]

senses.d: To mark or adorn with the representation of small branches; to work with sprigs; as, to sprig muslin.
To leap; to bound; to jump.
q: The mountain stag that springs From height to height, and bounds along the plains.

senses.d: To issue with speed and violence; to move with activity; to dart; to shoot.
q: And sudden light Sprung through the vaulted roof.

senses.d: To start or rise suddenly, as from a covert.
q: Watchful as fowlers when their game will spring.

senses.d: To fly back; as, a bow, when bent, springs back by its elastic power.
To bend from a straight direction or plane surface; to become warped; as, a piece of timber, or a plank, sometimes springs in seasoning.
To shoot up, out, or forth; to come to the light; to begin to appear; to emerge; as a plant from its seed, as streams from their source, and the like; — often followed by up, forth, or out.
q: Till well nigh the day began to spring.
To satisfy the desolate and waste ground, and to cause the bud of the tender herb to spring forth.
Do not blast my springing hopes.
O, spring to light; auspicious Babe, be born.

senses.d: To issue or proceed, as from a parent or ancestor; to result, as from a cause, motive, reason, or principle.
q: new hope to spring Out of despair, joy, but with fear yet linked.

senses.d: To grow; to thrive; to prosper.
q: What makes all this, but Jupiter the king, At whose command we perish, and we spring?

Spring.etym: [AS. springan; akin to D. & G. springen, OS. & OHG. springan, Icel. & Sw. springa, Dan. springe; cf. Gr. σπέρχεσθαι to hasten. Cf. Springe, Sprinkle.]

senses.d: To cause to spring up; to start or rouse, as game; to cause to rise from the earth, or from a covert; as, to spring a pheasant.
To produce or disclose suddenly or unexpectedly.
q: She starts, and leaves her bed, and springs a light.
The friends to the cause sprang a new project.

senses.d: To cause to explode; as, to spring a mine.
To crack or split; to bend or strain so as to weaken; as, to spring a mast or a yard.
To cause to close suddenly, as the parts of a trap operated by a spring; as, to spring a trap.

To bend by force, as something stiff or strong; to force or put by bending, as a beam into its sockets, and allowing it to straighten when in place; — often with in, out, etc.; as, to spring in a slat or a bar.
To pass over by leaping; as, to spring a fence.
A leap; a bound; a jump.
q: The prisoner, with a spring, from prison broke.

senses.d: A flying back; the resilience of a body recovering its former state by its elasticity; as, the spring of a bow.
Elastic power or force.
q: Heavens! what a spring was in his arm!

senses.d: An elastic body of any kind, as steel, India rubber, tough wood, or compressed air, used for various mechanical purposes, as receiving and imparting power, diminishing concussion, regulating motion, measuring weight or other force.
Any source of supply; especially, the source from which a stream proceeds; an issue of water from the earth; a natural fountain.
Any active power; that by which action, or motion, is produced or propagated; cause; origin; motive.
q: Our author shuns by vulgar springs to move The hero's glory, or the virgin's love.

senses.d: That which springs, or is originated, from a source;
That which causes one to spring; specifically, a lively tune.
The season of the year when plants begin to vegetate and grow; the vernal season, usually comprehending the months of March, April, and May, in the middle latitudes north of the equator.
The time of growth and progress; early portion; first stage.
q: O how this spring of love resembleth The uncertain glory of an April day.

senses.d: A crack or fissure in a mast or yard, running obliquely or transversely.

Spring.etym: [AS. spring a fountain, a leap. See Spring, v. i.]

senses.d: A noose fastened to an elastic body, and drawn close with a sudden spring, whereby it catches a bird or other animal; a gin; a snare.
q: As a woodcock to mine own springe.

Springe.etym: [From Spring, v. i.: cf. G. sprenkel, Prov. E. springle.]

senses.d: To catch in a springe; to insnare.
To sprinkle; to scatter.
q: He would sowen some difficulty, Or springen cockle in our cleane corn.

senses.d: The act or process of one who, or that which, springs.
Growth; increase; also, that which springs up; a shoot; a plant.
q: Thou blessest the springing thereof.

senses.d: To scatter in small drops or particles, as water, seed, etc.
To scatter on; to disperse something over in small drops or particles; to besprinkle; as, to sprinkle the earth with water; to sprinkle a floor with sand.
To baptize by the application of a few drops, or a small quantity, of water; hence, to cleanse; to purify.
q: Having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience.

Sprinkle.etym: [OE. sprenkelen, freq. of sprengen to sprinkle, to scatter, AS. sprengan, properly, to make to spring, causative of springan to spring; akin to D. sprenkelen to sprinkle, G. sprengen. See Spring, v. i., and cf. Sprent.]

senses.d: To scatter a liquid, or any fine substance, so that it may fall in particles.
q: And the priest shall . . . sprinkle of the oil with his finger seven times before the Lord.

senses.d: To rain moderately, or with scattered drops falling now and then; as, it sprinkles.
To fly or be scattered in small drops or particles.
A small quantity scattered, or sparsely distributed; a sprinkling.
A utensil for sprinkling; a sprinkler.
The act of one who, or that which, sprinkles.
q: Baptism may well enough be performed by sprinkling or effusion of water.

senses.d: A small quantity falling in distinct drops or particles; as, a sprinkling of rain or snow.
Hence, a moderate number or quantity distributed like separate drops, or as if scattered like drops.
To shoot, as the seed of a plant; to germinate; to push out new shoots; hence, to grow like shoots of plants.
To shoot into ramifications.

Sprout.etym: [OE. sprouten, spruten; akin to OFries. sprūta, AS. spreótan, D. spruiten, G. spriessen, Sw. spruta to squirt, to spout. Cf. Sprit, v. t. & i., Sprit a spar, Spout, v. t., Spurt.]

senses.d: To cause to sprout; as, the rain will sprout the seed.
To deprive of sprouts; as, to sprout potatoes.
The shoot of a plant; a shoot from the seed, from the stump, or from the root or tuber, of a plant or tree; more rarely, a shoot from the stem of a plant, or the end of a branch.
Young coleworts; Brussels sprouts.

Sprout.etym: [Cf. AS. sprote a sprout, sprig; akin to Icel. sproti, G. sprosse. See Sprout, v. i.]

senses.d: Said of a spar that has been cracked or strained.
A sponge.
To gain sight of; to discover at a distance, or in a state of concealment; to espy; to see.
q: One, in reading, skipped over all sentences where he spied a note of admiration.

senses.d: To discover by close search or examination.
q: Look about with your eyes; spy what things are to be reformed in the church of England.

senses.d: To explore; to view, inspect, and examine secretly, as a country; — usually with out.
q: Moses sent to spy out Jaazer, and they took the villages thereof.

Spy.etym: [OE. spien, espien, OF. espier, F. épier, OHG. spehōn, G. spähen; akin to L. specere to see, Skr. spaç. √169. Cf. Espy, v. t., Aspect, Auspice, Circumspect, Conspicuous, Despise, Frontispiece, Inspect, Prospect, Respite, Scope, Specimen, Spectacle, Specter, Speculate, Spice, Spite, Suspicion.]

senses.d: To search narrowly; to scrutinize.
q: It is my nature's plague To spy into abuses.

senses.d: One who keeps a constant watch of the conduct of others.

A person sent secretly into an enemy's camp, territory, or fortifications, to inspect his works, ascertain his strength, movements, or designs, and to communicate such intelligence to the proper officer.

Spy.etym: [See Spy, v., and cf. Espy, n.]

senses.d: The corner, or angle, of a figure.
Hence, anything which is square, or nearly so
q: He bolted his food down his capacious throat in squares of three inches.

senses.d: A pane of glass.
A certain number of lines, forming a portion of a column, nearly square; — used chiefly in reckoning the prices of advertisements in newspapers.
One hundred superficial feet.
An area of four sides, generally with houses on each side; sometimes, a solid block of houses; also, an open place or area for public use, as at the meeting or intersection of two or more streets.
q: The statue of Alexander VII. stands in the large square of the town.

senses.d: An instrument having at least one right angle and two or more straight edges, used to lay out or test square work. It is of several forms, as the T square, the carpenter's square, the try-square, etc.
Hence, a pattern or rule.
The product of a number or quantity multiplied by itself; thus, 64 is the square of 8, for 8 × 8 = 64; the square of a + b is a2 + 2ab + b2.
Exact proportion; justness of workmanship and conduct; regularity; rule.
q: They of Galatia much more out of square.
I have not kept my square.

senses.d: A body of troops formed in a square, esp. one formed to resist a charge of cavalry; a squadron.
Fig.: The relation of harmony, or exact agreement; equality; level.
q: We live not on the square with such as these.

Square.etym: [OF. esquarre, esquierre, F. équerre a carpenter's square (cf. It. squadra), fr. (assumed) LL. exquadrare to make square; L. ex + quadrus a square, fr. quattuor four. See Four, and cf. Quadrant, Squad, Squire a square.]

senses.d: Having four equal sides and four right angles; as, a square figure.
Forming a right angle; as, a square corner.
Having a shape broad for the height, with rectilineal and angular rather than curving outlines; as, a man of a square frame.
Exactly suitable or correspondent; true; just.
q: She's a most triumphant lady, if report be square to her.

senses.d: Rendering equal justice; exact; fair; honest; as, square dealing.
Even; leaving no balance; as, to make or leave the accounts square.
Leaving nothing; hearty; vigorous.
q: By Heaven, square eaters. More meat, I say.

senses.d: At right angles with the mast or the keel, and parallel to the horizon; — said of the yards of a square-rigged vessel when they are so braced.
To form with four equal sides and four right angles.
To form with right angles and straight lines, or flat surfaces; as, to square masons' work.
To compare with, or reduce to, any given measure or standard.
To adjust; to regulate; to mold; to shape; to fit; as, to square our actions by the opinions of others.
q: Square my trial To my proportioned strength.

senses.d: To make even, so as to leave no remainder or difference; to balance; as, to square accounts.
To multiply by itself; as, to square a number or a quantity.
To hold a quartile position respecting.
q: The icy Goat and Crab that square the Scales.

senses.d: To place at right angles with the keel; as, to square the yards.

Square.etym: [Cf. OF. escarrer, esquarrer. See Square, n.]

senses.d: To accord or agree exactly; to be consistent with; to conform or agree; to suit; to fit.
q: No works shall find acceptance . . . That square not truly with the Scripture plan.

senses.d: To go to opposite sides; to take an attitude of offense or defense, or of defiance; to quarrel.
q: Are you such fools To square for this?

senses.d: To take a boxing attitude; — often with up, sometimes with off.

The state or quality of being stable, or firm; steadiness; stableness; firmness; strength to stand without being moved or overthrown; as, the stability of a structure; the stability of a throne or a constitution.

Steadiness or firmness of character; firmness of resolution or purpose; the quality opposite to fickleness, irresolution, or inconstancy; constancy; steadfastness; as, a man of little stability, or of unusual stability.
Fixedness; — as opposed to fluidity.
q: Since fluidness and stability are contrary qualities.

Stability.etym: [L. stabilitas: cf. F. stabilité. See Stable, a.]

senses.d: Firmly established; not easily moved, shaken, or overthrown; fixed; as, a stable government.
q: In this region of chance, . . . where nothing is stable.

senses.d: Steady in purpose; constant; firm in resolution; not easily diverted from a purpose; not fickle or wavering; as, a man of stable character.
q: And to her husband ever meek and stable.

senses.d: Durable; not subject to overthrow or change; firm; as, a stable foundation; a stable position.

Stable.syn: Fixed; steady; constant; abiding; strong; durable; firm.
Stable.etym: [OF. estable, F. stable, fr. L. stabilis, fr. stare to stand. See Stand, v. i. and cf. Establish.]

senses.d: To fix; to establish.
A house, shed, or building, for beasts to lodge and feed in; esp., a building or apartment with stalls, for horses; as, a horse stable; a cow stable.

Stable.etym: [OF. estable, F. étable, from L. stabulum, fr. stare to stand. See Stand, v. i.]

senses.d: To put or keep in a stable.
To dwell or lodge in a stable; to dwell in an inclosed place; to kennel.
So placed as to resist forces tending to cause motion; of such structure as to resist distortion or molecular or chemical disturbance; — said of any body or substance.
To settle permanently in a state; to make firm; to establish; to fix.
A large pile of hay, grain, straw, or the like, usually of a nearly conical form, but sometimes rectangular or oblong, contracted at the top to a point or ridge, and sometimes covered with thatch.
q: But corn was housed, and beans were in the stack.

senses.d: A pile of poles or wood, indefinite in quantity.
q: Against every pillar was a stack of billets above a man's height.

senses.d: A pile of wood containing 108 cubic feet.
A number of flues embodied in one structure, rising above the roof. Hence:

Stack.etym: [Icel. stakkr; akin to Sw. stack, Dan. stak. Cf. Stake.]

senses.d: To lay in a conical or other pile; to make into a large pile; as, to stack hay, cornstalks, or grain; to stack or place wood.

Stack.etym: [Cf. Sw. stacka, Dan. stakke. See Stack, n.]

senses.d: One of the sweet spices used by the ancient Jews in the preparation of incense. It was perhaps an oil or other form of myrrh or cinnamon, or a kind of storax.

Stacte.etym: [L., fr. Gr. στακτή, strictly fem. of στακτόσ oozing out in drops, fr. στάζειν to drop.]

senses.d: A long piece of wood; a stick; the long handle of an instrument or weapon; a pole or stick, used for many purposes; as, a surveyor's staff; the staff of a spear or pike.
q: And he put the staves into the rings on the sides of the altar to bear it withal.
With forks and staves the felon to pursue.

senses.d: A stick carried in the hand for support or defense by a person walking; hence, a support; that which props or upholds.
q: The boy was the very staff of my age.
He spoke of it in “The Earnest Cry,” and likewise in the “Scotch Drink,” as one of the staffs of life which had been struck from the poor man's hand.

senses.d: A pole, stick, or wand borne as an ensign of authority; a badge of office; as, a constable's staff.
q: Methought this staff, mine office badge in court, Was broke in twain.
All his officers brake their staves; but at their return new staves were delivered unto them.

senses.d: A pole upon which a flag is supported and displayed.
The round of a ladder.
q: I ascended at one of six hundred and thirty-nine staves.

senses.d: A series of verses so disposed that, when it is concluded, the same order begins again; a stanza; a stave.
q: Cowley found out that no kind of staff is proper for an heroic poem, as being all too lyrical.

senses.d: The five lines and the spaces on which music is written; — formerly called stave.
An arbor, as of a wheel or a pinion of a watch.
The grooved director for the gorget, or knife, used in cutting for stone in the bladder.

An establishment of officers in various departments attached to an army, to a section of an army, or to the commander of an army. The general's staff consists of those officers about his person who are employed in carrying his commands into execution. See État Major.
Hence: A body of assistants serving to carry into effect the plans of a superintendent or manager; as, the staff of a newspaper.

Staff.etym: [AS. stæf a staff; akin to LG. & D. staf, OFries. stef, G. stab, Icel. stafr, Sw. staf, Dan. stav, Goth. stabs element, rudiment, Skr. sthāpay to cause to stand, to place. See Stand, and cf. Stab, Stave, n.]

senses.d: Plaster combined with fibrous and other materials so as to be suitable for sculpture in relief or in the round, or for forming flat plates or boards of considerable size which can be nailed to framework to make the exterior of a larger structure, forming joints which may afterward be repaired and concealed with fresh plaster.

Staff.etym: [G. staffiren to fill or fit out, adorn, fr. D. stoffeeren, OF. estoffer, F. étoffer, fr. OF. estoffe stuff, F. étoffe. See Stuff, n.]

senses.d: The adult male of the red deer (Cervus elaphus), a large European species closely related to the American elk, or wapiti.
A colt, or filly; also, a romping girl.
A castrated bull; — called also bull stag, and bull seg. See the Note under Ox.
An outside irregular dealer in stocks, who is not a member of the exchange.
The European wren.

Stag.etym: [Icel. steggr the male of several animals; or a doubtful AS. stagga. Cf. Steg.]

senses.d: To act as a “stag,” or irregular dealer in stocks.
To watch; to dog, or keep track of.
To move to one side and the other, as if about to fall, in standing or walking; not to stand or walk with steadiness; to sway; to reel or totter.
q: Deep was the wound; he staggered with the blow.

senses.d: To cease to stand firm; to begin to give way; to fail.
To begin to doubt and waver in purpose; to become less confident or determined; to hesitate.
q: He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief.

Stagger.etym: [OE. stakeren, Icel. stakra to push, to stagger, fr. staka to punt, push, stagger; cf. OD. staggeren to stagger. Cf. Stake, n.]

senses.d: To cause to reel or totter.
q: That hand shall burn in never-quenching fire That staggers thus my person.

senses.d: To cause to doubt and waver; to make to hesitate; to make less steady or confident; to shock.
q: Whosoever will read the story of this war will find himself much staggered.
Grants to the house of Russell were so enormous, as not only to outrage economy, but even to stagger credibility.

senses.d: To arrange (a series of parts) on each side of a median line alternately, as the spokes of a wheel or the rivets of a boiler seam.
An unsteady movement of the body in walking or standing, as if one were about to fall; a reeling motion; vertigo; — often in the plural; as, the stagger of a drunken man.
A disease of horses and other animals, attended by reeling, unsteady gait or sudden falling; as, parasitic staggers; apopletic or sleepy staggers.
Bewilderment; perplexity.
To discolor by the application of foreign matter; to make foul; to spot; as, to stain the hand with dye; armor stained with blood.

To color, as wood, glass, paper, cloth, or the like, by processes@ affecting, chemically or otherwise, the material itself; to tinge with a color or colors combining with, or penetrating, the substance; to dye; as, to stain wood with acids, colored washes, paint rubbed in, etc.; to stain glass.
To spot with guilt or infamy; to bring reproach on; to blot; to soil; to tarnish.
q: Of honor void, Of innocence, of faith, of purity, Our wonted ornaments now soiled and stained.

senses.d: To cause to seem inferior or soiled by comparison.
q: She stains the ripest virgins of her age.
That did all other beasts in beauty stain.

Stain.syn: To paint; dye; blot; soil; sully; discolor; disgrace; taint.

senses.d: To give or receive a stain; to grow dim.
A discoloration by foreign matter; a spot; as, a stain on a garment or cloth.
A natural spot of a color different from the gound.
q: Swift trouts, diversified with crimson stains.

senses.d: Taint of guilt; tarnish; disgrace; reproach.
q: Nor death itself can wholly wash their stains.
Our opinion . . . is, I trust, without any blemish or stain of heresy.

senses.d: Cause of reproach; shame.
A tincture; a tinge.
q: You have some stain of soldier in you.

Stain.syn: Blot; spot; taint; pollution; blemish; tarnish; color; disgrace; infamy; shame.

senses.d: One step of a series for ascending or descending to a different level; — commonly applied to those within a building.
A series of steps, as for passing from one story of a house to another; — commonly used in the plural; but originally used in the singular only.

Stair.etym: [OE. steir, steyer, AS. stǣger, from stīgan to ascend, rise. √164. See Sty to ascend.]

senses.d: A piece of wood, usually long and slender, pointed at one end so as to be easily driven into the ground as a support or stay; as, a stake to support vines, fences, hedges, etc.
q: A sharpened stake strong Dryas found.

senses.d: A stick inserted upright in a lo@op, eye, or mortise, at the side or end of a cart, a flat car, or the like, to prevent goods from falling off.
The piece of timber to which a martyr was affixed to be burned; hence, martyrdom by fire.
A small anvil usually furnished with a tang to enter a hole in a bench top, — used by tinsmiths, blacksmiths, etc., for light work, punching upon, etc.
That which is laid down as a wager; that which is staked or hazarded; a pledge.

Stake.etym: [AS. staca, from the root of E. stick; akin to OFries. & LG. stake, D. staak, Sw. @stake@, Dan. stage. See Stick, v. t., and cf. Estacade, Stockade.]

senses.d: To fasten, support, or defend with stakes; as, to stake vines or plants.
To mark the limits of by stakes; — with out; as, to stake out land; to stake out a new road.
To put at hazard upon the issue of competition, or upon a future contingency; to wager; to pledge.
q: I'll stake yon lamb, that near the fountain plays.

senses.d: To pierce or wound with a stake.
A territorial division; — called also stake of Zion.
q: Every city, or “stake,” including a chief town and surrounding towns, has its president, with two counselors; and this president has a high council of chosen men.

senses.d: Stole.
The stem or main axis of a plant; as, a stalk of wheat, rye, or oats; the stalks of maize or hemp.
That which resemb@les the stalk of a plant, as the stem of a quill.
An ornament in the Corinthian capital resembling the stalk of a plant, from which the volutes and helices spring.
One of the two upright pieces of a ladder.
q: To clim@b by the rungs and the stalks.

senses.d: A stem or peduncle, as of certain barnacles and crinoids.
An iron bar with projections inserted in a core to strengthen it; a core arbor.

Stalk.etym: [OE. stalke, fr. AS. stæl, stel, a stalk. See Stale a handle, Stall.]

senses.d: To walk slowly and cautiously; to walk in a stealthy, noiseless manner; — sometimes used with a reflexive pronoun.
q: Into the chamber he stalked him full still.
stalks close behind her, like a witch's fiend, Pressing to be employed.

senses.d: To walk behind something as a screen, for the purpose of approaching game; to proceed under c@over.
q: The king . . . crept under the shoulder of his led horse; . . . “I must stalk,” said he.
One underneath his horse, to get a shoot doth stalk.

senses.d: To walk with high and proud steps; @—usually implying the affectation of dignity, and indicating dislike. The word is used, however, especially by the poets, to express dignity of step.
q: With manly mien he stalked along the ground.
Then stalking through the deep, He fords the ocean.
I forbear myself from entering the lists in which he has long stalked alone and unchallenged.

Stalk.etym: [AS. stælcan, stealcian, to go slowly; cf. ste@al@c high, elevated, Dan. stalke to stalk; probably akin to 1st stalk.]

senses.d: To approach under cover of a screen, or by stealth, for the purpose of killing, as game.
q: As for shooting a man from behind a wall, it is cruelly like to stalking a deer.

senses.d: A high, proud, stately step or walk.
q: Thus twice before, . . . With martial stalk hath he gone by our watch.
The which with monstrous stalk behind him stepped.

senses.d: The act or process of stalking.
q: When the stalk was over (the antelope took alarm and ran off before I was within rifle shot) I came back.

senses.d: A stand; a station; a fixed spot; hence, the stand or place where a horse or an ox @is kept and fed; the division of a stable, or the compartment, for one horse, ox, or other animal.
A stable; a place for cattle.
q: At last he found a stall where oxen stood.

senses.d: A small apartment or shed in which merchandise is exposed for sale; as, a butcher's stall; a bookstall.
A bench or table on which small articles of merchandise are exposed for sale.
q: How peddlers' stalls with glittering toys are laid.

senses.d: A seat in the choir of a church, for one of the officiating clergy. It is inclosed, either wholly or partially, at the back and sides. The stalls are frequently very rich, with canopies and elaborate carving.
q: The dignifi@ed clergy, out of hum@ility, have called their thrones by the names of stalls.
Loud the monks @sang in their stalls.

senses.d: In the theater, a seat with arms or otherwise partly inclosed, as distinguished from the benches, sofas, etc.
The space left by excavation between pillars. See Post and stall, under Post.
q: Cries the stall reader, “Bless us! what a word on A titlepage is this!”

Stall.etym: [OE. stal, AS. steall, stall, a place, seat, or station, a stable; akin to D. & OHG. stal, G. & Sw. stall, @Icel. stallr, Dan. stald, originally, a standing place; akin @also to G. s@telle a place, stellen to place, Gr. στέλλειν to set, place, send, and E. stand. √ 163. See Stand, and cf. Apostle, E

senses.d: To put into a stall or stable; to keep in a stall or stalls; as, to stall an ox.
q: Where King Latinus then his oxen stalled.

senses.d: To fatten; as, to @stall@ cattle.
To place in an office with the customary formalities; to install.
To plunge into mire or snow so as not to be able to get on; to set; to fix; as, to stall a cart.
q: His horses had been stalled in the snow.

senses.d: To forestall; to anticip@ate.@
q: This @is not to be stall'd by my report.

senses.d: To keep close; to keep secret.
q: Stall this in your bosom.

senses.d: To live in, or as in, a stall; to dwell.
q: We could not stall together In the whole world.

senses.d: To kennel, as dogs.
To be set, as in mire or snow; to stick fast.
To be tired of eating, as cattle.

Stall.etym: [AS. steallian to have room. See Stall, @n.@]

senses.d: A covering or sheath, as of leather, horn, of iron, for a finger or thumb; a cot; as, a thumb stall; a finger stall.
Put or kept in a stall; hence, fatted.
To make involuntary stops in uttering syllables or words; to hesitate or falter in speaking; to speak with stops and diffi@culty; to stutter.
q: I would thou couldst stammer, that thou mightest pour this conc@ealed man out of thy mouth, as wine comes out of a narrow-mouthed bottle, either too much at once, or none at all.

Stammer.etym: [OE. stameren, fr. AS. stamur, stamer, stammering; akin to D. & LG. stameren to stammer, G. stammeln, OHG. stammalōn, stammēn, Dan. stamme, Sw. stamma, Icel. stama, stamma, OHG. & Dan. stam stammering, Icel. stamr, @Goth.@ stamms, and to G. stemmen to bear against, stumm dumb, D. stom. Cf. Stem to r

senses.d: To utter or pronounce with hesitation or imperfectly; — sometimes with out.
Defective utterance, or involuntary interruption of utterance; a stutter.
One who stammers.
Apt to stammer; hesitating in speech; stuttering.

A disturbance in the formation of sounds. It is due essentially to long-continued spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm, by which expiration is pre@vented, and hence it may be considered as a spasmodic inspiration.
To strike, beat, or press forcibly with the bottom of the foot, or by thrusting the foot downward.
q: He frets, he fumes, he stares, he stamps the ground.

senses.d: To bring down (the foot) forcibly on the ground or floor; as, he stamped his foot with rage.
To crush; to pulverize; specifically (Metal.), to crush by the blow of a heavy stamp, as ore in a mill.
q: I took your sin, the calf which ye had made, and burnt it with fire, and stamped it, and ground it very small.

senses.d: To impress with some mark or figure; as, to stamp a plate with arms or initials.
Fig.: To impress; to imprint; to fix deeply; as, to stamp virtuous principles on the heart.
q: God . . . has stamped no original characters on our minds wherein we may read his being.

senses.d: To cut out, bend, or indent, as paper, sheet metal, etc., into various forms, by a blow or suddenly applied pressure with a stamp or die, etc.; to mint; to coin.
To put a stamp on, as for postage; as, to stamp a letter; to stamp a legal document.

Stamp.etym: [OE. stampen; akin to LG. & D. stampen, G. stampfen, OHG. sta@mpfōn, Dan. stampe, Sw. stampa, Icel. stappa, G. stampf a pestle and E. step. See Step, v. i., and cf. Stampede.]

senses.d: To strike; to beat; to crush.
q: These cooks how they stamp and strain and grind.

senses.d: To strike the foot forcibly downward.
q: But starts, exclaims, and stamps, and raves, and dies.

senses.d: The act of stamping, as with the foot.
The which stamps; any instrument for making impressions on other bodies, as a die.
q: 'T is gold so pure It can not bear the stamp without alloy.

senses.d: The mark made by stamping; a mark imprinted; an impression.
q: That sacred name gives ornament and grace, And, like his stamp, makes basest metals pass.

senses.d: @That which is marked; a thing stamped.
q: @Hanging a golden stamp about their necks.

senses.d: A picture cut in wood or metal, or made by impression; a cut; a plate.
q: At Venice they put out very curious stamps of the several edifices which are most famous for their beauty and magnificence.

senses.d: An offic@ial mark set upon things chargeable with a duty or tax to government, as evidence that the duty or tax is paid; as, the stamp on a bill of exchange.

Hence, a stamped or printed device, issued by the government at a fixed price, and required by law to be affixed to, or stamped on, certain papers, as evidence that the government dues are paid; as, a postage stamp; a receipt stamp, etc.
An instrument for cutting out, or shaping, materials, as paper, leather, etc., by a downward pressure.

A character or reputation, good or bad, fixed on anything as if by an imprinted mark; current value; authority; as, these persons have the stamp of dishonesty; the Scriptures bear the stamp of a divine origin.
q: Of the same stamp is that which is obtruded on us, that an adamant suspends the attraction of the loadstone.

senses.d: Make; cast; form; character; as, a man of the same stamp, or of a different stamp.
q: A soldier of this season's stamp.

senses.d: A kind of heavy hammer, or pestle, raised by water or steam power, for beating ores to powder; anything like a pestle, used for pounding or b@eating.
A half-penny.
To stop the flowing of, as blood; to check; also, to stop the flowing of blood from; as, to stanch a wound.
q: Iron or a stone laid to the neck doth stanch the bleeding of the nose.

senses.d: To extinguish; to quench, as fire or thirst.

Stanch.etym: [OF. estanchier, F. étancher to st@op a liquid from flowing; akin to Pr., Sp., & Pg. estancar, It. stancare to weary, LL. stancare, stagnare, to stanch, fr. L. stagnare to be or make stagnant. See Stagnate.]

senses.d: To cease, as the flowing of blood.
q: Immediately her issue of blood stanched.

senses.d: That which stanches or checks.
A flood gate by which water is accumulated, for floating a boat over a shallow part of a stream by its release.
Strong and tight; sound; firm; as, a stanch ship.
q: One of the closets is parqueted with plain deal, set in diamond, exceeding stanch and pretty.

senses.d: Firm in principle; constant and zealous; loyal; hearty; steady; steadfast; as, a stanch churchman; a stanch friend or adherent.
q: In politics I hear you 're stanch.

senses.d: Close; secret; private.
q: This @is to be kept stanch.

Stanch.etym: [From Stanch, v. t., and hence literally signifying, stopped or stayed; cf. Sp. estanco stopped, tight, not leaky, as a ship. See Stanch, v. t.]

senses.d: To prop; to make stanch, or strong.
q: His gathered sticks to stanch the wall Of the snow tower when snow should fall.

senses.d: To be at rest in an erect position; to be fixed in an upright or firm position
q: It stands as it were to the ground yglued.
The ruined wall Stands when its wind@-worn battlements are gone.

senses.d: To occupy or hold a place; to have a situation; to be situated or located; as, Paris stands on the Seine.
q: Wite ye not where there stands a little town?

senses.d: To cease from progress; not to proceed; to stop; to pause; to halt; to remain stationary.
q: I charge thee, stand, And tell thy name.
The star, which they saw in the east, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was.

senses.d: To remain without ruin or injury; to hold good against tendencies to impair or injure; to be permanent; to endure; to last; hence, to find endurance, strength, or resources.
q: My mind on its own center stands unmoved.

senses.d: To maintain one's ground; to be acquitted; not to fail or yield; to be safe.
q: Readers by whose judgment I would stand or fall.

senses.d: To maintain an invincible or permanent attitude; to be fixed, steady, or firm; to take a position in resistance or opposition.
q: The king granted the Jews . . . to gather themselves together, and to stand for their life.

senses.d: To adhere to fixed principles; to maintain moral rectitude; to keep from falling into error or vice.
q: We must labor so as to stand with godliness, according to his appointment.

senses.d: To have or maintain a position, order, or rank; to be in a particular relation; as, Christian charity, or love, stands first in the rank of gifts.
To be in some particular state; to have essence or being; to be; to consist.
q: Accomplish what your signs foreshow; I stand resigned, and am prepared to go.
Thou seest how it stands with me, and that I may not tarry.

senses.d: To be consistent; to agree; to accord.
q: Doubt me not; by heaven, I will do nothing But what may stand with honor.

senses.d: To hold a course at sea; as, to stand from the shore; to stand for the harbor.
q: From the same parts of heaven his navy stands.

senses.d: To offer one's self, or to be offered, as a candidate.
q: He stood to be elected one of the proctors of the university.

Stand.etym: [OE. standen, AS. standan; akin to OFries. stonda, stān, D. staan, OS. standan, stān, @OHG. stantan, stān, G. stehen, Icel. standa, Dan. staae, Sw. stå, Goth. standan, Russ. stoiate, L. stare, Gr. ιστἄναι to cause to stand, στη̑ναι to stand, Skr. sthā. √163. Cf. Assist, Constant, Contrast, Desist, D

senses.d: To endure; to sustain; to bear; as, I can not stand the cold or the heat.
To resist, without yielding or receding; to withstand.
q: He stood the furious foe.

senses.d: To abide by; to submit to; to suffer.
q: Bid him disband his legions, . . . And stand the judgment of a Roman senate.

senses.d: To set upright; to cause to stand; as, to stand a book on the shelf; to stand a man on his feet.
To be at the expense of; to pay for; as, to stand a treat.
The act of standing.
q: I took my stand upon an eminence . . . to look into th@eir several ladings.

senses.d: A halt or stop for the purpose of defense, resistance, or opposition; as, to come to, or to make, a stand.
q: Vice is at stand, and at the highest flow.

senses.d: A place or post where one stands; a place where one may stand while observing or waiting for something.
q: I have found you out a stand most fit, Where you may have such vantage on the duke, He shall not pass you.

senses.d: A station in a city or town where carriages or wagons stand for hire; as, a cab stand.
A raised platform or station where a race or other outdoor spectacle may be viewed; as, the judges' or the grand stand at a race course.
A small table; also, something on or in which anything may be laid, hung, or placed upright; as, a hatstand; an umbrella stand; a music stand.
@The place where a witness stands to testify in court.
The situation of a shop, store, hotel, etc.; as, a good, bad, or convenient stand for business.
Rank; post; station; standing.
q: Father, since your fortune did attain So high a stand, I mean not to descend.

senses.d: A state of perplexity or embarrassment; as, to be at a stand what to do.

A young tree, usually reserved when other trees are cut; also, a tree growing or standing upon its own root, in distinction from one produced from a scion set in a stock, either of the same or another kind of tree.
A weight of from two hundred and fifty to three hundred pounds, — used in weighing pitch.

Stand.syn: Stop; halt; rest; interruption; obstruction; perplexity; difficulty; embarrassment; hesitation.

senses.d: To be, or signify that one is, willing to play with one's hand as dealt.
A flag; colors; a banner; especially, a national or other ensign.
q: His armies, in the following day, On those fair plains their standards proud display.

senses.d: That which is established by authority as a rule for the measure of quantity, extent, value, or quality; esp., the original specimen weight or measure sanctioned by government, as the standard pound, gallon, or yard.
That which is established as a rule or model by authority, custom, or general consent; criterion; test.
q: The court, which used to be the standard of prop@riety and correctness of speech.
A disposition to preserve, and an ability to improve, taken together, would be my standard of a statesman.

senses.d: The proportion of weights of fine metal and alloy established by authority.
q: By the present standard of the coinage, sixty-two shillings is coined out of one pound weight of silver.

senses.d: A tree of natural size supported by its own stem, and not dwarfed by grafting on the stock of a smaller species nor trained upon a wall or trellis.
q: In France part of their gardens is laid out for flowers, others for fruits; some standards, some against walls.

senses.d: The upper petal or banner of a papilionaceous corolla.
An upright support, as one of the poles of a scaffold; any upright in framing.
An inverted knee timber placed upon the deck instead of beneath it, with its vertical branch turned upward from that which lies horizontally.
The sheth of a plow.
A large drinking cup.

Standard.etym: [OF. estendart, F. étendard, probably fr. L. extendere to spread out, extend, but influenced by E. stand. See Extend.]

senses.d: Being, affording, or according with, a standard for comparison and judgment; as, standard time; standard weights and measures; a standard authority as to nautical terms; standard gold or silver.
Hence: Having a recognized and permanent value; as, standard works in history; standard authors.
Not supported by, or fastened to, a wall; as, standard fruit trees.
Remaining erect; not cut down; as, standing corn.
Not flowing; stagnant; as, standing water.
Not transitory; not liable to fade or vanish; lasting; as, a standing color.
Established by law, custom, or the like; settled; continually existing; permanent; not temporary; as, a standing army; legislative bodies have standing rules of proceeding and standing committees.
Not movable; fixed; as, a standing bed (distinguished from a trundle-bed).
The act of stopping, or coming to a stand; the state of being erect upon the feet; stand.
Maintenance of position; duration; duration or existence in the same place or condition; continuance; as, a custom of long standing; an officer of long standing.
q: An ancient thing of long standing.

senses.d: Place to stand in; station; stand.
q: I will provide you a good standing to see his entry.
I @sink in deep mire, where there is no standing.

senses.d: Condition in society; relative position; reputation; rank; as, a man of good standing, or of high standing.
Weak; worn out.

Stank.etym: [OF. estanc, or It. stanco. See Stanch, a.]

senses.d: To sigh.
Stunk.
Water retained by an embankment; a pool @of water.
A dam or mound to stop water.

Stank.etym: [OF. estang, F. étang, from L. stagnum a pool. Cf. Stagnate, Tank a cistern.]

senses.d: One of the innumerable luminous bodies seen in the heavens; any heavenly body other than the sun, moon, comets, and nebulæ.
q: His eyen twinkled in his head aright, As do the stars in the frosty night.

senses.d: The polestar; the north star.
A planet supposed to influence one's destiny; (usually pl.) a configuration of the planets, supposed to influence fortune.
q: O malignant and ill-brooding stars.
Blesses his stars, and thinks it luxury.

senses.d: That which resembles the figure of a star, as an ornament worn on the breast to indicate rank or honor.
q: On whom . . . Lavish Honor showered all her stars.

senses.d: Specifically, a radiated mark in writing or printing; an asterisk ; — used as a reference to a note, or to fill a blank where something is omitted, etc.
A composition of combustible matter used in the heading of rockets, in mines, etc., which, exploding in the air, presents a starlike appearance.
A person of brilliant and attractive qualities, especially on public occasions, as a distinguished orator, a leading theatrical performer, etc.

Star.etym: [OE. sterre, AS. steorra; akin to OFries. stera, OS. sterro, D. ster, OHG. sterno, sterro, G. stern, Icel. stjarna, Sw. stjerna, Dan. stierne, Goth. staírnō, Armor. & Corn. steren, L. stella, Gr. αστἤρ, ἄστρον, Skr. star; perhaps from a root meaning, to scatter, Skr. stṛ, L. sternere (cf. Stratum),

senses.d: To set or adorn with stars, or bright, radiating bodies; to bespangle; as, a robe starred with gems.
To be bright, or attract attention, as a star; to shine like a star; to be brilliant or prominent; to play a part as a theatrical star.
The starling.
To look with fixed eyes wide open, as through fear, wonder, surprise, impudence, etc.; to fasten an earnest and prolonged gaze on some object.
q: For ever upon the ground I see thee stare.
Look not big, nor stamp, nor stare, nor fret.

senses.d: To be very conspicuous on account of size, prominence, color, or brilliancy; as, staring windows or colors.
To stand out; to project; to bristle.
q: Makest my blood cold, and my hair to stare.
Take off all the staring straws and jags in the hive.

Stare.syn: To gaze; to look earnestly. See Gaze.
Stare.etym: [AS. starian; akin to LG. & D. staren, OHG. starēn, G. starren, Icel. stara; cf. Icel. stira, Dan. stirre, Sw. stirra, and G. starr stiff, rigid, fixed, Gr. στερεόσ solid (E. stereo-), Skr. sthira firm, strong. √166. Cf. Sterile.]

senses.d: To look earnestly at; to gaze at.
q: I will stare him out of his wits.

senses.d: The act of staring; a fixed look with eyes wide open.
The circumstances or condition of a being or thing at any given time.
q: State is a term nearly synonymous with “mode,” but of a meaning more extensive, and is not exclusively limited to the mutable and contingent.
Declare the past and present state of things.
Keep the state of the question in your eye.

senses.d: Rank; condition; quality; as, the state of honor.
q: Thy honor, state, and seat is due to me.

senses.d: Condition of prosperity or grandeur; wealthy or prosperous circumstances; social importance.
q: She instructed him how he should keep state, and yet with a modest sense of his misfortunes.
Can this imperious lord forget to reign, Quit all his state, descend, and serve again?

senses.d: Appearance of grandeur or dignity; pomp.
q: Where least of state there most of love is shown.

senses.d: A chair with a canopy above it, often standing on a dais; a seat of dignity; also, the canopy itself.
q: His high throne, . . . under state Of richest texture spread.
When he went to court, he used to kick away the state, and sit down by his prince cheek by jowl.

senses.d: Estate; possession.
q: Your state, my lord, again is yours.

senses.d: A person of high rank.

Any body of men united by profession, or constituting a community of a particular character; as, the civil and ecclesiastical states, or the lords spiritual and temporal and the commons, in Great Britain. Cf. Estate, n., 6.
The principal persons in a government.
q: The bold design Pleased highly those infernal states.

senses.d: The bodies that constitute the legislature of a country; as, the States-general of Holland.
A form of government which is not monarchial, as a republic.
q: Well monarchies may own religion's name, But states are atheists in their very fame.

senses.d: A political body, or body politic; the whole body of people who are united under one government, whatever may be the form of the government; a nation.
q: Municipal law is a rule of conduct prescribed by the supreme power in a state.
The Puritans in the reign of Mary, driven from their homes, sought an asylum in Geneva, where they found a state without a king, and a church without a bishop.

State.etym: [OE. stat, OF. estat, F. état, fr. L. status a standing, position, fr. stare, statum, to stand. See Stand, and cf. Estate, Status.]

senses.d: Stately.
Belonging to the state, or body politic; public.
To set; to settle; to establish.
q: I myself, though meanest stated, And in court now almost hated.
Who calls the council, states the certain day.

senses.d: To express the particulars of; to set down in detail or in gross; to represent fully in words; to narrate; to recite; as, to state the facts of a case, one's opinion, etc.
A statement; also, a document containing a statement.
Evincing state or dignity; lofty; majestic; grand; as, stately manners; a stately gait.
q: Here is a silly stately style indeed!

Stately.syn: Lofty; dignified; majestic; grand; august; magnificent.

senses.d: Majestically; loftily.
The act of standing; also, attitude or pose in standing; posture.
q: A station like the herald, Mercury.
Their manner was to stand at prayer, whereupon their meetings unto that purpose . . . had the names of stations given them.

senses.d: A state of standing or rest; equilibrium.
q: All progression is performed by drawing on or impelling forward some part which was before in station, or at quiet.

senses.d: The spot or place where anything stands, especially where a person or thing habitually stands, or is appointed to remain for a time; as, the station of a sentinel.
Post assigned; office; the part or department of public duty which a person is appointed to perform; sphere of duty or occupation; employment.
q: By spending this day in religious exercises, we acquire new strength and resolution to perform God's will in our several stations the week following.

senses.d: Situation; position; location.
q: The fig and date — why love they to remain In middle station, and an even plain?

senses.d: State; rank; condition of life; social status.
q: The greater part have kept, I see, Their station.
They in France of the best rank and station.

senses.d: The fast of the fourth and sixth days of the week, Wednesday and Friday, in memory of the council which condemned Christ, and of his passion.

Station.etym: [F., fr. L. statio, from stare, statum, to stand. See Stand.]

senses.d: To place; to set; to appoint or assign to the occupation of a post, place, or office; as, to station troops on the right of an army; to station a sentinel on a rampart; to station ships on the coast of Africa.
q: He gained the brow of the hill, where the English phalanx was stationed.

senses.d: In Australia, a sheep run or cattle run, together with the buildings belonging to it; also, the homestead and buildings belonging to such a run.
The natural height of an animal body; — generally used of the human body.
q: Foreign men of mighty stature came.

Stature.etym: [F. stature, OF. estature, from L. statura, originally, an upright posture; hence, height or size of the body, from stare, statum, to stand. See Stand.]

senses.d: An act of the legislature of a state or country, declaring, commanding, or prohibiting something; a positive law; the written will of the legislature expressed with all the requisite forms of legislation; — used in distinction from common law. See Common law, under Common, a.
An act of a corporation or of its founder, intended as a permanent rule or law; as, the statutes of a university.
An assemblage of farming servants (held possibly by statute) for the purpose of being hired; — called also statute fair.

Statute.syn: Act; regulation; edict; decree. See Law.
Statute.etym: [F. statut, LL. statutum, from L. statutus, p. p. of statuere to set, station, ordain, fr. status position, station, fr. stare, statum, to stand. See Stand, and cf. Constitute, Destitute.]

senses.d: One of a number of narrow strips of wood, or narrow iron plates, placed edge to edge to form the sides, covering, or lining of a vessel or structure; esp., one of the strips which form the sides of a cask, a pail, etc.
One of the cylindrical bars of a lantern wheel; one of the bars or rounds of a rack, a ladder, etc.
A metrical portion; a stanza; a staff.
q: Let us chant a passing stave In honor of that hero brave.

senses.d: The five horizontal and parallel lines on and between which musical notes are written or printed; the staff.

Stave.etym: [From Staff, and corresponding to the pl. staves. See Staff.]

senses.d: To break in a stave or the staves of; to break a hole in; to burst; — often with in; as, to stave a cask; to stave in a boat.
To push, as with a staff; — with off.
q: The condition of a servant staves him off to a distance.

senses.d: To delay by force or craft; to drive away; — usually with off; as, to stave off the execution of a project.
q: And answered with such craft as women use, Guilty or guiltless, to stave off a chance That breaks upon them perilously.

senses.d: To suffer, or cause, to be lost by breaking the cask.
q: All the wine in the city has been staved.

senses.d: To furnish with staves or rundles.
To render impervious or solid by driving with a calking iron; as, to stave lead, or the joints of pipes into which lead has been run.
To burst in pieces by striking against something; to dash into fragments.
q: Like a vessel of glass she stove and sank.

senses.d: A large, strong rope, employed to support a mast, by being extended from the head of one mast down to some other, or to some part of the vessel. Those which lead forward are called fore-and-aft stays; those which lead to the vessel's side are called backstays. See Illust. of Ship.

Stay.etym: [AS. stæg, akin to D., G., Icel., Sw., & Dan. stag; cf. OF. estai, F. étai, of Teutonic origin.]

senses.d: To stop from motion or falling; to prop; to fix firmly; to hold up; to support.
q: Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side.
Sallows and reeds . . . for vineyards useful found To stay thy vines.

senses.d: To support from sinking; to sustain with strength; to satisfy in part or for the time.
q: He has devoured a whole loaf of bread and butter, and it has not staid his stomach for a minute.

senses.d: To bear up under; to endure; to support; to resist successfully.
q: She will not stay the siege of loving terms, Nor bide the encounter of assailing eyes.

senses.d: To hold from proceeding; to withhold; to restrain; to stop; to hold.
q: Him backward overthrew and down him stayed With their rude hands and grisly grapplement.
All that may stay their minds from thinking that true which they heartily wish were false.

senses.d: To hinder; to delay; to detain; to keep back.
q: Your ships are stayed at Venice.
This business staid me in London almost a week.
I was willing to stay my reader on an argument that appeared to me new.

senses.d: To remain for the purpose of; to wait for.
To cause to cease; to put an end to.
q: Stay your strife.
For flattering planets seemed to say This child should ills of ages stay.

senses.d: To fasten or secure with stays; as, to stay a flat sheet in a steam boiler.
To tack, as a vessel, so that the other side of the vessel shall be presented to the wind.

Stay.etym: [OF. estayer, F. étayer to prop, fr. OF. estai, F. étai, a prop, probably fr. OD. stade, staeye, a prop, akin to E. stead; or cf. stay a rope to support a mast. Cf. Staid, a., Stay, v. i.]

senses.d: To remain; to continue in a place; to abide fixed for a space of time; to stop; to stand still.
q: She would command the hasty sun to stay.
Stay, I command you; stay and hear me first.
I stay a little longer, as one stays To cover up the embers that still burn.

senses.d: To continue in a state.
q: The flames augment, and stay At their full height, then languish to decay.

senses.d: To wait; to attend; to forbear to act.
q: I 'll tell thee all my whole device When I am in my coach, which stays for us.
The father can not stay any longer for the fortune.

senses.d: To dwell; to tarry; to linger.
q: I must stay a little on one action.

senses.d: To rest; to depend; to rely; to stand; to insist.
q: I stay here on my bond.
Ye despise this word, and trust in oppression and perverseness, and stay thereon.

senses.d: To come to an end; to cease; as, that day the storm stayed.
q: Here my commission stays.

senses.d: To hold out in a race or other contest; as, a horse stays well.
To change tack, as a ship.

Stay.etym: [√163. See Stay to hold up, prop.]

senses.d: That which serves as a prop; a support.
q: Trees serve as so many stays for their vines.
Lord Liverpool is the single stay of this ministry.

senses.d: A corset stiffened with whalebone or other material, worn by women, and rarely by men.
q: How the strait stays the slender waist constrain.

senses.d: Continuance in a place; abode for a space of time; sojourn; as, you make a short stay in this city.
q: Make haste, and leave thy business and thy care; No mortal interest can be worth thy stay.
Embrace the hero and his stay implore.

senses.d: Cessation of motion or progression; stand; stop.
q: Made of sphere metal, never to decay Until his revolution was at stay.
Affairs of state seemed rather to stand at a stay.

senses.d: Hindrance; let; check.
q: They were able to read good authors without any stay, if the book were not false.

senses.d: Restraint of passion; moderation; caution; steadiness; sobriety.
q: The wisdom, stay, and moderation of the king.
With prudent stay he long deferred The rough contention.

senses.d: Strictly, a part in tension to hold the parts together, or stiffen them.

Stay.etym: [Cf. OF. estai, F. étai support, and E. stay a rope to support a mast.]

senses.d: Staid; fixed; settled; sober; — now written staid. See Staid.
Place, or spot, in general.
q: Fly, therefore, fly this fearful stead anon.

senses.d: Place or room which another had, has, or might have.
q: In stead of bounds, he a pillar set.

senses.d: A frame on which a bed is laid; a bedstead.
q: The genial bed, Sallow the feet, the borders, and the stead.

senses.d: A farmhouse and offices.
q: The smallest act . . . shall stand us in great stead.
Here thy sword can do thee little stead.

Stead.etym: [OE. stede place, AS. stede; akin to LG. & D. stede, OS. stad, stedi, OHG. stat, G. statt, stätte, Icel. staðr, Dan. sted, Sw. stad, Goth. staþs, and E. stand. √163. See Stand, and cf. Staith, Stithy.]

senses.d: To help; to support; to benefit; to assist.
q: Perhaps my succour or advisement meet, Mote stead you much your purpose to subdue.
It nothing steads us To chide him from our eaves.

senses.d: To fill the place of.
Firm in standing or position; not tottering or shaking; fixed; firm.
q: Their feet steady, their hands diligent, their eyes watchful, and their hearts resolute.

senses.d: Constant in feeling, purpose, or pursuit; not fickle, changeable, or wavering; not easily moved or persuaded to alter a purpose; resolute; as, a man steady in his principles, in his purpose, or in the pursuit of an object.
Regular; constant; undeviating; uniform; as, the steady course of the sun; a steady breeze of wind.

Steady.syn: Fixed; regular; uniform; undeviating; invariable; unremitted; stable.
Steady.etym: [Cf. AS. stedig sterile, barren, stæððig, steady (in gestæððig), D. stedig, stadig, steeg, G. stätig, stetig. See Stead, n.]

senses.d: To make steady; to hold or keep from shaking, reeling, or falling; to make or keep firm; to support; to make constant, regular, or resolute.
To become steady; to regain a steady position or state; to move steadily.
q: Without a breeze, without a tide, She steadies with upright keel.

senses.d: A handle; a stale, or stele.
q: And in his hand a huge poleax did bear, Whose steale was iron-studded but not long.

senses.d: To take, and carry away, feloniously; to take without right or leave, and with intent to keep wrongfully; as, to steal the personal goods of another.
q: Maugre thy heed, thou must for indigence Or steal, or beg, or borrow, thy dispense.
The man who stole a goose and gave away the giblets in alms.

senses.d: To withdraw or convey clandestinely (reflexive); hence, to creep furtively, or to insinuate.
q: They could insinuate and steal themselves under the same by their humble carriage and submission.
He will steal himself into a man's favor.

senses.d: To gain by insinuating arts or covert means.
q: So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

senses.d: To get into one's power gradually and by imperceptible degrees; to take possession of by a gradual and imperceptible appropriation; — with away.
q: Variety of objects has a tendency to steal away the mind from its steady pursuit of any subject.

senses.d: To accomplish in a concealed or unobserved manner; to try to carry out secretly; as, to steal a look.
q: Always, when thou changest thine opinion or course, profess it plainly, . . . and do not think to steal it.
She yesterday wanted to steal a march of poor Liddy.
Fifty thousand men can not easily steal a march over the sea.

Steal.etym: [OE. stelen, AS. stelan; akin to OFries. stela, D. stelen, OHG. stelan, G. stehlen, Icel. stela, Sw. stjäla, Dan. stiæle, Goth. stilan.]

senses.d: To practice, or be guilty of, theft; to commit larceny or theft.
q: Thou shalt not steal.

senses.d: To withdraw, or pass privily; to slip in, along, or away, unperceived; to go or come furtively.
q: Fixed of mind to avoid further entreaty, and to fly all company, one night she stole away.
From whom you now must steal, and take no leave.
A soft and solemn breathing sound Rose like a steam of rich, distilled perfumes, And stole upon the air.

senses.d: The act of taking feloniously the personal property of another without his consent and knowledge; theft; larceny.
That which is stolen; stolen property; — chiefly used in the plural.
The act of stealing; theft.
q: The owner proveth the stealth to have been committed upon him by such an outlaw.

senses.d: The thing stolen; stolen property.
The bringing to pass anything in a secret or concealed manner; a secret procedure; a clandestine practice or action; — in either a good or a bad sense.
q: Do good by stealth, and blush to find it fame.
The monarch, blinded with desire of wealth, With steel invades the brother's life by stealth.
I told him of your stealth unto this wood.

senses.d: A variety of iron intermediate in composition and properties between wrought iron and cast iron (containing between one half of one per cent and one and a half per cent of carbon), and consisting of an alloy of iron with an iron carbide. Steel, unlike wrought iron, can be tempered, and retains magnetism. Its malleability decreases, and fusibility increases, with an increase in carbon.
An instrument or implement made of steel;
