A weapon, as a sword, dagger, etc.
q: While doubting thus he stood, Received the steel bathed in his brother's blood.

senses.d: An instrument of steel (usually a round rod) for sharpening knives.
A piece of steel for striking sparks from flint.
Fig.: Anything of extreme hardness; that which is characterized by sternness or rigor.
A chalybeate medicine.

Steel.etym: [AS. stēl, stȳl, stȳle; akin to D. staal, G. stahl, OHG. stahal, Icel. stāl, Dan. staal, Sw. stål, Old Prussian stakla.]

senses.d: To overlay, point, or edge with steel; as, to steel a razor; to steel an ax.
To make hard or strong; hence, to make insensible or obdurate.
q: Lies well steeled with weighty arguments.
O God of battles! steel my soldiers' hearts.
Why will you fight against so sweet a passion, And steel your heart to such a world of charms?

senses.d: To cause to resemble steel, as in smoothness, polish, or other qualities.
q: These waters, steeled By breezeless air to smoothest polish.

senses.d: To cover, as an electrotype plate, with a thin layer of iron by electrolysis. The iron thus deposited is very hard, like steel.

Steel.etym: [AS. stȳlan; cf. Icel. stæla. See Steel, n.]

senses.d: Bright; glittering; fiery.
q: His eyen steep, and rolling in his head.

senses.d: To soak in a liquid; to macerate; to extract the essence of by soaking; as, to soften seed by steeping it in water. Often used figuratively.
q: Let fancy still my sense in Lethe steep.
In refreshing dew to steep The little, trembling flowers.
The learned of the nation were steeped in Latin.

Steep.etym: [OE. stepen, probably fr. Icel. steypa to cause to stoop, cast down, pour out, to cast metals, causative of stūpa to stoop; cf. Sw. stöpa to cast, to steep, Dan. stöbe, D. & G. stippen to steep, to dip. Cf. Stoop, v. i.]

senses.d: To undergo the process of soaking in a liquid; as, the tea is steeping.
Something steeped, or used in steeping; a fertilizing liquid to hasten the germination of seeds.
A rennet bag.

Making a large angle with the plane of the horizon; ascending or descending rapidly with respect to a horizontal line or a level; precipitous; as, a steep hill or mountain; a steep roof; a steep ascent; a steep declivity; a steep barometric gradient.
Difficult of access; not easily reached; lofty; elevated; high.
Excessive; as, a steep price.

Steep.etym: [OE. steep, step, AS. steáp; akin to Icel. steypðr steep, and stūpa to stoop, Sw. stupa to fall, to tilt; cf. OFries. stap high. Cf. Stoop, v. i., Steep, v. t., Steeple.]

senses.d: A precipitous place, hill, mountain, rock, or ascent; any elevated object sloping with a large angle to the plane of the horizon; a precipice.
q: We had on each side naked rocks and mountains broken into a thousand irregular steeps and precipices.
Bare steeps, where desolation stalks.

senses.d: To gleam.
q: His head bald, that shone as any glass, . . . stemed as a furnace of a leed .

senses.d: A gleam of light; flame.
The principal body of a tree, shrub, or plant, of any kind; the main stock; the part which supports the branches or the head or top.
q: After they are shot up thirty feet in length, they spread a very large top, having no bough nor twig in the trunk or the stem.
The lowering spring, with lavish rain, Beats down the slender stem and breaded grain.

senses.d: A little branch which connects a fruit, flower, or leaf with a main branch; a peduncle, pedicel, or petiole; as, the stem of an apple or a cherry.
The stock of a family; a race or generation of progenitors.
q: While I do pray, learn here thy stem And true descent.

senses.d: A branch of a family.
q: This is a stem Of that victorious stock.

senses.d: A curved piece of timber to which the two sides of a ship are united at the fore end. The lower end of it is scarfed to the keel, and the bowsprit rests upon its upper end. Hence, the forward part of a vessel; the bow.
Fig.: An advanced or leading position; the lookout.
q: Wolsey sat at the stem more than twenty years.

senses.d: Anything resembling a stem or stalk; as, the stem of a tobacco pipe; the stem of a watch case, or that part to which the ring, by which it is suspended, is attached.
That part of a plant which bears leaves, or rudiments of leaves, whether rising above ground or wholly subterranean.
The entire central axis of a feather.
The short perpendicular line added to the body of a note; the tail of a crotchet, quaver, semiquaver, etc.
The part of an inflected word which remains unchanged (except by euphonic variations) throughout a given inflection; theme; base.

Stem.etym: [AS. stemn, stefn, stæfn; akin to OS. stamn the stem of a ship, D. stam stem, steven stem of a ship, G. stamm stem, steven stem of a ship, Icel. stafn, stamn, stem of a ship, stofn, stomn, stem, Sw. stam a tree trunk, Dan. stamme. Cf. Staff, Stand.]

senses.d: To remove the stem or stems from; as, to stem cherries; to remove the stem and its appendages (ribs and veins) from; as, to stem tobacco leaves.
To ram, as clay, into a blasting hole.
To oppose or cut with, or as with, the stem of a vessel; to resist, or make progress against; to stop or check the flow of, as a current.
q: stem the flood with their erected breasts.
Stemmed the wild torrent of a barbarous age.

Stem.etym: [Either from stem, n., or akin to stammer; cf. G. stemmen to press against.]

senses.d: To move forward against an obstacle, as a vessel against a current.
q: Stemming nightly toward the pole.

senses.d: To move the foot in walking; to advance or recede by raising and moving one of the feet to another resting place, or by moving both feet in succession.
To walk; to go on foot; esp., to walk a little distance; as, to step to one of the neighbors.
To walk slowly, gravely, or resolutely.
q: Home the swain retreats, His flock before him stepping to the fold.

senses.d: Fig.: To move mentally; to go in imagination.
q: They are stepping almost three thousand years back into the remotest antiquity.

Step.etym: [AS. stæppan; akin to OFries. steppa, D. stappen to step, stap a step, OHG. stepfen to step, G. stapfe a footstep, OHG. stapfo, G. stufe a step to step on; cf. Gr. � to shake about, handle roughly, stamp (?). Cf. Stamp, n. & a.]

senses.d: To set, as the foot.
To fix the foot of (a mast) in its step; to erect.
An advance or movement made by one removal of the foot; a pace.
A rest, or one of a set of rests, for the foot in ascending or descending, as a stair, or a round of a ladder.
q: The breadth of every single step or stair should be never less than one foot.

senses.d: The space passed over by one movement of the foot in walking or running; as, one step is generally about three feet, but may be more or less. Used also figuratively of any kind of progress; as, he improved step by step, or by steps.
q: To derive two or three general principles of motion from phenomena, and afterwards to tell us how the properties and actions of all corporeal things follow from those manifest principles, would be a very great step in philosophy.

senses.d: A small space or distance; as, it is but a step.
A print of the foot; a footstep; a footprint; track.
Gait; manner of walking; as, the approach of a man is often known by his step.
Proceeding; measure; action; an act.
q: The reputation of a man depends on the first steps he makes in the world.
Beware of desperate steps. The darkest day, Live till to-morrow, will have passed away.
I have lately taken steps . . . to relieve the old gentleman's distresses.

senses.d: Walk; passage.
q: Conduct my steps to find the fatal tree.

senses.d: A portable framework of stairs, much used indoors in reaching to a high position.
In general, a framing in wood or iron which is intended to receive an upright shaft; specif., a block of wood, or a solid platform upon the keelson, supporting the heel of the mast.
One of a series of offsets, or parts, resembling the steps of stairs, as one of the series of parts of a cone pulley on which the belt runs.
The intervak between two contiguous degrees of the csale.
At Eton College, England, a shallow step dividing the court into an inner and an outer portion.
One of the vast plains in Southeastern Europe and in Asia, generally elevated, and free from wood, analogous to many of the prairies in Western North America. See Savanna.

Steppe.etym: [From Russ. stepe, through G. or F. steppe.]

senses.d: Provided with a step or steps; having a series of offsets or parts resembling the steps of stairs; as, a stepped key.
The black tern.

Stern.etym: [AS. stearn a kind of bird. See Starling.]

senses.d: Having a certain hardness or severity of nature, manner, or aspect; hard; severe; rigid; rigorous; austere; fixed; unchanging; unrelenting; hence, serious; resolute; harsh; as, a sternresolve; a stern necessity; a stern heart; a stern gaze; a stern decree.
q: The sterne wind so loud gan to rout.
I would outstare the sternest eyes that look.
When that the poor have cried, Cæsar hath wept; Ambition should be made of sterner stuff.
Stern as tutors, and as uncles hard.
These barren rocks, your stern inheritance.

Stern.syn: Gloomy; sullen; forbidding; strict; unkind; hard-hearted; unfeeling; cruel; pitiless.
Stern.etym: [OE. sterne, sturne, AS. styrne; cf. D. stuurish stern, Sw. stursk refractory. √166.]

senses.d: The helm or tiller of a vessel or boat; also, the rudder.
The after or rear end of a ship or other vessel, or of a boat; the part opposite to the stem, or prow.
Fig.: The post of management or direction.
q: And sit chiefest stern of public weal.

senses.d: The hinder part of anything.
The tail of an animal; — now used only of the tail of a dog.

Stern.etym: [Icel. stjōrn a steering, or a doubtful AS. steórn. √166. See Steer, v. t.]

senses.d: Being in the stern, or being astern; as, the stern davits.
A man employed in a large family, or on a large estate, to manage the domestic concerns, supervise other servants, collect the rents or income, keep accounts, and the like.
q: Worthy to be stewards of rent and land.
They came near to the steward of Joseph's house.
As good stewards of the manifold grace of God.

senses.d: A person employed in a hotel, or a club, or on board a ship, to provide for the table, superintend the culinary affairs, etc. In naval vessels, the captain's steward, wardroom steward, steerage steward, warrant officers steward, etc., are petty officers who provide for the messes under their charge.
A fiscal agent of certain bodies; as, a steward in a Methodist church.
In some colleges, an officer who provides food for the students and superintends the kitchen; also, an officer who attends to the accounts of the students.
In Scotland, a magistrate appointed by the crown to exercise jurisdiction over royal lands.

Steward.etym: [OE. stiward, AS. stīweard, stigweard, literally, a sty ward; stigu sty + weard warden, guardian, — his first duty having been probably to attend to the domestic animals. √164. See Sty pen for swine, Ward.]

senses.d: To manage as a steward.
The office of a steward.
A small shoot, or branch, separated, as by a cutting, from a tree or shrub; also, any stem or branch of a tree, of any size, cut for fuel or timber.
q: Withered sticks to gather, which might serve Against a winter's day.

senses.d: Any long and comparatively slender piece of wood, whether in natural form or shaped with tools; a rod; a wand; a staff; as, the stick of a rocket; a walking stick.
Anything shaped like a stick; as, a stick of wax.
A derogatory expression for a person; one who is inert or stupid; as, an odd stick; a poor stick.
A composing stick. See under Composing. It is usually a frame of metal, but for posters, handbills, etc., one made of wood is used.
A thrust with a pointed instrument; a stab.

Stick.etym: [OE. sticke, AS. sticca; akin to stician to stab, prick, pierce, G. stecken a stick, staff, OHG. steccho, Icel. stik a stick. See Stick, v. t..]

senses.d: To penetrate with a pointed instrument; to pierce; to stab; hence, to kill by piercing; as, to stick a beast.
q: And sticked him with bodkins anon.
It was a shame . . . to stick him under the other gentleman's arm while he was redding the fray.

senses.d: To cause to penetrate; to push, thrust, or drive, so as to pierce; as, to stick a needle into one's finger.
q: Thou stickest a dagger in me.

senses.d: To fasten, attach, or cause to remain, by thrusting in; hence, also, to adorn or deck with things fastened on as by piercing; as, to stick a pin on the sleeve.
q: My shroud of white, stuck all with yew.
The points of spears are stuck within the shield.

senses.d: To set; to fix in; as, to stick card teeth.
To set with something pointed; as, to stick cards.
To fix on a pointed instrument; to impale; as, to stick an apple on a fork.
To attach by causing to adhere to the surface; as, to stick on a plaster; to stick a stamp on an envelope; also, to attach in any manner.
To compose; to set, or arrange, in a composing stick; as, to stick type.
To run or plane (moldings) in a machine, in contradistinction to working them by hand. Such moldings are said to be stuck.
To cause to stick; to bring to a stand; to pose; to puzzle; as, to stick one with a hard problem.
To impose upon; to compel to pay; sometimes, to cheat.

Stick.etym: [OE. stikien, v.t. & i., combined with steken, whence E. stuck), AS. stician, v.t. & i., and (assumed) stecan, v.t.; akin to OFries. steka, OS. stekan, OHG. stehhan, G. stechen, and to Gr. � to prick, Skr. tij to be sharp. Cf. Distinguish, Etiquette, Extinct, Instigate, Instinct, Prestige, Stake, St

senses.d: To adhere; as, glue sticks to the fingers; paste sticks to the wall.
q: The green caterpillar breedeth in the inward parts of roses not blown, where the dew sticketh.

senses.d: To remain where placed; to be fixed; to hold fast to any position so as to be moved with difficulty; to cling; to abide; to cleave; to be united closely.
q: A friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
I am a kind of bur; I shall stick.
If on your fame our sex a bolt has thrown, 'T will ever stick through malice of your own.

senses.d: To be prevented from going farther; to stop by reason of some obstacle; to be stayed.
q: I had most need of blessing, and “Amen” Stuck in my throat.
The trembling weapon passed Through nine bull hides, . . . and stuck within the last.

senses.d: To be embarrassed or puzzled; to hesitate; to be deterred, as by scruples; to scruple; — often with at.
q: They will stick long at part of a demonstration for want of perceiving the connection of two ideas.
Some stick not to say, that the parson and attorney forged a will.

senses.d: To cause difficulties, scruples, or hesitation.
q: This is the difficulty that sticks with the most reasonable.

senses.d: Not easily bent; not flexible or pliant; not limber or flaccid; rigid; firm; as, stiff wood, paper, joints.
q: rising on stiff pennons, tower The mid aërial sky.

senses.d: Not liquid or fluid; thick and tenacious; inspissated; neither soft nor hard; as, the paste is stiff.
Firm; strong; violent; difficult to oppose; as, a stiff gale or breeze.
Not easily subdued; unyielding; stubborn; obstinate; pertinacious; as, a stiff adversary.
q: It is a shame to stand stiff in a foolish argument.
A war ensues: the Cretans own their cause, Stiff to defend their hospitable laws.

senses.d: Not natural and easy; formal; constrained; affected; starched; as, stiff behavior; a stiff style.
q: The French are open, familiar, and talkative; the Italians stiff, ceremonious, and reserved.

senses.d: Harsh; disagreeable; severe; hard to bear.
Bearing a press of canvas without careening much; as, a stiff vessel; — opposed to crank.
Very large, strong, or costly; powerful; as, a stiff charge; a stiff price.

Stiff.syn: Rigid; inflexible; strong; hardly; stubborn; obstinate; pertinacious; harsh; formal; constrained; affected; starched; rigorous.
Stiff.etym: [OE. stif, AS. stīf; akin to D. stijf, G. steif, Dan. stiv, Sw. styf, Icel. stīfr, Lith. stipti to be stiff; cf. L. stipes a post, trunk of a tree, stipare to press, compress. Cf. Costive, Stifle, Stipulate, Stive to stuff.]

senses.d: To make stiff; to make less pliant or flexible; as, to stiffen cloth with starch.
q: Stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood.

senses.d: To inspissate; to make more thick or viscous; as, to stiffen paste.
To make torpid; to benumb.
To become stiff or stiffer, in any sense of the adjective.
q: Like bristles rose my stiffening hair.
The tender soil then stiffening by degrees.
Some souls we see, Grow hard and stiffen with adversity.

senses.d: Motionless; at rest; quiet; as, to stand still; to lie or sit still.
Uttering no sound; silent; as, the audience is still; the animals are still.
q: The sea that roared at thy command, At thy command was still.

senses.d: Not disturbed by noise or agitation; quiet; calm; as, a still evening; a still atmosphere.
Comparatively quiet or silent; soft; gentle; low.
Constant; continual.
q: By still practice learn to know thy meaning.

senses.d: Not effervescing; not sparkling; as, still wines.

Still.syn: Quiet; calm; noiseless; serene; motionless; inert; stagnant.
Still.etym: [OE. stille, AS. stille; akin to D. stil, OS. & OHG. stilli, G. still, Dan. stille, Sw. stilla, and to E. stall; from the idea of coming to a stand, or halt. Cf. Still, adv.]

senses.d: Freedom from noise; calm; silence; as, the still of midnight.
A steep hill or ascent.
To this time; until and during the time now present; now no less than before; yet.
q: It hath been anciently reported, and is still received.

senses.d: In the future as now and before.
q: Hourly joys be still upon you!

senses.d: In continuation by successive or repeated acts; always; ever; constantly; uniformly.
q: The desire of fame betrays an ambitious man into indecencies that lessen his reputation; he is still afraid lest any of his actions should be thrown away in private.
Chemists would be rich if they could still do in great quantities what they have sometimes done in little.

senses.d: In an increasing or additional degree; even more; — much used with comparatives.
q: The guilt being great, the fear doth still exceed.

senses.d: Notwithstanding what has been said or done; in spite of what has occured; nevertheless; — sometimes used as a conjunction. See Synonym of But.
q: As sunshine, broken in the rill, Though turned astray, is sunshine still.

senses.d: After that; after what is stated.
q: In the primitive church, such as by fear being compelled to sacrifice to strange gods, after repented, and kept still the office of preaching the gospel.
And like the watchful minutes to the hour, Still and anon cheered up the heavy time.

Still.etym: [AS. stille quietly. See Still, a. The modern senses come from the idea of stopping and staying still, or motionless.]

senses.d: To stop, as motion or agitation; to cause to become quiet, or comparatively quiet; to check the agitation of; as, to still the raging sea.
q: He having a full sway over the water, had power to still and compose it, as well as to move and disturb it.

senses.d: To stop, as noise; to silence.
q: With his name the mothers still their babies.

senses.d: To appease; to calm; to quiet, as tumult, agitation, or excitement; as, to still the passions.
q: Toil that would, at least, have stilled an unquiet impulse in me.

Still.syn: To quiet; calm; allay; lull; pacify; appease; subdue; suppress; silence; stop; check; restrain.
Still.etym: [AS. stillan, from stille still, quiet, firm. See Still, a.]

senses.d: A vessel, boiler, or copper used in the distillation of liquids; specifically, one used for the distillation of alcoholic liquors; a retort. The name is sometimes applied to the whole apparatus used in in vaporization and condensation.
A house where liquors are distilled; a distillery.

Still.etym: [Cf. OE. stillatorie. See Still, v., to distill.]

senses.d: To cause to fall by drops.
To expel spirit from by heat, or to evaporate and condense in a refrigeratory; to distill.
To drop, or flow in drops; to distill.

Any sharp organ of offense and defense, especially when connected with a poison gland, and adapted to inflict a wound by piercing; as the caudal sting of a scorpion. The sting of a bee or wasp is a modified ovipositor. The caudal sting, or spine, of a sting ray is a modified dorsal fin ray. The term is sometimes applied to the fang of a serpent. See Illust. of Scorpion.
A sharp-pointed hollow hair seated on a gland which secrets an acrid fluid, as in nettles. The points of these hairs usually break off in the wound, and the acrid fluid is pressed into it.
Anything that gives acute pain, bodily or mental; as, the stings of remorse; the stings of reproach.
q: The sting of death is sin.

senses.d: The thrust of a sting into the flesh; the act of stinging; a wound inflicted by stinging.
A goad; incitement.
The point of an epigram or other sarcastic saying.

Sting.etym: [AS. sting a sting. See Sting, v. t.]

senses.d: To pierce or wound with a sting; as, bees will sting an animal that irritates them; the nettles stung his hands.
To pain acutely; as, the conscience is stung with remorse; to bite.
To goad; to incite, as by taunts or reproaches.

Sting.etym: [AS. stingan; akin to Icel. & Sw. stinga, Dan. stinge, and probably to E. stick, v.t.; cf. Goth. usstiggan to put out, pluck out. Cf. Stick, v. t.]

senses.d: To emit a strong, offensive smell; to send out a disgusting odor.

Stink.etym: [AS. stinkan to have a smell (whether good or bad); akin to OHG. stinchan, G. & D. stinken to stink; of uncertain origin; cf. Icel. stökkva to leap, to spring, Goth. stigqan to push, strike, or Gr. � rancid. Cf. Stench.]

senses.d: To cause to stink; to affect by a stink.
A strong, offensive smell; a disgusting odor; a stench.
To change the place of in any manner; to move.
q: My foot I had never yet in five days been able to stir.

senses.d: To disturb the relative position of the particles of, as of a liquid, by passing something through it; to agitate; as, to stir a pudding with a spoon.
q: My mind is troubled, like a fountain stirred.

senses.d: To bring into debate; to agitate; to moot.
q: Stir not questions of jurisdiction.

senses.d: To incite to action; to arouse; to instigate; to prompt; to excite.
q: An Ate, stirring him to blood and strife.
And for her sake some mutiny will stir.

Stir.syn: To move; incite; awaken; rouse; animate; stimulate; excite; provoke.
Stir.etym: [OE. stiren, steren, sturen, AS. styrian; probably akin to D. storen to disturb, G. stören, OHG. stōren to scatter, destroy. √166.]

senses.d: To move; to change one's position.
q: I had not power to stir or strive, But felt that I was still alive.

senses.d: To be in motion; to be active or bustling; to exert or busy one's self.
q: All are not fit with them to stir and toil.
The friends of the unfortunate exile, far from resenting his unjust suspicions, were stirring anxiously in his behalf.

senses.d: To become the object of notice; to be on foot.
q: They fancy they have a right to talk freely upon everything that stirs or appears.

senses.d: To rise, or be up, in the morning.
The act or result of stirring; agitation; tumult; bustle; noise or various movements.
q: Why all these words, this clamor, and this stir?
Consider, after so much stir about genus and species, how few words we have yet settled definitions of.

senses.d: Public disturbance or commotion; tumultuous disorder; seditious uproar.
q: Being advertised of some stirs raised by his unnatural sons in England.

senses.d: Agitation of thoughts; conflicting passions.
The stem, or main body, of a tree or plant; the fixed, strong, firm part; the trunk.
q: Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground, yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant.

senses.d: The stem or branch in which a graft is inserted.
q: The scion overruleth the stock quite.

senses.d: A block of wood; something fixed and solid; a pillar; a firm support; a post.
q: All our fathers worshiped stocks and stones.
Item, for a stock of brass for the holy water, seven shillings; which, by the canon, must be of marble or metal, and in no case of brick.

senses.d: Hence, a person who is as dull and lifeless as a stock or post; one who has little sense.
q: Let's be no stoics, nor no stocks.

senses.d: The principal supporting part; the part in which others are inserted, or to which they are attached.
The wood to which the barrel, lock, etc., of a musket or like firearm are secured; also, a long, rectangular piece of wood, which is an important part of several forms of gun carriage.
The handle or contrivance by which bits are held in boring; a bitstock; a brace.
The block of wood or metal frame which constitutes the body of a plane, and in which the plane iron is fitted; a plane stock.
The wooden or iron crosspiece to which the shank of an anchor is attached. See Illust. of Anchor.
The support of the block in which an anvil is fixed, or of the anvil itself.
A handle or wrench forming a holder for the dies for cutting screws; a diestock.
The part of a tally formerly struck in the exchequer, which was delivered to the person who had lent the king money on account, as the evidence of indebtedness. See Counterfoil.

Stock.syn: Fund; capital; store; supply; accumulation; hoard; provision.
Stock.etym: [AS. stocc a stock, trunk, stick; akin to D. stok, G. stock, OHG. stoc, Icel. stokkr, Sw. stock, Dan. stok, and AS. stycce a piece; cf. Skr. tuj to urge, thrust. Cf. Stokker, Stucco, and Tuck a rapier.]

senses.d: To lay up; to put aside for future use; to store, as merchandise, and the like.

To provide with material requisites; to store; to fill; to supply; as, to stock a warehouse, that is, to fill it with goods; to stock a farm, that is, to supply it with cattle and tools; to stock land, that is, to occupy it with a permanent growth, especially of grass.
To suffer to retain milk for twenty-four hours or more previous to sale, as cows.
To put in the stocks.
Used or employed for constant service or application, as if constituting a portion of a stock or supply; standard; permanent; standing; as, a stock actor; a stock play; a stock sermon.
Raw material; that out of which something is manufactured; as, paper stock.
A plain soap which is made into toilet soap by adding perfumery, coloring matter, etc.
A stolon.
A long, loose garment reaching to the feet.
q: But when mild morn, in saffron stole, First issues from her eastern goal.

senses.d: A narrow band of silk or stuff, sometimes enriched with embroidery and jewels, worn on the left shoulder of deacons, and across both shoulders of bishops and priests, pendent on each side nearly to the ground. At Mass, it is worn crossed on the breast by priests. It is used in various sacred functions.

Stole.etym: [AS. stole, L. stola, Gr. � a stole, garment, equipment, fr. � to set, place, equip, send, akin to E. stall. See Stall.]

senses.d: An enlargement, or series of enlargements, in the anterior part of the alimentary canal, in which food is digested; any cavity in which digestion takes place in an animal; a digestive cavity. See Digestion, and Gastric juice, under Gastric.
The desire for food caused by hunger; appetite; as, a good stomach for roast beef.
Hence appetite in general; inclination; desire.
q: He which hath no stomach to this fight, Let him depart.

senses.d: Violence of temper; anger; sullenness; resentment; willful obstinacy; stubbornness.
q: Stern was his look, and full of stomach vain.
This sort of crying proceeding from pride, obstinacy, and stomach, the will, where the fault lies, must be bent.

senses.d: Pride; haughtiness; arrogance.
q: He was a man Of an unbounded stomach.

Stomach.etym: [OE. stomak, F. estomac, L. stomachus, fr. Gr. στόμαχοσ stomach, throat, gullet, fr. στόμα a mouth, any outlet or entrance.]

senses.d: To resent; to remember with anger; to dislike.
q: The lion began to show his teeth, and to stomach the affront.
The Parliament sit in that body . . . to be his counselors and dictators, though he stomach it.

senses.d: To bear without repugnance; to brook.

Stomach.etym: [Cf. L. stomachari, v.t. & i., to be angry or vexed at a thing.]

senses.d: To be angry.
One who stomachs.
An ornamental covering for the breast, worn originally both by men and women. Those worn by women were often richly decorated.
q: A stately lady in a diamond stomacher.

senses.d: Concreted earthy or mineral matter; also, any particular mass of such matter; as, a house built of stone; the boy threw a stone; pebbles are rounded stones.
q: They had brick for stone, and slime . . . for mortar.

senses.d: A precious stone; a gem.
Something made of stone. Specifically: -
The glass of a mirror; a mirror.
q: Lend me a looking-glass; If that her breath will mist or stain the stone, Why, then she lives.

senses.d: A monument to the dead; a gravestone.
q: Should some relenting eye Glance on the where our cold relics lie.

senses.d: A calculous concretion, especially one in the kidneys or bladder; the disease arising from a calculus.
One of the testes; a testicle.
The hard endocarp of drupes; as, the stone of a cherry or peach. See Illust. of Endocarp.
A weight which legally is fourteen pounds, but in practice varies with the article weighed.
Fig.: Symbol of hardness and insensibility; torpidness; insensibility; as, a heart of stone.
q: I have not yet forgot myself to stone.

senses.d: A stand or table with a smooth, flat top of stone, commonly marble, on which to arrange the pages of a book, newspaper, etc., before printing; — called also imposing stone.

Stone.etym: [OE. ston, stan, AS. stān; akin to OS. & OFries. stēn, D. steen, G. stein, Icel. steinn, Sw. sten, Dan. steen, Goth. stains, Russ. stiena a wall, Gr. �, �, a pebble. √167. Cf. Steen.]

senses.d: To pelt, beat, or kill with stones.
q: And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.

senses.d: To make like stone; to harden.
q: O perjured woman! thou dost stone my heart.

senses.d: To free from stones; also, to remove the seeds of; as, to stone a field; to stone cherries; to stone raisins.
To wall or face with stones; to line or fortify with stones; as, to stone a well; to stone a cellar.
To rub, scour, or sharpen with a stone.

Stone.etym: [From Stone, n.: cf. AS. st�nan, Goth. stainjan.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to stone, consisting of, or abounding in, stone or stones; resembling stone; hard; as, a stony tower; a stony cave; stony ground; a stony crust.
Converting into stone; petrifying; petrific.
q: The stony dart of senseless cold.

senses.d: Inflexible; cruel; unrelenting; pitiless; obdurate; perverse; cold; morally hard; appearing as if petrified; as, a stony heart; a stony gaze.
A plant from which layers are propagated by bending its branches into the soil.
To ramfy; to tiller, as grain; to shoot out suckers.
A single seat with three or four legs and without a back, made in various forms for various uses.
A seat used in evacuating the bowels; hence, an evacuation; a discharge from the bowels.
A stool pigeon, or decoy bird.
A small channel on the side of a vessel, for the dead-eyes of the backstays.
A bishop's seat or see; a bishop-stool.
A bench or form for resting the feet or the knees; a footstool; as, a kneeling stool.
Material, such as oyster shells, spread on the sea bottom for oyster spat to adhere to.

Stool.etym: [AS. stōl a seat; akin to OFries. & OS. stōl, D. stoel, G. stuhl, OHG. stuol, Icel. stōll, Sw. & Dan. stol, Goth. stōls, Lith. stalas a table, Russ. stol'; from the root of E. stand. √163. See Stand, and cf. Fauteuil.]

senses.d: Originally, a covered porch with seats, at a house door; the Dutch stoep as introduced by the Dutch into New York. Afterward, an out-of-door flight of stairs of from seven to fourteen steps, with platform and parapets, leading to an entrance door some distance above the street; the French perron. Hence, any porch, platform, entrance stairway, or small veranda, at a house door.
A vessel of liquor; a flagon.
q: Fetch me a stoop of liquor.

Stoop.etym: [OE. stope, Icel. staup; akin to AS. steáp, D. stoop, G. stauf, OHG. stouph.]

senses.d: A post fixed in the earth.
To bend the upper part of the body downward and forward; to bend or lean forward; to incline forward in standing or walking; to assume habitually a bent position.
To yield; to submit; to bend, as by compulsion; to assume a position of humility or subjection.
q: Mighty in her ships stood Carthage long, . . . Yet stooped to Rome, less wealthy, but more strong.
These are arts, my prince, In which your Zama does not stoop to Rome.

senses.d: To descend from rank or dignity; to condescend.
q: Where men of great wealth stoop to husbandry, it multiplieth riches exceedingly.

senses.d: To come down as a hawk does on its prey; to pounce; to souse; to swoop.
q: The bird of Jove, stooped from his aëry tour, Two birds of gayest plume before him drove.

senses.d: To sink when on the wing; to alight.
q: And stoop with closing pinions from above.
Cowering low With blandishment, each bird stooped on his wing.

Stoop.syn: To lean; yield; submit; condescend; descend; cower; shrink.
Stoop.etym: [OE. stoupen; akin to AS. st�pian, OD. stuypen, Icel. stūpa, Sw. stupa to fall, to tilt. Cf 5th Steep.]

senses.d: To bend forward and downward; to bow down; as, to stoop the body.
To cause to incline downward; to slant; as, to stoop a cask of liquor.
To cause to submit; to prostrate.
q: Many of those whose states so tempt thine ears Are stooped by death; and many left alive.

senses.d: To degrade.
The act of stooping, or bending the body forward; inclination forward; also, an habitual bend of the back and shoulders.
Descent, as from dignity or superiority; condescension; an act or position of humiliation.
q: Can any loyal subject see With patience such a stoop from sovereignty?

senses.d: The fall of a bird on its prey; a swoop.
To close, as an aperture, by filling or by obstructing; as, to stop the ears; hence, to stanch, as a wound.
To obstruct; to render impassable; as, to stop a way, road, or passage.
To arrest the progress of; to hinder; to impede; to shut in; as, to stop a traveler; to stop the course of a stream, or a flow of blood.

To hinder from acting or moving; to prevent the effect or efficiency of; to cause to cease; to repress; to restrain; to suppress; to interrupt; to suspend; as, to stop the execution of a decree, the progress of vice, the approaches of old age or infirmity.
q: Whose disposition all the world well knows Will not be rubbed nor stopped.

senses.d: To regulate the sounds of, as musical strings, by pressing them against the finger board with the finger, or by shortening in any way the vibrating part.
To point, as a composition; to punctuate.
q: If his sentences were properly stopped.

senses.d: To make fast; to stopper.

Stop.syn: To obstruct; hinder; impede; repress; suppress; restrain; discontinue; delay; interrupt.
Stop.etym: [OE. stoppen, AS. stoppian (in comp.); akin to LG. & D. stoppen, G. stopfen, Icel. stoppa, Sw. stoppa, Dan. stoppe; all probably fr. LL. stopare, stupare, fr. L. stuppa the coarse part of flax, tow, oakum. Cf. Estop, Stuff, Stupe a fomentation.]

senses.d: To cease to go on; to halt, or stand still; to come to a stop.
q: He bites his lip, and starts; Stops on a sudden, looks upon the ground; Then lays his finger on his temple: strait Springs out into fast gait; then stops again.

senses.d: To cease from any motion, or course of action.
q: Stop, while ye may, suspend your mad career!

senses.d: To spend a short time; to reside temporarily; to stay; to tarry; as, to stop with a friend.
q: By stopping at home till the money was gone.

senses.d: The act of stopping, or the state of being stopped; hindrance of progress or of action; cessation; repression; interruption; check; obstruction.
q: It is doubtful . . . whether it contributed anything to the stop of the infection.
Occult qualities put a stop to the improvement of natural philosophy.
It is a great step toward the mastery of our desires to give this stop to them.

senses.d: That which stops, impedes, or obstructs; as obstacle; an impediment; an obstruction.
q: A fatal stop traversed their headlong course.
So melancholy a prospect should inspire us with zeal to oppose some stop to the rising torrent.

senses.d: A device, or piece, as a pin, block, pawl, etc., for arresting or limiting motion, or for determining the position to which another part shall be brought.

The closing of an aperture in the air passage, or pressure of the finger upon the string, of an instrument of music, so as to modify the tone; hence, any contrivance by which the sounds of a musical instrument are regulated.
q: The organ sound a time survives the stop.

senses.d: In the organ, one of the knobs or handles at each side of the organist, by which he can draw on or shut off any register or row of pipes; the register itself; as, the vox humana stop.

A member, plain or molded, formed of a separate piece and fixed to a jamb, against which a door or window shuts. This takes the place, or answers the purpose, of a rebate. Also, a pin or block to prevent a drawer from sliding too far.
A point or mark in writing or printing intended to distinguish the sentences, parts of a sentence, or clauses; a mark of punctuation. See Punctuation.
The diaphragm used in optical instruments to cut off the marginal portions of a beam of light passing through lenses.
The depression in the face of a dog between the skull and the nasal bones. It is conspicuous in the bulldog, pug, and some other breeds.

Some part of the articulating organs, as the lips, or the tongue and palate, closed (a) so as to cut off the passage of breath or voice through the mouth and the nose (distinguished as a lip-stop, or a front-stop, etc., as in p, t, d, etc.), or (b) so as to obstruct, but not entirely cut off, the passage, as in l, n, etc.; also, any of the consonants so formed.

Stop.syn: Cessation; check; obstruction; obstacle; hindrance; impediment; interruption.

senses.d: Made by complete closure of the mouth organs; shut; — said of certain consonants (p, b, t, d, etc.).
That which is accumulated, or massed together; a source from which supplies may be drawn; hence, an abundance; a great quantity, or a great number.
q: The ships are fraught with store of victuals.
With store of ladies, whose bright eyes Rain influence, and give the prize.

senses.d: A place of deposit for goods, esp. for large quantities; a storehouse; a warehouse; a magazine.
Any place where goods are sold, whether by wholesale or retail; a shop.
Articles, especially of food, accumulated for some specific object; supplies, as of provisions, arms, ammunition, and the like; as, the stores of an army, of a ship, of a family.
q: His swine, his horse, his stoor, and his poultry.
In his needy shop a tortoise hung, An alligator stuffed, and other skins Of ill-shaped fishes; and about his shelves A beggarly account of empty boxes.
Sulphurous and nitrous foam, . . . Concocted and adjusted, they reduced To blackest grain, and into store conveyed.

Store.syn: Fund; supply; abundance; plenty; accumulation; provision.
Store.etym: [OE. stor, stoor, OF. estor, provisions, supplies, fr. estorer to store. See Store, v. t.]

senses.d: Accumulated; hoarded.
To collect as a reserved supply; to accumulate; to lay away.
q: Dora stored what little she could save.

senses.d: To furnish; to supply; to replenish; esp., to stock or furnish against a future time.
q: Her mind with thousand virtues stored.
Wise Plato said the world with men was stored.
Having stored a pond of four acres with carps, tench, and other fish.

senses.d: To deposit in a store, warehouse, or other building, for preservation; to warehouse; as, to store goods.

Store.etym: [OE. storen, OF. estorer to construct, restore, store, LL. staurare, for L. instaurare to renew, restore; in + staurare (in comp.) Cf. Instore, Instaurate, Restore, Story a floor.]

senses.d: A building for keeping goods of any kind, especially provisions; a magazine; a repository; a warehouse.
q: Joseph opened all the storehouses, and sold unto Egyptians.
The Scripture of God is a storehouse abounding with estimable treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

senses.d: A mass or quality laid up.

Any one of several species of large wading birds of the family Ciconidæ, having long legs and a long, pointed bill. They are found both in the Old World and in America, and belong to Ciconia and several allied genera. The European white stork (Ciconia alba) is the best known. It commonly makes its nests on the top of a building, a chimney, a church spire, or a pillar. The black stork (C. nigra) is native of Asia, Africa, and Europe.

Stork.etym: [AS. storc; akin to G. storch, OHG. storah, Icel. storkr, Dan. & Sw. stork, and perhaps to Gr. � a vulture.]

senses.d: A violent disturbance of the atmosphere, attended by wind, rain, snow, hail, or thunder and lightning; hence, often, a heavy fall of rain, snow, or hail, whether accompanied with wind or not.
q: We hear this fearful tempest sing, Yet seek no shelter to avoid the storm.

senses.d: A violent agitation of human society; a civil, political, or domestic commotion; sedition, insurrection, or war; violent outbreak; clamor; tumult.
q: I will stir up in England some black storm.
Her sister Began to scold and raise up such a storm.

senses.d: A heavy shower or fall, any adverse outburst of tumultuous force; violence.
q: A brave man struggling in the storms of fate.

senses.d: A violent assault on a fortified place; a furious attempt of troops to enter and take a fortified place by scaling the walls, forcing the gates, or the like.
q: Storms beat, and rolls the main; O! beat those storms, and roll the seas, in vain.
What at first was called a gust, the same Hath now a storm's, anon a tempest's name.

Storm.etym: [AS. storm; akin to D. storm, G. sturm, Icel. stormr; and perhaps to Gr. � assault, onset, Skr. s� to flow, to hasten, or perhaps to L. sternere to strew, prostrate (cf. Stratum). √166.]

senses.d: To assault; to attack, and attempt to take, by scaling walls, forcing gates, breaches, or the like; as, to storm a fortified town.
To raise a tempest.
To blow with violence; also, to rain, hail, snow, or the like, usually in a violent manner, or with high wind; — used impersonally; as, it storms.
To rage; to be in a violent passion; to fume.
q: The master storms, the lady scolds.

senses.d: Characterized by, or proceeding from, a storm; subject to storms; agitated with furious winds; biosterous; tempestous; as, a stormy season; a stormy day or week.
Proceeding from violent agitation or fury; as, a stormy sound; stormy shocks.
Violent; passionate; rough; as, stormy passions.
q: Stormy chiefs of a desert but extensive domain.

senses.d: A set of rooms on the same floor or level; a floor, or the space between two floors. Also, a horizontal division of a building's exterior considered architecturally, which need not correspond exactly with the stories within.

Story.etym: [OF. estoré, estorée, built, erected, p. p. of estorer to build, restore, to store. See Store, v. t.]

senses.d: A narration or recital of that which has occurred; a description of past events; a history; a statement; a record.
q: One malcontent who did indeed get a name in story.
Venice, with its unique city and its Impressive story.
The four great monarchies make the subject of ancient story.

senses.d: The relation of an incident or minor event; a short narrative; a tale; especially, a fictitious narrative less elaborate than a novel; a short romance.
A euphemism or child's word for “a lie;” a fib; as, to tell a story.

Story.etym: [OE. storie, OF. estoire, F. histoire, fr. L. historia. See History.]

senses.d: To tell in historical relation; to make the subject of a story; to narrate or describe in story.
q: How worthy he is I will leave to appear hereafter, rather than story him in his own hearing.
It is storied of the brazen colossus in Rhodes, that it was seventy cubits high.

senses.d: Strong; lusty; vigorous; robust; sinewy; muscular; hence, firm; resolute; dauntless.
q: With hearts stern and stout.
A stouter champion never handled sword.
He lost the character of a bold, stout, magnanimous man.
The lords all stand To clear their cause, most resolutely stout.

senses.d: Proud; haughty; arrogant; hard.
q: Your words have been stout against me.
Commonly . . . they that be rich are lofty and stout.

senses.d: Firm; tough; materially strong; enduring; as, a stout vessel, stick, string, or cloth.
Large; bulky; corpulent.

Stout.etym: [D. stout bold (or OF. estout bold, proud, of Teutonic origin); akin to AS. stolt, G. stolz, and perh. to E. stilt.]

senses.d: A strong malt liquor; strong porter.
The state or quality of being stout.

Stoutness.syn: Strength; bulk; courage; force; valor; lustiness; brawniness; boldness; fortitude; stubbornness.

senses.d: A variant of Strait, a.
q: Egypt is a long country, but it is straight, that is to say, narrow.

senses.d: Right, in a mathematical sense; passing from one point to another by the nearest course; direct; not deviating or crooked; as, a straight line or course; a straight piece of timber.
q: And the crooked shall be made straight.
There are many several sorts of crooked lines, but there is only one which is straight.

senses.d: Approximately straight; not much curved; as, straight ribs are such as pass from the base of a leaf to the apex, with a small curve.
Composed of cards which constitute a regular sequence, as the ace, king, queen, jack, and ten-spot; as, a straight hand; a straight flush.
Conforming to justice and rectitude; not deviating from truth or fairness; upright; as, straight dealing.
Unmixed; undiluted; as, to take liquor straight.

Making no exceptions or deviations in one's support of the organization and candidates of a political party; as, a straight Republican; a straight Democrat; also, containing the names of all the regularly nominated candidates of a party and no others; as, a straight ballot.

Straight.etym: [OE. strei�t, properly p. p. of strecchen to stretch, AS. streht, p. p. of streccan to stretch, to extend. See Stretch.]

senses.d: In a straight manner; directly; rightly; forthwith; immediately; as, the arrow went straight to the mark.
q: I know thy generous temper well; Fling but the appearance of dishonor on it, It straight takes fire, and mounts into a blaze.
Everything was going on straight.

senses.d: A hand of five cards in consecutive order as to value; a sequence. When they are of one suit, it is calles straight flush.
To straighten.
Immediately; without loss of time; without delay.
q: He took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi. . . . And straightway the damsel arose.

senses.d: Race; stock; generation; descent; family.
q: He is of a noble strain.
With animals and plants a cross between different varieties, or between individuals of the same variety but of another strain, gives vigor and fertility to the offspring.

senses.d: Hereditary character, quality, or disposition.
q: Intemperance and lust breed diseases, which, propogated, spoil the strain of nation.

senses.d: Rank; a sort.
To draw with force; to extend with great effort; to stretch; as, to strain a rope; to strain the shrouds of a ship; to strain the cords of a musical instrument.
To act upon, in any way, so as to cause change of form or volume, as forces on a beam to bend it.
To exert to the utmost; to ply vigorously.
q: He sweats, Strains his young nerves.
They strain their warbling throats To welcome in the spring.

senses.d: To stretch beyond its proper limit; to do violence to, in the matter of intent or meaning; as, to strain the law in order to convict an accused person.
q: There can be no other meaning in this expression, however some may pretend to strain it.

senses.d: To injure by drawing, stretching, or the exertion of force; as, the gale strained the timbers of the ship.
To injure in the muscles or joints by causing to make too strong an effort; to harm by overexertion; to sprain; as, to strain a horse by overloading; to strain the wrist; to strain a muscle.
q: Prudes decayed about may track, Strain their necks with looking back.

senses.d: To squeeze; to press closely.
q: Evander with a close embrace Strained his departing friend.

senses.d: To make uneasy or unnatural; to produce with apparent effort; to force; to constrain.
q: He talks and plays with Fatima, but his mirth Is forced and strained.
The quality of mercy is not strained.

senses.d: To urge with importunity; to press; as, to strain a petition or invitation.
q: Note, if your lady strain his entertainment.

senses.d: To press, or cause to pass, through a strainer, as through a screen, a cloth, or some porous substance; to purify, or separate from extraneous or solid matter, by filtration; to filter; as, to strain milk through cloth.

Strain.etym: [OF. estraindre, estreindre, F. étreindre, L. stringere to draw or bind tight; probably akin to Gr. � a halter, � that which is squeezwd out, a drop, or perhaps to E. strike. Cf. Strangle, Strike, Constrain, District, Strait, a. Stress, Strict, Stringent.]

senses.d: To make violent efforts.
q: To build his fortune I will strain a little.

senses.d: To percolate; to be filtered; as, water straining through a sandy soil.
The act of straining, or the state of being strained.

A violent effort; an excessive and hurtful exertion or tension, as of the muscles; as, he lifted the weight with a strain; the strain upon a ship's rigging in a gale; also, the hurt or injury resulting; a sprain.
q: Whether any poet of our country since Shakespeare has exerted a greater variety of powers with less strain and less ostentation.
Credit is gained by custom, and seldom recovers a strain.

senses.d: A change of form or dimensions of a solid or liquid mass, produced by a stress.
A portion of music divided off by a double bar; a complete musical period or sentence; a movement, or any rounded subdivision of a movement.
q: Their heavenly harps a lower strain began.

senses.d: Any sustained note or movement; a song; a distinct portion of an ode or other poem; also, the pervading note, or burden, of a song, poem, oration, book, etc.; theme; motive; manner; style; also, a course of action or conduct; as, he spoke in a noble strain; there was a strain of woe in his story; a strain of trickery appears in his career.
q: Such take too high a strain at first.
The genius and strain of the book of Proverbs.
It seems a novelty, and yet contains Nothing but sound and honest gospel strains.

senses.d: Turn; tendency; inborn disposition. Cf. 1st Strain.
q: Because heretics have a strain of madness, he applied her with some corporal chastisements.

senses.d: A cultural subvariety that is only slightly differentiated.
A variant of Straight.
Narrow; not broad.
q: Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
Too strait and low our cottage doors.

senses.d: Tight; close; closely fitting.
Close; intimate; near; familiar.
Strict; scrupulous; rigorous.
q: Some certain edicts and some strait decrees.
The straitest sect of our religion.

senses.d: Difficult; distressful; straited.
q: To make your strait circumstances yet straiter.

senses.d: Parsimonious; niggargly; mean.
q: I beg cold comfort, and you are so strait, And so ingrateful, you deny me that.

Strait.etym: [OE. straight, streyt, streit, OF. estreit, estroit, F. étroit, from L. strictus drawn together, close, tight, p. p. of stringere to draw tight. See 2nd Strait, and cf. Strict.]

senses.d: Strictly; rigorously.
A narrow pass or passage.
q: He brought him through a darksome narrow strait To a broad gate all built of beaten gold.
Honor travels in a strait so narrow Where one but goes abreast.

senses.d: A (comparatively) narrow passageway connecting two large bodies of water; — often in the plural; as, the strait, or straits, of Gibraltar; the straits of Magellan; the strait, or straits, of Mackinaw.
q: We steered directly through a large outlet which they call a strait, though it be fifteen miles broad.

senses.d: A neck of land; an isthmus.
q: A dark strait of barren land.

senses.d: Fig.: A condition of narrowness or restriction; doubt; distress; difficulty; poverty; perplexity; — sometimes in the plural; as, reduced to great straits.
q: For I am in a strait betwixt two.
Let no man, who owns a Providence, grow desperate under any calamity or strait whatsoever.
Ulysses made use of the pretense of natural infirmity to conceal the straits he was in at that time in his thoughts.

Strait.etym: [OE. straight, streit, OF. estreit, estroit. See Strait, a.]

senses.d: To put to difficulties.
To make strait; to make narrow; hence, to contract; to confine.
q: Waters, when straitened, as at the falls of bridges, give a roaring noise.
In narrow circuit, straitened by a foe.

senses.d: To make tense, or tight; to tighten.
q: They straiten at each end the cord.

senses.d: To restrict; to distress or embarrass in respect of means or conditions of life; — used chiefly in the past participle; — as, a man straitened in his circumstances.
In a strait manner; narrowly; strictly; rigorously.
Closely; intimately.
The quality or condition of being strait; especially, a pinched condition or situation caused by poverty; as, the straitnessof their circumstances.
A streak.
An iron band by which the fellies of a wheel are secured to each other, being not continuous, as the tire is, but made up of separate pieces.
One breadth of planks or plates forming a continuous range on the bottom or sides of a vessel, reaching from the stem to the stern; a streak.
A trough for washing broken ore, gravel, or sand; a launder.
Strong.
Belonging to another country; foreign.
q: One of the strange queen's lords.
I do not contemn the knowledge of strange and divers tongues.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to others; not one's own; not pertaining to one's self; not domestic.
q: So she, impatient her own faults to see, Turns from herself, and in strange things delights.

senses.d: Not before known, heard, or seen; new.
q: Here is the hand and seal of the duke; you know the character, I doubt not; and the signet is not strange to you.

senses.d: Not according to the common way; novel; odd; unusual; irregular; extraordinary; unnatural; queer.
q: Sated at length, erelong I might perceive Strange alteration in me.

senses.d: Reserved; distant in deportment.
q: She may be strange and shy at first, but will soon learn to love thee.

senses.d: Backward; slow.
q: Who, loving the effect, would not be strange In favoring the cause.

senses.d: Not familiar; unaccustomed; inexperienced.
q: In thy fortunes am unlearned and strange.
Strange! what extremes should thus preserve the snow High on the Alps, or in deep caves below.

Strange.syn: Foreign; new; outlandish; wonderful; astonishing; marvelous; unusual; odd; uncommon; irregular; queer; eccentric.
Strange.etym: [OE. estrange, F. étrange, fr. L. extraneus that is without, external, foreign, fr. extra on the outside. See Extra, and cf. Estrange, Extraneous.]

senses.d: Strangely.
q: Most strange, but yet most truly, will I speak.

senses.d: To alienate; to estrange.
To be estranged or alienated.
To wonder; to be astonished.
As something foreign, or not one's own; in a manner adapted to something foreign and strange.
In the manner of one who does not know another; distantly; reservedly; coldly.
q: You all look strangely on me.
I do in justice charge thee . . . That thou commend it strangely to some place Where chance may nurse or end it.

senses.d: In a strange manner; in a manner or degree to excite surprise or wonder; wonderfully.
q: How strangely active are the arts of peace!
It would strangely delight you to see with what spirit he converses.

senses.d: One who is strange, foreign, or unknown.
One who comes from a foreign land; a foreigner.
q: I am a most poor woman and a stranger, Born out of your dominions.

senses.d: One whose home is at a distance from the place where he is, but in the same country.
One who is unknown or unacquainted; as, the gentleman is a stranger to me; hence, one not admitted to communication, fellowship, or acquaintance.
q: Melons on beds of ice are taught to bear, And strangers to the sun yet ripen here.
My child is yet a stranger in the world.
I was no stranger to the original.

senses.d: One not belonging to the family or household; a guest; a visitor.
q: To honor and receive Our heavenly stranger.

senses.d: One not privy or party an act, contract, or title; a mere intruder or intermeddler; one who interferes without right; as, actual possession of land gives a good title against a stranger having no title; as to strangers, a mortgage is considered merely as a pledge; a mere stranger to the levy.
To estrange; to alienate.
To compress the windpipe of (a person or animal) until death results from stoppage of respiration; to choke to death by compressing the throat, as with the hand or a rope.
q: Our Saxon ancestors compelled the adulteress to strangle herself.

senses.d: To stifle, choke, or suffocate in any manner.
q: Shall I not then be stifled in the vault, . . . And there die strangled ere my Romeo comes?

senses.d: To hinder from appearance; to stifle; to suppress.

Strangle.etym: [OF. estrangler, F. étrangler, L. strangulare, Gr. �, �, fr. � a halter; and perhaps akin to E. string, n. Cf. Strain, String.]

senses.d: To be strangled, or suffocated.
To spread or scatter. See Strew, and Strow.
A stalk or stem of certain species of grain, pulse, etc., especially of wheat, rye, oats, barley, more rarely of buckwheat, beans, and pease.
The gathered and thrashed stalks of certain species of grain, etc.; as, a bundle, or a load, of rye straw.
Anything proverbially worthless; the least possible thing; a mere trifle.
q: I set not a straw by thy dreamings.

Straw.etym: [OE. straw, stre, stree, AS. streáw, from the root of E. strew; akin to OFries. strē, D. stroo, G. stroh, OHG. strō, Icel. strā, Dan. straa, Sw. strå. √166. See Strew.]

senses.d: Straw.

A current of water or other fluid; a liquid flowing continuously in a line or course, either on the earth, as a river, brook, etc., or from a vessel, reservoir, or fountain; specifically, any course of running water; as, many streams are blended in the Mississippi; gas and steam came from the earth in streams; a stream of molten lead from a furnace; a stream of lava from a volcano.
A beam or ray of light.
Anything issuing or moving with continued succession of parts; as, a stream of words; a stream of sand.
A continued current or course; as, a stream of weather.
Current; drift; tendency; series of tending or moving causes; as, the stream of opinions or manners.

Stream.etym: [AS. streám; akin to OFries. strām, OS. strōm, D. stroom, G. strom, OHG. stroum, strūm, Dan. & Sw. ström, Icel. straumr, Ir. sroth, Lith. srove, Russ. struia, Gr. ρὕσισ a flowing, ρεἱ̑ν to flow, Skr. sru. √174. Cf. Catarrh, Diarrhea, Rheum, Rhythm.]

senses.d: To issue or flow in a stream; to flow freely or in a current, as a fluid or whatever is likened to fluids; as, tears streamed from her eyes.
q: Beneath those banks where rivers stream.

senses.d: To pour out, or emit, a stream or streams.
q: A thousand suns will stream on thee.

senses.d: To issue in a stream of light; to radiate.
To extend; to stretch out with a wavy motion; to float in the wind; as, a flag streams in the wind.
To send forth in a current or stream; to cause to flow; to pour; as, his eyes streamed tears.
q: It may so please that she at length will stream Some dew of grace into my withered heart.

senses.d: To mark with colors or embroidery in long tracts.
q: The herald's mantle is streamed with gold.

senses.d: To unfurl.
Originally, a paved way or road; a public highway; now commonly, a thoroughfare in a city or village, bordered by dwellings or business houses.
q: He removed Amasa from the street unto the field.
At home or through the high street passing.
His deserted mansion in Duke Street.

Street.etym: [OE. strete, AS. strǣt, fr. L. strata (sc. via) a paved way, properly fem. p. p. of sternere, stratum, to spread; akin to E. strew. See Strew, and cf. Stratum, Stray, v. & a.]

senses.d: The quality or state of being strong; ability to do or to bear; capacity for exertion or endurance, whether physical, intellectual, or moral; force; vigor; power; as, strength of body or of the arm; strength of mind, of memory, or of judgment.
q: All his strength in his hairs were.
Thou must outlive Thy youth, thy strength, thy beauty.

senses.d: Power to resist force; solidity or toughness; the quality of bodies by which they endure the application of force without breaking or yielding; — in this sense opposed to frangibility; as, the strength of a bone, of a beam, of a wall, a rope, and the like.
Power of resisting attacks; impregnability.

That quality which tends to secure results; effective power in an institution or enactment; security; validity; legal or moral force; logical conclusiveness; as, the strength of social or legal obligations; the strength of law; the strength of public opinion; strength of evidence; strength of argument.
One who, or that which, is regarded as embodying or affording force, strength, or firmness; that on which confidence or reliance is based; support; security.
q: God is our refuge and strength.
What they boded would be a mischief to us, you are providing shall be one of our principal strengths.
Certainly there is not a greater strength against temptation.

senses.d: Force as measured; amount, numbers, or power of any body, as of an army, a navy, and the like; as, what is the strength of the enemy by land, or by sea?
Vigor or style; force of expression; nervous diction; — said of literary work.
q: And praise the easy vigor of a life Where Denham's strength and Waller's sweetness join.

senses.d: Intensity; — said of light or color.
q: Bright Phœbus in his strength.

senses.d: Intensity or degree of the distinguishing and essential element; spirit; virtue; excellence; — said of liquors, solutions, etc.; as, the strength of wine or of acids.
A strong place; a stronghold.

Strength.syn: Force; robustness; toughness; hardness; stoutness; brawniness; lustiness; firmness; puissance; support; spirit; validity; authority. See Force.
Strength.etym: [OE. strengthe, AS. strengðu, fr. strang strong. See Strong.]

senses.d: To strengthen.
To make strong or stronger; to add strength to; as, to strengthen a limb, a bridge, an army; to strengthen an obligation; to strengthen authority.
q: Let noble Warwick, Cobham, and the rest, . . . With powerful policy strengthen themselves.

senses.d: To animate; to encourage; to fix in resolution.
q: Charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him.

Strengthen.syn: To invigorate; confirm; establish; fortify; animate; encourage.

senses.d: To grow strong or stronger.
q: The young disease, that must subdue at length, Grows with his growth, and strengthens with his strength.

senses.d: That strengthens; giving or increasing strength.
To reach out; to extend; to put forth.
q: And stretch forth his neck long and small.
I in conquest stretched mine arm.

senses.d: To draw out to the full length; to cause to extend in a straight line; as, to stretch a cord or rope.
To cause to extend in breadth; to spread; to expand; as, to stretch cloth; to stretch the wings.
To make tense; to tighten; to distend forcibly.
q: The ox hath therefore stretched his yoke in vain.

senses.d: To draw or pull out to greater length; to strain; as, to stretch a tendon or muscle.
q: Awake, my soul, stretch every nerve.

senses.d: To exaggerate; to extend too far; as, to stretch the truth; to stretch one's credit.
q: They take up, one day, the most violent and stretched prerogative.

Stretch.etym: [OE. strecchen, AS. streccan; akin to D. strekken, G. strecken, OHG. strecchen, Sw. sträcka, Dan. strække; cf. AS. stræck, strec, strong, violent, G. strack straight; of uncertain origin, perhaps akin to E. strong. Cf. Straight.]

senses.d: To be extended; to be drawn out in length or in breadth, or both; to spread; to reach; as, the iron road stretches across the continent; the lake stretches over fifty square miles.
q: As far as stretcheth any ground.

senses.d: To extend or spread one's self, or one's limbs; as, the lazy man yawns and stretches.
To be extended, or to bear extension, without breaking, as elastic or ductile substances.
q: The inner membrane . . . because it would stretch and yield, remained umbroken.

senses.d: To strain the truth; to exaggerate; as, a man apt to stretch in his report of facts.
To sail by the wind under press of canvas; as, the ship stretched to the eastward.
Act of stretching, or state of being stretched; reach; effort; struggle; strain; as, a stretch of the limbs; a stretch of the imagination.
q: By stretch of arms the distant shore to gain.
Those put a lawful authority upon the stretch, to the abuse of yower, under the color of prerogative.

senses.d: A continuous line or surface; a continuous space of time; as, grassy stretches of land.
q: A great stretch of cultivated country.
But all of them left me a week at a stretch.

senses.d: The extent to which anything may be stretched.
q: Quotations, in their utmost stretch, can signify no more than that Luther lay under severe agonies of mind.
This is the utmost stretch that nature can.

senses.d: The reach or extent of a vessel's progress on one tack; a tack or board.
Course; direction; as, the stretch of seams of coal.
Struck; smitten; wounded; as, the stricken deer.
Worn out; far gone; advanced. See Strike, v. t., 21.
q: Abraham was old and well stricken in age.

senses.d: Whole; entire; — said of the hour as marked by the striking of a clock.
q: He persevered for a stricken hour in such a torrent of unnecessary tattle.
Speeches are spoken by the stricken hour, day after day, week, perhaps, after week.

senses.d: The act of striving; earnest endeavor.
Exertion or contention for superiority; contest of emulation, either by intellectual or physical efforts.
q: Doting about questions and strifes of words.
Thus gods contended — noble strife - Who most should ease the wants of life.

senses.d: Altercation; violent contention; fight; battle.
q: Twenty of them fought in this black strife.
These vows, thus granted, raised a strife above Betwixt the god of war and queen of love.

senses.d: That which is contended against; occasion of contest.
To touch or hit with some force, either with the hand or with an instrument; to smite; to give a blow to, either with the hand or with any instrument or missile.
q: He at Philippi kept His sword e'en like a dancer; while I struck The lean and wrinkled Cassius.

senses.d: To come in collision with; to strike against; as, a bullet struck him; the wave struck the boat amidships; the ship struck a reef.
To give, as a blow; to impel, as with a blow; to give a force to; to dash; to cast.
q: They shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two sideposts.
Who would be free, themselves must strike the blow.

senses.d: To stamp or impress with a stroke; to coin; as, to strike coin from metal: to strike dollars at the mint.
To thrust in; to cause to enter or penetrate; to set in the earth; as, a tree strikes its roots deep.
To punish; to afflict; to smite.
q: To punish the just is not good, nor strike princes for equity.

senses.d: To cause to sound by one or more beats; to indicate or notify by audible strokes; as, the clock strikes twelve; the drums strike up a march.

To lower; to let or take down; to remove; as, to strike sail; to strike a flag or an ensign, as in token of surrender; to strike a yard or a topmast in a gale; to strike a tent; to strike the centering of an arch.
To make a sudden impression upon, as by a blow; to affect sensibly with some strong emotion; as, to strike the mind, with surprise; to strike one with wonder, alarm, dread, or horror.
q: Nice works of art strike and surprise us most on the first view.
They please as beauties, here as wonders strike.

senses.d: To affect in some particular manner by a sudden impression or impulse; as, the plan proposed strikes me favorably; to strike one dead or blind.
q: How often has stricken you dumb with his irony!

senses.d: To cause or produce by a stroke, or suddenly, as by a stroke; as, to strike a light.
q: Waving wide her myrtle wand, She strikes a universal peace through sea and land.

senses.d: To cause to ignite; as, to strike a match.

Strike.etym: [OE. striken to strike, proceed, flow, AS. strīcan to go, proceed, akin to D. strijken to rub, stroke, strike, to move, go, G. streichen, OHG. strīhhan, L. stringere to touch lightly, to graze, to strip off (but perhaps not to L. stringere in sense to draw tight), striga a row, a furrow. Cf. Streak,

senses.d: To move; to advance; to proceed; to take a course; as, to strike into the fields.
q: A mouse . . . struck forth sternly .

senses.d: To deliver a quick blow or thrust; to give blows.
q: And fiercely took his trenchant blade in hand, With which he stroke so furious and so fell.
Strike now, or else the iron cools.

senses.d: To hit; to collide; to dush; to clash; as, a hammer strikes against the bell of a clock.
To sound by percussion, with blows, or as with blows; to be struck; as, the clock strikes.
q: A deep sound strikes like a rising knell.

senses.d: To make an attack; to aim a blow.
q: A puny subject strikes At thy great glory.
Struck for throne, and striking found his doom.

senses.d: To touch; to act by appulse.
q: Hinder light but from striking on it , and its colors vanish.

senses.d: To run upon a rock or bank; to be stranded; as, the ship struck in the night.
To pass with a quick or strong effect; to dart; to penetrate.
q: Till a dart strike through his liver.
Now and then a glittering beam of wit or passion strikes through the obscurity of the poem.

senses.d: To break forth; to commence suddenly; — with into; as, to strike into reputation; to strike into a run.
To lower a flag, or colors, in token of respect, or to signify a surrender of a ship to an enemy.
q: That the English ships of war should not strike in the Danish seas.

senses.d: To quit work in order to compel an increase, or prevent a reduction, of wages.
To become attached to something; — said of the spat of oysters.
The act of striking.
An instrument with a straight edge for leveling a measure of grain, salt, and the like, scraping off what is above the level of the top; a strickle.
A bushel; four pecks.
An old measure of four bushels.
Fullness of measure; hence, excellence of quality.
q: Three hogsheads of ale of the first strike.

senses.d: An iron pale or standard in a gate or fence.
The act of quitting work; specifically, such an act by a body of workmen, done as a means of enforcing compliance with demands made on their employer.
q: Strikes are the insurrections of labor.

senses.d: A puddler's stirrer.
The horizontal direction of the outcropping edges of tilted rocks; or, the direction of a horizontal line supposed to be drawn on the surface of a tilted stratum. It is at right angles to the dip.
The extortion of money, or the attempt to extort money, by threat of injury; blackmailing.
A sudden finding of rich ore in mining; hence, any sudden success or good fortune, esp. financial.
Act of leveling all the pins with the first bowl; also, the score thus made. Sometimes called double spare.

Any actual or constructive striking at the pitched ball, three of which, if the ball is not hit fairly, cause the batter to be put out; hence, any of various acts or events which are ruled as equivalent to such a striking, as failing to strike at a ball so pitched that the batter should have struck at it.
Same as Ten-strike.
One who, or that which, strikes; specifically, a blacksmith's helper who wields the sledge.
A harpoon; also, a harpooner.
q: Wherever we come to an anchor, we always send out our strikers, and put out hooks and lines overboard, to try fish.

senses.d: A wencher; a lewd man.
A workman who is on a strike.
A blackmailer in politics; also, one whose political influence can be bought.

A small cord, a line, a twine, or a slender strip of leather, or other substance, used for binding together, fastening, or tying things; a cord, larger than a thread and smaller than a rope; as, a shoe string; a bonnet string; a silken string.
q: Round Ormond's knee thou tiest the mystic string.

senses.d: A thread or cord on which a number of objects or parts are strung or arranged in close and orderly succession; hence, a line or series of things arranged on a thread, or as if so arranged; a succession; a concatenation; a chain; as, a string of shells or beads; a string of dried apples; a string of houses; a string of arguments.
A strip, as of leather, by which the covers of a book are held together.

The cord of a musical instrument, as of a piano, harp, or violin; specifically (pl.), the stringed instruments of an orchestra, in distinction from the wind instruments; as, the strings took up the theme.
q: Me softer airs befit, and softer strings Of lute, or viol still.

senses.d: The line or cord of a bow.
q: He twangs the grieving string.

senses.d: A fiber, as of a plant; a little, fibrous root.
q: Duckweed putteth forth a little string into the water, from the bottom.

senses.d: A nerve or tendon of an animal body.
q: The string of his tongue was loosed.

senses.d: An inside range of ceiling planks, corresponding to the sheer strake on the outside and bolted to it.
The tough fibrous substance that unites the valves of the pericap of leguminous plants, and which is readily pulled off; as, the strings of beans.
A small, filamentous ramification of a metallic vein.
Same as Stringcourse.
The points made in a game.

String.etym: [OE. string, streng, AS. streng; akin to D. streng, G. strang, Icel. strengr, Sw. sträng, Dan. stræng; probably from the adj., E. strong (see Strong); or perhaps originally meaning, twisted, and akin to E. strangle.]

senses.d: To furnish with strings; as, to string a violin.
q: Has not wise nature strung the legs and feet With firmest nerves, designed to walk the street?

senses.d: To put in tune the strings of, as a stringed instrument, in order to play upon it.
q: For here the Muse so oft her harp has strung, That not a mountain rears its head unsung.

senses.d: To put on a string; to file; as, to string beads.
To make tense; to strengthen.
q: Toil strung the nerves, and purified the blood.

senses.d: To deprive of strings; to strip the strings from; as, to string beans. See String, n., 9.
In various indoor games, a score or tally, sometimes, as in American billiard games, marked by buttons threaded on a string or wire.
The line from behind and over which the cue ball must be played after being out of play as by being pocketed or knocked off the table; — called also string line.
A hoax; a trumped-up or “fake” story.
To hoax; josh; jolly.
To form into a string or strings, as a substance which is stretched, or people who are moving along, etc.
Having strings; as, a stringed instrument.
Produced by strings.

To deprive; to bereave; to make destitute; to plunder; especially, to deprive of a covering; to skin; to peel; as, to strip a man of his possession, his rights, his privileges, his reputation; to strip one of his clothes; to strip a beast of his skin; to strip a tree of its bark.
q: And strippen her out of her rude array.
They stripped Joseph out of his coat.
Opinions which . . . no clergyman could have avowed without imminent risk of being stripped of his gown.

senses.d: To divest of clothing; to uncover.
q: Before the folk herself strippeth she.
Strip your sword stark naked.

senses.d: To dismantle; as, to strip a ship of rigging, spars, etc.
To pare off the surface of, as land, in strips.
To deprive of all milk; to milk dry; to draw the last milk from; hence, to milk with a peculiar movement of the hand on the teats at the last of a milking; as, to strip a cow.
To pass; to get clear of; to outstrip.
q: When first they stripped the Malean promontory.
Before he reached it he was out of breath, And then the other stripped him.

senses.d: To pull or tear off, as a covering; to remove; to wrest away; as, to strip the skin from a beast; to strip the bark from a tree; to strip the clothes from a man's back; to strip away all disguisses.
q: To strip bad habits from a corrupted heart, is stripping off the skin.

senses.d: To tear off (the thread) from a bolt or nut; as, the thread is stripped.
To remove the metal coating from (a plated article), as by acids or electrolytic action.
To remove fiber, flock, or lint from; — said of the teeth of a card when it becomes partly clogged.
To pick the cured leaves from the stalks of (tobacco) and tie them into “hands”; to remove the midrib from (tobacco leaves).

Strip.etym: [OE. stripen, strepen, AS. str�pan in bestr�pan to plunder; akin to D. stroopen, MHG. stroufen, G. streifen.]

senses.d: To take off, or become divested of, clothes or covering; to undress.
To fail in the thread; to lose the thread, as a bolt, screw, or nut. See Strip, v. t., 8.
A narrow piece, or one comparatively long; as, a strip of cloth; a strip of land.
A trough for washing ore.
The issuing of a projectile from a rifled gun without acquiring the spiral motion.

A line, or long, narrow division of anything of a different color or structure from the ground; hence, any linear variation of color or structure; as, a stripe, or streak, of red on a green ground; a raised stripe.
A pattern produced by arranging the warp threads in sets of alternating colors, or in sets presenting some other contrast of appearance.
A strip, or long, narrow piece attached to something of a different color; as, a red or blue stripe sewed upon a garment.
A stroke or blow made with a whip, rod, scourge, or the like, such as usually leaves a mark.
q: Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed.

senses.d: A long, narrow discoloration of the skin made by the blow of a lash, rod, or the like.
q: Cruelty marked him with inglorious stripes.

senses.d: Color indicating a party or faction; hence, distinguishing characteristic; sign; likeness; sort; as, persons of the same political stripe.
The chevron on the coat of a noncommissioned officer.

Stripe.etym: [OD. strijpe a stripe, streak; akin to LG. stripe, D. streep, Dan. stribe, G. strief, striefen, MHG. striefen to glide, march.]

senses.d: To make stripes upon; to form with lines of different colors or textures; to variegate with stripes.
To strike; to lash.
A youth in the state of adolescence, or just passing from boyhood to manhood; a lad.
q: Inquire thou whose son the stripling is.

Stripling.etym: [Dim. of strip; as if a small strip from the main stock or steam.]

senses.d: To make efforts; to use exertions; to endeavor with earnestness; to labor hard.
q: Was for this his ambition strove To equal Cæsar first, and after, Jove?

senses.d: To struggle in opposition; to be in contention or dispute; to contend; to contest; — followed by against or with before the person or thing opposed; as, strive against temptation; strive for the truth.
q: My Spirit shall not always strive with man.
Why dost thou strive against him?
Now private pity strove with public hate, Reason with rage, and eloquence with fate.

senses.d: To vie; to compete; to be a rival.
q: that sweet grove Of Daphne, by Orontes and the inspired Castalian spring, might with this paradise Of Eden strive.

Strive.syn: To contend; vie; struggle; endeavor; aim.
Strive.etym: [OF. estriver; of Teutonic origin, and akin to G. streben, D. streven, Dan. stræbe, Sw. sträfva. Cf. Strife.]

senses.d: An effort; a striving.
Strife; contention.
Striven.
