q: Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel.

senses.d: Struck.
The act of striking; a blow; a hit; a knock; esp., a violent or hostile attack made with the arm or hand, or with an instrument or weapon.
q: His hand fetcheth a stroke with the ax to cut down the tree.
A fool's lips enter into contention and his mouth calleth for strokes.
He entered and won the whole kingdom of Naples without striking a stroke.

senses.d: The result of effect of a striking; injury or affliction; soreness.
q: In the day that Lord bindeth up the breach of his people, and healeth the stroke of their wound.

senses.d: The striking of the clock to tell the hour.
q: Well, but what's o'clock? - Upon the stroke of ten. — Well, let is strike.

senses.d: A gentle, caressing touch or movement upon something; a stroking.
A mark or dash in writing or printing; a line; the touch of a pen or pencil; as, an up stroke; a firm stroke.
q: O, lasting as those colors may they shine, Free as thy stroke, yet faultless as thy line.

senses.d: Hence, by extension, an addition or amandment to a written composition; a touch; as, to give some finishing strokes to an essay.
A sudden attack of disease; especially, a fatal attack; a severe disaster; any affliction or calamity, especially a sudden one; as, a stroke of apoplexy; the stroke of death.
q: At this one stroke the man looked dead in law.

senses.d: A throb or beat, as of the heart.

One of a series of beats or movements against a resisting medium, by means of which movement through or upon it is accomplished; as, the stroke of a bird's wing in flying, or an oar in rowing, of a skater, swimmer, etc.

A powerful or sudden effort by which something is done, produced, or accomplished; also, something done or accomplished by such an effort; as, a stroke of genius; a stroke of business; a master stroke of policy.

The movement, in either direction, of the piston plunger, piston rod, crosshead, etc., as of a steam engine or a pump, in which these parts have a reciprocating motion; as, the forward stroke of a piston; also, the entire distance passed through, as by a piston, in such a movement; as, the piston is at half stroke.
Power; influence.
q: He has a great stroke with the reader.

Stroke.etym: [OE. strok, strook, strak, fr. striken. See Strike, v. t.]

senses.d: To strike.
q: Ye mote with the plat sword again Stroken him in the wound, and it will close.

senses.d: To rib gently in one direction; especially, to pass the hand gently over by way of expressing kindness or tenderness; to caress; to soothe.
q: He dried the falling drops, and, yet more kind, He stroked her cheeks.

senses.d: To make smooth by rubbing.
To give a finely fluted surface to.
To row the stroke oar of; as, to stroke a boat.

Stroke.etym: [OE. stroken, straken, AS. strācian, fr. strīcan to go over, pass. See Strike, v. t., and cf. Straggle.]

senses.d: Having active physical power, or great physical power to act; having a power of exerting great bodily force; vigorous.
q: That our oxen may be strong to labor.
Orses the strong to greater strength must yield.

senses.d: Having passive physical power; having ability to bear or endure; firm; hale; sound; robust; as, a strong constitution; strong health.
Solid; tough; not easily broken or injured; able to withstand violence; able to sustain attacks; not easily subdued or taken; as, a strong beam; a strong rock; a strong fortress or town.
Having great military or naval force; powerful; as, a strong army or fleet; a nation strong at sea.
Having great wealth, means, or resources; as, a strong house, or company of merchants.
Reaching a certain degree or limit in respect to strength or numbers; as, an army ten thousand strong.
Moving with rapidity or force; violent; forcible; impetuous; as, a strong current of water or wind; the wind was strong from the northeast; a strong tide.

Adapted to make a deep or effectual impression on the mind or imagination; striking or superior of the kind; powerful; forcible; cogent; as, a strong argument; strong reasons; strong evidence; a strong example; strong language.
Ardent; eager; zealous; earnestly engaged; as, a strong partisan; a strong Whig or Tory.
q: Her mother, ever strong against that match.

senses.d: Having virtues of great efficacy; or, having a particular quality in a great degree; as, a strong powder or tincture; a strong decoction; strong tea or coffee.
Full of spirit; containing a large proportion of alcohol; intoxicating; as, strong liquors.
Affecting any sense powerfully; as, strong light, colors, etc.; a strong flavor of onions; a strong scent.

Strong.syn: Vigorous; powerful; stout; solid; firm; hardy; muscular; forcible; cogent; valid. See Robust.
Strong.etym: [AS. strang, strong; akin to D. & G. streng strict, rigorous, OHG. strengi strong, brave, harsh, Icel. strangr strong, severe, Dan. streng, Sw. sträng strict, severe. Cf. Strength, Stretch, String.]

senses.d: In a strong manner; so as to be strong in action or in resistance; with strength; with great force; forcibly; powerfully; firmly; vehemently; as, a town strongly fortified; he objected strongly.
Same as Strew.
q: Thick as autumnal leaves that strow the brooks In Vallombrosa.
A manner turbid . . . and strown with blemished.

senses.d: To strive, or to make efforts, with a twisting, or with contortions of the body.
To use great efforts; to labor hard; to strive; to contend forcibly; as, to struggle to save one's life; to struggle with the waves; to struggle with adversity.
q: The brave men, living and dead, who struggled here, have consecrated it far above our power to add or detract.

senses.d: To labor in pain or anguish; to be in agony; to labor in any kind of difficulty or distress.
q: 'T is wisdom to beware, And better shun the bait than struggle in the snare.

Struggle.etym: [OE. strogelen; cf. Icel. strj�ka to stroke, to beat, to flog, Sw. stryka to stroke, to strike, Dan. stryge, G. straucheln to stumble. Cf. Stroll.]

senses.d: A violent effort or efforts with contortions of the body; agony; distress.
Great labor; forcible effort to obtain an object, or to avert an evil.
Contest; contention; strife.
q: An honest might look upon the struggle with indifference.

senses.d: The stumps of wheat, rye, barley, oats, or buckwheat, left in the ground; the part of the stalk left by the scythe or sickle.

Stubble.etym: [OE. stobil, stoble, OF. estouble, estuble, F. étuele, LL. stupla, stupula, L. stipula stubble, stalk; cf. D. & G. stopped, OHG. stupfila. Cf. Stipule.]

senses.d: Firm as a stub or stump; stiff; unbending; unyielding; persistent; hence, unreasonably obstinate in will or opinion; not yielding to reason or persuasion; refractory; harsh; — said of persons and things; as, stubborn wills; stubborn ore; a stubborn oak; as stubborn as a mule.
q: And I was young and full of ragerie Stubborn and strong, and jolly as a pie.
These heretics be so stiff and stubborn.
Your stubborn usage of the pope.

Stubborn.syn: Obstinate; inflexible; obdurate; headstrong; stiff; hardy; firm; refractory; intractable; rugged; contumacious; heady.
Stubborn.etym: [OE. stoburn, stiborn; probably fr. AS. styb a stub. See Stub.]

senses.d: A thrust.
A collection of breeding horses and mares, or the place where they are kept; also, a number of horses kept for a racing, riding, etc.
q: In the studs of Ireland, where care is taken, we see horses bred of excellent shape, vigor, and size.
He had the finest stud in England, and his delight was to win plates from Tories.

Stud.etym: [OE. stod, stood, AS. stōd; akin to OHG. stuota, G. stute a mare, Icel. stō� stud, Lith. stodas a herd, Russ. stado, and to E. stand. The sense is properly, a stand, an establishment. √163. See Stand, and cf. Steed.]

senses.d: A stem; a trunk.
q: Seest not this same hawthorn stud?

senses.d: An upright scanting, esp. one of the small uprights in the framing for lath and plaster partitions, and furring, and upon which the laths are nailed.
A kind of nail with a large head, used chiefly for ornament; an ornamental knob; a boss.
q: A belt of straw and ivy buds, With coral clasps and amber studs.
Crystal and myrrhine cups, embossed with gems And studs of pearl.

senses.d: An ornamental button of various forms, worn in a shirt front, collar, wristband, or the like, not sewed in place, but inserted through a buttonhole or eyelet, and transferable.
A short rod or pin, fixed in and projecting from something, and sometimes forming a journal.
An iron brace across the shorter diameter of the link of a chain cable.

Stud.etym: [AS. studu a post; akin to Sw. stöd a prop, Icel. sto� a post, sty�ja to prop, and probably ultimately to E. stand; cf. D. stut a prop, G. stütze. See Stand.]

senses.d: To adorn with shining studs, or knobs.
q: Thy horses shall be trapped, Their harness studded all with gold and pearl.

senses.d: To set with detached ornaments or prominent objects; to set thickly, as with studs.
q: The sloping sides and summits of our hills, and the extensive plains that stretch before our view, are studded with substantial, neat, and commodious dwellings of freemen.

senses.d: A setting of the mind or thoughts upon a subject; hence, application of mind to books, arts, or science, or to any subject, for the purpose of acquiring knowledge.
q: Hammond . . . spent thirteen hours of the day in study.
Study gives strength to the mind; conversation, grace.

senses.d: Mental occupation; absorbed or thoughtful attention; meditation; contemplation.
q: Just men they seemed, and all their study bent To worship God aright, and know his works.

senses.d: Any particular branch of learning that is studied; any object of attentive consideration.
q: The Holy Scriptures, especially the New Testament, are her daily study.
The proper study of mankind is man.

senses.d: A building or apartment devoted to study or to literary work.

A representation or rendering of any object or scene intended, not for exhibition as an original work of art, but for the information, instruction, or assistance of the maker; as, a study of heads or of hands for a figure picture.
A piece for special practice. See Etude.

Study.etym: [OE. studie, L. studium, akin to studere to study; possibly akin to Gr. � haste, zeal, � to hasten; cf. OF. estudie, estude, F. étude. Cf. Etude, Student, Studio, Study, v. i.]

senses.d: To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to dwell upon anything in thought; to muse; to ponder.
q: I found a moral first, and then studied for a fable.

senses.d: To apply the mind to books or learning.
To endeavor diligently; to be zealous.

Study.etym: [OE. studien, OF. estudier, F. étudier. See Study, n.]

senses.d: To apply the mind to; to read and examine for the purpose of learning and understanding; as, to study law or theology; to study languages.
To consider attentively; to examine closely; as, to study the work of nature.
q: Study thyself; what rank or what degree The wise Creator has ordained for thee.

senses.d: To form or arrange by previous thought; to con over, as in committing to memory; as, to study a speech.
To make an object of study; to aim at sedulously; to devote one's thoughts to; as, to study the welfare of others; to study variety in composition.
q: For their heart studieth destruction.

senses.d: Material which is to be worked up in any process of manufacture.
q: For the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much.
Ambitions should be made of sterner stuff.
The workman on his stuff his skill doth show, And yet the stuff gives not the man his skill.

senses.d: The fundamental material of which anything is made up; elemental part; essence.
q: Yet do I hold it very stuff o' the conscience To do no contrived murder.

senses.d: Woven material not made into garments; fabric of any kind; specifically, any one of various fabrics of wool or worsted; sometimes, worsted fiber.
q: What stuff wilt have a kirtle of?
It was of stuff and silk mixed, though, superior kinds were of silk exclusively.

senses.d: Furniture; goods; domestic vessels or utensils.
q: He took away locks, and gave away the king's stuff.

senses.d: A medicine or mixture; a potion.
Refuse or worthless matter; hence, also, foolish or irrational language; nonsense; trash.
q: Anger would indite Such woeful stuff as I or Shadwell write.

senses.d: A melted mass of turpentine, tallow, etc., with which the masts, sides, and bottom of a ship are smeared for lubrication.
Paper stock ground ready for use.

Stuff.etym: [OF. estoffe, F. étoffe; of uncertain origin, perhaps of Teutonic origin and akin to E. stop, v.t. Cf. Stuff, v. t.]

senses.d: To fill by crowding something into; to cram with something; to load to excess; as, to stuff a bedtick.
q: Sometimes this crook drew hazel bought adown, And stuffed her apron wide with nuts so brown.
Lest the gods, for sin, Should with a swelling dropsy stuff thy skin.

senses.d: To thrust or crowd; to press; to pack.
q: Put roses into a glass with a narrow mouth, stuffing them close together . . . and they retain smell and color.

senses.d: To fill by being pressed or packed into.
q: With inward arms the dire machine they load, And iron bowels stuff the dark abode.

senses.d: To fill with a seasoning composition of bread, meat, condiments, etc.; as, to stuff a turkey.
To obstruct, as any of the organs; to affect with some obstruction in the organs of sense or respiration.
q: I'm stuffed, cousin; I can not smell.

senses.d: To fill the skin of, for the purpose of preserving as a specimen; — said of birds or other animals.
To form or fashion by packing with the necessary material.
q: An Eastern king put a judge to death for an iniquitous sentence, and ordered his hide to be stuffed into a cushion, and placed upon the tribunal.

senses.d: To crowd with facts; to cram the mind of; sometimes, to crowd or fill with false or idle tales or fancies.
To put fraudulent votes into (a ballot box).

Stuff.etym: [OE. stoffen; cf. OF. estoffer, F. étoffer, to put stuff in, to stuff, to line, also, OF. estouffer to stifle, F. étouffer; both perhaps of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. stop. Cf. Stop, v. t., Stuff, n.]

senses.d: To feed gluttonously; to cram.
q: Taught harmless man to cram and stuff.

senses.d: To trip in walking or in moving in any way with the legs; to strike the foot so as to fall, or to endanger a fall; to stagger because of a false step.
q: There stumble steeds strong and down go all.
The way of the wicked is as darkness: they know at what they stumble.

senses.d: To walk in an unsteady or clumsy manner.
q: He stumbled up the dark avenue.

senses.d: To fall into a crime or an error; to err.
q: He that loveth his brother abideth in the light, and there is none occasion og stumbling in him.

senses.d: To strike or happen (upon a person or thing) without design; to fall or light by chance; — with on, upon, or against.
q: Ovid stumbled, by some inadvertency, upon Livia in a bath.
Forth as she waddled in the brake, A gray goose stumbled on a snake.

Stumble.etym: [OE. stumblen, stomblen; freq. of a word akin to E. stammer. See Stammer.]

senses.d: To cause to stumble or trip.
Fig.: To mislead; to confound; to perplex; to cause to err or to fall.
q: False and dazzling fires to stumble men.
One thing more stumbles me in the very foundation of this hypothesis.

senses.d: A trip in walking or running.
A blunder; a failure; a fall from rectitude.
q: One stumble is enough to deface the character of an honorable life.

senses.d: The part of a tree or plant remaining in the earth after the stem or trunk is cut off; the stub.
The part of a limb or other body remaining after a part is amputated or destroyed; a fixed or rooted remnant; a stub; as, the stump of a leg, a finger, a tooth, or a broom.
The legs; as, to stir one's stumps.
One of the three pointed rods stuck in the ground to form a wicket and support the bails.

A short, thick roll of leather or paper, cut to a point, or any similar implement, used to rub down the lines of a crayon or pencil drawing, in shading it, or for shading drawings by producing tints and gradations from crayon, etc., in powder.

A pin in a tumbler lock which forms an obstruction to throwing the bolt, except when the gates of the tumblers are properly arranged, as by the key; a fence; also, a pin or projection in a lock to form a guide for a movable piece.

Stump.etym: [OE. stumpe, stompe; akin to D. stomp, G. stumpf, Icel. stumpr, Dan. & Sw. stump, and perhaps also to E. stamp.]

senses.d: To cut off a part of; to reduce to a stump; to lop.
q: Around the stumped top soft moss did grow.

senses.d: To strike, as the toes, against a stone or something fixed; to stub.
To challenge; also, to nonplus.
To travel over, delivering speeches for electioneering purposes; as, to stump a State, or a district. See To go on the stump, under Stump, n.
To put (a batsman) out of play by knocking off the bail, or knocking down the stumps of the wicket he is defending while he is off his allotted ground; — sometimes with out.
q: A herd of boys with clamor bowled, And stumped the wicket.

senses.d: To walk clumsily, as if on stumps.
To bring under; to conquer by force or the exertion of superior power, and bring into permanent subjection; to reduce under dominion; to vanquish.
q: I will subdue all thine enemies.

senses.d: To overpower so as to disable from further resistance; to crush.
q: Nothing could have subdued nature To such a lowness, but his unkind daughters.
If aught . . . were worthy to subdue The soul of man.

senses.d: To destroy the force of; to overcome; as, medicines subdue a fever.
To render submissive; to bring under command; to reduce to mildness or obedience; to tame; as, to subdue a stubborn child; to subdue the temper or passions.
To overcome, as by persuasion or other mild means; as, to subdue opposition by argument or entreaties.
To reduce to tenderness; to melt; to soften; as, to subdue ferocity by tears.
To make mellow; to break, as land; also, to destroy, as weeds.
To reduce the intensity or degree of; to tone down; to soften; as, to subdue the brilliancy of colors.

Subdue.syn: To conquer; overpower; overcome; surmount; vanquish. See Conquer.
Subdue.etym: [OE. soduen, OF. sosduire to seduce, L. subtus below (fr. sub under) + ducere to lead. See Duke, and cf. Subduct.]

senses.d: Conquered; overpowered; crushed; submissive; mild.
Not glaring in color; soft in tone.
Placed or situated under; lying below, or in a lower situation.
Placed under the power of another; specifically (International Law), owing allegiance to a particular sovereign or state; as, Jamaica is subject to Great Britain.
q: Esau was never subject to Jacob.

senses.d: Exposed; liable; prone; disposed; as, a country subject to extreme heat; men subject to temptation.
q: All human things are subject to decay.

senses.d: Obedient; submissive.
q: Put them in mind to be subject to principalities.

Subject.syn: Liable; subordinate; inferior; obnoxious; exposed. See Liable.
Subject.etym: [OE. suget, OF. souzget, sougit (in which the first part is L. subtus below, fr. sub under), subgiet, subject, F. sujet, from L. subjectus lying under, subjected, p. p. of subjicere, subicere, to throw, lay, place, or bring under; sub under + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.]

senses.d: That which is placed under the authority, dominion, control, or influence of something else.

Specifically: One who is under the authority of a ruler and is governed by his laws; one who owes allegiance to a sovereign or a sovereign state; as, a subject of Queen Victoria; a British subject; a subject of the United States.
q: Was never subject longed to be a king, As I do long and wish to be a subject.
The subject must obey his prince, because God commands it, human laws require it.

senses.d: That which is subjected, or submitted to, any physical operation or process; specifically (Anat.), a dead body used for the purpose of dissection.
That which is brought under thought or examination; that which is taken up for discussion, or concerning which anything is said or done.
q: Make choice of a subject, beautiful and noble, which . . . shall afford an ample field of matter wherein to expatiate.
The unhappy subject of these quarrels.

senses.d: The person who is treated of; the hero of a piece; the chief character.
q: Writers of particular lives . . . are apt to be prejudiced in favor of their subject.

senses.d: That of which anything is affirmed or predicated; the theme of a proposition or discourse; that which is spoken of; as, the nominative case is the subject of the verb.
q: The subject of a proposition is that concerning which anything is affirmed or denied.

senses.d: That in which any quality, attribute, or relation, whether spiritual or material, inheres, or to which any of these appertain; substance; substratum.
q: That which manifests its qualities — in other words, that in which the appearing causes inhere, that to which they belong — is called their subject or substance, or substratum.

senses.d: Hence, that substance or being which is conscious of its own operations; the mind; the thinking agent or principal; the ego. Cf. Object, n., 2.
q: The philosophers of mind have, in a manner, usurped and appropriated this expression to themselves. Accordingly, in their hands, the phrases conscious or thinking subject, and subject, mean precisely the same thing.

senses.d: The principal theme, or leading thought or phrase, on which a composition or a movement is based.
q: The earliest known form of subject is the ecclesiastical cantus firmus, or plain song.

senses.d: The incident, scene, figure, group, etc., which it is the aim of the artist to represent.

Subject.etym: [From L. subjectus, through an old form of F. sujet. See Subject, a.]

senses.d: To bring under control, power, or dominion; to make subject; to subordinate; to subdue.
q: Firmness of mind that subjects every gratification of sense to the rule of right reason.
In one short view subjected to our eye, Gods, emperors, heroes, sages, beauties, lie.
He is the most subjected, the most �nslaved, who is so in his understanding.

senses.d: To expose; to make obnoxious or liable; as, credulity subjects a person to impositions.
To submit; to make accountable.
q: God is not bound to subject his ways of operation to the scrutiny of our thoughts.

senses.d: To make subservient.
q: Subjected to his service angel wings.

senses.d: To cause to undergo; as, to subject a substance to a white heat; to subject a person to a rigid test.
Subjacent.
Reduced to subjection; brought under the dominion of another.
Exposed; liable; subject; obnoxious.
The act of subjecting, or of bringing under the dominion of another; the act of subduing.
q: The conquest of the kingdom, and subjection of the rebels.

senses.d: The state of being subject, or under the power, control, and government of another; a state of obedience or submissiveness; as, the safety of life, liberty, and property depends on our subjection to the laws.
q: Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands.

Because the subjection of the body to the will is by natural necessity, the subjection of the will unto God voluntary, we stand in need of direction after what sort our wills and desires may be rightly conformed to His.

Subjection.etym: [L. subjectio: cf. OF. subjection, F. subjétion. See Subject, a.]

senses.d: To let down; to lower.
q: Sometimes the hill submits itself a while.

senses.d: To put or place under.
q: The bristled throat Of the submitted sacrifice with ruthless steel he cut.

senses.d: To yield, resign, or surrender to power, will, or authority; — often with the reflexive pronoun.
q: Ye ben submitted through your free assent.
The angel of the Lord said unto her, Return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands.
Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands.

senses.d: To leave or commit to the discretion or judgment of another or others; to refer; as, to submit a controversy to arbitrators; to submit a question to the court; — often followed by a dependent proposition as the object.
q: Whether the condition of the clergy be able to bear a heavy burden, is submitted to the house.
We submit that a wooden spoon of our day would not be justified in calling Galileo and Napier blockheads because they never heard of the differential calculus.

Submit.etym: [L. submittere; sub under + mittere to send: cf. F. soumettre. See Missile.]

senses.d: To yield one's person to the power of another; to give up resistance; to surrender.
q: The revolted provinces presently submitted.

senses.d: To yield one's opinion to the opinion of authority of another; to be subject; to acquiesce.
q: To thy husband's will Thine shall submit.

senses.d: To be submissive or resigned; to yield without murmuring.
q: Our religion requires from us . . . to submit to pain, disgrace, and even death.

senses.d: To procure or cause to take a false oath amounting to perjury, such oath being actually taken.
To procure privately, or by collusion; to procure by indirect means; to incite secretly; to instigate.
q: Thou art suborned against his honor.
Those who by despair suborn their death.

Suborn.etym: [F. suborner, L. subornare; sub under, secretly + ornare to furnish, provide, equip, adorn. See Ornament.]

senses.d: To write underneath, as one's name; to sign (one's name) to a document.
q: subscribed their names under them.

senses.d: To sign with one's own hand; to give consent to, as something written, or to bind one's self to the terms of, by writing one's name beneath; as, parties subscribe a covenant or contract; a man subscribes a bond.
q: All the bishops subscribed the sentence.

senses.d: To attest by writing one's name beneath; as, officers subscribe their official acts, and secretaries and clerks subscribe copies or records.
To promise to give, by writing one's name with the amount; as, each man subscribed ten dollars.
To sign away; to yield; to surrender.
To declare over one's signature; to publish.
q: Either or must shortly hear from him, or I will subscribe him a coward.

Subscribe.etym: [L. subscribere, subscriptum; sub under + scribere to write: cf. F. souscrire. See Scribe.]

senses.d: To sign one's name to a letter or other document.
To give consent to something written, by signing one's name; hence, to assent; to agree.
q: So spake, so wished, much humbled Eve; but Fate Subscribed not.

senses.d: To become surely; — with for.
To yield; to admit one's self to be inferior or in the wrong.
q: I will subscribe, and say I wronged the duke.

senses.d: To set one's name to a paper in token of promise to give a certain sum.
To enter one's name for a newspaper, a book, etc.

That which underlies all outward manifestations; substratum; the permanent subject or cause of phenomena, whether material or spiritual; that in which properties inhere; that which is real, in distinction from that which is apparent; the abiding part of any existence, in distinction from any accident; that which constitutes anything what it is; real or existing essence.
q: These cooks, how they stamp, and strain, and grind, And turn substance into accident!
Heroic virtue did his actions guide, And he the substance, not the appearance, chose.

senses.d: The most important element in any existence; the characteristic and essential components of anything; the main part; essential import; purport.
q: This edition is the same in substance with the Latin.
It is insolent in words, in manner; but in substance it is not only insulting, but alarming.

senses.d: Body; matter; material of which a thing is made; hence, substantiality; solidity; firmness; as, the substance of which a garment is made; some textile fabrics have little substance.
Material possessions; estate; property; resources.
q: And there wasted his substance with riotous living.
Thy substance, valued at the highest rate, Can not amount unto a hundred marks.
We are destroying many thousand lives, and exhausting our substance, but not for our own interest.

senses.d: Same as Hypostasis, 2.

Substance.etym: [F., fr. L. substantia, fr. substare to be under or present, to stand firm; sub under + stare to stand. See Stand.]

senses.d: To furnish or endow with substance; to supply property to; to make rich.
The quality or state of being subtile; thinness; fineness; as, the subtility of air or light.
Refinement; extreme acuteness; subtlety.
q: Intelligible discourses are spoiled by too much subtility in nice divisions.

senses.d: Cunning; skill; craft.
q: To learn a lewd man this subtility.

senses.d: Slyness in design; artifice; guile; a cunning design or artifice; a trick; subtlety.
q: O full of all subtility and all mischief.

senses.d: An outlying part of a city or town; a smaller place immediately adjacent to a city; in the plural, the region which is on the confines of any city or large town; as, a house stands in the suburbs; a garden situated in the suburbs of Paris.
q: could hardly have contained less than thirty or forty thousand souls within its walls; and the suburbs were very populous.

senses.d: Hence, the confines; the outer part; the environment.
q: The suburb of their straw-built citadel.

Suburb.etym: [L. suburbium; sub under, below, near + urbs a city. See Urban.]

senses.d: To overturn from the foundation; to overthrow; to ruin utterly.
q: These are his substance, sinews, arms, and strength, With which he yoketh your rebellious necks, Razeth your cities, and subverts your towns.
This would subvert the principles of all knowledge.

senses.d: To pervert, as the mind, and turn it from the truth; to corrupt; to confound.

Subvert.syn: To overturn; overthrow; destroy; invert; reverse; extinguish.
Subvert.etym: [L. subvertere, subversum; sub under + vertere to turn: cf. F. subvertir. See Verse.]

senses.d: To overthrow anything from the foundation; to be subversive.
q: They have a power given to them like that of the evil principle, to subvert and destroy.

senses.d: To follow in order; to come next after; hence, to take the place of; as, the king's eldest son succeeds his father on the throne; autumn succeeds summer.
q: As he saw him nigh succeed.

senses.d: To fall heir to; to inherit.
To come after; to be subsequent or consequent to; to follow; to pursue.
q: Destructive effects . . . succeeded the curse.

senses.d: To support; to prosper; to promote.
q: Succeed my wish and second my design.

Succeed.etym: [L. succedere, successum; sub under + cedere to go, to go along, approach, follow, succeed: cf. F. succéder. See Cede, and cf. Success.]

senses.d: To come in the place of another person, thing, or event; to come next in the usual, natural, or prescribed course of things; to follow; hence, to come next in the possession of anything; — often with to.
q: If the father left only daughters, they equally succeeded to him in copartnership.
Enjoy till I return Short pleasures; for long woes are to succeed!

senses.d: Specifically: To ascend the throne after the removal the death of the occupant.
q: No woman shall succeed in Salique land.

senses.d: To descend, as an estate or an heirloom, in the same family; to devolve.
To obtain the object desired; to accomplish what is attempted or intended; to have a prosperous issue or termination; to be successful; as, he succeeded in his plans; his plans succeeded.
q: It is almost impossible for poets to succeed without ambition.
Spenser endeavored it in Shepherd's Kalendar; but neither will it succeed in English.

senses.d: To go under cover.
q: Will you to the cooler cave succeed!

senses.d: Act of succeeding; succession.
q: Then all the sons of these five brethren reigned By due success.

senses.d: That which comes after; hence, consequence, issue, or result, of an endeavor or undertaking, whether good or bad; the outcome of effort.
q: Men . . . that are like to do that, that is committed to them, and to report back again faithfully the success.
Perplexed and troubled at his bad success The tempter stood.

senses.d: The favorable or prosperous termination of anything attempted; the attainment of a proposed object; prosperous issue.
q: Dream of success and happy victory!
Or teach with more success her son The vices of the time to shun.
Military successes, above all others, elevate the minds of a people.

senses.d: That which meets with, or one who accomplishes, favorable results, as a play or a player.

Success.etym: [L. successus: cf. F. succès. See Succeed.]

senses.d: Of that kind; of the like kind; like; resembling; similar; as, we never saw such a day; — followed by that or as introducing the word or proposition which defines the similarity, or the standard of comparison; as, the books are not such that I can recommend them, or, not such as I can recommend; these apples are not such as those we saw yesterday; give your children such precepts as tend to make them better.
q: And in his time such a conqueror That greater was there none under the sun.
His misery was such that none of the bystanders could refrain from weeping.

senses.d: Having the particular quality or character specified.
q: That thou art happy, owe to God; That thou continuest such, owe to thyself.

senses.d: The same that; — with as; as, this was the state of the kingdom at such time as the enemy landed.
Certain; — representing the object as already particularized in terms which are not mentioned.
q: In rushed one and tells him such a knight Is new arrived.
To-day or to-morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year.
And many other such like things ye do.

Such.etym: [OE. such, sich, sech, sik, swich, swilch, swulch, swilc, swulc, AS. swelc, swilc, swylc; akin to OFries. selik, D. zulk, OS. sulic, OHG. sulih, solih, G. solch, Icel. slīkr, OSw. salik, Sw. slik, Dan. slig, Goth. swaleiks; originally meaning, so shaped. √192. See So, Like, a., and cf. Which.]

senses.d: To draw, as a liquid, by the action of the mouth and tongue, which tends to produce a vacuum, and causes the liquid to rush in by atmospheric pressure; to draw, or apply force to, by exhausting the air.

To draw liquid from by the action of the mouth; as, to suck an orange; specifically, to draw milk from (the mother, the breast, etc.) with the mouth; as, the young of an animal sucks the mother, or dam; an infant sucks the breast.
To draw in, or imbibe, by any process resembles sucking; to inhale; to absorb; as, to suck in air; the roots of plants suck water from the ground.
To draw or drain.
q: Old ocean, sucked through the porous globe.

senses.d: To draw in, as a whirlpool; to swallow up.
q: As waters are by whirlpools sucked and drawn.

Suck.etym: [OE. suken, souken, AS. s�can, s�gan; akin to D. zuigen, G. saugen, OHG. s�gan, Icel. s�ga, sj�ga, Sw. suga, Dan. suge, L. sugere. Cf. Honeysuckle, Soak, Succulent, Suction.]

senses.d: To draw, or attempt to draw, something by suction, as with the mouth, or through a tube.
q: Where the bee sucks, there suck I.

senses.d: To draw milk from the breast or udder; as, a child, or the young of an animal, is first nourished by sucking.
To draw in; to imbibe; to partake.
q: The crown had sucked too hard, and now, being full, was like to draw less.

senses.d: The act of drawing with the mouth.
That which is drawn into the mouth by sucking; specifically, mikl drawn from the breast.
A small draught.
Juice; succulence.
Drawing milk from the mother or dam; hence, colloquially, young, inexperienced, as, a sucking infant; a sucking calf.
q: I suppose you are a young barrister, sucking lawyer, or that sort of thing.

senses.d: A teat.
To give suck to; to nurse at the breast.
q: The breasts of Hecuba When she did suckle Hector, looked not lovelier.
They are not weak, suckled by Wisdom.

senses.d: To nurse; to suck.
A young child or animal nursed at the breast.
A small kind of yellow clover (Trifolium filiforme) common in Southern Europe.
Happening without previous notice or with very brief notice; coming unexpectedly, or without the common preparation; immediate; instant; speedy.
q: Sudden fear troubleth thee.

senses.d: Hastly prepared or employed; quick; rapid.
q: Never was such a sudden scholar made.
The apples of Asphaltis, appearing goodly to the sudden eye.

senses.d: Hasty; violent; rash; precipitate.

Sudden.etym: [OE. sodian, sodein, OF. sodain, sudain, F. soudain, L. subitaneus, fr. subitus sudden, that has come unexpectedly, p. p. of subire to come on, to steal upon; sub under, secretly + ire to go. See Issue, and cf. Subitaneous.]

senses.d: Suddenly; unexpectedly.
q: Herbs of every leaf that sudden flowered.

senses.d: An unexpected occurrence; a surprise.
q: How art thou lost! how on a sudden lost!
He withdrew his opposition all of a sudden.

senses.d: To follow up; to chase; to seek after; to endeavor to win; to woo.
q: For yet there was no man that haddle him sued.
I was beloved of many a gentle knight, And sued and sought with all the service due.
Sue me, and woo me, and flatter me.

senses.d: To seek justice or right from, by legal process; to institute process in law against; to bring an action against; to prosecute judicially.
To clean, as the beak; — said of a hawk.
To leave high and dry on shore; as, to sue a ship.

Sue.etym: [OE. suen, sewen, siwen, OF. sivre (pres.ind. 3d sing. il siut, suit, he follows, nous sevons we follow), LL. sequere, for L. sequi, secutus; akin to Gr. �, Skr. sac to accompany, and probably to E. see, v.t. See See, v. t., and cf. Consequence, Ensue, Execute, Obsequious, Pursue, Second, Sect in re

senses.d: To seek by request; to make application; to petition; to entreat; to plead.
q: By adverse destiny constrained to sue For counsel and redress, he sues to you.
Cæsar came to Rome to sue for the double honor of a triumph and the consulship.
The Indians were defeated and sued for peace.

senses.d: To prosecute; to make legal claim; to seek (for something) in law; as, to sue for damages.
To woo; to pay addresses as a lover.
To be left high and dry on the shore, as a ship.
To feel, or endure, with pain, annoyance, etc.; to submit to with distress or grief; to undergo; as, to suffer pain of body, or grief of mind.
To endure or undergo without sinking; to support; to sustain; to bear up under.
q: Our spirit and strength entire, Strongly to suffer and support our pains.

senses.d: To undergo; to be affected by; to sustain; to experience; as, most substances suffer a change when long exposed to air and moisture; to suffer loss or damage.
q: If your more ponderous and settled project May suffer alteration.

senses.d: To allow; to permit; not to forbid or hinder; to tolerate.
q: Thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him.
I suffer them to enter and possess.

Suffer.syn: To permit; bear; endure; support; sustain; allow; admit; tolerate. See Permit.
Suffer.etym: [OE. suffren, soffren, OF. sufrir, sofrir, F. souffrir, (assumed) LL. sofferire, for L. sufferre; sub under + ferre to bear, akin to E. bear. See Bear to support.]

senses.d: To feel or undergo pain of body or mind; to bear what is inconvenient; as, we suffer from pain, sickness, or sorrow; we suffer with anxiety.
q: O well for him whose will is strong! He suffers, but he will not suffer long.

senses.d: To undergo punishment; specifically, to undergo the penalty of death.
q: The father was first condemned to suffer upon a day appointed, and the son afterwards the day following.

senses.d: To be injured; to sustain loss or damage.
q: Public business suffers by private infirmities.

senses.d: The bearing of pain, inconvenience, or loss; pain endured; distress, loss, or injury incurred; as, sufferings by pain or sorrow; sufferings by want or by wrongs.
Being in pain or grief; having loss, injury, distress, etc.
To be enough, or sufficient; to meet the need (of anything); to be equal to the end proposed; to be adequate.
q: To recount almighty works, What words or tongue of seraph can suffice?

Suffice.etym: [OE. suffisen, OF. soufire, F. suffire (cf. suffisant, p. pr.), L. sufficere to put under, to substitute, to avail for, to suffice; sub under + facere to make. See Fact.]

senses.d: To satisfy; to content; to be equal to the wants or demands of.
q: Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter.

senses.d: To furnish; to supply adequately.
q: The power appeased, with winds sufficed the sail.

senses.d: The quality or state of being sufficient, or adequate to the end proposed; adequacy.
q: His sufficiency is such that he bestows and possesses, his plenty being unexhausted.

senses.d: Qualification for any purpose; ability; capacity.
q: A substitute or most allowed sufficiency.
I am not so confident of my own sufficiency as not willingly to admit the counsel of others.

senses.d: Adequate substance or means; competence.
Supply equal to wants; ample stock or fund.
Conceit; self-confidence; self-sufficiency.
q: Sufficiency is a compound of vanity and ignorance.

Sufficiency.etym: [L. sufficientia: cf. F. suffisance. See Suffice.]

senses.d: Equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants; enough; ample; competent; as, provision sufficient for the family; an army sufficient to defend the country.
q: My grace is sufficient for thee.

senses.d: Possessing adequate talents or accomplishments; of competent power or ability; qualified; fit.
q: Who is sufficient for these things?

senses.d: Capable of meeting obligations; responsible.
q: The man is, notwithstanding, sufficient . . . I think I may take his bond.

senses.d: Self-sufficient; self-satisfied; content.
q: Thou art the most sufficient (I'll say for thee), Not to believe a thing.

Sufficient.syn: Enough; adequate; competent; full; satisfactory; ample.
Sufficient.etym: [L. sufficiens, -entis, p. pr. of sufficere: cf. F. suffisant. See Suffice.]

senses.d: To a sufficient degree; to a degree that answers the purpose, or gives content; enough; as, we are sufficiently supplied with food; a man sufficiently qualified for the discharge of his official duties.
The act of following or pursuing, as game; pursuit.
The act of suing; the process by which one endeavors to gain an end or an object; an attempt to attain a certain result; pursuit; endeavor.
q: Thenceforth the suit of earthly conquest shone.

senses.d: The act of wooing in love; the solicitation of a woman in marriage; courtship.
q: Rebate your loves, each rival suit suspend, Till this funereal web my labors end.

senses.d: The attempt to gain an end by legal process; an action or process for the recovery of a right or claim; legal application to a court for justice; prosecution of right before any tribunal; as, a civil suit; a criminal suit; a suit in chancery.
q: I arrest thee at the suit of Count Orsino.
In England the several suits, or remedial instruments of justice, are distinguished into three kinds — actions personal, real, and mixed.

senses.d: That which follows as a retinue; a company of attendants or followers; the assembly of persons who attend upon a prince, magistrate, or other person of distinction; — often written suite, and pronounced swēt.

Things that follow in a series or succession; the individual objects, collectively considered, which constitute a series, as of rooms, buildings, compositions, etc.; — often written suite, and pronounced swēt.

A number of things used together, and generally necessary to be united in order to answer their purpose; a number of things ordinarily classed or used together; a set; as, a suit of curtains; a suit of armor; a suit of clothes.
One of the four sets of cards which constitute a pack; — each set consisting of thirteen cards bearing a particular emblem, as hearts, spades, clubs, or diamonds.
q: To deal and shuffle, to divide and sort Her mingled suits and sequences.

senses.d: Regular order; succession.
q: Every five and thirty years the same kind and suit of weather comes again.

Suit.etym: [OE. suite, F. suite, OF. suite, sieute, fr. suivre to follow, OF. sivre; perhaps influenced by L. secta. See Sue to follow, and cf. Sect, Suite.]

senses.d: To fit; to adapt; to make proper or suitable; as, to suit the action to the word.
To be fitted to; to accord with; to become; to befit.
q: Ill suits his cloth the praise of railing well.
Raise her notes to that sublime degree Which suits song of piety and thee.

senses.d: To dress; to clothe.
q: So went he suited to his watery tomb.

senses.d: To please; to make content; as, he is well suited with his place; to suit one's taste.
To agree; to accord; to be fitted; to correspond; — usually followed by with or to.
q: The place itself was suiting to his care.
Give me not an office That suits with me so ill.

Suit.syn: To agree; accord; comport; tally; correspond; match; answer.

senses.d: The aggregate of two or more numbers, magnitudes, quantities, or particulars; the amount or whole of any number of individuals or particulars added together; as, the sum of 5 and 7 is 12.
q: Take ye the sum of all the congregation.

senses.d: A quantity of money or currency; any amount, indefinitely; as, a sum of money; a small sum, or a large sum.
q: With a great sum obtained I this freedom.

senses.d: The principal points or thoughts when viewed together; the amount; the substance; compendium; as, this is the sum of all the evidence in the case; this is the sum and substance of his objections.
Height; completion; utmost degree.
q: Thus have I told thee all my state, and brought My story to the sum of earthly bliss.

senses.d: A problem to be solved, or an example to be wrought out.
q: A sum in arithmetic wherein a flaw discovered at a particular point is ipso facto fatal to the whole.
A large sheet of paper . . . covered with long sums.

Sum.etym: [OE. summe, somme, OF. sume, some, F. somme, L. summa, fr. summus highest, a superlative from sub under. See Sub-, and cf. Supreme.]

senses.d: To bring together into one whole; to collect into one amount; to cast up, as a column of figures; to ascertain the totality of; — usually with up.
q: The mind doth value every moment, and then the hour doth rather sum up the moments, than divide the day.

senses.d: To bring or collect into a small compass; to comprise in a few words; to condense; — usually with up.
q: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard,” in few words sums up the moral of this fable.
He sums their virtues in himself alone.

senses.d: To have (the feathers) full grown; to furnish with complete, or full-grown, plumage.
q: But feathered soon and fledge They summed their pens .

Sum.syn: To cast up; collect; comprise; condense; comprehend; compute.

senses.d: One who sums; one who casts up an account.

A large stone or beam placed horizontally on columns, piers, posts, or the like, serving for various uses. Specifically: (a) The lintel of a door or window. (b) The commencement of a cross vault. (c) A central floor timber, as a girder, or a piece reaching from a wall to a girder. Called also summertree.

Summer.etym: [F. sommier a rafter, the same word as sommier a beast of burden. See Sumpter.]

senses.d: The season of the year in which the sun shines most directly upon any region; the warmest period of the year.

Summer.etym: [OE. sumer, somer, AS. sumor, sumer; akin to OFries. sumur, D. zomer, OS. sumar, G. sommer, OHG. & Icel. sumar, Dan. sommer, Sw. sommar, W. haf, Zend hama, Skr. samā year. √292.]

senses.d: To pass the summer; to spend the warm season; as, to summer in Switzerland.
q: The fowls shall summer upon them.

senses.d: To keep or carry through the summer; to feed during the summer; as, to summer stock.
Involving large outlay or expense; costly; expensive; hence, luxurious; splendid; magnificient; as, a sumptuous house or table; sumptuous apparel.
q: We are too magnificient and sumptuous in our tables and attendance.
She spoke, and turned her sumptuous head, with eyes Of shining expectation fixed on mine.

Sumptuous.etym: [L. sumptuosus, fr. sumptus expanse, cost: cf. F. somptueux. See Sumptuary.]

senses.d: The luminous orb, the light of which constitutes day, and its absence night; the central body round which the earth and planets revolve, by which they are held in their orbits, and from which they receive light and heat. Its mean distance from the earth is about 92,500,000 miles, and its diameter about 860,000.
Any heavenly body which forms the center of a system of orbs.
The direct light or warmth of the sun; sunshine.
q: Lambs that did frisk in the sun.

senses.d: That which resembles the sun, as in splendor or importance; any source of light, warmth, or animation.
q: For the Lord God is a sun and shield.
I will never consent to put out the sun of sovereignity to posterity.

Sun.etym: [OE. sunne, sonne, AS. sunne; akin to OFries. sunne, D. zon, OS. & OHG. sunna, G. sonne, Icel. sunna, Goth. sunna; perh. fr. same root as L. sol. √297. Cf. Solar, South.]

senses.d: To expose to the sun's rays; to warm or dry in the sun; as, to sun cloth; to sun grain.
q: Then to sun thyself in open air.

senses.d: To disunite in almost any manner, either by rending, cutting, or breaking; to part; to put or keep apart; to separate; to divide; to sever; as, to sunder a rope; to sunder a limb; to sunder friends.
q: It is sundered from the main land by a sandy plain.

Sunder.etym: [OE. sundren, AS. sundrain (in āsundrain, gesundrain), from sundor asunder, separately, apart; akin to D. zonder, prep., without, G. sonder separate, as prep., without, sondern but, OHG. suntar separately, Icel. sundr asunder, Sw. & Dan. sönder, Goth. sundrō alone, separately.]

senses.d: To part; to separate.
A separation into parts; a division or severance.

Sunder.etym: [See Sunder, v. t., and cf. Asunder.]

senses.d: To expose to the sun and wind.
Several; divers; more than one or two; various.
q: With many a sound of sundry melody.
Sundry foes the rural realm surround.

senses.d: Separate; diverse.
q: Every church almost had the Bible of a sundry translation.

Sundry.etym: [OE. sundry, sondry, AS. syndrig, fr. sundor asunder. See Sunder, v. t.]

senses.d: The first appearance of the sun above the horizon in the morning; more generally, the time of such appearance, whether in fair or cloudy weather; as, to begin work at sunrise.
Hence, the region where the sun rises; the east.
q: Which were beyond Jordan toward the sunrising.
Full hot and fast the Saxon rides, with rein of travel slack, And, bending o'ev his saddle, leaves the sunrise at his back.

senses.d: To take into the mouth with the lips, as a liquid; to take or drink by a little at a time; to sip.
q: There I'll sup Balm and nectar in my cup.

Sup.etym: [OE. soupen to drink, AS. s�pan; akin to D. zuipen, G. saufen, OHG. s�fan, Icel. s�pa, Sw. supa, Dan. söbe. Cf. Sip, Sop, Soup, Supper.]

senses.d: A small mouthful, as of liquor or broth; a little taken with the lips; a sip.
q: Tom Thumb had got a little sup.

senses.d: To eat the evening meal; to take supper.
q: I do entreat that we may sup together.

senses.d: To treat with supper.
q: Sup them well and look unto them all.

senses.d: A greater quantity than is wanted; superabundance; as, a superfluity of water; a superfluity of wealth.
q: A quiet mediocrity is still to be preferred before a troubled superfluity.

senses.d: The state or quality of being superfluous; excess.
Something beyond what is needed; something which serves for show or luxury.
More than is wanted or is sufficient; rendered unnecessary by superabundance; unnecessary; useless; excessive; as, a superfluous price.
q: An authority which makes all further argument or illustration superfluous.

Superfluous.syn: Unnecessary; useless; exuberant; excessive; redundant; needless.
Superfluous.etym: [L. superfluus overflowing; super over, above + fluere to flow. See Super-, and Fluent.]

senses.d: The act of superscribing.
That which is written or engraved on the surface, outside, or above something else; specifically, an address on a letter, envelope, or the like.
q: The superscription of his accusation was written over, The King of the Jews.

senses.d: That part of a prescription which contains the Latin word recipe (Take) or the sign �.
An excessive reverence for, or fear of, that which is unknown or mysterious.

An ignorant or irrational worship of the Supreme Deity; excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples in the observance of religious rites not commanded, or of points of minor importance; also, a rite or practice proceeding from excess of sculptures in religion.
q: And the truth With superstitions and traditions taint.

senses.d: The worship of a false god or gods; false religion; religious veneration for objects.
q: had certain questions against him of their own superstition.

senses.d: Belief in the direct agency of superior powers in certain extraordinary or singular events, or in magic, omens, prognostics, or the like.
Excessive nicety; scrupulous exactness.

Superstition.etym: [F. superstition, L. superstitio, originally, a standing still over or by a thing; hence, amazement, wonder, dread, especially of the divine or supernatural, fr. superstare to stand over; super over + stare to stand. See Super-, and Stand.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to superstition; proceeding from, or manifesting, superstition; as, superstitious rites; superstitious observances.
Evincing superstition; overscrupulous and rigid in religious observances; addicted to superstition; full of idle fancies and scruples in regard to religion.
q: Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious.

senses.d: Overexact; scrupulous beyond need.
A meal taken at the close of the day; the evening meal.

Supper.etym: [OE. soper, super, OF. super, soper, F. souper; originally an infinitive, to sup, take a meal. See Soup, and cf. Sup to take supper.]

senses.d: To take supper; to sup.
To supply with supper.
To trip up.
To remove or displace by stratagem; to displace and take the place of; to supersede; as, a rival supplants another in the favor of a mistress or a prince.
q: Suspecting that the courtier had supplanted the friend.

senses.d: To overthrow, undermine, or force away, in order to get a substitute in place of.
q: You never will supplant the received ideas of God.

Supplant.syn: To remove; displace; overpower; undermine; overthrow; supersede.
Supplant.etym: [F. supplanter, L. supplantare to trip up one's heels, to throw down; sub under + planta the sole of the foot, also, a sucker, slip, sprout. Cf. Plant, n.]

senses.d: Pliant; flexible; easily bent; as, supple joints; supple fingers.
Yielding; compliant; not obstinate; submissive to guidance; as, a supple horse.
q: If punishment . . . makes not the will supple, it hardens the offender.

senses.d: Bending to the humor of others; flattering; fawning; obsequious.

Supple.syn: Pliant; flexible; yielding; compliant; bending; flattering; fawning; soft.
Supple.etym: [OE. souple, F. souple, from L. supplex suppliant, perhaps originally, being the knees. Cf. Supplicate.]

senses.d: To make soft and pliant; to render flexible; as, to supple leather.
q: The flesh therewith she suppled and did steep.

senses.d: To make compliant, submissive, or obedient.
q: A mother persisting till she had bent her daughter's mind and suppled her will.
They should supple our stiff willfulness.

senses.d: To become soft and pliant.
q: The stones . . . Suppled into softness as they fell.

senses.d: Asking earnestly and submissively; entreating; beseeching; supplicating.
q: The rich grow suppliant, and the poor grow proud.

senses.d: Manifesting entreaty; expressive of supplication.
q: To bow and sue for grace With suppliant knee.

Suppliant.syn: Entreating; beseeching; suing; begging; supplicating; imploring.
Suppliant.etym: [F., p. pr. of supplier to entreat, L. supplicare. See Supplicate, and cf. Supplicant.]

senses.d: One who supplicates; a humble petitioner; one who entreats submissively.
q: Hear thy suppliant's prayer.

senses.d: The act of supplicating; humble and earnest prayer, as in worship.
A humble petition; an earnest request; an entreaty.
A religious solemnity observed in consequence of some military success, and also, in times of distress and danger, to avert the anger of the gods.

To fill up, or keep full; to furnish with what is wanted; to afford, or furnish with, a sufficiency; as, rivers are supplied by smaller streams; an aqueduct supplies an artificial lake; — often followed by with before the thing furnished; as, to supply a furnace with fuel; to supply soldiers with ammunition.
To serve instead of; to take the place of.
q: Burning ships the banished sun supply.
The sun was set, and Vesper, to supply His absent beams, had lighted up the sky.

senses.d: To fill temporarily; to serve as substitute for another in, as a vacant place or office; to occupy; to have possession of; as, to supply a pulpit.
To give; to bring or furnish; to provide; as, to supply money for the war.

Supply.syn: To furnish; provide; administer; minister; contribute; yield; accommodate.
Supply.etym: [For older supploy, F. suppléer, OF. also supployer, (assumed) LL. suppletare, from L. supplere, suppletum; sub under + plere to fill, akin to plenus full. See Plenty.]

senses.d: The act of supplying; supplial.
That which supplies a want; sufficiency of things for use or want.
Auxiliary troops or reënforcements.
The food, and the like, which meets the daily necessities of an army or other large body of men; store; — used chiefly in the plural; as, the army was discontented for lack of supplies.
An amount of money provided, as by Parliament or Congress, to meet the annual national expenditures; generally in the plural; as, to vote supplies.
A person who fills a place for a time; one who supplies the place of another; a substitute; esp., a clergyman who supplies a vacant pulpit.
Serving to contain, deliver, or regulate a supply of anything; as, a supply tank or valve.

To bear by being under; to keep from falling; to uphold; to sustain, in a literal or physical sense; to prop up; to bear the weight of; as, a pillar supports a structure; an abutment supports an arch; the trunk of a tree supports the branches.
To endure without being overcome, exhausted, or changed in character; to sustain; as, to support pain, distress, or misfortunes.
q: This fierce demeanor and his insolence The patience of a god could not support.

senses.d: To keep from failing or sinking; to solace under affictive circumstances; to assist; to encourage; to defend; as, to support the courage or spirits.
To assume and carry successfully, as the part of an actor; to represent or act; to sustain; as, to support the character of King Lear.
To furnish with the means of sustenance or livelihood; to maintain; to provide for; as, to support a family; to support the ministers of the gospel.
To carry on; to enable to continue; to maintain; as, to support a war or a contest; to support an argument or a debate.
To verify; to make good; to substantiate; to establish; to sustain; as, the testimony is not sufficient to support the charges; the evidence will not support the statements or allegations.
q: To urge such arguments, as though they were sufficient to support and demonstrate a whole scheme of moral philosophy.

senses.d: To vindicate; to maintain; to defend successfully; as, to be able to support one's own cause.
To uphold by aid or countenance; to aid; to help; to back up; as, to support a friend or a party; to support the present administration.
q: Wherefore, bold pleasant, Darest thou support a published traitor?

senses.d: A attend as an honorary assistant; as, a chairman supported by a vice chairman; O'Connell left the prison, supported by his two sons.

Support.syn: To maintain; endure; verify; substantiate; countenance; patronize; help; back; second; succor; relieve; uphold; encourage; favor; nurture; nourish; cherish; shield; defend; protect; stay; assist; forward.
Support.etym: [F. supporter, L. supportare to carry on, to convey, in LL., to support, sustain; sub under + portare to carry. See Port demeanor.]

senses.d: The act, state, or operation of supporting, upholding, or sustaining.
That which upholds, sustains, or keeps from falling, as a prop, a pillar, or a foundation of any kind.

That which maintains or preserves from being overcome, falling, yielding, sinking, giving way, or the like; subsistence; maintenance; assistance; reënforcement; as, he gave his family a good support, the support of national credit; the assaulting column had the support of a battery.

Support.syn: Stay; prop; maintenance; subsistence; assistance; favor; countenance; encouragement; patronage; aid; help; succor; nutriment; sustenance; food.

senses.d: To represent to one's self, or state to another, not as true or real, but as if so, and with a view to some consequence or application which the reality would involve or admit of; to imagine or admit to exist, for the sake of argument or illustration; to assume to be true; as, let us suppose the earth to be the center of the system, what would be the result?
q: Suppose they take offence without a cause.
When we have as great assurance that a thing is, as we could possibly, supposing it were, we ought not to make any doubt of its existence.

senses.d: To imagine; to believe; to receive as true.
q: How easy is a bush supposed a bear!
Let not my lord suppose that they have slain all the young men, the king's sons; for Amnon only is dead.

senses.d: To require to exist or to be true; to imply by the laws of thought or of nature; as, purpose supposes foresight.
q: One falsehood always supposes another, and renders all you can say suspected.

senses.d: To put by fraud in the place of another.

Suppose.syn: To imagine; believe; conclude; judge; consider; view; regard; conjecture; assume.
Suppose.etym: [F. supposer; pref. sub- under + poser to place; — corresponding in meaning to L. supponere, suppositum, to put under, to substitute, falsify, counterfeit. See Pose.]

senses.d: To make supposition; to think; to be of opinion.
Supposition.
Highest in authority; holding the highest place in authority, government, or power.
q: He that is the supreme King of kings.

senses.d: Highest; greatest; most excellent or most extreme; utmost; greatist possible (sometimes in a bad sense); as, supreme love; supreme glory; supreme magnanimity; supreme folly.
q: Each would be supreme within its own sphere, and those spheres could not but clash.

senses.d: Situated at the highest part or point.

Supreme.etym: [L. supremus, superlative of superus that is above, upper, fr. super above: cf. F. suprême. See Super-, and cf. Sum.]

senses.d: Certainly knowing and believing; confident beyond doubt; implicity trusting; unquestioning; positive.
q: We are sure that the judgment of God is according to truth against them which commit such things.
I'm sure care 's an enemy of life.

senses.d: Certain to find or retain; as, to be sure of game; to be sure of success; to be sure of life or health.
Fit or worthy to be depended on; certain not to fail or disappoint expectation; unfailing; strong; permanent; enduring.
q: The Lord will certainly make my lord a sure house; because my lord fighteth the battles of the Lord.
The testimony of the Lord is sure.
Which put in good sure leather sacks.

senses.d: Betrothed; engaged to marry.
q: The king was sure to Dame Elizabeth Lucy, and her husband before God.
I presume . . . that you had been sure as fast as faith could bind you, man and wife.

senses.d: Free from danger; safe; secure.
q: Fear not; the forest is not three leagues off; If we recover that we are sure enough.
She that's made sure to him she loves not well.

Sure.syn: Certain; unfailing; infallible; safe; firm; permanent; steady; stable; strong; secure; indisputable; confident; positive.
Sure.etym: [OE. sur, OF. seür, F. sûr, L. securus; se aside, without + cura care. See Secure, and cf. Assure, Insure, Sicker sure.]

senses.d: In a sure manner; safely; certainly.
q: 'T is pleasant, sure, to see one's name in print.

senses.d: In a sure or certain manner; certainly; infallibly; undoubtedly; assuredly.
q: In the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.
He that created something out of nothing, surely can raise great things out of small.

senses.d: Without danger; firmly; steadly; securely.
q: He that walketh uprightly walketh surely.

senses.d: Suretyship.
The state of being sure; certainty; security.
q: Know of a surety, that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs.
For the more surety they looked round about.

senses.d: That which makes sure; that which confirms; ground of confidence or security.
q: our happy state Hold, as you yours, while our obedience holds; On other surety none.

senses.d: Security against loss or damage; security for payment, or for the performance of some act.
q: There remains unpaid A hundred thousand more; in surety of the which One part of Aquitaine is bound to us.

senses.d: One who is bound with and for another who is primarily liable, and who is called the principal; one who engages to answer for another's appearance in court, or for his payment of a debt, or for performance of some act; a bondsman; a bail.
q: He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it.

senses.d: Hence, a substitute; a hostage.
Evidence; confirmation; warrant.
q: She called the saints to surety, That she would never put it from her finger, Unless she gave it to yourself.

Surety.etym: [OE. seurte, OF. seürté, F. sûreté. See Sure, Security.]

senses.d: To act as surety for.
Excess in eating and drinking.
q: Let not Sir Surfeit sit at thy board.
Now comes the sick hour that his surfeit made.

senses.d: Fullness and oppression of the system, occasioned often by excessive eating and drinking.
q: To prevent surfeit and other diseases that are incident to those that heat their blood by travels.

senses.d: Disgust caused by excess; satiety.
q: Matter and argument have been supplied abundantly, and even to surfeit.

Surfeit.etym: [OE. surfet, OF. surfait, sorfait, excess, arrogance, crime, fr. surfaire, sorfaire, to augment, exaggerate, F. surfaire to overcharge; sur over + faire to make, do, L. facere. See Sur-, and Fact.]

senses.d: To load the stomach with food, so that sickness or uneasiness ensues; to eat to excess.
q: They are as sick that surfeit with too much as they that starve with nothing.

senses.d: To indulge to satiety in any gratification.
To feed so as to oppress the stomach and derange the function of the system; to overfeed, and produce satiety, sickness, or uneasiness; — often reflexive; as, to surfeit one's self with sweets.
To fill to satiety and disgust; to cloy; as, he surfeits us with compliments.
A name or appellation which is added to, or over and above, the baptismal or Christian name, and becomes a family name.
An appellation added to the original name; an agnomen.

Surname.etym: [Pref. sur + name; really a substitution for OE. sournoun, from F. surnom. See Sur-, and Noun, Name.]

senses.d: To name or call by an appellation added to the original name; to give a surname to.
q: Another shall subscribe with his hand unto the Lord, and surname himself by the name of Israel.
And Simon he surnamed Peter.

senses.d: The act of coming upon, or taking, unawares; the act of seizing unexpectedly; surprisal; as, the fort was taken by surprise.

The state of being surprised, or taken unawares, by some act or event which could not reasonably be foreseen; emotion excited by what is sudden and strange; a suddenly excited feeling of wonder or astonishment.
q: Pure surprise and fear Made me to quit the house.

senses.d: Anything that causes such a state or emotion.
A dish covered with a crust of raised paste, but with no other contents.

Surprise.etym: [F. surprise, fr. surprendre, surpris; sur over + prendre to take, L. prehendere. See Sur-, and Prehensile.]

senses.d: To come or fall suddenly and unexpectedly; to take unawares; to seize or capture by unexpected attack.
q: Fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites.
The castle of Macduff I will surprise.
Who can speak The mingled passions that surprised his heart?

senses.d: To strike with wonder, astonishment, or confusion, by something sudden, unexpected, or remarkable; to confound; as, his conduct surprised me.
q: I am surprised with an uncouth fear.
Up he starts, Discovered and surprised.

senses.d: To lead (one) to do suddenly and without forethought; to bring (one) into some unexpected state; — with into; as, to be surprised into an indiscretion; to be surprised into generosity.
To hold possession of; to hold.
q: Not with me, That in my hands surprise the sovereignity.

Surprise.etym: [From Surprise, n.: cf. F. surprendre, p. p. surpris.]

senses.d: To keep from falling; to bear; to uphold; to support; as, a foundation sustains the superstructure; a beast sustains a load; a rope sustains a weight.
q: Every pillar the temple to sustain.

senses.d: Hence, to keep from sinking, as in despondence, or the like; to support.
q: No comfortable expectations of another life to sustain him under the evils in this world.

senses.d: To maintain; to keep alive; to support; to subsist; to nourish; as, provisions to sustain an army.
To aid, comfort, or relieve; to vindicate.
q: His sons, who seek the tyrant to sustain.

senses.d: To endure without failing or yielding; to bear up under; as, to sustain defeat and disappointment.
To suffer; to bear; to undergo.
q: Shall Turnus, then, such endless toil sustain?
You shall sustain more new disgraces.

senses.d: To allow the prosecution of; to admit as valid; to sanction; to continue; not to dismiss or abate; as, the court sustained the action or suit.
To prove; to establish by evidence; to corroborate or confirm; to be conclusive of; as, to sustain a charge, an accusation, or a proposition.

Sustain.syn: To support; uphold; subsist; assist; relieve; suffer; undergo.
Sustain.etym: [OE. sustenen, susteinen, OF. sustenir, sostenir, F. soutenir (the French prefix is properly fr. L. subtus below, fr. sub under), L. sustinere; pref. sus- (see Sub-) + tenere to hold. See Tenable, and cf. Sustenance.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, upholds or sustains; a sustainer.
q: I waked again, for my sustain was the Lord.

senses.d: Held up to a certain pitch, degree, or level; uniform; as, sustained pasion; a sustained style of writing; a sustained note in music.
The act of sustaining; support; maintenance; subsistence; as, the sustenance of the body; the sustenance of life.
That which supports life; food; victuals; provisions; means of living; as, the city has ample sustenance.
q: For lying is thy sustenance, thy food.

Sustenance.etym: [OF. sustenance, sostenance, soustenance: cf. L. sustenentia endurance. See Sustain.]

senses.d: Anything used to swaddle with, as a cloth or band; a swaddling band.
q: They put me in bed in all my swaddles.

Swaddle.etym: [AS. swe�il, swe�el, fr. swe�ain to bind. See Swathe.]

senses.d: To bind as with a bandage; to bind or warp tightly with clothes; to swathe; — used esp. of infants; as, to swaddle a baby.
q: They swaddled me up in my nightgown with long pieces of linen.

senses.d: To beat; to cudgel.

Any one of numerous species of passerine birds of the family Hirundinidæ, especially one of those species in which the tail is deeply forked. They have long, pointed wings, and are noted for the swiftness and gracefulness of their flight.
Any one of numerous species of swifts which resemble the true swallows in form and habits, as the common American chimney swallow, or swift.
The aperture in a block through which the rope reeves.

Swallow.etym: [OE. swalowe, AS. swalewe, swealwe; akin to D. zwaluw, OHG. swalawa, G. schwalbe, Icel. & Sw. svala, Dan. svale.]

senses.d: To take into the stomach; to receive through the gullet, or esophagus, into the stomach; as, to swallow food or drink.
q: As if I had swallowed snowballs for pills.

senses.d: To draw into an abyss or gulf; to ingulf; to absorb — usually followed by up.
q: The earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up, and their houses.

senses.d: To receive or embrace, as opinions or belief, without examination or scruple; to receive implicitly.
q: Though that story . . . be not so readily swallowed.

senses.d: To engross; to appropriate; — usually with up.
q: Homer excels . . . in this, that he swallowed up the honor of those who succeeded him.

senses.d: To occupy; to take up; to employ.
q: The necessary provision of the life swallows the greatest part of their time.

senses.d: To seize and waste; to exhaust; to consume.
q: Corruption swallowed what the liberal hand Of bounty scattered.

senses.d: To retract; to recant; as, to swallow one's opinions.
To put up with; to bear patiently or without retaliation; as, to swallow an affront or insult.

Swallow.syn: To absorb; imbibe; ingulf; engross; consume. See Absorb.
Swallow.etym: [OE. swolewen, swolwen, swolhen, AS. swelgan; akin to D. zwelgen, OHG. swelahan, swelgan, G. schwelgen to feast, to revel, Icel. svelgia to swallow, SW. svälja, Dan. svælge. Cf. Groundsel a plant.]

senses.d: To perform the act of swallowing; as, his cold is so severe he is unable to swallow.
The act of swallowing.
The gullet, or esophagus; the throat.
Taste; relish; inclination; liking.
q: I have no swallow for it.

senses.d: Capacity for swallowing; voracity.
q: There being nothing too gross for the swallow of political rancor.

senses.d: As much as is, or can be, swallowed at once; as, a swallow of water.
That which ingulfs; a whirlpool.

Any one of numerous species of large aquatic birds belonging to Cygnus, Olor, and allied genera of the subfamily Cygninæ. They have a large and strong beak and a long neck, and are noted for their graceful movements when swimming. Most of the northern species are white. In literature the swan was fabled to sing a melodious song, especially at the time of its death.
Fig.: An appellation for a sweet singer, or a poet noted for grace and melody; as Shakespeare is called the swan of Avon.
The constellation Cygnus.

Swan.etym: [AS. swan; akin to D. zwaan, OHG. swan, G. schwan, Icel. svanr, Sw. svan, Dan. svane; and perhaps to E. sound something audible.]

senses.d: To climb a tree, pole, or the like, by embracing it with the arms and legs alternately. See Shin.
q: At the top was placed a piece of money, as a prize for those who could swarm up and seize it.

senses.d: A large number or mass of small animals or insects, especially when in motion.
Especially, a great number of honeybees which emigrate from a hive at once, and seek new lodgings under the direction of a queen; a like body of bees settled permanently in a hive.
Hence, any great number or multitude, as of people in motion, or sometimes of inanimate objects; as, a swarm of meteorites.
q: Those prodigious swarms that had settled themselves in every part of it .

Swarm.etym: [OE. swarm, AS. swearm; akin to D. zwerm, G. schwarm, OHG. swaram, Icel. svarmr a tumult, Sw. svärm a swarm, Dan. sværm, and G. schwirren to whiz, to buzz, Skr. svar to sound, and perhaps to E. swear. √177. Cf. Swerve, Swirl.]

senses.d: To collect, and depart from a hive by flight in a body; — said of bees; as, bees swarm in warm, clear days in summer.
To appear or collect in a crowd; to throng together; to congregate in a multitude.
To be crowded; to be thronged with a multitude of beings in motion.
q: Every place swarms with soldiers.

senses.d: To abound; to be filled (with).
To breed multitudes.
q: Not so thick swarmed once the soil Bedropped with blood of Gorgon.

senses.d: To crowd or throng.

To affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed; to make a promise, threat, or resolve on oath; also, to affirm solemnly by some sacred object, or one regarded as sacred, as the Bible, the Koran, etc.
q: Ye shall swear by my name falsely.
I swear by all the Roman gods.

senses.d: To give evidence on oath; as, to swear to the truth of a statement; he swore against the prisoner.
To make an appeal to God in an irreverant manner; to use the name of God or sacred things profanely; to call upon God in imprecation; to curse.
q: swore little; diced not above seven times a week.

Swear.etym: [OE. swerien, AS. swerian; akin to D. zweren, OS. swerian, OHG. swerien, G. schwören, Icel. sverja, Sw. svärja, Dan. sværge, Icel. & Sw. svara to answer, Dan. svare, Dan. & Sw. svar an answer, Goth. swaran to swear, and perhaps to E. swarm. √177. Cf. Answer.]

senses.d: To utter or affirm with a solemn appeal to God for the truth of the declaration; to make (a promise, threat, or resolve) under oath.
q: Swear unto me here by God, that thou wilt not deal falsely with me.
He swore consent to your succession.

senses.d: To put to an oath; to cause to take an oath; to administer an oath to; — ofetn followed by in or into; as, to swear witnesses; to swear a jury; to swear in an officer; he was sworn into office.
To declare or charge upon oath; as, he swore treason against his friend.
To appeal to by an oath.
q: Now, by Apollo, king, Thou swear'st thy gods in vain.

senses.d: One who swears; one who calls God to witness for the truth of his declaration.
A profane person; one who uses profane language.
q: Then the liars and swearers are fools.

senses.d: To excrete sensible moisture from the pores of the skin; to perspire.
Fig.: To perspire in toil; to work hard; to drudge.
q: He 'd have the poets sweat.

senses.d: To emit moisture, as green plants in a heap.

Sweat.etym: [OE. sweten, AS. swætan, fr. swāt, n., sweat; akin to OFries. & OS. swēt, D. zweet, OHG. sweiz, G. schweiss, Icel. sviti, sveiti, Sw. svett, Dan. sved, L. sudor sweat, sudare to sweat, Gr. �, �, sweat, � to sweat, Skr. svēda sweat, svid to sweat. √178. Cf. Exude, Sudary, Sudorific.]

senses.d: To cause to excrete moisture from the skin; to cause to perspire; as, his physicians attempted to sweat him by most powerful sudorifics.
To emit or suffer to flow from the pores; to exude.
q: It made her not a drop for sweat.
With exercise she sweat ill humors out.

senses.d: To unite by heating, after the application of soldier.
To get something advantageous, as money, property, or labor from (any one), by exaction or oppression; as, to sweat a spendthrift; to sweat laborers.
q: The only use of it which is interdicted is to put it in circulation again after having diminished its weight by “sweating”, or otherwise, because the quantity of metal contains is no longer consistent with its impression.

senses.d: The fluid which is excreted from the skin of an animal; the fluid secreted by the sudoriferous glands; a transparent, colorless, acid liquid with a peculiar odor, containing some fatty acids and mineral matter; perspiration. See Perspiration.
q: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.

senses.d: The act of sweating; or the state of one who sweats; hence, labor; toil; drudgery.
Moisture issuing from any substance; as, the sweat of hay or grain in a mow or stack.
The sweating sickness.
A short run by a race horse in exercise.

Sweat.etym: [Cf. OE. swot, AS. swāt. See Sweat, v. i.]

senses.d: To pass a broom across (a surface) so as to remove loose dirt, dust, etc.; to brush, or rub over, with a broom for the purpose of cleaning; as, to sweep a floor, the street, or a chimney. Used also figuratively.
q: I will sweep it with the besom of destruction.

senses.d: To drive or carry along or off with a broom or a brush, or as if with a broom; to remove by, or as if by, brushing; as, to sweep dirt from a floor; the wind sweeps the snow from the hills; a freshet sweeps away a dam, timber, or rubbish; a pestilence sweeps off multitudes.
q: The hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies.
I have already swept the stakes.

senses.d: To brush against or over; to rub lightly along.
q: Their long descending train, With rubies edged and sapphires, swept the plain.
