senses.d: To carry with a long, swinging, or dragging motion; hence, to carry in a stately or proud fashion.
q: And like a peacock sweep along his tail.

senses.d: To strike with a long stroke.
q: Wake into voice each silent string, And sweep the sounding lyre.

senses.d: To draw or drag something over; as, to sweep the bottom of a river with a net.
To pass over, or traverse, with the eye or with an instrument of observation; as, to sweep the heavens with a telescope.

Sweep.etym: [OE. swepen; akin to AS. swāpan. See Swoop, v. i.]

senses.d: To clean rooms, yards, etc., or to clear away dust, dirt, litter, etc., with a broom, brush, or the like.

To brush swiftly over the surface of anything; to pass with switness and force, as if brushing the surface of anything; to move in a stately manner; as, the wind sweeps across the plain; a woman sweeps through a drawing-room.
To pass over anything comprehensively; to range through with rapidity; as, his eye sweeps through space.
The act of sweeping.
The compass or range of a stroke; as, a long sweep.
The compass of any turning body or of any motion; as, the sweep of a door; the sweep of the eye.
The compass of anything flowing or brushing; as, the flood carried away everything within its sweep.
Violent and general destruction; as, the sweep of an epidemic disease.
Direction and extent of any motion not rectlinear; as, the sweep of a compass.
Direction or departure of a curve, a road, an arch, or the like, away from a rectlinear line.
q: The road which makes a small sweep.

senses.d: One who sweeps; a sweeper; specifically, a chimney sweeper.
A movable templet for making molds, in loam molding.
The mold of a ship when she begins to curve in at the rungheads; any part of a ship shaped in a segment of a circle.
The almond furnace.
A long pole, or piece of timber, moved on a horizontal fulcrum fixed to a tall post and used to raise and lower a bucket in a well for drawing water.

Cleaning off surfaces, or cleaning away dust, dirt, or litter, as a broom does; moving with swiftness and force; carrying everything before it; including in its scope many persons or things; as, a sweeping flood; a sweeping majority; a sweeping accusation.
Having an agreeable taste or flavor such as that of sugar; saccharine; — opposed to sour and bitter; as, a sweet beverage; sweet fruits; sweet oranges.
Pleasing to the smell; fragrant; redolent; balmy; as, a sweet rose; sweet odor; sweet incense.
q: The breath of these flowers is sweet to me.

senses.d: Pleasing to the ear; soft; melodious; harmonious; as, the sweet notes of a flute or an organ; sweet music; a sweet voice; a sweet singer.
q: To make his English sweet upon his tongue.
A voice sweet, tremulous, but powerful.

senses.d: Pleasing to the eye; beautiful; mild and attractive; fair; as, a sweet face; a sweet color or complexion.
q: Sweet interchange Of hill and valley, rivers, woods, and plains.

senses.d: Fresh; not salt or brackish; as, sweet water.
Not changed from a sound or wholesome state. Specifically: (a) Not sour; as, sweet milk or bread. (b) Not state; not putrescent or putrid; not rancid; as, sweet butter; sweet meat or fish.
Plaesing to the mind; mild; gentle; calm; amiable; winning; presuasive; as, sweet manners.
q: Canst thou bind the sweet influence of Pleiades?
Mildness and sweet reasonableness is the one established rule of Christian working.

Sweet.etym: [OE. swete, swote, sote, AS. swēte; akin to OFries. swēte, OS. swōti, D. zoet, G. süss, OHG. suozi, Icel. sætr, sœtr, Sw. söt, Dan. söd, Goth. suts, L. suavis, for suadvis, Gr. �, Skr. svādu sweet, svad, svād, to sweeten. √175. Cf. Assuage, Suave, Suasion.]

senses.d: That which is sweet to the taste; — used chiefly in the plural.
That which is sweet or pleasant in odor; a perfume.
That which is pleasing or grateful to the mind; as, the sweets of domestic life.
q: A little bitter mingled in our cup leaves no relish of the sweet.

senses.d: One who is dear to another; a darling; — a term of endearment.
Sweetly.
To sweeten.
In a sweet manner.
The quality or state of being sweet (in any sense of the adjective); gratefulness to the taste or to the smell; agreeableness.

To grow larger; to dilate or extend the exterior surface or dimensions, by matter added within, or by expansion of the inclosed substance; as, the legs swell in dropsy; a bruised part swells; a bladder swells by inflation.
To increase in size or extent by any addition; to increase in volume or force; as, a river swells, and overflows its banks; sounds swell or diminish.
To rise or be driven into waves or billows; to heave; as, in tempest, the ocean swells into waves.
To be puffed up or bloated; as, to swell with pride.
q: You swell at the tartan, as the bull is said to do at scarlet.

senses.d: To be inflated; to belly; as, the sails swell.
To be turgid, bombastic, or extravagant; as, swelling words; a swelling style.
To protuberate; to bulge out; as, a cask swells in the middle.
To be elated; to rise arrogantly.
q: Your equal mind yet swells not into state.

senses.d: To grow upon the view; to become larger; to expand.
To become larger in amount; as, many little debts added, swell to a great amount.
To act in a pompous, ostentatious, or arrogant manner; to strut; to look big.
q: Here he comes, swelling like a turkey cock.

Swell.etym: [AS. swellan; akin to D. zwellen, OS. & OHG. swellan, G. schwellen, Icel. svella, Sw. svälla.]

senses.d: To increase the size, bulk, or dimensions of; to cause to rise, dilate, or increase; as, rains and dissolving snow swell the rivers in spring; immigration swells the population.
q: swells her high, heart-cheering tone.

senses.d: To aggravate; to heighten.
q: It is low ebb with his accuser when such peccadilloes are put to swell the charge.

senses.d: To raise to arrogance; to puff up; to inflate; as, to be swelled with pride or haughtiness.
To augment gradually in force or loudness, as the sound of a note.
The act of swelling.
Gradual increase.
q: Little River affords navigation during a swell to within three miles of the Miami.

senses.d: Increase of force, intensity, or volume of sound.
q: Music arose with its voluptuous swell.

senses.d: Increase of power in style, or of rhetorical force.
q: The swell and subsidence of his periods.

senses.d: A gradual ascent, or rounded elevation, of land; as, an extensive plain abounding with little swells.
A wave, or billow; especially, a succession of large waves; the roll of the sea after a storm; as, a heavy swell sets into the harbor.
q: The swell Of the long waves that roll in yonder bay.
The gigantic swells and billows of the snow.

senses.d: A gradual increase and decrease of the volume of sound; the crescendo and diminuendo combined; — generally indicated by the sign.
A showy, dashing person; a dandy.
Having the characteristics of a person of rank and importance; showy; dandified; distinguished; as, a swell person; a swell neighborhood.
The act of that which swells; as, the swelling of rivers in spring; the swelling of the breast with pride.
q: Rise to the swelling of the voiceless sea.

senses.d: A protuberance; a prominence
q: The superficies of such plates are not even, but have many cavities and swellings.

senses.d: To stray; to wander; to rope.
q: A maid thitherward did run, To catch her sparrow which from her did swerve.

senses.d: To go out of a straight line; to deflect.
To wander from any line prescribed, or from a rule or duty; to depart from what is established by law, duty, custom, or the like; to deviate.
q: I swerve not from thy commandments.
They swerve from the strict letter of the law.
Many who, through the contagion of evil example, swerve exceedingly from the rules of their holy religion.

senses.d: To bend; to incline.
To climb or move upward by winding or turning.
q: The tree was high; Yet nimbly up from bough to bough I swerved.

Swerve.etym: [OE. swerven, AS. sweorfan to wipe off, to file, to polish; akin to OFries. swerva to creep, D. zwerven to swerve, to rope, OS. swerban to wipe off, MHG. swerben to be whirled, OHG. swerban to wipe off, Icel. sverfa to file, Goth. swaírban (in comp.) to wipe, and perhaps to E. swarm. Cf. Swarm.]

senses.d: To turn aside.
Moving a great distance in a short time; moving with celerity or velocity; fleet; rapid; quick; speedy; prompt.
q: My beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.
Swift of dispatch and easy of access.
And bring upon themselves swift destruction.

senses.d: Of short continuance; passing away quickly.

Swift.etym: [AS. swift; akin to swāpan to sweep, swipu a whip; cf. swīfan to move quickly, to revolve. See Swoop, v. i., and cf. Swivel, Squib.]

senses.d: Swiftly.
q: Ply swift and strong the oar.

senses.d: The current of a stream.

Any one of numerous species of small, long-winged, insectivorous birds of the family Micropodidæ. In form and habits the swifts resemble swallows, but they are destitute of complex vocal muscles and are not singing birds, but belong to a widely different group allied to the humming birds.
Any one of several species of lizards, as the pine lizard.
The ghost moth. See under Ghost.
A reel, or turning instrument, for winding yarn, thread, etc.; — used chiefly in the plural.
The main card cylinder of a flax-carding machine.
A rope used to retain the bars of the capstan in their sockets while men are turning it.
A rope used to encircle a boat longitudinally, to strengthen and defend her sides.
The forward shroud of a lower mast.
To tighten, as slack standing rigging, by bringing the opposite shrouds nearer.
In a swift manner; with quick motion or velocity; fleetly.
To be supported by water or other fluid; not to sink; to float; as, any substance will swim, whose specific gravity is less than that of the fluid in which it is immersed.
To move progressively in water by means of strokes with the hands and feet, or the fins or the tail.
q: Leap in with me into this angry flood, And swim to yonder point.

senses.d: To be overflowed or drenched.
q: Sudden the ditches swell, the meadows swim.

senses.d: Fig.: To be as if borne or floating in a fluid.
q: now swim in joy.

senses.d: To be filled with swimming animals.
q: that swim full of small fishes.

Swim.etym: [AS. swimman; akin to D. zwemmen, OHG. swimman, G. schwimmen, Icel. svimma, Dan. swömme, Sw. simma. Cf. Sound an air bladder, a strait.]

senses.d: To pass or move over or on by swimming; as, to swim a stream.
q: Sometimes he thought to swim the stormy main.

senses.d: To cause or compel to swim; to make to float; as, to swim a horse across a river.
To immerse in water that the lighter parts may float; as, to swim wheat in order to select seed.
The act of swimming; a gliding motion, like that of one swimming.
The sound, or air bladder, of a fish.
A part of a stream much frequented by fish.
To be dizzy; to have an unsteady or reeling sensation; as, the head swims.

Swim.etym: [OE. swime dizziness, vertigo, AS. swīma; akin to D. zwijm, Icel. svimi dizziness, svina to subside, svīa to abate, G. schwindel dizziness, schwinden to disappear, to dwindle, OHG. swīnan to dwindle. Cf. Squemish, Swindler.]

senses.d: Any animal of the hog kind, especially one of the domestical species. Swine secrete a large amount of subcutaneous fat, which, when extracted, is known as lard. The male is specifically called boar, the female, sow, and the young, pig. See Hog.

Swine.etym: [OE. swin, AS. swīn; akin to OFries. & OS. swin, D. zwijn, G. schwein, OHG. swīn, Icel. svīn, Sw. svin, Dan. sviin, Goth. swein; originally a diminutive corresponding to E. sow. See Sow, n.]

senses.d: Enlarged by swelling; immoderately increased; as, swollen eyes; swollen streams.
To sink into a fainting fit, in which there is an apparent suspension of the vital functions and mental powers; to faint; — often with away.
q: The sucklings swoon in the streets of the city.
The most in years . . . swooned first away for pain.
He seemed ready to swoon away in the surprise of joy.

Swoon.etym: [OE. swounen, swoghenen, for swo�nien, fr. swo�en to sigh deeply, to droop, AS. swōgan to sough, sigh; cf. geswōgen senseless, swooned, geswōwung a swooning. Cf. Sough.]

senses.d: A fainting fit; syncope.
An offensive weapon, having a long and usually sharp-pointed blade with a cutting edge or edges. It is the general term, including the small sword, rapier, saber, scimiter, and many other varieties.
Hence, the emblem of judicial vengeance or punishment, or of authority and power.
q: He beareth not the sword in vain.
She quits the balance, and resigns the sword.

senses.d: Destruction by the sword, or in battle; war; dissension.
q: I came not to send peace, but a sword.

senses.d: The military power of a country.
q: He hath no more authority over the sword than over the law.

senses.d: One of the end bars by which the lay of a hand loom is suspended.

Sword.etym: [OE. swerd, AS. sweord; akin to OFries. swerd, swird, D. zwaard, OS. swerd, OHG. swert, G. schwert, Icel. sverð, Sw. svärd, Dan. sværd; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: Saw.
A congregation or assembly of Jews met for the purpose of worship, or the performance of religious rites.
The building or place appropriated to the religious worship of the Jews.

The council of, probably, 120 members among the Jews, first appointed after the return from the Babylonish captivity; — called also the Great Synagogue, and sometimes, though erroneously, the Sanhedrin.
A congregation in the early Christian church.
q: My brethren, . . . if there come into your synagogue a man with a gold ring.

senses.d: Any assembly of men.

Synagogue.etym: [F., from L. synagoga, Gr. � a bringing together, an assembly, a synagogue, fr. � to bring together; σύν with + � to lead. See Syn-, and Agent.]

senses.d: A red wine of Italy.
Of or pertaining to Syria; Syriac.
A native of Syria.
Same as Skee.
A wet place; a river inlet.
q: The praire round about is wet, at times almost marshy, especially at the borders of the great reedy slews.

senses.d: In the western United States, one who settles on government land before it is legally open to settlement in order to gain the prior claim that the law gives to the first settler when the land is opened to settlement; hence, any one who does a thing prematurely or anticipates another in acting in order to gain an unfair advantage.
